text:
In the sample, the first protocol, Protocol1, records the DMA_RD message
protocol. You can see that the related signals of Protocol1 are recorded under the
[ProtocolConfig.Protocol1.RelatedSignals] sub-section. The scope variable Scope1
records the hierarchy of the first scope. Sig1 and Sig2 are two signals under this scope
and use this variable Scope1 to show the full hierarchy. If you need to change the
hierarchy, you just need to change Scope1 in most cases. This helps to reuse this setting
over different projects.

Abnormal Analysis

Binding Related Signals to Message Protocol in Batch Mode
For experienced users or users who just want to refine the existing binding signals, for
example, change the hierarchy of each signal, using the GUI is less efficient. In this
case, you can edit the protocol .rc files directly. The file users can import these .rc files
as needed. The PureLog DB users can apply the protocolCompile utility with the
protocol .rc files to save the binding information in the PureLog DB. Then you can export
protocols with the binding signals from the PureLog DB as needed.
If you already bound dumped signals to a certain protocol, you can visualize message
protocol transactions along with binding signals as shown in the following sample:
Figure 522

Message Protocol Transactions with Binding Signals

Abnormal Analysis
When a log file includes enormous lines and messages, it becomes very difficult to find
the abnormal points. The Abnormal Analysis feature of PureLog sums up the abnormal
points in a log. You only need to feed PureLog with some golden logs that are related to
the current error log.

Launching Abnormal Analysis
To launch Abnormal Analysis, set the following environment variables:
setenv PYTHONPATH
setenv VL_VERSION TD
setenv PYTHONPATH $VERDI_HOME/share/NPI/
python:$PYTHONPATH
setenv LD_LIBRARY_PATH $VERDI_HOME/share/NPI/lib/linux64:$LD_LIBRARY_PATH
module load cmlp/2021.06-py36

Abnormal Analysis

Using Abnormal Analysis
1. Keep daily record in the database.
For example, if you have case1, case2, and case3 in your daily regression, you can
use PureLog every day to save the record of each testcase in the database through
the PureLog TCL process. The high-level features extracted by partition rules are also
saved in the database for abnormal analysis.
The database used by abnormal analysis is not integrated into the PureLog
database. In other words, abnormal analysis uses its own database that is
different from the PureLog database.
2. Apply abnormal analysis when there is a failure.
For example, there is a failure of case1. You can use PureLog to analyze the abnormal
points as follows:
Open the error log with PureLog.
Launch the abnormal engine, as shown in the following figure.
Figure 523

Launching Abnormal Engine

In the Input Case Name dialog box, specify the DB Path and Case Name.
Figure 524

Input Case Name Dialog Box

Abnormal Analysis

Click OK to apply the changes.
After the analysis is complete, you can navigate the different abnormal points, as
shown in the following figures.
Abnormal Sequence
Figure 525

Abnormal Sequence

Abnormal Digit
Figure 526

Abnormal Digit

Abnormal Data
Figure 527

Abnormal Data

SaveDB.tcl: TCL Process to Save Testcase Record
To use the TCL process, run the following command:
pureLog -play SaveDB.tcl

TCL Process
set win [viaCreateLogViewer]
## Record Case1

viaLogViewerOpenLog
-window $win
pureLogAAExtractLog
## Record Case2
viaLogViewerOpenLog
-window $win
pureLogAAExtractLog
## Record Case3
viaLogViewerOpenLog
-window $win
pureLogAAExtractLog
debExit

text:
The SmartSheet feature available with PureLog allows you to view data in a spreadsheet
format, analyze it, and link it to the HDL design. You can choose to either open a new
sheet in SmartSheet or import an existing .csv file. Furthermore, in case you use
SmartLog to open the log with partition rules, you can save the partition results into the
CSV format and then open the file in SmartSheet. To save the file in CSV format, use the
File > Save Contents menu option in SmartLog.
SmartSheet offers the following features for viewing the data:
* Sorting the data entries based on number
Sort Smallest to Largest
Sort Largest to Smallest
* Filtering the data entries based on number
* Filtering the data entries based on text
* Finding data by column

Launching SmartSheet
To launch SmartSheet without design information, you can type PureLogDB. In case you
need design information, you can open Verdi with the design as usual and then click the
Tools > SmartSheet menu option in the Verdi GUI.

The SmartSheet pane opens, as shown in the following figure:
Figure 528

SmartSheet Pane

Toolbar and Menu Options
SmartSheet provides a toolbar with frequently used options to navigate the files, as
illustrated in the following figure:
Figure 529

SmartSheet Toolbar

The SmartSheet window provides the following menu options:
File Menu Options
* Open File
Menu Bar: File -> Open File
This option opens the Open CSV form to help you open an existing .csv file.

title: 2 200 Info Rx IP2
text:
* New Sheet
Menu Bar: File -> New Sheet
This option opens a new sheet in the SmartSheet pane.
* Save
Menu Bar: File -> Save
This option saves the currently open sheet.
* Save As
Menu Bar: File -> Save As
This option saves the currently open sheet as a different sheet.
Edit Menu Options
* Copy
Menu Bar: Edit -> Copy
This option copies the selected data/entries.
* Paste
Menu Bar: Edit -> Paste
This option pastes the copied data/entries.
* Undo
Menu Bar: Edit -> Undo
This option cancels the previously performed action.
* Redo
Menu Bar: Edit -> Redo
This option redo the previously performed action.
* Insert Row
Menu Bar: Edit -> Insert Row -> Up
This option inserts a new row above the selected row.
Menu Bar: Edit -> Insert Row -> Down
This option inserts a new row below the selected row.
Menu Bar: Edit -> Insert Row -> Insert Multiple Row

title: 2 200 Info Rx IP2
text:
This option inserts multiple rows as specified in the Insert Multiple Rows form.
Figure 530

Insert Multiple Rows Form

title: 2 200 Info Rx IP2
text:
* Insert Column
Menu Bar: Edit -> Insert Column -> Right
This option inserts a new column on the right side of the selected column.
Menu Bar: Edit -> Insert Column -> Left
This option inserts a new column on the left side of the selected column.
Menu Bar: Edit -> Insert Column -> Right Check-box
This option inserts a new column with check-box on the right side of the selected
column.
Menu Bar: Edit -> Insert Column -> Left Check-box
This option inserts a new column with check-box on the left side of the selected
column.
Menu Bar: Edit -> Insert Column -> Insert Multiple Columns

title: 2 200 Info Rx IP2
text:
This option inserts multiple columns as specified in the Insert Multiple Columns
form.
Figure 531

Insert Multiple Columns Form

title: 2 200 Info Rx IP2
text:
* Delete
Menu Bar: Edit -> Delete -> Row
This option deletes the selected row.
Menu Bar: Edit -> Delete -> Column
This option deletes the selected column.
Tools Menu Options
* Customize Menu/Toolbar
Menu Bar: Tools -> Customize Menu/Toolbar

title: 2 200 Info Rx IP2
text:
This option customizes the menu or the toolbar as specified in the Customize Menu/
Toolbar form.
Figure 532

Customize Menu/Toolbar Form

title: 2 200 Info Rx IP2
text:
Window Menu Options
* Dock To
Menu Bar: Window -> Dock To -> New Container Window
This option docks the current window to a new container window.

title: 2 200 Info Rx IP2
text:
Use Model of SmartSheet
You can build your own spreadsheet in the SmartSheet window as follows:
Figure 533

A Customized Spreadsheet

SmartSheet takes each number column as <categories> and text/check-box column as
<properties> or <series>.

The following flow shows how to specify text/check-box column as <properties> or
<series>.

The PureLog timing violation solution helps you find and fix timing violations in your design
more intelligently and efficiently.
The major features are as follows:
* Summarize the timing violations based on components.
Easy to dispatch task to the right owner.
* Prioritize timing violations in different scenarios wherein, you can pick the best one for
the particular scenario.
The corrupted flip-flop with the higher number of violations.
Active drivers associated with a higher number of violations.
* Support waive or unwaive operations effectively.
Waive conditions are saved or restored for the next run.
All waiver justifications are logged into the database for projectlevel review.
* Enable rapid debug workflows for timing violation analysis.
Oneclick access to related signals, violation messages in the simulation log, and
TFV trace results.
* Selectively compile simulation logs from large regression trees using path include and
exclude filters.
You need to set environment variable

PURELOG_ENABLE_TIMING_VIOLATION_REPORT = 1

Generate Timing Violation Report
The Generate Timing Violation Report topic includes the following detail:

Leverage the logCompile Utility
Run the timing violation analysis by using the logCompile command:
logCompile time_violation -storage_path db_storage -project PROJ1005
-root_dir PROJ1005/0326 -log sim.log -config configFile

where.
* -storage_path: Path to store the database.
* -project: Project name.
* -root_dir: Root directory for the test cases.
* -log: Simulation log file.
* -config: Configuration file path that includes mapping information.

scope's mapping. All non mapping instances are included in the report "others.vio.rpt".

Some timing violations happen before the reset stage. You can ignore these violations.
In the TimeCheckEnable section, you can set the message after which timing violations for
the selected instance are captured.

Open or Check Timing Violation Report
To open or check the Timing Violation Report, perform the following steps:
1. Under the Tools menu, click New Timing Violation Report to open the timing violation

2. Click Open database icon in the timing violation window. Follow the guidelines that
appears in the dialog box, to open reports within the database.

3. The summary reports for each component appears and sorted by the count of
violations.

4. Use check or uncheck to record the violations which are checked.

5. Use waive or unwaive violations to record the reason and username for the projectlevel review.

The waived violations are moved to the root node <Waived> in the bottom.

6. Click View Details to see raw messages in the SmartLog.

The action is only available in the node of simulation log.
7. Click the link of SmartLog to access related signals in nWave.

In the common active fan-in path report (refer to Check Common Active
Fan-in for Timing Violation), it helps to display the temporal flow view result.

Save or Load the Waived Result
Save or Load the Waived Result has the following sections:
Save or Load wavied result of current opened report

To save or restore waived results for current opened reports, use the actions listed below:
* Under File menu,
Click Load Timing Violation Waive Status to restore the waived result.
Click Save Timing Violation Waive Status to save the waived result.

Save or Load whole Database.
Use msgdbControl to export the waived result from the database.
msgdbControl export_data -storage_path $storagePath -type timingWaiveFile
-project_name $projName [-date yyyy-mm-dd] -output $outputFile

* -date: Is optional. If not specified, it exports waive file based on the latest date. -date
is in yyyy-mm-dd format.
For example, 2025-09-17.
* -output: Is the option to specify the destination path for the exported file.
Feed the overall waive file into logCompile in the next run.
logCompile timing_violation -waive $waiveFile

Check Common Active Fan-in for Timing Violation
In certain cases, timing violations affect many Flip-Flops.
However, the issue comes from just a few active drivers.

The tool summarizes the common active fan-in path, and they are sorted by the number of
associated corrupted Flip-Flop.
Perform the following steps to generate a report:
1. Import design.
2. Open the waveform file that contains the logs for active fan-in path analysis.
3. Open summary reports (refer to Open or Check Timing Violation Report.)
4. Click Analyze Common Active Fan-in from Opened FSDB files icon to open the
dialog box as follows:

5. Enter the mapping of log details with corresponding FSDB entries.
The report appears and is organized by the number of related corrupted Flip-Flops.

Regression Debug Automation (RDA)
The following sections describe the LCA features supported by RDA as a part of this
release:
* Static Bug Finding Root Cause Analysis (SBRCA)
* RDA Integration With Verdi VMS

During RTL simulation, Dynamic SDC Verification in VCS detects domain crossing and
glitch issues, such as reset domain crossing (RDC) or glitches. Static bug finding is a part
of RTL sign off and saves weeks of efforts in a project cycle.
Debugging violations found by static bug finding can be difficult, especially when RDC
bugs appear in large numbers, such as during MCP verification. RDA offers a Static Bug
Finding Root Cause Analysis (SBRCA) solution that automatically organizes violations into
fewer groups. This solution connects violations to waveform, source code, and simulation
log for further debugging and uses Verdi for analysis.
* Technology Overview
* SBRCA Usage
* Smart Waiver

Technology Overview
SBRCA helps you to debug the static bug findings using Verdi. VCS complies with the
SDC commands containing RDC/Glitch property. After completing simulation with VCSSDC, SBRCA checks the results of VCS-SDC and helps in finding out the violations.
SBRCA extracts details of a violation message and displays the information in a binstructured report.
RDA provides Verdi GUI to review SBRCA reports generated after analyzing violations
from the log file. Use the Verdi GUI to continue debugging in the source code, logs, and
waveform.

SBRCA Debug Flow

The VCS compilation runs with the dynamic SDC verification infrastructure in the static
bug finding mode and VCS-MCP mode. However, they are implemented with different
mechanism and cannot be executed in the same way. Therefore, SBRCA has a different
configuration template from VCS-MCP. The following figure displays the flow from VCSSDC to :

Schematic from VCS to autorca

Requirements
The following are the requirements for the SBRCA setup:
* VCS compilation with SDC commands which contain RDC/Glitch property.
* Run simulation. The property can pass or fail.

SBRCA Usage
The following steps are required to perform SBRCA:
1. Prepare a configuration file for SBRCA. Refer to the Preparing RDA Configuration File
for SBRCA section for more details.
2. Invoke SBRCA. Refer to the Invoking SBRCA in RDA Flow section for more details.
3. Review the SBRCA results in Verdi. Refer to the Reviewing SBRCA in Verdi GUI
section for more details.

Verdi GUI Features
You can perform the following actions in Verdi GUI:
* Grouping
* Debugging Type (RDC/Glitch)
* Directing to the Target Violation in SmartLog
* Invoking the Target Violation Waveform in nWave
* Directing to the Target Signal in nTrace
* Directing to the Target SDC command in nTrace
Grouping
The Grouping feature is a core part of SBRCA. It helps to review all the violations grouped
into bins with different information, which means that the same bin might have the same
bug.
You can group violations using the following grouping rules for RDC and Glitch:
RDC
* signal_to: Group by the same signal(TO) names
* signal_from: Group by the same signal(FROM) names
* signal_both: Group by the same signal(TO) and same signal(FROM) names
* reset: Group by the same reset signals name
* sdc_command: Group by the same SDC command

Glitch
* signal_to: Group by the same signal(TO) names
* signal_from: Group by the same signal(FROM) names
* signal_both: Group by the same signal(TO) and same signal(FROM) names
* sdc_command: Group by the same SDC command
On Verdi GUI, you can select the Group by option to choose the grouping rule. Using the
Grouping feature, you can review the results of different grouping rules in the active report
window as shown in the following figure:
Figure 570

Selecting Grouping Rules

Debugging Type (RDC/Glitch)
SBRCA provides the Violation Type field to select the debugging type. You can choose
between Glitch and RDC violation types as shown in the following figure:
Figure 571

Selecting Debugging Type

Directing to the Target Violation in SmartLog
You can review the raw simulation log by directing to the target violation in SmartLog.
You can activate SmartLog in the following ways:
* Click the SmartLog Entry icon in the Action column.
* Right-click Recommend Debug Index or any entry under All Violation Index and
select Open in SmartLog.

The following figure displays selecting Open in SmartLog:
Figure 572

Ways to Direct to the Target Violation Message

The activated SmartLog performs the following steps:
1. Jumps to the line of the target violation message.
2. Highlights all the keywords to group. For example, highlights top.d1.b1.scrc[0]
while grouping with signal(TO).
3. Lists all the matching keywords which you can click and jumps to other violations in the
same bin on the right-hand side.
4. Reuses only one SmartLog window when you operate on other indexes.
Figure 573

The SmartLog View

Invoking the Target Violation Waveform in nWave
The violation waveforms Tcls are dumped after VCS-SDC annotate the violation details in
nWave. SBRCA provides entries to invoke them.

You can activate nWave in the following ways:
* Click the nWave Entry icon in the Action column.
* Right-click the Recommend Debug Index or entries under All Violation Index and
select Open in nWave as shown in the following figure:
Figure 574

Ways to Invoke the Target Violation Waveform

The corresponding waveform details such as violation index, FROM-TO signals, and
their value change are displayed. The same nWave window can be used again, which
means that after clearing the old information, new information is displayed.
Figure 575

The nWave View

Directing to the Target Signal in nTrace
SBRCA provides the cross-reference of signals from the report to nTrace. You can activate
this feature in one of the following ways:
* Click the nTrace Entry icon in the Action column.
* Double-click Signal(TO) or Signal(FROM).
* Right-click Signal(TO) or Signal(FROM) and select Open in nTrace.
Figure 576

The View of Directing the Target Signal

Directing to the Target SDC command in nTrace
SBRCA provides the cross-reference of SDC command from the report to nTrace. You can
activate this feature using one of the following ways:
* Click the nTrace Entry icon in the Action column.
* Double-click Clock or SDC Command Type.
* Right-click Clock or SDC Command Type, and select Open in nTrace.
The content of the SDC command file is displayed in the new tab in nTrace, and the target
command is highlighted. The tab can be re-used when another SDC command action is
triggered.

Figure 577

The View of Directing SDC Command

Loading RDA in Verdi VMS
You need to use RDA plugin to load RDA in Verdi VMS. To invoke the RDA plugin, perform
the following steps:
1. Add RDA plugin to synopsys_eman.setup.
plugins:
- rda:
<VERDI_HOME>/platform/linux64/bin/rcaIntgrFlow/python38/rca_plugin.so

where <VERDI_HOME> is the full path of Verdi.
2. Load the RDA plugin in your .emc file.
plugins:
- rda

3. Register a load RDA report template using the following command:
vms admin register_custom_template -t $VERDI_HOME/share/autoRCA/
python38/etc/vms/web_template/load_rda_report.emd -a

The Open RDA report button is added to the Verdi VMS GUI.

When you run the vms -gui command, select a session. Click the Open RDA report
button to open the RCA Manager window, as shown in the following figure:
Figure 579

Loading RDA in Verdi VMS

Enabling RDA Binning
RDA binning is always enabled in the RDA plugin.

Enabling Debug Facilitator/RCA
Define the debug engines Debug Facilitator and DUTRCA. Enable these engines for the
error patterns that you want to analyze.
Debug facilitator is defined by default; you need to include DF.emc as shown in the
following command:
include:
- $VERDI_HOME/share/autoRCA/python38/etc/vms/engine_template/DF.emc

However, you need to define DUTRCA as shown in the following commands:
debug_engines :
- name: DUTRCA
cmd: $current_dir/dutrca_debug_engine_cmd.sh
log_file: $${EMAN_TEST_NAME}_dutrca_debug_engine.log
run_dir: $current_dir/DUTRCA/$$EMAN_TEST_PATH
custom_values:
REF_CL_WORK_DIR: $$EMAN_REF_FIND_CL_WORK_DIR
DUTRCA_CONFIG: $current_dir/dutrca.yaml

TARGET_SCOPE: minsoc_tb_top.minsoc_top_0
REPORT_PATH: $current_dir/DUTRCA/$$EMAN_TEST_PATH/dutrca_report.xml

After defining the debug engines, enable them for the specific error patterns. In the
following example, DF and DUTRCA are enabled for the uvm_error error pattern:
error_patterns:
- name: uvm_error
pattern:
(?P<Type>UVM_ERROR)\s+.*\s+\[(?P<Code>\S+)\]\s+(?P<Description>.*)
base_status: fail
custom_status: uvm_error
priority: 0
debug_rerun_count: 1
debug_engines: DF DUTRCA

You need to create your scripts based on your environment.
dutrca_debug_engine_cmd.sh
#!/bin/sh
TARGET_BUILD_DIR=$EMAN_COMPILE_DIR
TARGET_TEST_DIR=$TARGET_BUILD_DIR/${EMAN_TEST_NAME}_debug
REF_BUILD_DIR=$EMAN_TOP_RUN_DIR/reference_finder/$EMAN_REF_FIND_ID/${EMAN
_REF_FIND_CL}_build_debug
REF_TEST_DIR=$REF_BUILD_DIR/${EMAN_TEST_NAME}_debug
# Set up env var used in dutrca.yaml
export TARGET_SIMV_DAIDIR=$TARGET_BUILD_DIR/simv.daidir
export TARGET_WAVEFORM=$TARGET_TEST_DIR/inter.fsdb
export TARGET_SIM_LOG=$EMAN_DEBUG_LOG_FILE
export REF_SIMV_DAIDIR=$REF_BUILD_DIR/simv.daidir
export REF_WAVEFORM=$REF_TEST_DIR/novas.fsdb
export REF_SIM_LOG=$REF_TEST_DIR/sim.log
DUTRCA_CONFIG=$EMAN_EXECUTION_DIR/dutrca.yaml
autorca -cfg $DUTRCA_CONFIG -work rca.work_dir
if [ $? -eq 0 ]; then
echo "DUTRCA succeeded"
else
echo "DUTRCA failed"
fi

dutrca.yaml
dutrca:
## 1: auto mode, 2: manual mode, 3: auto + manual mode ##
mode: 1
# default is 3
## set fail/pass case to debug ##

target_simv_daidir:
$TARGET_SIMV_DAIDIR
# [full path], required
field
target_waveform:
$TARGET_WAVEFORM # [full path], required field
target_sim_log:
$TARGET_SIM_LOG
#
[full path], required field for "auto mode"
#original log: case2/0705_TB_0705_DUT/run.log
reference_simv_daidir: $REF_SIMV_DAIDIR
# [full path], required
field
reference_waveform:
$REF_WAVEFORM
# [full path], required field
reference_sim_log:
$REF_SIM_LOG
# [full path],
required field for "auto mode"
design_based_root_cause: true # [true/false], required field
target_scope: $TARGET_SCOPE #minsoc_tb_top.minsoc_top_0 # [full
scope], required field
max_signal_depth: 3
# default is "3"
slack_time: 0ns
# default is "0ns"
time_bound: auto
# default is "auto"
enable_transaction_diff: True

Reference Finder
The Verdi VMS feature, Reference Finder, allows connecting Verdi VMS to any source
control. For each failed test, you can find the most recent changelist where the test passed
and use this changelist as the reference for the test.

The following figure displays the flow that it follows for DUTRCA:
Figure 580

Reference Finder Flow

The Target for DUTRCA is generated using the following command in the Regular Debug
Test: debug_run_cmd
The Reference for DUTRCA is generated using the following command in the Reference
Debug Test: ref_debug_run_cmd
The debug engine DUTRCA needs a reference, so you need to define a reference finder
for a build. You can define a reference finder by adding the following scripts to your Verdi
VMS configuration file:
* init
[Optional] Specifies a script or command to initialize the reference finder. If this
command is defined, it is executed only after you start using the reference finder.
* list_cls
[Required] Specifies a script or command to get the list of changelist IDs. If this
command is defined, it is executed once at the beginning to allow loading these
changelists later. After the script is executed, its log file is parsed for getting the
changelist IDs.

* load_cl
[Required] Specifies a script or command that defines how to load a specific changelist.
It is called every time a changelist is required.

#!/bin/sh
ROOT_DIR=$(realpath "${BASH_SOURCE%/*}")
if [ -z $EMAN_REF_FIND_WORK_DIR ]; then
echo "EMAN_REF_FIND_WORK_DIR is empty. Skip loading cl"
exit 1
fi
if [ -z $EMAN_REF_FIND_CL ]; then
echo "EMAN_REF_FIND_CL is empty. Skip loading cl"
exit 1
fi
mkdir -p $EMAN_REF_FIND_WORK_DIR/${EMAN_REF_FIND_CL}
find_cl_dir=realpath $EMAN_REF_FIND_WORK_DIR/${EMAN_REF_FIND_CL}
echo "find_cl_dir:$find_cl_dir"

cd $find_cl_dir
P4CLIENT_SUFFIX=echo $find_cl_dir | md5sum | awk '{print $1}'
export P4CLIENT="labRDA_${USER}_${P4CLIENT_SUFFIX}"
echo "P4CLIENT:$P4CLIENT"
rm -rf $P4CONFIG
echo "P4PORT=$P4PORT"
> $P4CONFIG
echo "P4CLIENT=$P4CLIENT" >> $P4CONFIG
source $ROOT_DIR/create_template
p4 client -i < p4_client_templete
p4 sync -f @$EMAN_REF_FIND_CL

Applying Incremental Binning on Verdi VMS Parallel Debug
The Verdi VMS feature, Parallel Debug, allows you to run debug tests immediately after
the test fails in its custom failure category. Parallel debug provides the following benefits:
* Overlapping of the regular run and the debug run saves the overall turnaround time.
* Analyzing the RDA report and debugging before the regular run finishes.
The following figure displays the difference when you enable and disable the parallel
debug feature:
Figure 581

Difference Between Parallel Debug Off and On

* Incremental Binning
* RDA Behavior After Enabling Parallel Debug
* Requirement for Incremental Binning

Incremental Binning
The Once Binning feature allows categorizing all tests together and provides enhanced
clustering results as all the tests are considered. Once binning always provides the same
clustering results. However, it does not support the Verdi VMS Parallel Debug feature.
Incremental binning categorizes tests one by one and supports the Verdi VMS Parallel
Debug feature. The Bucket ID of a test remains unchanged after it is decided. Therefore,
incremental binning and once binning might have different clustering results. For example,
in the following figure, before test4 finishes, test3 is kept in bucket2. After test4 finishes,
the test3 stays in bucket2.
Figure 582

Difference Between Once And Incremental Binning

RDA Behavior After Enabling Parallel Debug
After the Parallel Debug feature is enabled, you can notice the following RDA behavior:
1. When Verdi VMS identifies the first failed test and sends the test to RDA for binning,
RDA report is created. You can open the RDA report using RCA Manager as shown in
Figure 583

RDA Report

2. RCA Manager checks every minute whether the report is updated. When the report is
updated, it displays the New Update Available! information in the toolbar, as shown in
Figure 584

RCA Manager Displaying "New Update Available"

3. Click File > Reload to reload the report in the RCA Manager. When you click Reload,
RCA Manager displays the latest updates. The New Update Available! information
in the toolbar disappears until the next update becomes available, as shown in the
Figure 585

"New Update Available" Disappears

The RDA report gets updated with the following changes:
* New bucket or buckets appear.
* New remaining case or cases display.
* New action buttons include:
RCA button when the debug engine DUTRCA finishes.
Post-sim mode button when the Debug Facilitator finishes.
Interactive mode button when the Debug Facilitator finishes.

text:
DesignDiff
The DesignDiff feature introduces a GUI to compare the source code of two designs:
the reference design and the target design. You can analyze the comparison results.
DesignDiff shows differences between the two designs based on the semantics of the HDL
code, rather than the text of the HDL code. The DesignDiff feature includes the following
functions:
* Integrates the RTL difference (XML format) into DesignDiff.
* Adds the difference functionality.
* Displays the number of design changes in the nTrace hierarchy.
* Allows you to click each scope to view related design changes.
* Shows the target source code in Verdi.
The DesignDiff feature provides options to calculate and display the number of design
changes in the Instance View pane and ignore any module or source code file.
This section provides details on the following topics:
* DesignDiff Requirements
* Enabling DesignDiff
* Reviewing DesignDiff
* Ignoring the Module and Source Code Files
* DesignDiff Limitations

DesignDiff Requirements

DesignDiff Requirements
The following are the requirements for the DesignDiff feature:
* The RTL difference generates the DesignDiff report only when the VSO folder is
available; otherwise, it throws errors.
* You must provide the target and reference designs as two versions of the same
design. It allows DesignDiff to generate meaningful reports for review and analysis. To
generate the target and reference design directories, refer to the Generating Required
Directories section.

Generating Required Directories
The DesignDiff feature requires simv.daidir and ref.daidir directories for the current
and reference designs, respectively. To generate these directories, use the following
compile options for the respective simulator:
* VCS
When VCS is used for simulation, compile the design using the -kdb=designdiff
compile-time option, as shown in the following command:
% vcs -kdb=designdiff -lca [other_options]

Where, [other_options] are the other compile-time options.
* VCS with VSO.ai
When VCS is used with VSO.ai, compile the design using the -vso cso -kdb option
along with other compile-time options, as shown in the following command:
% vcs -vso cso -kdb -lca [other_options]

After compilation, the *.vso folder is generated along with *.daidir in the same
directory.
You must save these two files at the same directory level.
* Third-Party Simulators

Enabling DesignDiff

For third-party simulators, elaborate the design using the -useius=adv -designdiff
or -usemti=adv -designdiff option along with other compile-time options, as shown
in the following command:
For IUS flow,
% elabcom -useius=adv -designdiff [other_options]

title: 2 200 Info Rx IP2
text:
Enabling DesignDiff
After generating the target and reference design directories using the compile-time options
provided in the Generating Required Directories section, enable the DesignDiff feature
using the designdiff command.
Use the following syntax to compare the two simv.daidir design directories:
% designdiff -dbdir <target_simv.daidir> -refdir <reference_simv.daidir>
[other_options]

Where, [other_options] are the DesignDiff runtime options. You can add the following
DesignDiff runtime options:
* -diffreport <filename>: Specify the file name for the report. By default, the file
name is designdiff_report.xml.
* -ignore_module <filename>: Specify the file name that contains the list of module
names to filter out. For more details on the -ignore_module <filename> option, refer
to the Ignoring the Module and Source Code Files section.
* -ignore_file <filename>: Specify the file name that contains the list of source code
files to filter out. For more details on the -ignore_file <filename> option, refer to
the Ignoring the Module and Source Code Files section.
* -with_score: Calculates the design change score for the report. For more details,
refer to the -with_score section.
For example, % designdiff -dbdir ./target/simv.daidir -refdir ./reference/
ref.daidir.
The designdiff command analyzes the design difference details and generates the
corresponding report in an XML format, designdiff_report.xml.

title: 2 200 Info Rx IP2
text:
To view the generated report, designdiff_report.xml, in Verdi, run the following
command:
% verdi -load_trace_report <generated_xml_report>, or
% designdiff -load_report <generated_xml_report>

title: 2 200 Info Rx IP2
text:
You must load Designdiff reports using the command line; the GUI Load RDA
Trace Report option is not supported for DesignDiff reports.
For example, % verdi -load_trace_report designdiff_report.xml

The following figure displays the GUI overview of the DesignDiff report uploaded to Verdi
using the % verdi -load_trace_report designdiff_report.xml command:
Figure 586

DesignDiff Report Overview in Verdi GUI

The GUI of the DesignDiff report consists of the following three main components:
* Instance View
* Source View
* Source Code Changes
You can debug a design in the following two ways:
* Instance: To check the design difference of an instance with a large number of designdifference changes, click the scope in the Instance View pane. This synchronizes the
Source View pane with the source code of the module and displays the design-change
entries in the Source Code Changes section.
* Source code changes: When you click an entry in the Source Code Changes section,
the Source View pane displays the corresponding difference between the two designs.

Instance View
The Instance View pane displays the hierarchy tree of the design. The instance table
provides the name of the module, and the inclusive and exclusive change for the selected
instance, as shown in the following figure:
Figure 587

Instance View

When you run the designdiff command with the -with_score option, the DesignDiff
feature calculates the design changes and displays the score in the Instance View
pane, as shown in Figure 588. The score indicates the summation of the design changes
(addition, deletion, and modification).
% designdiff -dbdir <target>.daidir -refdir <reference>.dbdir -with_score

The exclusive change indicates the number of current scope changes, and the inclusive
change indicates the number of current scope and the child scope changes. A higher
count for an instance means that the instance contains a higher number of design
changes.

Figure 588

Instance View With -with_score

When you run the designdiff command without the -with_score option, the scores for
the design changes are not displayed in the Instance View pane. However, the design

change scope and the modules with design changes are highlighted in yellow, as shown in
Figure 589

Instance View Without -with_score

Source View
When you click an entry in the Instance View or Source Code Changes pane, the
Source View pane displays the source code difference between the two designs. The
following figure displays the Source View pane:
Figure 590

Source View Pane

The Source View pane is split into two vertical views, where the left view displays the
reference design view and the right view displays the target design view. The right-arrow
icon,

, in the Source View pane highlights the active difference.

The Source View pane consists of the following information:
* Status string
It displays the name of the module in the ignore list.
* Icons

The following icons are available:

: The colors indicate the following types of design

changes:

Red: The red background color indicates that the highlighted lines are deleted.
Green: The green background color indicates that the highlighted lines are
added.
Blue: The blue background color indicates that the highlighted lines are
modified.

: Select the check box to synchronize the scroll bars of the
reference and target views.

: The jump action icons -- Go to Next, Go to Previous, Go to Top,
and Current Active Difference -- allow you to jump to the next, previous, topmost,
and currently active design difference, respectively.
Their availability depends on the current difference status as follows:

unavailable.

: If the scope diff count is one, only Current Active
Difference is available.

: If the scope has more than one difference and the current
difference is not the last one, Go to Next is available.

: If the scope has more than one difference and the current
difference is not the first one, Go to Previous and Go to Top are available.

* If there is no reference code for the selected target design, the reference view displays
No reference source code to show in red, as shown in the following figure:
Figure 591

No Reference Code to Show

Source Code Changes
The Source Code Changes section in the RCA report displays the following:
* All the RTL changes grouped by the file names.
* Module names and line numbers for the design changes.
You can collapse or expand the listed file entries. The following figure displays the source
code changes:
Figure 592

Source Code Changes

The Source Code Changes section consists of the following items:
* Four columns: File, Module, Line, and Syntax.
* The Line column displays the specific line number or a range of line numbers from the
source code.

If you see (Deleted from Ref) after the line number, it means that the line numbers
refer to the reference source code. If there is no such note, the line numbers refer to
the target source code.
* All source code changes are categorized in the RTL Changes parent item.
* The Syntax column appears when you set the TDC_DIFFCHECK_ASSERTION
environment variable to 1. This supports the Assertion feature.
It can display the following values: Signal, Port, Parameter, Stmt, ContAssign,
Instance, PortConn, Task, Function, Gate, GatePortConn, Assert, Assume, Cover,
Property, and Sequence.
* When the same line contains multiple syntax values, they are separated by a dash '|'
separator.
* The elide mode is set to left style.
Sorting Source Code Changes
You can sort entries in the following ways:
* Click the File, Module, and Syntax headers to sort the columns.
* The comparison includes several elements, such as the File column, the Module
column, and the source code changes (add, delete, or edit). It also displays the target
begin and end lines, and the reference begin and end lines.
* The following priority is used for comparison:

title: 2 200 Info Rx IP2
text:
everal elements, such as the File column, the Module
column, and the source code changes (add, delete, or edit). It also displays the target
begin and end lines, and the reference begin and end lines.
* The following priority is used for comparison:
File column = Module column > Source code difference (add, delete, edit) > begin line

> end line.

* The following priority is followed for sorting when Syntax is available:
1. Syntax
2. File
3. Edit mode
4. Begin line
5. End line
If two items match on one sorting element, use the next element to decide the order.
* You can sort entries alphabetically by file name or module name.
* If the file name or module name is the same, entries are sorted based on differences in
the source code. Entries that are not deleted appear before entries that are deleted.

Ignoring the Module and Source Code Files

* When comparing two deleted items, Verdi uses the following order of priority:
1. Target view begin line
2. Target view end line
3. Reference view begin line
4. Reference view end line
* When comparing two items that are not deleted, first compare the target view begin
line. If these lines match, compare the target view end line next.
* Sort keys are case-sensitive.
* The initial view sorts by the File column.
* The Line column does not support sorting.

Ignoring the Module and Source Code Files
To ignore a module file and a source code file, use the -ignore_module
<ignore_module_file> and -ignore_file <ignore_source_code_file> options,
respectively, and run the following command:
% designdiff -dbdir <target_simv.daidir> -refdir <reference_simv.daidir>
-ignore_module <ignore_module_file> -ignore_file <ignore_source code
file>

The -ignore_module <ignore_module_file> option reads modules listed in the userspecified module list and excludes them from comparison. The following is the format of
the ignored module list:
module list name
ModuleName1
ModuleName2
ModuleName3

module.list
ALUB
PCU
CCU

DesignDiff Limitations

DesignDiff Limitations
The following are the limitations of the DesignDiff feature:
* Supported versions
The DesignDiff feature is supported for the following VCS release versions:
V-2023.12-SP2-8, W-2024.09-SP2-3, and later.
* File location requirements
The simv.vso folder must be saved in the same place as the simv.daidir.
* Unsupported languages and features
SystemC, Unified Power Format (UPF), Testbench, and VHDL languages are not
The scores of unnamed statements might not be accurate.
The Source View pane displays differences where a MACRO is used but not
defined.
DesignDiff cannot identify the exact changed line within an encrypted (protected)
block. It can only highlight the first line of that block as the changed location.
* Design reloading
To reload a design, you must run the srcDiffView -on Tcl command; otherwise,
Verdi cannot read the reference design.
* Scroll bar synchronization
When you select the SyncScrollBar check box, you can synchronize only from the
target view to the reference view, and not vice versa.
* Reference view limitations
Most of the reference view options, such as setting the active view, the right-click
options, and the drag option, are not available.
The reference view does not support the parameter annotation.
Non-manual scroll bar options, such as the srcGotoLine Tcl command, are not
When you jump to the target file line in the target design, the target line does not fall
in the range of a valid scope. The reference view does not get refreshed because of
the outdated data.
* Unsupported compilation flows

DesignDiff Limitations

VCS compilation is not supported with the -preserve_path option and in the
Scalene and PCH flows.
The -kdb=only and -kdb=common_elab:off flows are not supported.
The Verdi full-load mode is not supported when the design is compiled using the
-kdb=postelab flow.
* Design change detection
Any change in value format is treated as a design change. For example, if 3'b001
changes to 1'h1, the tool considers it as a design change.
A change in the order of the sensitive list is considered a design change.
A difference in the initial value in a declaration is not considered a design change.
Modules with different parameterizations cannot be combined for comparison.
DesignDiff does not detect modport changes within interfaces. Changes to modport
declarations, such as adding or removing signals from a modport, are not identified.
DesignDiff maps blocks at the process level (initial, always, final). When
multiple sequential blocks exist within the same process, DesignDiff does not map
sibling blocks individually. To ensure accurate mapping, place each sequential block
in a separate process.
* Scope of analysis
DesignDiff checks for differences in the Design Under Test (DUT). It does not check
the testbench for differences.

Verdi Formal Navigator
This chapter contains the following topics:
* Overview of Verdi Formal Navigator
* Launch Verdi Formal Navigator
* Setting Up Verdi Formal Navigator

Overview of Verdi Formal Navigator
As designers, you want to perform what-if analyses to test hypothetical scenarios and
observe the potential effects of specific changes without the need to rerun an entire
simulation. This approach saves time and allows you to quickly assess the impact of a
design change. It helps you make informed decisions and identify potential issues before
you progress in the verification process. You can leverage the Navigator feature of VC
Formal in Verdi for waveform manipulation, plotting, and design exploration, without
requiring detailed knowledge of how to use the complete VC Formal tool.
The Navigator feature is designed to enhance waveform analysis for design verification.
The Navigator view enables you to do the following:
* Generate Waveforms From Design Signals: To understand how the design signals
interact and confirm that the design operates as intended under various conditions, you
need to visualize the signal behavior over time. This feature offers a clear, graphical
representation of signal transitions and interactions by generating waveforms from the
design signals. Thus, you can spot any unexpected behavior in the design.
* View Specific Properties: This feature enables you to view specific properties, such
as assert or cover properties for targets and assume properties for constraints. By
doing so, it enables you to track the fulfillment of these properties during simulation.
* Add, Modify, or Delete Constraints and Targets: You often need the flexibility to
adapt your verification environment to different scenarios by adding, modifying, or
removing constraints and targets. This feature helps you to test the design under
various conditions and ensures comprehensive coverage.
* Edit Signal Values in a Waveform: You may want to perform what-if analyses by
adjusting signal values to observe the impact of these changes on the design. This

Launch Verdi Formal Navigator

feature enables you to edit signal values directly within the waveform and visualize the
effects of hypothetical adjustments. You can also generate a new waveform based on
these changes.
* Generate Counter-Example Waveforms for Failing Properties: This feature
generates counter-example waveforms and shows how and why a SystemVerilog
Assertions (SVA) property fails.

these changes.
* Generate Counter-Example Waveforms for Failing Properties: This feature
generates counter-example waveforms and shows how and why a SystemVerilog
Assertions (SVA) property fails.
In addition to the above-mentioned tasks, you can experiment with different verification
scenarios without changing the testbench and recompiling to run the simulation again,
thereby increasing productivity.
After you load the design into Verdi and launch Navigator, VC Formal runs in the
background automatically. When the VC Formal engine is ready, the Navigator window
opens in Verdi, allowing you to generate waveforms without a testbench.
You can edit the signal values in a waveform cycle-by-cycle, plot the waveform again, and
generate a new scenario, or extend the current waveform for additional cycles. If you write
SVA, you can also independently create SVA assert and cover properties. It allows you to
generate a waveform to verify whether assert properties fail or cover properties are met.
For more information about how to use the Navigator feature, refer to the VC Formal User
Guide.

Using the Verdi Flow
To launch Verdi Formal Navigator from Verdi, do the following:
* Import the design by running the following command:
% verdi -lca -sverilog -f <filelist>

Verdi Assistant
Verdi Assistant is an AI-powered feature that integrates a Large Language Model (LLM)
into the Verdi environment. It provides a chatbot interface for conversational debugging.
This feature allows you to interact with Verdi by using natural language. As a result, you
can find commands, execute them, obtain documentation or answers to usage questions
easily. Verdi Assistant automates command execution and provides instant support. It
reduces the learning curve for new users and increases productivity of experienced users.
Verdi Assistant provides the following benefits:
* Simplifies command discovery and execution through natural language prompts.
* Reduces the need to consult documentation or application engineers for common
tasks.
* Supports both new and experienced users by streamlining workflows.
* Executes multiple commands with a single prompt, saving time.
* Provides context-aware assistance based on the current GUI state.
* Offers feedback mechanisms to improve the responses generated by the assistant.

Understanding the Chat History Database
This section describes the chat history database, which stores all Verdi Assistant
promptresponse interactions in an SQLite3 file. This file also includes the configuration
of the Verdi Assistant directory, file name, data format, and the fields recorded for each
conversation turn.
This section contains the following topics:
* Database File Configuration and Format
* Data Stored Per Prompt

Database File Configuration and Format
This section explains how the Chat History Database file is configured, including how the
directory and file name are determined through environment variables. The database is
stored in SQLite3 format for easy access and compatibility.
* File Directory
Set the VERDI_ASSISTANT_CHAT_DB_DIR environment variable to specify the database
directory.
If you do not set this variable, the directory defaults to your home directory under
.verdi (for example, ~/.verdi).
* File Name
Set the VERDI_ASSISTANT_CHAT_DB_NAME environment variable to specify the
database file name.
If you do not set this variable, the file name defaults to chat_<username>.db, where
<username> is your operating system username.

* File Format
The database uses the SQLite3 format. Access the database by using SQLite3 scripts
or any SQLite3-compatible browser.

Data Stored Per Prompt
For every prompt and response, Verdi Assistant records one row in the sessions table of
the Chat History Database. Each row includes the following columns, with a composite
primary key on (chat_id, idx).

chat_id

Unique identifier of a chat session (UUID-style
string). All turns in the same conversation share
the same chat_id.

For example, 0 for the first turn, 1 for the
second and so on.
Together with chat_id, this identifies a single
row.

the interaction.

User prompt text sent to Verdi Assistant.

where -1 indicates unknown or not recorded.

The Waveform Agent is an intelligent sub-agent in Verdi Assistant. It uses AI-driven
agentic techniques to enhance waveform analysis.

The new capabilities are specifically designed to streamline the analysis of complex user
waveform files with enhanced precision and efficiency. These capabilities help users
identify potential issues earlier and ensure faster, more reliable design verification.
You can submit natural-language queries to request detailed information about a waveform
file. The agent processes these requests and retrieves relevant data.
In GUI mode, you interact with both a chatbot and a waveform view. This mode is also
called Waveform-Viewer-Integrated mode.
It enables contextual queries and visual signal analysis. You can reference items in the
waveform view using phrases such as "the selected signals," "the cursor time," or "the
waveform".
The waveform view updates based on the chatbot's responses. This provides instant
visual confirmation.
This chapter covers the following topics:
* Getting Started
* Prompting Basics
* Prompting for Common Debug Tasks
* Prompting Guidelines
* Known Issues and Limitations of Waveform Agent

Getting Started
This section describes how to define default prompt settings. The settings help tailor
responses to your design context, making prompts more effective and reducing repetition.

Set Default Debugging Target
Before querying signal debugging information, you can set the default debugging target,
such as FSDB file path and time unit. This eliminates the need to repeat the information in
every prompt.
Set Default FSDB
You can set the active FSDB for debugging once, eliminating the need to specify the full
FSDB path in each prompt. In GUI mode, the active FSDB is automatically synchronized
with the active FSDB in the waveform window.
In MCP mode, when an FSDB is not explicitly provided in the prompt, the most recently
mentioned FSDB is used. To change the default FSDB file path, enter the new FSDB file
path in a new prompt.

Set Default Time Unit
You can set the default time unit for debugging instead of specifying the time unit in each
prompt. If the default time unit is not set and no time unit is specified, Waveform Agent
processes the prompt with the default FSDB scale unit.

active waveform window. In MCP mode, when the time unit is not explicitly provided in the

Prompting Guidelines
This section provides guidance on optimizing prompt formulation to achieve optimal results
in waveform analysis. It outlines best practices and strategies for constructing precise,
well-structured prompts that enhance the efficiency and accuracy of the agentic debug
process.
Default Waveform and Time Unit
Default settings for waveform and time unit can be configured to streamline repeated
prompts. These defaults are synchronized with the active waveform window and are
applied automatically unless new values are specified. Refer to the Set Default Debugging
Target section for more details.
Radix
To ensure consistent interpretation, always include the radix specifier when writing values.
* 'h for hexadecimal
* 'd for decimal
* 'b for binary
* 'o for octal
For example, to specify the decimal value 17, use 'h11, 'd17, or 'b10001.
You can also specify the width of the bit before the radix specifier. For example, 8'h3C
represents an 8-bit hexadecimal value.

When a number is written without a radix specifier, it is interpreted based on its value:
1. If the value contains only 0 and 1, it is treated as binary.
Example: 1010 Interpreted as binary.
2. If the value contains any digits from 2 to 9, it is treated as decimal.
Example: 123 Interpreted as decimal.
3. If the value contains any letters from A to F (case-insensitive), it is treated as
hexadecimal.
Example: 3C Interpreted as hexadecimal.
Simple and Full Hierarchical Name
Full hierarchical name is required unless the signal is already visible in the active window
within Verdi. For example, the following prompt uses full hierarchical signal name
'tb_CPU.system.m1':
Find the value of signal "tb_CPU.system.m1.CARD" at 0 ns.
Alternatively, you can add signal tb_CPU.system.m1.CARD to the waveform window then
the signal can be referenced using the simple name:
Find the value of signal "CARD" at 0ns.
Delimiter
Only the dot (.) character is supported as a delimiter for hierarchy. The slash (/) character
is not supported.
Bus Signals with Unknowns (Xs)
When searching for unknown values in a bus signal, any value that contains 'x' is identified
as unknown. For example, 'bxxxx, 'b010x, and 'b1x11 are all identified as unknown values.
Matching Value Including Unknowns
To search for a specific value that includes unknown (X) values, the value must be written
in binary format. Note that an unknown value needs to be specified by a lowercase 'x'. For
example, 8'b10x01100.
Complex Scenarios
When describing a complex scenario, break it down into clear steps. Avoid including
unnecessary expertise, for more effective outcomes.
The following is an example on paired-signal timing validation.
[Original Prompt]

Analyze the timing relationship between the 3rd and 4th grant-request pairs for signals
ubus_tb_top.dut.ubus_gnt_master_0 and ubus_tb_top.dut.ubus_req_master_0 in /u/user/
fsdb/ex.fsdb, and determine if each request occurs before its corresponding grant.
[Preferred Prompt]
In the /u/user/fsdb/ex.fsdb FSDB:
1. Find the timestamps of the 3rd and 4th request events (rising edges) in signal
ubus_tb_top.dut.ubus_req_master_0.
2. Find the timestamps of the 3rd and 4th grant events (rising edges) in signal
ubus_tb_top.dut.ubus_gnt_master_0.
3. Compare the timestamps to determine if each request event occurs before its
corresponding grant event (3rd request before 3rd grant, 4th request before 4th grant).
Limited Number of Returned Results
The results are capped and only partially displayed due to chat limitations. However, the
total number of matches are provided. You are advised to revise the prompt to narrow the
scope or improve result relevance.
[Prompt]
List all timestamps of tb_CPUsystem.i_CPUsystem.addr in CPU.fsdb
[Answer]
Here are the first 30 timestamps of value changes for the signal
tb_CPUsystem.i_CPUsystem.addr in CPU.fsdb:
1. 0 ns: 8'bxxxxxxxx
2. 12 ns: 8'b00000000

29. 3726 ns: 8'b01010101
30. 3926 ns: 8'b00001101
The data is truncated to the first 30 items. There is a total of 96 transitions.
To retrieve the timestamps of value changes after 3926ns, revise the prompt to the
following.
List all timestamps of scope.sig1 in ex.fsdb starting from 3926ns.

Known Issues and Limitations of Waveform Agent
This section describes the known issues and limitations of Waveform Agent.
Assertion and Transaction Waveform
Waveform analysis for assertion signals and transaction waveform is not supported.
[Prompt] Find the first assertion failure timestamp for the signal system.i_cpu.INCPC2.
Phase Between Clock Signals
Phase measurement between clock signals is not supported.
[Prompt] Measure the phase between clock signals
tb_CPUsystem.i_CPUsystem.CLOCK1 and tb_CPUsystem.i_CPUsystem.CLOCK2.
Gated Clock and Multiple Clock Frequency
Retrieving clock-related information is not supported for gated clocks.
This limitation also applies to clock signals with multiple clock frequencies. Examples
include clock frequency and cycle length.
[Prompt] Obtain the period of the system.gated_clock clock signal.
The system.gated_clock is assumed to be a gated clock signal in the waveform.
Member Signals
For composite objects such as SystemVerilog structs, unions, and interfaces, individual
member signals cannot be accessed; only the parent signal is supported.

Design Agent is an intelligent sub-agent in Verdi Assistant. It uses agentic AI to automate
and speed up HDL (Hardware Description Language) design analysis. You can submit
natural-language queries to explore RTL (Register-Transfer Level) codebases, extract
insights, and find structural patterns.
Design Agent is designed to streamline the analysis of complex hardware designs.
It enhances precision and helps engineers gain a deeper understanding of module

hierarchies, signal interactions, and potential design issues. By identifying issues earlier
in the development cycle, Design Agent reduces manual effort and accelerates design
verification.
This chapter covers the following topics:
* Getting Started
* Prompting Basics
* Advanced Prompting

Getting Started

responses to your design context, making prompts more effective and reducing repetition.
Import Design
Before using Design Agent, you need to import designs into the Verdi Assistant
environment. This ensures the agent has access to the full RTL codebase for accurate
analysis.

Prompting Basics
Design Agent uses natural language prompts to analyze RTL design data, facilitating both
structural and functional exploration. This section introduces how to write clear, effective
prompts through simple examples.
Design Agent offers two primary functionalities: Design Exploration and Signal Tracing.
* Design Exploration allows you to query and extract structural information from RTL
designs using natural language inputs, streamlining the process of understanding
design architecture.
* Signal Tracing assists in analyzing the connectivity of signals within the design,
focusing on the propagation of signal values. Signal tracing is divided into two
categories: static signal tracing and active signal tracing, each serving distinct
purposes in signal analysis.

Design Exploration
Design Exploration comprises three primary functions: identifying design objects, retrieving
object properties and accessing module source code. Supported objects include signals,
instances, modules, ports, and other RTL design elements.

Design Exploration also supports netlist-level analysis, allowing users to explore
components like flip-flops, registers, latches, and finite state machines (FSMs). This
capability helps engineers gain deeper insight into sequential logic and control structures
within the design.
In both MCP and GUI modes, the system automatically generates an output file to prevent
excessively large response content from being displayed directly in the interface. For
responses that exceed the display limit, only the primary objectives are shown in the
chatbot, while the full details are provided in the attached file. You can conveniently
review the generated file through SmartLog in Verdi by clicking the file link provided in the
response.
In GUI mode, the selected scope from the Instance View can be referenced directly by
prompting with "selected scope/instance", without using the full hierarchical name.
Limitations:
* Design Exploration currently supports SystemVerilog only.
* Interface element analysis is not supported.

Prompting Guidelines
This section provides guidance on optimizing prompt formulation to achieve optimal results
in waveform analysis. It outlines best practices and strategies for constructing precise,
well-structured prompts that enhance the efficiency and accuracy of the agentic debug
process.
Default Waveform and Time Unit
Default settings for waveform and time unit can be configured to streamline repeated
prompts. These defaults are synchronized with the active waveform window and are
applied automatically unless new values are specified.

efault Waveform and Time Unit
Default settings for waveform and time unit can be configured to streamline repeated
prompts. These defaults are synchronized with the active waveform window and are
applied automatically unless new values are specified. Refer to the Set Default Debugging
Target section for more details.
Radix
To ensure consistent interpretation, always include the radix specifier when writing values.
* 'h for hexadecimal
* 'd for decimal
* 'b for binary
* 'o for octal
For example, to specify the decimal value 17, use 'h11, 'd17, or 'b10001.
You can also specify the width of the bit before the radix specifier. For example, 8'h3C
represents an 8-bit hexadecimal value.

When a number is written without a radix specifier, it is interpreted based on its value:
1. If the value contains only 0 and 1, it is treated as binary.
Example: 1010 Interpreted as binary.
2. If the value contains any digits from 2 to 9, it is treated as decimal.
Example: 123 Interpreted as decimal.
3. If the value contains any letters from A to F (case-insensitive), it is treated as
hexadecimal.
Example: 3C Interpreted as hexadecimal.
Simple and Full Hierarchical Name
Full hierarchical name is required unless the signal is already visible in the active window
within Verdi. For example, the following prompt uses full hierarchical signal name
'tb_CPU.system.m1':
Find the value of signal "tb_CPU.system.m1.CARD" at 0 ns.
Alternatively, you can add signal tb_CPU.system.m1.CARD to the waveform window then
the signal can be referenced using the simple name:
Find the value of signal "CARD" at 0ns.
Delimiter
Only the dot (.) character is supported as a delimiter for hierarchy. The slash (/) character
is not supported.
Bus Signals with Unknowns (Xs)
When searching for unknown values in a bus signal, any value that contains 'x' is identified
as unknown. For example, 'bxxxx, 'b010x, and 'b1x11 are all identified as unknown values.
Matching Value Including Unknowns
To search for a specific value that includes unknown (X) values, the value must be written
in binary format. Note that an unknown value needs to be specified by a lowercase 'x'. For
example, 8'b10x01100.
Complex Scenarios
When describing a complex scenario, break it down into clear steps. Avoid including
unnecessary expertise, for more effective outcomes.
The following is an example on paired-signal timing validation.
[Original Prompt]

Analyze the timing relationship between the 3rd and 4th grant-request pairs for signals
ubus_tb_top.dut.ubus_gnt_master_0 and ubus_tb_top.dut.ubus_req_master_0 in /u/user/
fsdb/ex.fsdb, and determine if each request occurs before its corresponding grant.
[Preferred Prompt]
In the /u/user/fsdb/ex.fsdb FSDB:
1. Find the timestamps of the 3rd and 4th request events (rising edges) in signal
ubus_tb_top.dut.ubus_req_master_0.
2. Find the timestamps of the 3rd and 4th grant events (rising edges) in signal
ubus_tb_top.dut.ubus_gnt_master_0.
3. Compare the timestamps to determine if each request event occurs before its
corresponding grant event (3rd request before 3rd grant, 4th request before 4th grant).
Limited Number of Returned Results
The results are capped and only partially displayed due to chat limitations. However, the
total number of matches are provided. You are advised to revise the prompt to narrow the
scope or improve result relevance.

Known Issues and Limitations of Waveform Agent
This section describes the known issues and limitations of Waveform Agent.
Assertion and Transaction Waveform
Waveform analysis for assertion signals and transaction waveform is not supported.
[Prompt] Find the first assertion failure timestamp for the signal system.i_cpu.INCPC2.
Phase Between Clock Signals
Phase measurement between clock signals is not supported.
[Prompt] Measure the phase between clock signals
tb_CPUsystem.i_CPUsystem.CLOCK1 and tb_CPUsystem.i_CPUsystem.CLOCK2.
Gated Clock and Multiple Clock Frequency
Retrieving clock-related information is not supported for gated clocks.
This limitation also applies to clock signals with multiple clock frequencies. Examples
include clock frequency and cycle length.
[Prompt] Obtain the period of the system.gated_clock clock signal.
The system.gated_clock is assumed to be a gated clock signal in the waveform.
Member Signals
For composite objects such as SystemVerilog structs, unions, and interfaces, individual
member signals cannot be accessed; only the parent signal is supported.

Design Agent is an intelligent sub-agent in Verdi Assistant. It uses agentic AI to automate
and speed up HDL (Hardware Description Language) design analysis. You can submit
natural-language queries to explore RTL (Register-Transfer Level) codebases, extract
insights, and find structural patterns.
Design Agent is designed to streamline the analysis of complex hardware designs.
It enhances precision and helps engineers gain a deeper understanding of module

hierarchies, signal interactions, and potential design issues. By identifying issues earlier
in the development cycle, Design Agent reduces manual effort and accelerates design
verification.
This chapter covers the following topics:
* Getting Started
* Prompting Basics
* Advanced Prompting

Getting Started
This section describes how to define default prompt settings. The settings help tailor
responses to your design context, making prompts more effective and reducing repetition.
Import Design
Before using Design Agent, you need to import designs into the Verdi Assistant
environment. This ensures the agent has access to the full RTL codebase for accurate
analysis.
You can prompt the agent to load a design by providing the path to simv.daidir.

Import the design from /path/to/simv.daidir

The design has been successfully imported
from the directory path/to/simv.daidir

Design loading is currently supported only through the -dbdir option, which requires the
path to the compiled simulation database (for example, simv.daidir).
Reload Design
Reloading the design ensures that the Design Agent operates on the latest RTL code after
any modifications. This action re-imports the compiled simulation database and all existing
applications into Verdi.

Reload the design

The design has been successfully reloaded

Import FSDB
To change the default FSDB file path, enter a new FSDB path in a new prompt.
Certain Design Agent capabilities depend on FSDB files. If the required FSDB files are not
available, the system notifies you.
Waveform Agent handles FSDB file import. It loads and processes waveform data to
support analysis.

Import /path/to/my.fsdb

The FSDB file located at /path/to/my.fsdb has
been successfully imported and is now active.

The following example illustrates the scenario and response when the required FSDB file
has not been imported for Design Agent.

ns

need the FSDB (waveform database) file name
associated with the design. Could you provide
this information?

Prompting Basics
Design Agent uses natural language prompts to analyze RTL design data, facilitating both
structural and functional exploration. This section introduces how to write clear, effective
prompts through simple examples.
Design Agent offers two primary functionalities: Design Exploration and Signal Tracing.
* Design Exploration allows you to query and extract structural information from RTL
designs using natural language inputs, streamlining the process of understanding
design architecture.
* Signal Tracing assists in analyzing the connectivity of signals within the design,
focusing on the propagation of signal values. Signal tracing is divided into two
categories: static signal tracing and active signal tracing, each serving distinct
purposes in signal analysis.

Design Exploration
Design Exploration comprises three primary functions: identifying design objects, retrieving
object properties and accessing module source code. Supported objects include signals,
instances, modules, ports, and other RTL design elements.

Design Exploration also supports netlist-level analysis, allowing users to explore
components like flip-flops, registers, latches, and finite state machines (FSMs). This
capability helps engineers gain deeper insight into sequential logic and control structures
within the design.
In both MCP and GUI modes, the system automatically generates an output file to prevent
excessively large response content from being displayed directly in the interface. For
responses that exceed the display limit, only the primary objectives are shown in the
chatbot, while the full details are provided in the attached file. You can conveniently
review the generated file through SmartLog in Verdi by clicking the file link provided in the
response.
In GUI mode, the selected scope from the Instance View can be referenced directly by
prompting with "selected scope/instance", without using the full hierarchical name.
Limitations:
* Design Exploration currently supports SystemVerilog only.
* Interface element analysis is not supported.
Identifying Design Objects
You can search, retrieve, and count specific targets within the design. Queries might be
constrained to a defined scope and revised using conditions to enable more focused and
precise analysis.

Static Signal Tracing
Static signal tracing enables analysis of signal connectivity within the RTL design without
requiring simulation data.
Static signal tracing analyzes the structural connectivity of signals within the RTL
design. This type of tracing does not require simulation data and focuses on the design's
connectivity graph.
In GUI mode, static tracing automatically adapts the visualization to the tracing objective:
single-level tracing is shown in Source View, while multi-level tracing is shown in
Schematic View. During tracing, related signals are also recorded to a file.
Trace Forward (Trace Loads/Fanouts)
Trace forward follows a signal from its source to all its loads (fanouts). This helps identify
which parts of the design are affected by a particular signal.

Active Signal Tracing
Active signal tracing analyzes signal behavior using simulation data to identify active
drivers and trace unknown values.
Active signal tracing requires simulation data (FSDB) to analyze signal behavior at a
specific simulation time. This type of tracing focuses on the dynamic behavior of signals
during simulation.
In GUI mode, Temporal Flow View (TFV) is used to visualize active tracing results, and
relevant traced signals are recorded to a file during the tracing process.
Trace Active Driver
Trace active driver identifies which driver is actively driving a signal at a specific simulation
time. This is essential for debugging signal contention and understanding multiplexed
signal paths.
Tracing active drivers or value-change causes can be time-consuming. By default, the
agent traces only direct drivers. If you request a value-change cause, the trace continues
deeper. When a one-time tracing limit is reached, the agent prompts for confirmation
before continuing, and then resumes from the previous stop point.

Explains the advanced prompting techniques for signal tracing, including filters and stop
criteria based on name, scope, type, size, and location.

Signal Tracing with Particular Filter/Stop Criteria
Static and active signal tracing support filtering signals or stopping tracing based on
specific conditions. This helps users narrow down signal candidates for debugging.
Signal tracing supports filtering based on the following attributes:
* Name - Match signals by naming patterns or keywords.
* Scope - Limit tracing to a specific hierarchical scope.
* Type - Filter by signal type (for example, wire, reg, port).

* Size - Specify bit-width or array dimensions.
* Location - Restrict by file or line location in the design.
Clear and simple conditions improve accuracy. Avoid combining multiple
conditions in a single query for best results.

Active Signal Tracing
Active signal tracing analyzes signal behavior using simulation data to identify active
drivers and trace unknown values.
Active signal tracing requires simulation data (FSDB) to analyze signal behavior at a
specific simulation time. This type of tracing focuses on the dynamic behavior of signals
during simulation.
In GUI mode, Temporal Flow View (TFV) is used to visualize active tracing results, and
relevant traced signals are recorded to a file during the tracing process.
Trace Active Driver
Trace active driver identifies which driver is actively driving a signal at a specific simulation
time. This is essential for debugging signal contention and understanding multiplexed
signal paths.
Tracing active drivers or value-change causes can be time-consuming. By default, the
agent traces only direct drivers. If you request a value-change cause, the trace continues
deeper. When a one-time tracing limit is reached, the agent prompts for confirmation
before continuing, and then resumes from the previous stop point.

Advanced Prompting
Explains the advanced prompting techniques for signal tracing, including filters and stop
criteria based on name, scope, type, size, and location.

Signal Tracing with Particular Filter/Stop Criteria
Static and active signal tracing support filtering signals or stopping tracing based on
specific conditions. This helps users narrow down signal candidates for debugging.
Signal tracing supports filtering based on the following attributes:
* Name - Match signals by naming patterns or keywords.
* Scope - Limit tracing to a specific hierarchical scope.
* Type - Filter by signal type (for example, wire, reg, port).

* Size - Specify bit-width or array dimensions.
* Location - Restrict by file or line location in the design.
Clear and simple conditions improve accuracy. Avoid combining multiple
conditions in a single query for best results.
In GUI mode, signals that meet stop criteria are highlighted in the Schematic window or in
Temporal Flow View.

Setup Environment and Launch FastAgent
This section explains how to configure FastAgent and launch the MCP Client using the
FastAgent framework.
Edit Configuration
Open the fastagent.config.yaml file and follow the instructions provided in the file to fill
in the necessary settings.
The configuration is divided into two main sections. Complete all required fields based on
user's local LLM setup. The detailed guidance is included within the YAML file.
Launch FastAgent
After preparing the configuration file, run the following command:
fastagent

This launches the MCP Client using the FastAgent framework. It automatically connects
to Verdi Agentic by using the settings in fastagent.config.yaml. After the connection is
established, you can start testing the MCP Client.

Glossary
This glossary defines important terms, signals, and concepts referenced in the Verdi
Assistant documentation.

Model Context Protocol

A communication protocol that defines how a client interacts with an AI model or
system. MCP ensures structured data exchange, command handling and process
control.
MCP can operate in different modes depending on the communication method. For
example, STDIO Mode and SSE Mode.

Glossary

Standard Input/Output Mode

A mode in which the MCP communicates with the AI model process through standard
input and output streams. This setup is commonly used for local or embedded
integrations where data is exchanged via terminal-like interfaces rather than network
sockets.

SSE Mode (Server-Sent Events Mode)

A mode in which the MCP communicates over HTTP using Server-Sent Events. This
allows the server to push real-time updates, such as progress messages or streaming
responses, to the client in a continuous connection.

API key

A unique authentication token used to identify and authorize a user or application when
accessing an API service or system API.
API keys help control access, track usage and enforce rate limits.

Endpoint

A specific URL or network address where a service or API can be accessed.
In the context of SCS (Service Control System), the endpoint defines the connection
target for structured requests. Examples include job creation, model queries, and
debug commands.

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
FSDB Format
The Verdi platform supports a file format called Fast Signal Database (FSDB). FSDB has
these advantages over the standard format:
* An FSDB file is more compact than a standard VCD file. Typically, an FSDB file is
about 5 to 50 times smaller than a VCD file.
* FSDB files let the Verdi platform display waveforms and back-annotated signal values
faster.
Synopsys provides object and support files in the Verdi package. You can link these files
with popular simulators to dump FSDB files directly during simulation, instead of using
VCD files. For existing VCD files, the Verdi package includes the vfast conversion utility.
Use it to convert VCD files into FSDB files. The Verdi platform also converts VCD files
to FSDB automatically when you open a VCD file with the File -> Open Waveform File
command in nTrace or the File -> Open command in nWave. The Verdi package also
includes fsdb2vcd, a utility that converts FSDB files back to VCD format.
If FSDB dumper support for a simulator version is over 18 months old, and that vendor has
more than three major simulator versions, Synopsys moves that FSDB dumper into the
legacy dumper.
For older simulator versions, contact Synopsys support:
https://solvnetplus.synopsys.com/s/contactsupport
