Switch Dumping With Simulator Restore
The FSDB dumper switches the dump file when the simulator executes the restore
command. When the simulator executes restore (or restart) for the first time, FSDB
dumping redirects to a new file named <original_FSDB_name>.restore.FSDB. The
dumper saves and closes the original dump files. If you dump multiple FSDB files, the
dumper redirects each one to a different restore file. If the simulator executes restore
several times, each run overwrites the <original_FSDB_name>.restore.FSDB files.
* ModelSim Simulator
* Cadence IUS Simulator
* Miscellaneous Rules

ModelSim Simulator
When the restore command is executed for the first time, the dumping is redirected to a
new FSDB file named as <original_FSDB_name>.restore.FSDB. If multiple FSDB files
are being dumped, each of them is redirected to a different restore FSDB file.
Simulator Commands
* checkpoint
* restore
Refer to the ModelSim User's Manual for details of checkpoint and restore commands.
vsim> fsdbDumpvars +fsdbfile+save.fsdb

Create the save.fsdb FSDB file.
vsim> run 10ns
vsim> checkpoint saveData

Save a copy of the simulation data at the time for later restore.

Appendix A: Switch Dumping With Simulator Restore
Cadence IUS Simulator

vsim> run 20ns
vsim> restore saveData

When the simulation is restored to the previously saved time point, the save.fsdb file is
saved and closed, and the new file save.restore.fsdb is created.
vsim> run 30ns
vsim> quit

The following FSDB files and associated time ranges are the result:
* save.fsdb: 0ns ~ 30ns
* save.restore.fsdb: 10ns ~ 40ns

Cadence IUS Simulator
When the restart command is executed for the first time, the dumping is redirected to a
new FSDB file named as <original_FSDB_name>.restore.FSDB. If multiple FSDB files
are being dumped, each of them is redirected to a different restore FSDB file.
Simulator Commands
* save
* restart
Refer to the IUS user's manual for details of the save and restart commands.
ncsim> call fsdbDumpvars +fsdbfile+save.fsdb

Create the save.fsdb FSDB file.
ncsim> run 20ns
ncsim> save saveData

Save a copy of the simulation data at the time for later restore.
ncsim> run 20ns
ncsim> restart saveData

When the simulation is restored to the previously saved time point, the save.fsdb file is
saved and closed, and the new file save.restore.fsdb is created.
ncsim> run 10ns
ncsim> exit

Appendix A: Switch Dumping With Simulator Restore
Miscellaneous Rules

The following FSDB files and associated time ranges are the result:
* save.fsdb: 0ns ~ 40ns
* save.restore.fsdb: 20ns ~ 30ns

Miscellaneous Rules
The miscellaneous rules apply in the following situations:
* When the restore command is executed several times.
* When the FSDB name happens to have a restore.fsdb extension.
* When restoring in a new simulation session.

restore Command Executed Multiple Times
When the restore command is executed several times, the
<original_FSDB_name>.restore.FSDB files are overridden.
Example in IUS
ncsim> call fsdbDumpvars +fsdbfile+save.fsdb

Create the save.fsdb FSDB file.
ncsim> run 20ns
ncsim> save saveData

Save a copy of the simulation data at the time for later restore.
ncsim> run 20ns
ncsim> restart saveData

When the simulation is restored to the previously saved time point, the save.fsdb file is
saved and closed, and the new file save.restore.fsdb is created.
ncsim> run 10ns
ncsim> restart saveData

When the simulation is restored to the previously saved time point, the
save.restore.fsdb file is re-created and this file overwrites the previous one.
ncsim> run 40ns
ncsim> exit

Appendix A: Switch Dumping With Simulator Restore
Miscellaneous Rules

FSDB File With restore.fsdb Extension
When the FSDB name happens to have a restore.fsdb extension, then the restore
FSDB file name is the same.

Restore in a New Simulation Session
For IUS and Modelsim, restoring in a new simulation session is an independent dumper
process.
Example in IUS
* The first simulation session:
ncsim> call fsdbDumpvars +fsdbfile+save.fsdb

The save.fsdb file is created.
ncsim>
ncsim>
ncsim>
ncsim>

run 20ns
save saveData
run 20ns
restart saveData

The save.restore.fsdb file is created.
ncsim> run 10ns
ncsim> exit

* The second simulation session:
ncsim> restart saveData
ncsim> call fsdbDumpvars +fsdbfile+save.fsdb

The save.fsdb file is created.

$fsdbDumpPSL
Dumps the PSL assert directives in the Verilog or VHDL design to the FSDB file.

This command supports the dumper for IUS 13.1 and ModelSim 10.2 and their
later versions.
If the IUS simulator is used, the +psl_prop option is used to dump the PSL
properties in the Verilog or VHDL design.
$fsdbDumpPSL([ depth, | "level=",depth_var, ]
[instance | "instance=",instance_var]);
[ ,"option" | ,"option=",option_var ]*);

Specify the levels of hierarchy to dump for the subsequent scopes. If the subsequent
arguments are signals, only these signals are dumped.
"level="

Keyword to identify the next argument is a number.
depth_var

Specify how many levels of hierarchy to dump for the subsequent scopes in a variable.

Specify the instance name for which all SVA assertions below it are dumped.
"instance="

Keyword to identify the content of the next argument is a module scope or signal.
instance_var

This definition gives the module scope or signal represented by the instance_var that
specifies the object to dump. The HDL type should be string.

+psl_prop

Dump the PSL properties.

"option="

Keyword to identify the next argument is a string.

Specify the option in a variable.

The $fsdbDumpPSL command supports dumping for the following verification unit types:
* vunit
* vprop
* vmode
# inline
Assume that the file name is case.v:
reg clk = 0;
//psl property p1 = {clk==1;clk==0} @(posedge clk); ---(A)
//psl assert always {clk==1;clk==0} @(posedge clk); ---(B)
endmodule

By default, (B) is dumped. If the "+fsdb+psl_prop" option is specified, (A) is also
dumped.
# vunit / vprop / vmode
Assume that the file name is case.v.
reg clk = 0;
endmodule

Assume that the file name is casevunit.v and this file can only be loaded and compiled
with the option:
vunit v1 (top) {
default clock = @(posedge top.clk);
property p2 = {clk==1;clk==0} @(posedge clk);
assert always {clk==1;clk==0};
}

---(C)
---(D)

By default, (D) is dumped. If the "+fsdb+psl_prop" option is specified, (C) is also
dumped.
Extra Scope Creation
An extra scope is created when binding the verification unit with the instance, for example:
File: unit.v
vunit VUNIT_NAME(top.sub_Inst){

}
File: top.v

sub sub_Inst();
endmodule
module sub;

endmodule

In this case, an extra scope named "VUNIT_NAME" is created under top.sub_Inst. The
same result is obtained in vprop and vmode.
Naming Rules
When naming the design, the following rules must be followed:
* assert/assume/cover should be keywords when naming the design. For example:
top.A1_$assert // (This is an assert.)
top.6_case302_v_cover // (This is a cover.)
* The restrict directive is not dumped. When the +psl_prop option is specified, the
property under the restrict directive is created.
* The cover directive does not have an underlying property.
# Unnamed Assertion
[case1]
//psl property p1 = {clk} @(posedge clk);
//psl assert always {clk} @(posedge clk);

If the +psl_prop option is not specified, the dumping result is:
top.7_case302_v_assert.

top.7_case302_v_assert
top.p1

[case2]

//psl property p1 = {clk} @(posedge clk);
//psl assert always p1;

If the +psl_prop option is not specified, the dumping result is:
top.7_case302_v_assert

top.7_case302_v_assert
top.p1

# Named Assertion
[case1]
//psl property p1 = {clk} @(posedge clk);
//psl A1: assert always {clk} @(posedge clk);

If the +psl_prop option is not specified, the dumping result is:
top.A1_$assert
top.A1
// (This module has the same value change as
top.A1_$assert.)

top.A1_$assert
top.A1
top.p1

[case2]

//psl property p1 = {clk} @(posedge clk);
//psl A1: assert always p1;

If the +psl_prop option is not specified, the dumping result is:
top.A1_$assert
top.A1

top.A1_$assert
top.A1
top.p1

The "-assert" option should be specified for PSL execution.
> irun -assert design_files -propfile_vlog vlog_vunit_file
-propfile_vhdl vhdl_vunit_file

Bind the vunit in the irun command line.
> ncvlog -assert -propfile vlog_vunit_file

Bind the vunit in the ncvlog command line.
> ncvhdl -assert -propfile vhdl_vunit_file

Bind the vunit in the ncvhdl command line.

The Novas object files for FSDB dumping provide the following FSDB dumping commands
for VHDL. Call these procedures from your VHDL testbench to control FSDB signal
dumping during simulation.
* $fsdbDumpvars -- Specifies which signals or hierarchy levels to dump.
* fsdbDumpvarsES -- Dumps signals with extended scope support.
* fsdbDumpMDA -- Dumps multi-dimensional array (MDA) or memory signals.
* $fsdbDumpSVA -- Dumps SystemVerilog Assertion (SVA) results.
* $fsdbDumpvarsByFile -- Dumps signals specified in a file list.
* fsdbSuppress -- Suppresses specific FSDB dumper warning messages.
* $fsdbDumpon, $fsdbDumpoff -- Enables or disables FSDB dumping during simulation.
* fsdbSwitchDumpfile -- Manually switches dumping to a new FSDB file.
* $fsdbDumpfile -- Specifies the FSDB output file name and opens it for dumping.
* fsdbAutoSwitchDumpfile -- Automatically switches to a new FSDB file at a size limit.
* $fsdbDumpFinish -- Closes the FSDB file and finishes the dump session.
* $fsdbDumpflush -- Flushes buffered data to the FSDB file.
* fsdbDumpVariable -- Dumps a specific VHDL variable by name.
* fsdbDumpVariableByFile -- Dumps VHDL variables specified in a file list.

General Dumping Commands
Dump signals under the specified scopes with the arguments instance and depth. The
signals are saved in the FSDB file created by fsdbDumpfile command or the +fsdbfile
+filename option. If an FSDB file name is not specified, the default file name is novas.fsdb.
When there are multiple fsdbDumpvars and have performance issues, it is
recommended to use fsdbDumpvarsByFile instead of fsdbDumpvars.
$fsdbDumpvars(depth, "instance"[,"option,*"]);

call fsdbDumpvars
call fsdbDumpvars [depth][instance][option]*

Modelsim:
fsdbDumpvars [depth] [instance]

Specify how many sub-scope levels under the given scope you want to dump. Specify this
argument as 1 to dump the signals under the given scope. Specify this argument as 0 to
dump all signals under the given scope and its descendant scopes.

Specify the complete path name of the scope you want to dump. Different simulators have
different naming rules for describing the complete path name of a scope. You can refer to
the simulator documents for complete details.
Assume the VHDL root scope is root_scope, scope1 is the child scope under root_scope,
and scope2 is the child scope under scope1. In IUS, the complete path name of a scope
is:scope1:scope2. The left-most colon indicates the root scope and the other colons are

used to separate the scope name. In ModelSim, the complete path name of a scope can
be either root_scope.scope1.scope2 or /root_scope/scope1/scope2.

Only IO port signals are dumped.

Enable dumping of functions in the design.

Only reg type signals are dumped.

title: 3 top.type_dut.logicInst
text:
Specify the es list filename.
The file format of the Essential Signal file is as follows:
#ESD
# The first line should be "#ESD".
# Used to recognize the file format.
#V2
# The second line should be "#V2".
# The following is the signal list.
# The first character '<' means the beginning of a scope.
# The scope name is specified sequentially.
<scope_instance_name
# List all signals under the same scope.
signal_instance_name

title: 3 top.type_dut.logicInst
text:
>
# The first character '>' indicates move to the next
# higher scope.

>
# The following are option values you want to save in FSDB.
# They are saved under a hidden scope called
# $$ESD_OPTIONS.
# Syntax - $var_name="value"
$op1="system.i_cpu.i_PCU"
# The first character '$' means an option and its value are
# specified sequentially.

title: 3 top.type_dut.logicInst
text:
Specify one or more of the following options:

de"

mode implies:
0: Disable functionality.
1 or 2: Skip all cell information.

The following example uses the syntax for calling the system task in the design.
Refer to the syntax section for the correct format for the simulator command
line.

fsdbDumpvarsES(0, ":", "myeslist.list");

Dumps all signals in the Essential Signal list to the FSDB. Hierarchical format is used in
myeslist.list.
fsdbDumpvarsES(1, "system.i_CPU.i_ALUB", "+fsdbfile+target.fsdb" ,
"myeslist.list")

Dumps all signals in the Essential Signal file (myeslist.list) which are also within the
specified scope(s) and level to target.fsdb. The immediate child scope(s) of the specified
scope(s) and level are identified. If the child scope is a library cell instance, it is ignored.
For other immediate child scopes, the external nets of output boundary signals are
dumped.

fsdbDumpMDA
Dump value changes of SystemVerilog MDA (one or multi-dimensional array) signals to
the FSDB file.
fsdbDumpMDA supports MDA statements that are specified in the Verilog/
SystemVerilog portion of a mixed language design only. For pure VHDL arrays,
which can be dumped by fsdbDumpvars, there is no specific command for
performing this action.
fsdbDumpMDA needs to be added in the initial block. Invoking fsdbDumpMDA
multiple times in the source code, for example specifying inside the always
block, for example, cause the FSDB size to be increased, since fsdbDumpMDA
traverses the design each time it is invoked and saves the hierarchy tree into
the FSDB file.
$fsdbDumpMDA( depth, "instance" [,"option,*"] );

Inside quotation marks, use a comma to separate options and no space should
be left between options.
The first two arguments depth and instance are required. You can place a
delimiter in the instance argument to represent the design top. For example,
fsdbDumpMDA(0, ":"). For ModelSim users, the delimiter between the
hierarchical names is slash (/).

call fsdbDumpMDA [depth] [instance]
call fsdbDumpMDA [depth] [instance] [option]*

Modelsim:
fsdbDumpMDA [depth] [instance]
fsdbDumpMDA [depth] [instance] [option]*

fsdbSuppress
Specify the scopes that is not dumped by the fsdbDumpvars, fsdbDumpvarsByFile,
fsdbDumpMDA or fsdbDumpVariable commands. fsdbSuppress supports suppressing
by file name or the target scopes passed as arguments. The supported target scope can
be modules, instances, scopes, or signals in complete hierarchical format. Each format is
called in different fsdbSuppress calls respectively.
fsdbSuppress should be specified before fsdbDumpvars, fsdbDumpvarsByFile,
fsdbDumpMDA, or fsdbDumpVariable; if not, fsdbSuppress does not work.
The setting of fsdbSuppress are reset after fsdbDumpFinish is executed.
$fsdbSuppress( "suppress_file" | "instance,*");
$fsdbSuppress("suppress_file");
$fsdbSuppress("instance,*");

Use a comma to separate instances or signal_names and no space should be
left between the instances or signal_names.
call fsdbSuppress suppress_file
call fsdbSuppress instance*

fsdbSuppress suppress_file
fsdbSuppress instance*

suppress_file

Specify the file containing the names of the scopes that are not dumped.
"instance"

Specify one or more scopes that are not dumped.
"signal_name"

Specify the signal in full hierarchical format that are not dumped.
All supported suppression methods should be used separately for each
fsdbSuppress called; cannot combine multiple suppression types in one
fsdbSuppress command. For file syntax, each line of the file is the complete
name of a scope that you do not want to be dumped.

fsdbDumpvars(0,dump_top);

specifying the specific file name.
$fsdbDumpon( ["+fsdbfile+filename"] );
$fsdbDumpoff( ["+fsdbfile+filename"] );

call fsdbDumpon [+fsdbfile+filename]
call fsdbDumpoff [+fsdbfile+filename]

fsdbDumpon [+fsdbfile+filename]
fsdbDumpoff [+fsdbfile+filename]

fsdbSwitchDumpfile
Support multiple FSDB files during a simulation run by specifying the currently active
FSDB file name. When this command is executed, the previously opened FSDB file is
closed and the new FSDB file is created to continue saving the values change data and
act as current active FSDB file.
Since the FSDB dumper supports more then one open file for saving data simultaneously,
the source file that is supposed to be switched can be specified by the "+fsdbfile
+sourcefilename" option, if not the source file must be the currently active FSDB file.
$fsdbSwitchDumpfile("NewFileName" [ ,"+fsdbfile+src_file"] );
$fsdbSwitchDumpfile("NewFileName");
$fsdbSwitchDumpfile("NewFileName", "+fsdbfile+src_file");

fsdbSwitchDumpfile NewFileName
fsdbSwitchDumpfile NewFileName +fsdbfile+src_file

call fsdbSwitchDumpfile NewFileName
call fsdbSwitchDumpfile NewFileName +fsdbfile+src_file

NewFileName

The target new name of the FSDB file generating by the Novas object files for FSDB
dumping.
+fsdbfile+src_file

Specify the source FSDB file to be switched.
(include the .fsdb file extension in the name). This
is optional; if it is not specified, the FSDB dumper
switches dump finish on all active FSDB files.

fsdbDumpfile("test0.fsdb");
fsdbDumpvars(0, "system");
fsdbDumpvars(3, "system", "+fsdbfile+f1.fsdb);
wait for 100 ns
fsdbSwitchDumpfile("test1.fsdb", "+fsdbfile+test0.fsdb");
wait for 100 ns
fsdbSwitchDumpfile("test2.fsdb", "+fsdbfile+f1.fsdb");

Create test0.fsdb to dump the design initially. Create f1.fsdb to dump different depth of
design. Switch test0.fsdb to test1.fsdb at the simulation time 100 ns. Then switch
f1.fsdb to test2.fsdb at the simulation time 200 ns.

fsdbDumpfile
Specify the FSDB file name created by the Novas object files for FSDB dumping. If it is not
specified, the default FSDB file name is "novas.fsdb". This command is valid only before
fsdbDumpvars is executed and is ignored if specified after fsdbDumpvars.
To restrict the largest dump-file size to the user-defined size limitation, specify the limit size
in megabyte format. This function affects the FSDB file that is specified in "FSDB_Name".
The FSDB dumper uses the sliding window scheme to keep the last signal values in the
FSDB file. It drops the old values if the file size exceeds the user-specified limitation.

For fsdbDumpvars, fsdbDumpMDA, fsdbDumpvarsES, fsdbDumpSVA, and
fsdbDumpvarsByFile, you can use the "+fsdbfile+filename.fsdb" option to specify the target
FSDB file to dump. It is similar to using fsdbDumpfile then fsdbDumpvars.
To leverage the memory consumption, the maximum number of opened FSDB
files for dumping in one simulation run should not be more than 32 files.
$fsdbDumpfile( "FSDB_Name" [ ,limit_size] );

call fsdbDumpfile FSDB_Name [limit_size]

fsdbDumpfile FSDB_Name [limit_size]

FSDB_Name

Specify the name of the FSDB file generated by the Novas object files for FSDB dumping.
limit_size

Specify the maximum FSDB file size in megabyte.
The minimum file size of the FSDB file is 10M. If you set the size less than 10M,
it is set to 10M instead.
fsdbDumpfile("novas.fsdb", 32);
/* dumpfile novas.fsdb, limit 32 megabyte */
fsdbDumpvars(0, "design_top");

fsdbAutoSwitchDumpfile
Automatically switch to a new dump file when the working FSDB file hits the specified size
limitation. The unit associated with the fsdbAutoSwitchDumpfile File_Size parameter is a
megabyte.
$fsdbAutoSwitchDumpfile must be used before $fsdbDumpvars as per the
implementation.
$fsdbAutoSwitchDumpfile( File_Size, "FSDB_Name", Number_of_Files
[,"log_filename"] );

call fsdbAutoSwitchDumpfile File_Size FSDB_name Number_of_Files
[log_filename]

fsdbAutoSwitchDumpfile File_Size FSDB_name Number_of_Files [log_filename]

File_Size

The FSDB file size limit in MB.
The minimum file size of the FSDB file is 10MB. If you set the size less than
10MB, it is set to 10MB instead.
FSDB_name

FSDB file generating by the Novas object files for FSDB dumping.
Number_of_Files

The maximum number of FSDB files you want to be created.
If the number is put as 0, the FSDB dumper creates new FSDB files without file
number limitation.
log_filename

This argument is optional. You can specify the filename for the log file.
in the VDHL design. Refer to the syntax section for the correct format for the
simulator command line.
process
fsdbAutoSwitchDumpfile(10, "test.fsdb", 20);
fsdbDumpvars(0, ":system");
wait;

The first FSDB file is named as test_000.fsdb. The second FSDB file test_001.fsdb is
created when the file size of test_000.fsdb reaches near 10MB. The third FSDB file
test_002.fsdb is created when the file size of test_001.fsdb reaches near 10MB, and so
on. The first FSDB file test_000.fsdb is overwritten when the file size of test_019.fsdb
reaches near 10MB. The default test.log file lists the time range of each FSDB file.
process begin
fsdbAutoSwitchDumpfile(10, "test.fsdb", 20, "my.log");
fsdbDumpvars(0, "system");
wait;

The number and the maximum file size of the FSDB file are the same as the previous
example, but the log file is set to my.log.

This FSDB dumping command for example, be used in the HDL code and also through the
command line for interactive simulation control. The command forces the signal values to
be flushed to the FSDB file while the simulation is running. This allows you to check the
current simulation results whenever it is ready instead of waiting for the simulation to end
or the internal buffer to be filled.

The Novas object files for FSDB dumping automatically flushes the value
change data to the FSDB file on disk under the following conditions:

- The Ctrl-C is used to break the simulation.

A novas_dump.log file gets created during simulation to record some essential
simulation/dumping information, such as simulation options used, environment
variable settings, and Novas object directories linked. This log file is needed to
report a dumper related issue effectively.

IUS (15.1 or Later Versions) - Verilog Only
The Novas object file for FSDB dumping supports signal dumping in pure Verilog designs
with IUS. The object file for pure Verilog designs with IUS is called libpli.so and is
located under the <VERDI_HOME>/share/PLI/IUS/${PLATFORM} directory. To link this
object file, set the LD_LIBRARY_PATH environment variable to point to the correct directory
and then the correct file is loaded for FSDB Dumping.
Starting from Verdi-2020.03, IUS versions before 15.10 are not supported.

Dynamic Linking
If the IUS execution files (ncelab and ncsim) being used do not statically link with any
other applications, dynamic linking can be used to link the Novas shared library file
(libpli.so or libpli.sl) for FSDB dumping with IUS for pure Verilog designs. These
files can be found under the <VERDI_HOME>/share/PLI/IUS/${PLATFORM}/ directories.

IUS searches and loads only one libpli.so (libpli.sl) file from the shared library paths. The
system shared library search path must be set before running ncelab, ncsim or ncverilog.
${VERDI_HOME}/share/PLI/IUS/${PLATFORM}/: \

Perform Elaboration and Run Simulation
If you use the ncverilog command to run IUS, you must specify the -access +r
(+ncaccess+r) or +linedebug options to enable read access of the design object.
> ncverilog +ncaccess+r -f run.f

or
> ncverilog +linedebug -f run.f

You must specify +linedebug when running the ncverilog command if you want to
set line breakpoints or run the design step by step using interactive mode in the Verdi
platform.
If you use the ncvlog, ncelab and ncsim trilogy to run the IUS simulation, you must specify
the -access +r option with ncelab or specify the -linedebug option with ncvlog to enable
read access of the design object.
> ncvlog -linedebug -f ncvlog.args
> ncelab -f ncelab.args

or
> ncvlog -f ncvlog.args
> ncelab -access +r -f ncelab.args

Then,
> ncsim -f ncsim.args

You must specify -linedebug with ncvlog to compile the designs if you want to set line
breakpoints or run the design step by step using interactive mode in the Verdi platform.
You can check whether IUS linked with the Novas object file for FSDB dumping
successfully by using the call command at the ncsim prompt (use ncsim top -tcl to
enter ncsim prompt). Specifying the call command without any option lists all the Verilog
FSDB dumping commands that are available in the IUS simulation. For example:
> ncsim -f ncsim.args -tcl

Dynamic Loading
Dynamic loading is another easy way to link the Novas shared library file for FSDB
dumping and other applications with IUS simultaneously. For dynamic loading with IUS,
the Novas shared library file for FSDB dumping is libIUS.so These files can be found
under the <VERDI_HOME>/share/PLI/IUS/${PLATFORM}/ directories.

Set the system shared library search path to include the directory for the Novas object file
for FSDB dumping.
${VERDI_HOME}/share/PLI/IUS/${PLATFORM}/boot: \

Load and Link the Novas Object File
If you use the ncverilog command to run IUS, specify the
+loadpli1=debpli:novas_pli_boot option with ncverilog. debpli as the library file
name of the dynamic loading version of the FSDB dumper. novas_pli_boot is the booting
function of the FSDB dumper. You must also specify the +ncaccess+r or +linedebug
option to enable read access of the design object.
> ncverilog +ncaccess+r \
+loadpli1=debpli:novas_pli_boot -f run.f

or
> ncverilog +linedebug \
+loadpli1=debpli:novas_pli_boot -f run.f

To load the CFC function library, add the additional option -loadcfc
debcfc:novas_cfc_boot as follows:
> ncverilog +ncaccess+r \
+loadpli1=debpli:novas_pli_boot \
-loadcfc debcfc:novas_cfc_boot \
-f run.f

IUS (IUS15.1 and Later Versions) - Verilog, VHDL or Mixed
The Novas object file for FSDB dumping in the ${VERDI_HOME}/share/PLI/IUS/
${PLATFORM} directory is for both a VPI-based and VHPI-based FSDB dumping and
supports signal dumping in pure VHDL or mixed-HDL designs.
There are several files included in the directory.
libpli.so

${VERDI_HOME}/share/PLI/IUS/${ FSDB dumping
PLATFORM}/
task library

libcfc.so

${VERDI_HOME}/share/PLI/IUS/${ C command
PLATFORM}/
library

libfmi.so

${VERDI_HOME}/share/PLI/IUS/${ VHDL procedure
PLATFORM}/
library

novas.vhd

${VERDI_HOME}/share/PLI/IUS/${ VHDL procedure
PLATFORM}/

libsscore_iusXXX
.so

${VERDI_HOME}/share/PLI/lib/${ FSDB dumper
PLATFORM}/
engine library

The libpli.so file provides the FSDB Verilog FSDB dumping commands. The
libfmi.so file provides the FSDB VHDL foreign functions, and the libcfc.so file
provides the FSDB C commands. The novas.vhd file contains the FSDB dumping

commands in VHDL procedure format. The libsscore_iusXXX.so file is the FSDB
dumper engine library.
If you use any of the three previously mentioned programming interfaces as provided by
other vendors or your own, you for example, have to merge and rebuild these shared
libraries. Otherwise, you can link the FSDB dumper with the Dynamic Loading (bootstrap)
method. The detailed steps for merging these files with other vendors are discussed later.

Dynamic Linking
By default, IUS automatically searches for and loads the libpli.so, libfmi.so, and
libcfc.so files according to the LD_LIBRARY_PATH setting. If you do not use any PLI,

CFC or FMI programs from other vendors or your own, you can directly use these files
from the Novas package.
To link the Novas object files for FSDB dumping with IUS, specify the shared library path,
and then compile and include the FSDB dumping commands.

Set the system shared library search path to include the directory of the Novas object file
for FSDB dumping before running ncelab and ncsim.
${VERDI_HOME}/share/PLI/IUS/${PLATFORM}: \

Compile and Include FSDB Dumping Commands
When invoking FSDB dumping commands at the simulator command prompt ("ncsim >")
or in VHDL design is needed, one of the following methods must be used to compile and
include the FSDB dumping commands.
Method 1: Using ncvhdl, ncvlog, ncelab and ncsim:
1. Compile the novas.vhd file into the default design working library. This VHDL file is
found in the <VERDI_HOME>/share/PLI/IUS/${PLATFORM} directory.
> ncvhdl -message \
${VERDI_HOME}/share/PLI/IUS/${PLATFORM}/novas.vhd

The novas.vhd file contains the declarations of the FSDB foreign functions in the pkg
and novas packages.

2. Use the novas package in any VHDL files that call any FSDB foreign functions.
Assume the novas.vhd file is compiled into the default working library. Use the novas
package in the VHDL code as shown in the following example:
library IEEE;
use IEEE.std_logic_1164.all;
library work;
use work.novas.all;

The following example shows how to include the FSDB foreign functions in the VHDL
code.
process
fsdbDumpfile("test.fsdb");
fsdbDumpvars(0, ":");
wait ;

Recompile any VHDL files that were modified. To learn more about the usage and syntax
of the FSDB foreign functions, refer to the FSDB Dumping Commands Used in VHDL
section.
Enable Read Access
To enable read access of the design objects, the -linedebug option must be included with
ncvhdl, ncvlog, or the -access +r option specified with ncelab. For example:
> ncvlog -message -linedebug test.v

or
> ncvhdl -message -linedebug test.vhd

or
> ncelab -message -access +r WORK.TOP:BLK

The -linedebug command line option must be specified with ncvhdl or ncvlog to compile
the design if you want to set line breakpoints or run the design step by step using
interactive mode in the Verdi platform.
Method 2: Using irun:
Use the novas package in any VHDL files that call any FSDB foreign functions. Assume
the novas.vhd file is compiled into the default working library. Use the novas package in
the VHDL code as shown in the following example:
library IEEE;
use IEEE.std_logic_1164.all;
library work;
use work.novas.all;

The following example shows how to include the FSDB foreign functions in the VHDL
code.
process
fsdbDumpfile("test.fsdb");
fsdbDumpvars(0, ":");
wait ;

It is convenient to directly use the FSDB dumper without rebuilding new libraries to merge
with other third party programs. To dynamically load the FSDB dumper with IUS, specify
the shared library path, and then compile and include the FSDB dumping commands.

Set the system shared library search path to include the directory of the dynamic loading
version of the FSDB dumper before running ncelab and ncsim.
${VERDI_HOME}/share/PLI/IUS/${PLATFORM}/boot:\

Compile and Include FSDB Dumping Commands
This is optional. However, if the FSDB dumping commands are invoked at the simulator
prompt in the VHDL design or the simulation is run using interactive mode in the Verdi
platform, the following method must be used to compile and include the FSDB dumping
commands:
Method: Using ncvhdl, ncvlog, ncelab and ncsim:
1. Compile the novas.vhd file into the default design working library. You can find this
VHDL file in the <VERDI_HOME>/share/PLI/IUS/${PLATFORM} directory.
> ncvhdl -message \
${VERDI_HOME}/share/PLI/IUS/${PLATFORM}/novas.vhd

The novas.vhd file contains the declarations of the FSDB foreign functions in the pkg
and novas packages.

2. Use the novas package in any VHDL files that call any FSDB foreign functions.
Assume the novas.vhd file is compiled with the default working library. Use the novas
package in the VHDL code as shown in the following example:
library IEEE;
use IEEE.std_logic_1164.all;
library work;
use work.novas.all;

The following example shows how to include the FSDB foreign functions in the VHDL
code:
process
fsdbDumpfile("test.fsdb");
fsdbDumpvars(0, ":");
wait ;

Recompile any VHDL files that were modified. To learn more about the usage and
syntax of the FSDB foreign functions, refer to the FSDB Dumping Commands Used in
VHDL section.
3. To enable read access of the design objects, the -linedebug option must be included
with ncvhdl, ncvlog, or the -access +r option specified with ncelab. For example:
> ncvlog -message -linedebug test.v

or
> ncvhdl -message -linedebug test.vhd

or
> ncelab -message -access +r WORK.TOP:BLK

This is optional. However, if you want to set line breakpoints or run the design step by
step using interactive mode in the Verdi platform, the -linedebug command line option
must be specified with ncvlog to compile the design.
> ncvlog -message -linedebug test.v

or
> ncvhdl -message -linedebug test.vhd

4. Specify the -loadpli1 debpli:novas_pli_boot option with ncelab. The -access +r
option must also be specified with ncelab to enable read access of the design object.
> ncelab -access +r -loadpli1 debpli:novas_pli_boot \
-VHDLEXPAND WORK.TOP:BLK

From Cadence IUS 5.5 and later versions, the symbols in PLI applications
are not exported by default. This for example, cause a crash if you load
several PLI applications that contain the FSDB writer library. To avoid the
crash, you can add the :export qualifier to each -loadpli option. This
exports the symbols in the PLI applications.
For example:
> ncelab -access +r \
-loadpli1 debpli:novas_pli_boot:export\
-VHDLEXPAND WORK.TOP:BLK

To load the CFC function library with irun, add the additional option -loadcfc

<file(s)>

Calling CFC Functions From the ncsim Prompt
To check whether IUS linked the Novas object file for FSDB dumping successfully, use the
call command at the ncsim prompt. Specifying the call command without any options
lists all CFC commands and Verilog FSDB dumping commands that are available in
ncsim. For example:
ncsim> call
*** Registering Novas CFC commands
Available C function names:
fsdbDumpvarsES
fsdbDumpMDA
fsdbDumpvarsByFile
fsdbSuppress
fsdbDumpon
fsdbDumpoff
fsdbSwitchDumpfile
fsdbDumpfile
fsdbAutoSwitchDumpfile
$fsdbDumpvars
$fsdbDumpMDA
$fsdbDumpSVA
$fsdbSuppress
$fsdbDumpon
$fsdbDumpoff
$fsdbSwitchDumpfile
$fsdbDumpfile
$fsdbAutoSwitchDumpfile
$fsdbDumpFinish
$fsdbDumpflush
$fsdbLog

The FSDB dumping commands can be called at the ncsim prompt to dump the design
directly. In the following example, two FSDB dumping commands are called at the ncsim
prompt to dump the entire design to test.fsdb:
ncsim> call fsdbDumpfile test.fsdb
ncsim> call fsdbDumpvars 0 :

For more usage information about these FSDB commands, refer to the FSDB Dumping
Commands Used in VHDL section.

If you run a pure Verilog design or mixed-HDL design with a Verilog top module
and Novas VHPI/VPI, follow the IUS signals/scopes naming convention for pure
Verilog design to call Novas VHPI/VPI FSDB dumping commands. If you run
a pure VHDL design or mixed-HDL design with VHDL top module and Novas
VHPI/VPI, follow the NC-SIM signals/scopes naming convention for pure VHDL
design to call Novas VHPI/VPI FSDB dumping commands.

Linking FSDB Dumper Library With NC-SystemC Simulator
The following steps use Linux and IUS 15.1 as an example. They apply only
when you specify dumping commands inside the SystemC source code (a .cpp
file).
To link the FSDB Dumper Library with the NC-SystemC simulator, follow these steps:
1. Include the header file fsdb_nc_mix.h.
#include "systemc.h"
#include "fsdb_nc_mix.h"

2. Call dumping functions to dump module instances or signals explicitly.
fsdbDumpSC(0,"my_system");

3. Set the library path.
>setenv LD_LIBRARY_PATH
<VERDI_HOME>/share/PLI/IUS/<PLATFORM>: \

Simulate SystemC Design With ncsc_run
1. Compile your SystemC design with ncsc_run and run the simulation.
>ncsc_run *.cpp *.v *.vhdl -TOP <top module>

To dump signals in your mixed SystemC/HDL design, modify your SystemC code as
follows:
-I<VERDI_HOME>/share/PLI/IUS/<PLATFORM> \
-L<VERDI_HOME>/share/PLI/IUS/<PLATFORM> \
-lfsdbSC

Mixed SystemC/HDL Dumping Limitations
If you do not pass signal names in a member initializer, non-intuitive names such as
signal_1 appear as signal names.

SystemC Dumper for Cadence SCV Transaction
To dump transactions, your SystemC code must be modified with the following steps:
1. Include the header file scv_tr_fsdb.h.
#include "scv.h"
#include "scv_tr_fsdb.h"

Include -I<VERDI_HOME>/share/PLI/IUS/LINUX in the c++ compiler option you
specify to compile your design.
2. Invoke scv_tr_fsdb_init() before opening a file for recording the transactions.
int sc_main (int argc , char *argv[]) {
scv_tr_fsdb_init();
scv_tr_db db("my_db");
scv_tr_db::set_default_db(&db);

}

Then the transaction which records the classes and methods you invoked in your design is
saved in an FSDB file.

Simulation creates a novas_dump.log file. This file records simulation and
dumping information, such as options used, environment variable settings, and
linked Novas object directories. Use this log when you report a dumper-related
issue.

ModelSim (10.6 or Later Versions) - Verilog Only
The Novas object files for FSDB dumping support signal dumping in pure Verilog designs
with ModelSim. Use FSDB dumping commands at the vsim prompt or in Verilog code to
dump signals to FSDB files.
Files for FSDB dumping of pure Verilog designs with ModelSim are in the <VERDI_HOME>/
share/PLI/MODELSIM/${PLATFORM} directory. The FSDB dumper is a shared library
called novas_fli.so. Load it in vsim when you run the ModelSim simulation.
To link the Novas object files for FSDB dumping with ModelSim, specify the shared library
path and then load the FSDB dumper.

Set the shared library search path to include the Novas object files directory for FSDB
dumping.
${VERDI_HOME}/share/PLI/MODELSIM/${PLATFORM}:\

Load the FSDB Dumper
You can load the FSDB dumper novas_fli.so into vsim during simulation in three ways.

Method 1: -pli Option
Use the -pli option with vsim. For example:
> vsim -pli novas_fli.so top

Method 2: veriuser Entry
Set the veriuser entry in the modelsim.ini file. For example:
[vsim]

veriuser=novas_fli.so

Method 3: PLIOBJS Environment Variable
Set the PLIOBJS system environment variable before running vsim. For example:
> setenv PLIOBJS "novas_fli.so"

When linking succeeds, vsim shows a Novas banner indicating that the FSDB dumper
engine is loading. Otherwise, vsim shows a failed-to-load message.
Succeeds:
*Novas* Loading libssocre_mtiXXX.so

Fails:
*Novas* Failed to load FSDB dumper.

Linking With Other Applications
Other vendors often provide applications as standalone shared library files. Use one of the
following methods to load different PLI programs into vsim at the same time.
Method 1: -pli Option
Use the -pli option with vsim. For example:
> vsim -pli novas_fli.so -pli third_party.so top

Method 2: veriuser Entry
Set the veriuser entry in the modelsim.ini file. For example:

[vsim]

veriuser=novas_fli.so third_party.so

Method 3: PLIOBJS Environment Variable
Set the PLIOBJS system environment variable before running vsim. For example:
> setenv PLIOBJS "novas_fli.so third_party.so"

ModelSim (SE 10.6 or Later Versions) - VHDL or Mixed Only
The Novas object files for FSDB dumping support signal dumping in pure VHDL or mixedHDL designs with ModelSim. To dump VHDL and Verilog signals to the FSDB files, you
can use the FSDB dumping commands at the vsim prompt, invoke the FSDB foreign
functions in the VHDL code or invoke the FSDB dumping commands in the Verilog code.
The related files for FSDB dumping of VHDL or mixed-HDL designs with ModelSim are
in the <VERDI_HOME>/share/PLI/MODELSIM/${PLATFORM} directory. The FSDB dumper
is a shared library file called novas_fli.so. You have to load it in vsim when running the
ModelSim simulation.
Limitation: The FSDB dumper for ModelSim cannot automatically record each
value change of variable types. You must use fsdbDumpVariable to repeatedly
dump the current value of a variable.
To link the Novas object files for FSDB dumping with ModelSim, specify the shared
library path, compile and include the FSDB dumping commands, and then load the FSDB
dumper.

Set the system shared library search path to include the directory for the Novas object files
for FSDB dumping.
${VERDI_HOME}/share/PLI/MODELSIM/${PLATFORM}:\

Compile and Include Novas FSDB Dumping Commands
Compile Novas FSDB Dumping Commands to Design Library
Compile the VHDL file novas.vhd into the default design working library or the novas
design library. This VHDL file is found in the <VERDI_HOME>/share/PLI/MODELSIM/
${PLATFORM} directory.
For example, compile novas.vhd into the specific design library:
> setenv MTI_VCO_MODE 32 // Enable 32-bit simulation

or
> setenv MTI_VCO_MODE 64 // Enable 64-bit simulation
> vlib novas
> vcom -work novas \
${VERDI_HOME}/share/PLI/MODELSIM/${PLATFORM}/novas.vhd

Or, compile novas.vhd into the default working design library:
> vcom ${VERDI_HOME}/share/PLI/MODELSIM/${PLATFORM}/novas.vhd

The novas.vhd file contains the declarations of the FSDB foreign functions in the pkg
package and the definition of the novas entity.
Include Novas FSDB Dumping Commands in Design Files
Alternatively, use the pkg package in any VHDL design files that include FSDB foreign
functions. For example, if the novas.vhd is compiled into the novas library:
library IEEE;
use IEEE.std_logic_1164.all;
library novas;
use novas.pkg.all;

Otherwise, if the novas.vhd is compiled into the default working library:
library IEEE;
use IEEE.std_logic_1164.all;
library work;
use work.pkg.all;

The following example shows how to invoke the FSDB foreign functions in the VHDL code.
process
fsdbDumpfile("test.fsdb");
fsdbDumpvars(0, "system");
wait ;

Recompile all VHDL files you modified.
To learn more about the usage and syntax of the FSDB foreign functions, you can refer to
the FSDB Dumping Commands Used in VHDL section.

Loading the FSDB dumper is optional. However, if FSDB commands are invoked at the
vsim prompt, or if the ModelSim simulation is run using interactive mode in the Verdi
platform, the novas entity must be loaded when starting the ModelSim simulation with
vsim. For example, assume novas.vhd is compiled into the novas library:
> vsim novas.novas top

Then the FSDB commands can be invoked at the vsim prompt. For example:
VSIM 1> fsdbDumpfile test.fsdb (Creates the FSDB file)
VSIM 2> fsdbDumpvars 0 system (Dump all signals from the system region)

ModelSim Simulator
The Novas object files for FSDB dumping support signal dumping in mixed SystemC/
HDL designs with ModelSim. To dump signals to FSDB files, you can either use FSDB
commands at the vsim prompt and include FSDB foreign functions in VHDL code, or
include FSDB dumping commands in Verilog code. Files for FSDB dumping of mixed
SystemC/HDL designs with ModelSim are in the <VERDI_HOME>/share/PLI/MODELSIM/
${PLATFORM} directory. The FSDB dumper is a shared library called novas_fli.so. Load
it in vsim when you run the ModelSim simulation.

Linking the Novas Library With the ModelSim Simulator
The following steps use Linux and ModelSim 10.6 as examples.
1. Set the shared library search path to include the Novas object files directory for FSDB
dumping.
>setenv LD_LIBRARY_PATH
<VERDI_HOME>/share/PLI/MODELSIM/${PLATFORM}:

Compile Design
2. Create the library.
>vlib novas

3. Do common elaboration on Verilog design.
>vlog +define+NEW_PLI=1 -sv *.v

4. Compile the *.cpp codes.
>sccom -g *.cpp
Link the *.o files to be "systemc.so".
>sccom -link

5. Load the Novas object files for FSDB dumping while running the simulation:
>vsim -pli \
<VERDI_HOME>/share/PLI/MODELSIM/<PLATFORM>/novas_fli.so \
sc_main -c -do "fsdbDumpfile sc.fsdb; fsdbDumpSC 0; run 1000 ns; exit"

Using the Automatic SystemC Dumper to Dump SystemC Designs
The libfsdbSC.a library provides the dumping functions that let you create an FSDB file
containing the values of signals as they change during the simulation. Access to the
dumping functions are provided in the header file named fsdb_trace_file.h.
The following functions are provided:
Functions:
* fsdbDumpfile
* fsdbDumpAll
* fsdbDumpvars
* fsdbDumpAllTrans
* fsdbDumpTrans
* fsdbDumpon
* fsdbDumpoff
* fsdbEnableDumpVariable
* fsdbDumpFinish
* fsdbSwitchDumpfile
* fsdbAutoSwitchDumpfile
To dump the signals in your SystemC design, you must modify your SystemC code with
the following steps:
1. Include the header file fsdb_trace_file.h.
#include "systemc.h"
#include "fsdb_trace_file.h"

2. Invoke the dumping functions to dump module instances or signals explicitly.
fsdbDumpvars(5,top);

3. Link the libnffw.a and libfsdbSC.a libraries.
You can find libnffw.a in the <VERDI_HOME>/share/FsdbWriter/$PLATFORM
subdirectory.

SystemC Dumping Limitations
1. This library only supports pure SystemC designs.
2. Non-intuitive names, such as, signal_0, are shown as signal names if no signal names
declared in sc_main function have been passed. For example:
int sc_main(int argc, int argv[]){
sc_signal<int> var1;
sc_signal<int> var2("var2");

The name of var1 is "signal_0", and the name of var2 is "var2".

Using the SystemC Dumper to Dump SystemC Designs
The libfsdbSC.a library provides the dumping class and functions that let you
create an FSDB file containing the values of signals as they change during the simulation.
Access to the dumping class and functions are provided in the signal header file named
fsdb_trace_file.h.

The following class and functions are provided:
Class
* fsdb_trace_file
Functions
* fsdbDumpvars
* fsdbDumpOn
* fsdbDumpOff
* fsdb_trace
To dump the signals in your SystemC design, you must modify your SystemC code with
the following steps:
1. Include the header file fsdb_trace_file.h.
#include "systemc.h"
#include " fsdb_trace_file.h "

2. Create the trace file at the top level after all modules and signals have been
instantiated.
fsdb_trace_file *my_trace_file;
my_trace_file = new fsdb_trace_file("dump.fsdb");

3. Invoke the dumping functions to dump module instances or signals explicitly.
fsdbDumpvars(my_trace_file)

4. Link the libnffw.a and libfsdbSC.a libraries.
You can find libnffw.a in the <VERDI_HOME>/share/FsdbWriter/$PLATFORM
subdirectory.

Switch Dumping With Simulator Restore
The FSDB dumper switches the dump file when the simulator executes the restore
command. When the simulator executes restore (or restart) for the first time, FSDB
dumping redirects to a new file named <original_FSDB_name>.restore.FSDB. The
dumper saves and closes the original dump files. If you dump multiple FSDB files, the
dumper redirects each one to a different restore file. If the simulator executes restore
several times, each run overwrites the <original_FSDB_name>.restore.FSDB files.
* ModelSim Simulator
* Cadence IUS Simulator
* Miscellaneous Rules

ModelSim Simulator

new FSDB file named as <original_FSDB_name>.restore.FSDB. If multiple FSDB files
are being dumped, each of them is redirected to a different restore FSDB file.

* restore

Appendix A: Switch Dumping With Simulator Restore
Cadence IUS Simulator

title: 3 top.type_dut.logicInst
text:
vsim> run 20ns
vsim> restore saveData

When the simulation is restored to the previously saved time point, the save.fsdb file is
saved and closed, and the new file save.restore.fsdb is created.
vsim> run 30ns
vsim> quit

title: 3 top.type_dut.logicInst
text:
The following FSDB files and associated time ranges are the result:
* save.fsdb: 0ns ~ 30ns
* save.restore.fsdb: 10ns ~ 40ns

Cadence IUS Simulator
When the restart command is executed for the first time, the dumping is redirected to a
new FSDB file named as <original_FSDB_name>.restore.FSDB. If multiple FSDB files
are being dumped, each of them is redirected to a different restore FSDB file.
Simulator Commands
* save
* restart
Refer to the IUS user's manual for details of the save and restart commands.
ncsim> call fsdbDumpvars +fsdbfile+save.fsdb

Create the save.fsdb FSDB file.
ncsim> run 20ns
ncsim> save saveData

Save a copy of the simulation data at the time for later restore.
ncsim> run 20ns
ncsim> restart saveData

When the simulation is restored to the previously saved time point, the save.fsdb file is
saved and closed, and the new file save.restore.fsdb is created.
ncsim> run 10ns
ncsim> exit

Appendix A: Switch Dumping With Simulator Restore
Miscellaneous Rules

The following FSDB files and associated time ranges are the result:
* save.fsdb: 0ns ~ 40ns
* save.restore.fsdb: 20ns ~ 30ns

Miscellaneous Rules
The miscellaneous rules apply in the following situations:
* When the restore command is executed several times.
* When the FSDB name happens to have a restore.fsdb extension.
* When restoring in a new simulation session.

restore Command Executed Multiple Times
When the restore command is executed several times, the
<original_FSDB_name>.restore.FSDB files are overridden.
Example in IUS
ncsim> call fsdbDumpvars +fsdbfile+save.fsdb

Create the save.fsdb FSDB file.
ncsim> run 20ns
ncsim> save saveData

Save a copy of the simulation data at the time for later restore.
ncsim> run 20ns
ncsim> restart saveData

When the simulation is restored to the previously saved time point, the save.fsdb file is
saved and closed, and the new file save.restore.fsdb is created.
ncsim> run 10ns
ncsim> restart saveData

When the simulation is restored to the previously saved time point, the
save.restore.fsdb file is re-created and this file overwrites the previous one.
ncsim> run 40ns
ncsim> exit

Appendix A: Switch Dumping With Simulator Restore
Miscellaneous Rules

FSDB File With restore.fsdb Extension
When the FSDB name happens to have a restore.fsdb extension, then the restore
FSDB file name is the same.

Restore in a New Simulation Session
For IUS and Modelsim, restoring in a new simulation session is an independent dumper
process.
Example in IUS
* The first simulation session:
ncsim> call fsdbDumpvars +fsdbfile+save.fsdb

The save.fsdb file is created.
ncsim>
ncsim>
ncsim>
ncsim>

run 20ns
save saveData
run 20ns
restart saveData

The save.restore.fsdb file is created.
ncsim> run 10ns
ncsim> exit

* The second simulation session:
ncsim> restart saveData
ncsim> call fsdbDumpvars +fsdbfile+save.fsdb

The save.fsdb file is created.

Preface
This book is designed to help you to become proficient in the nAnalyzer module, an addon to the Verdi platform. You should already be familiar with the Verdi platform before
beginning this book. If you do not feel comfortable with basic Verdi operations, review the
Verdi User Guide and Tutorial document first.
This book focuses on the most commonly used commands without going into detail on
everything. For detailed descriptions of individual commands, refer to the appropriate
chapter of the Verdi and Siloti Command Reference Manual.
The manual should be read from beginning to end, although you may skip any sections
with which you are already familiar.

Audience
The audience for this manual includes engineers who are familiar with languages and
tools used in design and verification and are frequently required to do further analysis of
clock and reset trees, timing issues and signal switching activity.
This document assumes that you have a basic knowledge of the platform on which your
version of the Verdi platform runs: UNIX or Linux and that you are knowledgeable in
Verilog or VHDL, simulation software, and digital logic design.

Customer Support

Introduction
Verdi helps engineers find, isolate, and fix sim bugs fast.
Engineers also inspect and debug design implementation issues.
These tasks differ from pure functional debug.
Many analysis tasks need sign-off before a design is done.

These tasks include clock/reset tree and clock domain analysis.

timing

They also include timing debug and signal activity review.
The nAnalyzer module supports these tasks.
Its features appear as menu items on Verdi tools.
Some menu items open extra windows.
Verdi and nAnalyzer help teams work faster and cut costs.
They also help you get chips to market sooner.
This section describes the following topics:
* Technology
* Before You Begin

parasitics on timing becomes critical.

Technology
The nAnalyzer module provides support in the following implementation related areas.

Timing Analysis Debug
As die size continues to decrease and speed continues to increase, the effects of
parasitics on timing becomes critical. The ability to view and understand the timing is

Chapter 1: Introduction
Before You Begin

timing

important. The nAnalyzer module provides the following functionality in the area of timing
analysis debug:
SDF

Format

Standard

* Load Standard Delay Format (SDF) files and annotate the delay information onto
nSchema.

* Load timing results from standard timing tools (e.g. Synopsys' PrimeTime), view a list
of critical paths, and display a flat schematic view for the critical paths.
* Perform simple delay analysis (e.g. longest/shortest path between points).

Clock/Reset Tree Analysis

* Create a schematic view displaying the clock/reset tree and then annotate timing for
skew analysis.

skew

During the design process, you'll want to investigate the clock and reset trees to confirm
proper balancing. The nAnalyzer module provides the following functionality in the area of
clock/reset tree analysis:

* Analyze the different clock domains in your design.
* Check clock domains for proper synchronization and locate crossing paths.

Switching Analysis
Low power needs and tight schedules make late power analysis hard.

signal

Switching analysis lets you study signal activity early.
With design data and an FSDB file, the nAnalyzermodule can:

* Determine which nets have the most transitions over a specified time range (switching
activity).

peak

* Identify the times with the most transitions (peak activity).

4. All of the tutorial data resides in the $VERDI_HOME/demo directory. Make a copy of
these demo files in your working directory:
% cp -r $VERDI_HOME/demo <working_dir>

Timing Analysis Debug
Debug timing violations and analyze SDF delay paths using the Verdi nAnalyzer module to
visualize critical paths, slack times, and cell delays on gate-level designs.
Key workflows include loading and annotating SDF data on nSchema, calculating longest/
shortest paths between two points, debugging PrimeTime STA results, comparing timing
reports with SDF, and attaching clock domain information. Requires a gate-level netlist
with an SDF file or a timing analysis report. Operates through the Verdi GUI (nSchema,
nWave).
This section describes the following topics:
* Overview
* Use Models
* Tutorials

Overview
SDF

Format

Standard

timing

In the area of timing analysis debug, nAnalyzer supports two primary functions: viewing
and analyzing Standard Delay Format (SDF) data in the context of the design and
debugging timing analysis results.

Standard Delay Format (SDF)
Depending on a company's design flow one sign-off criteria can be a successful gate-level
timing simulation with SDF enabled. The chip's timing must be accurate to meet setup
and hold times of registers and the timing conditions of memories. Trying to visualize and
understand the SDF is tedious and time consuming.
FSDB

The two main requirements for analyzing SDF data are a gate-level design with a
corresponding SDF file. You may also have an FSDB file that was generated with SDF

Overview

enabled. After loading this information in the Verdi platform, you have several options for
using the nAnalyzer module to view and analyze SDF:

* View the delay paths (PATHCONSTRAINT in the SDF) in the nSchema frame.

cell

interconnect

* Annotate the interconnect and cell delay (INTERCONNECT and IOPATH in the SDF)
on nSchema with the following options:
Select the preferred corner case (if multiple exist in the SDF).
Modify the precision.
Check the cell delay.

shortest

longest

* Calculate the longest/shortest paths between two points and display the results
textually or schematically.
nWave

* View the SDF annotated FSDB results in nWave.
The Verdi platform currently supports version 3.0 as the primary supported
version. Older versions are also supported to allow existing SDF files to be
used without any modification.
A warning message will be displayed to let you know which version is
parsed if the SDF file is not in version 3.0 format. This is because some
statements (even though they are not needed), which are supported in the
old version but not in version 3.0, may be missed.

Timing Analysis Results

timing

There is a wide range of timing analysis tools each with their own timing report format. The
timing analysis results are typically in text format and difficult to understand and visualize.

The two main requirements for debugging timing analysis results is a gate-level design
with a corresponding timing analysis results file. The various report formats can be
converted with a utility to an XML format (for example, pt2Xml.pl for PrimeTime). The
results can then be loaded into the Verdi platform. After loading the design and timing
analysis report in the Verdi platform, you have several options for using nAnalyzer to
debug the timing analysis results:
time

slack

* Sort and filter the timing results by start point, slack time or other specified options.
* Select any start/end point combination and display the results textually or
schematically.
SDF

* Compare the timing analysis results with an equivalent SDF.

Utilities (Perl script) to convert timing analysis results are provided for the following tools:

* PrimeTime: pt2Xml.pl
Although a utility is provided for PrimeTime, the PrimeTime timing analysis
report format can be directly read by the Verdi platform.
These timing report formats are available but are still in beta:

Compiler

Magma

Pearl

* Pearl: pearl.pl
* RTL Compiler: RTLC2Xml.pl
* Silicon Ensemble: SE2Xml.pl
Perl

The syntax for any of the provided Perl scripts is as follows:
perl_script -o <xml_filename> <report_filename>

Import

After the timing analysis results are converted, you can load the results into the Verdi
platform by choosing the File -> Import Path Data File command from the main window.
In the Import Timing Report form, you would select the XML file name and click OK.

This opens the Timing Report form as follows:

start point or start/end clock point. After selecting a result, the related report details are
summarized in the Information box. Refer to the Debug PrimeTime Results tutorial for
details on analyzing and viewing the loaded results.

Clock/Reset Tree Analysis
This section describes the following topics:
* Overview
* Clock Domain Analysis Background
* Tutorials

Overview

In clock/reset tree analysis, nAnalyzer supports two primary functions.
It lets you view clock/reset trees in the schematic view.

It also lets you analyze the clock domains in the design.

Clock/Reset Tree
Because the complexity of the clock/reset tree is increasing in VLSI designs, implementing
an ideal clock/reset tree has become an important task. In most designs, the clock and
reset trees have heavy fan-out loads. If the loads are not balanced among each branch,
clock/reset skew may occur.
The main requirement for analyzing clock or reset trees is a gate-level design. You can
also use an RTL design.
SDF

You may also have a SDF file.
After loading this information in the Verdi platform, you have several options to view clock/
reset trees with the nAnalyzer module:
view

register

compressed

* Extract the clock/reset tree and display the results in a compressed register view in the
nSchema frame.
polarity

* Use the compressed register views to understand the polarity of the clock/reset tree.
* Expand the compressed register symbol to view the flip-flops or latches connected to
the net.

* Highlight the clock/reset trees for easier viewing across schematic views.
* Analyze the clock/reset skew between branches if you have SDF information.

Clock Domain Analysis
A complex chip design may consist of several clock domains and analyzing the different
domains is critical. You need to understand how many clock domains exist, how many
gates are connected to each domain and determine if any paths cross clock domains.
The main requirement for analyzing clock domains is a gate-level design.
SDC

Constraint

You may also have a Synopsys Design Constraint (SDC) file.
After loading this information in the Verdi platform, you have several options to understand
your clock domains with nAnalyzer:

can be used if you have one.

* Extract the clock domains and determine whether the domains are resolved or not. See
the Clock Domain Analysis Background section for more details.
* Analyze the clock domains for crossing paths and indicate whether a synchronizer is
included or not.
* Display a selected clock domain or crossing path result textually or schematically.
* Highlight the clock domains or crossing paths for easier viewing across schematic

* Identify the clock source for a selected flip-flop or latch.

Terminology
Clock Signal
signal

A clock signal is a signal directly connected to the clock pin of a storage element in the
design. The storage element could be flip-flop, latch or other memory storage element.

Internal Clock Source
input

primary

The internal clock source is the signal closest to the primary input port driving the clock
signals by passing through design hierarchy and the optional logic. The type of logic
passed through is variable. In general, the logic could be a buffer, inverter, reduced buffer
or inverter after constant value propagation, and so on.

Clock Domain

A clock domain consists of groups of storage elements. Under an internal clock source,
there might be two clock domains. One is triggered by the positive edge of the internal
clock source. The other is triggered by the negative edge of the internal clock source. All
the flip-flops, latches or other storage elements in a clock domain are triggered by the
same edge of the internal clock source.

Clock Source Tree
node

The clock source tree is a tree structure. The tree node is an internal clock source. If a
clock source is derived from another internal clock source by passing through some logic,
it is child node of the internal clock source that drives it in the tree.
There are two ways for an internal clock source to be derived from its parent.
logic

combinational

If the internal clock source is derived from its parent by passing through combinational
logic, the derived type relative to its parent is Level0. This typically means it is a gated
clock as demonstrated in the following figure.

Figure 25

Parent Clock Source and Child Clock Source with Level0

In this figure, there are two internal clock sources, CLKi with clock domain Domain_i and
CLKj with clock domain Domain_j. Comb represents combinational logic other than a
buffer or inverter. The internal clock source CLKj is generated by CLKi by passing through
combinational logic. So, internal clock source CLKj is the child of internal clock source
CLKi in the clock source tree. A Level0 type is used to indicate the derived type of the
internal clock source CLKj relative to its parent.
shift

phase

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
In addition to the derived type, another property is the phase shift of the internal clock
source relative to its parent. For a Level0 type child internal clock source, the phase
difference to the parent internal clock source should be extracted. In the following figure,
clock source CLK1 has T/2 phase shift compared to parent internal clock source CLK.

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Figure 26

Phase Shift between Clock Sources

generated

If the internal clock source is generated from the combinational output of some flip-flops,
which are triggered by the parent internal clock source, the derived type relative to its
parent is LevelN. This typically means it is a generated clock, as demonstrated in the
following figure.
Figure 27

Parent Clock Source and Child Clock Source with LevelN

In this figure, there are three internal clock sources, CLKi with clock domain Domain_i,
rising edge triggered, and CLKi with clock domain Domain_j, falling edge triggered. The
internal clock source CLKk is generated by combinational logic whose inputs are the
output of flip-flops in Domain_i or Domain_j. The internal clock source CLKi does not pass
into the combinational logic to generate the clock source CLKk directly. Thus in the clock
source tree, clock source CLKk is child of clock source CLKi and a LevelN type is used to
indicate the derived type of the internal clock source CLKk relative to its parent.

For LevelN derived types, the phase shift of the internal clock source relative to its parent
cannot be extracted automatically.

Clock Source

un-resolved

resolved

The root of the clock source tree is the clock source. A resolved clock source can be a
primary input, a user specified clock source or the output of a register. Other sources
such as a floating wire or the output of combinational logic are unresolved clock sources.
If more than one clock source drives an internal clock source, it is treated as multiple
resolved. Multiple resolved internal clock sources are the root of a clock source tree.
The following shows an example for the definition of clock sources. Assume the signal
system.clock is the specified clock source.
Figure 28

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
The clock domains are extracted as follows.

Figure 29

Extracted Clocks Domains for the Example

The signal system.clock is specified as a clock source, so it is a root of the clock source
tree. The flip-flops (FFs) under this domain have been marked as domain 1.f and 1.r
where `f' represents FFs driven by the falling edge and `r' means rising edge.
A derived clock source, system.i_cpu.i_CCU.C1 resides under the root source
system.clock. system.i_cpu.i_CCU.C1 was generated from a FF output so the domains
under this source are identified as 1.1, which represents the sub domains belonging to the
root domain 1.

Extract Clock Source Tree

The clock analyzer is used as the engine to extract the clock source tree. There are two
primary steps in the engine:

* Extract clock domains with internal clock source.
* Build the clock source tree based on the clock domain and extracted internal clock
source.

Constant Value Propagation
Before any steps, the design can be reduced using constant value propagation.
Figure 30

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
In this figure, if scan_enable is specified as 0, the MUX is reduced to a buffer (or inverter)
with only one input CLK. If scan_enable is specified as 1, the MUX is reduced to a buffer
with only one input scan_clk.

Extract Clock Domain
The engine collects all flip-flops (and latches) and find their clock signal. All the flip-flops
(and latches) from the same clock signal are merged into a group. Then the engine traces
backward to find the internal clock source from the clock signals.

After the engine finds the internal clock source, all groups of flip-flops with the same
internal clock source are merged into at most two clock domains under the internal clock
source. One domain is triggered by the positive edge of the extracted internal clock
source. The other domain is triggered by the negative edge of the extracted internal clock
source.
When finding the internal clock source of the flip-flop (and latches) groups, there are some
options to guide the engine to pass through certain types of logic.

Pass Through Logic
When finding the internal clock source of groups of flip-flops (and latches), some logic can
be passed through just like a wire connection.
* Pass through assignment.
* Pass through buffer.
* Pass through reduced buffer. Here reduced means that the logic is reduced by
constant value setting.
* Pass through inverters.
* Pass through a specific gated clock cell. Here the specific gated clock cell means a
library cell which has an input clock pin and output clock pin. The cell is designed to be
used specifically as the gated cell for gated clocks to reduce the power consumption
and reduce timing problems.
* Pass through cell with one input port and one output port.
* Pass through cell with one input port after specifying non-concerned signal.

Build Clock Source Tree

After extracting the clock domain, the engine will use the results to build the clock source
tree, to find the clock sources and construct the parent-child relationship of all internal
clock sources under the same clock source.

For each internal clock source signal, the engine will trace its fan in cone. When tracing, it
will stop at:
* primary inputs,
* floating wires or output ports of unknown logic,
* flip-flop outputs,
* and specified clock sources.

In the path to the fan in cone, there may be some internal clock sources extracted during
the first step. The engine will construct the parent-child relationship according to the
derived type and extract the phase shift between them.
After the root of the clock source tree is found, the clock source is resolved if the clock
source is a:
input

primary

* primary input,
* flip-flop output,

* or specified clock source.
The clock source is unresolved if it is a:
* floating wire
* or output port of complex (or unknown) logic.
The clock source is multiple resolved if it is driven by more than one clock source.

Specify Clock Source
When building the clock source tree, you can specify a clock source to guide the engine.
It is not a requirement but it may help the engine to determine the real clock source when
more than one input is encountered for a cell.
The primary port or any signal in the design can be specified as a clock source with full
hierarchy name. The specified clock source will be a root of a clock source tree. This
allows you to treat some special clock sources different than others under the same root.

Mix-Clock Domain Crossing-Path
A mix-clock domain path crosses from the start point of one clock domain to the end point
of another clock domain.
The following two figures show two different mix-clock domain paths.

Figure 31

Mix-Clock Domain Path

Figure 32

Mix-clock Domain Path 2

crossing

Here the clock domain is a general concept. You may have different interests in different
applications. For example, if you are concerned with a timing problem, in the above clock
source tree analysis, you can find that the clock source in the same clock source tree
may have fixed frequency and phase relationship. Based on this, the timing in the clock
domains with clock sources in the same clock source tree can be analyzed accurately.
Thus, you can focus on the crossing path between different clock domains with clock
sources in different clock source trees.

In extracting mix-clock domain paths, generally, from domain and to domain pairs should
be specified to be applied to the extraction. Both the from domain and to domain could be
a root of the tree, an internal clock source in the tree or a clock domain in the tree.

No matter how the from domain and to domain is specified, after extraction, the crossing
path is listed under the from and to domain pairs with detailed path information from the
start flip-flop to the end flip-flop. The specifying of the root of the tree and internal clock
source will be expanded as all the clock domains under the specified node.

Appendix A: Synchronizer Template
This appendix introduces the synchronizer template used for the following purposes:
* To verify whether mixed clock domain paths are synchronized correctly.
* To find out which paths satisfy some user-specified rules.
* To report violations when a path violates some user-specified rules.
In real designs, there are many kinds of synchronizers that can be used to synchronize
the data propagation between different clock domains. Some synchronizers are simple
and some are very complex. The template is a set of constraints. It does not use dynamic
values such as stimuli of design and simulation results.
This section describes the following topics:
* Elements in Synchronizer Template
* Template Types
* Default Template

Elements in Synchronizer Template
A synchronizer template may contain the following major elements.

StartPoint
The start point is the output of sequential logic such as a flop or latch or primary input.

EndPoint
The end point is the input of sequential logic such as a flop or latch or primary output.

Template Types

CrossPath
The cross path connects a StartPoint and an EndPoint if the StartPoint and EndPoint
belong to different clock domains. Generally, it can be achieved by checking mixed clock
domain paths in the design.

FromDomain
A FromDomain can be any clock domain or level-sensitive (latch) clock domain in the
design. It must be specified by domain name.

ToDomain
A ToDomain can be any clock domain or level-sensitive (latch) clock domain in the design.
It must be specified by domain name.

Template
The template is a set of user-specified constraints for proving. The proving action is
applied to the CrossPath.

Template Types
For single bit data propagating between asynchronous clock domains, the synchronizer is
used to reduce the probability for the ToDomain to sample a meta-stability value. In such
cases, the synchronizer could be simple.
For bus data propagating between asynchronous clock domains, the synchronizer is
not only used to resolve the meta-stability issue, but also the synchronization between
different bits if more than one bit of the bus changes value at the same clock edge. In such
cases, the communication protocol should be introduced into the synchronizer; so the
synchronizer will become very complex.
If the data is propagating from a fast clock domain to slower clock domain, the
synchronizer may be used to avoid missing data in the ToDomain. In such cases, the

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
uld be introduced into the synchronizer; so the
synchronizer will become very complex.
If the data is propagating from a fast clock domain to slower clock domain, the
synchronizer may be used to avoid missing data in the ToDomain. In such cases, the
communication protocol should be introduced into the synchronizer and it will become very
complex.
Here we can only prove the simple synchronizer using the template. The constraints are
used to verify the simple synchronizer. We extended the use of constraints by design
hierarchy. If the synchronizer (simple or complex) is described in a module (cell), we can
check whether the crossing path passes through the synchronizer module (cell) or not.

Template Types

There are two types of templates. One is a set of constraints specifying the detailed cells
in the crossing path, which is called a flatten synchronizer template. The other is the
synchronizer module.

Synchronizer Module Template
It is a good coding practice to enclose a protocol-based synchronizer into an isolated
module considering:
* Code reuse.
* Design verification and debug.
If the protocol to synchronize data between different clock domains is written in an isolated
module, you can check whether the crossing path passes through the module or not. The
only thing to be customized is the synchronizer module names.

Flatten Synchronizer Template
The main purpose for this template is to reduce the meta-stability issue. So the primary
concern is the flip-flop in the path. Together with the StartPoint and EndPoint, the path is
divided into several segments as shown in the following figure.
Figure 57

Synchronizer Template

In the above figure, FF indicates a flip-flop or latch and Seg1, Seg2, Seg n+1 are the
segments between two FF and they can only be combinational logic cells.
The constraints specify the following:
* The number of synchronizer FF (flip-flop or latch).
* The combinational cell types (or cell names) in the segments.

Default Template

In addition to customizing the above constraints, the following constraints should also be
satisfied:
* All the clock ports of the FF in the synchronizer section should be connected to the
clock signal of the ToDomain.
* The fan out of all FF in the synchronizer section should not exceed one.

Default Template
The following default templates are provided.

Template sync_1 Type A & B
Figure 58

Template sync_1

In this template, the following constraints should be followed:
* At least one synchronizer FF (flip-flop or latch) between the asynchronous clock
domains.
* The clock port of the synchronizer FF Sync1 should be connected to the clock signal of
the ToDomain.
* Type A: In Seg1, there can be zero or any number of combinational logic cells.
* Type B: In Seg1, only a buffer/inverter/assignment is allowed.
* Type A: In Seg2, only a buffer/inverter/assignment is allowed.
* Type B: In Seg2, there can be zero or any number of combinational logic cells.

Default Template

Template sync_2 Type A & B
Figure 59

Template sync_2

In this template, the following constraints should be followed:
* At least two synchronizer FF's (flip-flop or latch) between the asynchronous clock
domains.
* The clock port of the synchronizer FF Sync1 should be connected to the clock signal of
the ToDomain.
* The fan out of Sync1 in the synchronizer section should not exceed one.
* Type A: In Seg1, there can be zero or any number of combinational logic cells.
* Type B: In Seg1, only a buffer/inverter/assignment is allowed.
* In Seg2, only a buffer/inverter/assignment is allowed.
* In Seg3, there can be zero or any number of combinational logic cells.

Default Template

Mux (D-Mux) Synchronizer
Figure 60

D-Mux Synchronizer

In this template, the following constraints should be followed:
* The selected input of MUX comes from the To domain, and is synchronized by two flipflops (control path synchronizer). See Rule 1 as an example.
* One of the MUX inputs comes from the To domain via the holding loop. See Rule 2 as
an example.
* The MUX inputs are From domain, To domain or user-specified static signals. See Rule
3 as an example.
* The logic between the MUX synchronizer and the To flop is driven by the To domain or
static signals. See Rule 4 as an example.

Default Template

Template sync_module
Figure 61

Template sync_module

In this template, the module name should be configured before it is used for synchronizer
proving. The module name may be changed according to the design. The only constraint
is that the crossing path should pass through the specified synchronizer module.
Limitation: In the synchronizer module, there must be synchronizer flip-flop or
latch on the crossing path. Otherwise, the crossing path cannot be proved to be
synchronized even though it is passing through the synchronizer module.

Preface
This book is designed to allow you to quickly become proficient in the nECO module, an
add-on to the Verdi platform. You should already be familiar with the Verdi platform (in
particular nSchema) before beginning this book. If you do not feel comfortable with basic
Verdi operations, review the Verdi User Guide and Tutorial document first.
This book focuses on the most commonly used commands without going into detail on
everything. For detailed descriptions of individual commands, refer to the appropriate
chapter of the Verdi and Siloti Command Reference Manual.
The manual should be read from beginning to end, although you may skip any sections
which you are already familiar.

Audience
The audience for this manual includes engineers who are familiar with languages and
tools used in design and verification and are frequently required to complete Engineering
Change Orders (ECOs) on gate-level netlists.
This document assumes that you have a basic knowledge of the platform on which your
version of the Verdi platform runs: UNIX or Linux and that you are knowledgeable in
Verilog or VHDL, simulation software, and digital logic design.

Customer Support
Customer support is available through SolvNetPlus.

Accessing SolvNetPlus
The SolvNetPlus site includes a knowledge base of technical articles and answers to
frequently asked questions about Synopsys tools. The SolvNetPlus site also gives you
access to a wide range of Synopsys online services including software downloads,
documentation, and technical support.
To access the SolvNetPlus site, go to the following address:
