Support for Boundary MUX Cells in Temporal Flow View
Temporal Flow View also supports tracing power boundary MUX cells. The usage of
instrument Boundary Cell (BC) type is similar to ISO/SPA/SRSN instrument cell types.
The instrument cell is dependent on the XML file. The instrument cell color is same as the
power domain color; the cell shape is illustrated in the following figure:
Figure 135

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Power Corruption Model in Temporal Flow View
If the value of power corrupted cell is random, it's value is obtained from the FSDB file
directly. The automatic tracing feature supported by Temporal Flow Viewallows you to
trace this value for power net when the power is corrupted. You can use the Trace This
Value right-click option to trace the corrupted power signal's value instead of using the
Trace Active X option.
The Trace Active X right-click option is disabled in power-aware Temporal Flow
View if the signal value is not X.

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
When tracing the fanout signal for which the power supply set is corrupted, the value is
obtained from the FSDB file directly, and trace is performed to the power supply set to
detect the root cause of power corruption.
For example, in the following figure, the power of the cell is corrupt.
Figure 136

Corrupted Power Cell

When the Trace This Value right-click option is used for the A_reg signal, the automatic
tracing functionality traces to the corrupted power supply set to debug the root cause of
power corruption. In this case, the root cause of power corruption is the power switch
which changes from 1 -> 0, as illustrated in the following figure:
Figure 137

Tracing Corrupted Power Supply Set

In some scenarios, even though the power model is corrupted, the output may
not be X due to which the Trace Active X option is not enabled. In such cases,
you can use the Trace This Value option instead of Trace Active X.

Limitations
The following limitations apply to this feature for Temporal Flow View:
* The following UPF types are only supported:
Power Port
Power Net
Power Logic Net
i. ack_port of power switch
ii. control_port of power switch
iii. isolation_signal of isolation
iv. save_signal/restore_signal of retention
Power Supply
Power Switch
ISO
SRSN
SPA
Retention (edge trigger only)
* The connect_logic_net power logic net and Level Shift UPF types are not supported.
* Single-pin, zero-pin, and level sensitive retention type cells are not supported.

Directly Importing Liberty Files and Displaying Power Cell Information

* When tracing is performed in Temporal Flow View with partially dumping the FSDB file,
If there is no dumping on certain signals, the value is calculated by the register
signal. If it cannot be calculated or the signal is a sync signal, such as, register
signal, then "NF" is shown in the Value pane.
When trace reaches a scope that does not contain any dumped signals, the path
stops expanding at the boundary and results in the symbol, as illustrated in the

When the mouse hovers over the symbol, the tooltip message notifies that the trace
is stopped because it traced into a scope without any dumped simulation results
(which is required for tracing).
* Automatic power-aware tracing feature in Temporal Flow View does not support
Transition based mode (tracing the power corruption triggering path).

Set the search priority for Liberty File (*.lib), NOVAS Library (*.lib++), and Synopsys

also illustrated in Figure 138.

Displaying Power State Group in Power State Table Frame
Overview
The following enhancements are provided with Verdi Power-Aware Debug:
* The add_power_state command is enhanced to define a Power State Table. The
create_pst and add_pst_state commands are no longer required to create a Power
State Table.
* The power states displayed in the Power State Table are composed hierarchically to
avoid exponential explosion of the size of the Power State Table.
* The Power State Table frame and the Power Domain List frame displays the related
power states in the complete design under a single user-defined group as Power State
Group List.
* The Power State Group List supports dynamic debug functionalities like active
annotation, drag and drop, and so on.

Displaying Power State Group in Power State Table Frame

Use Model
To view the related power states in a design, create a Power State Group List for the entire
design. The Power State Table frame displays the Power State Group List as illustrated in
Figure 149.
Figure 149

Power State Group Displayed in the PST Frame

Use the create_group command to create a group of related power states and define a
group name that can be used in the add_power_state command.
Syntax:
create_group group_name

Use the add_power_state command to add power states for the functional nets (power,
ground and so on) and create power state tables and define them hierarchically.
Syntax:
add_power_state [-supply|-domain|-group] object_name [-update]
-state {[parent_state_name] state_name [-legal|illegal]
[-simstate simstate]

Displaying Power State Group in Power State Table Frame

[-supply_expr {Boolean_expression}]
[-logic_expr {Boolean_expression}]
}]*
[-complete]

The following is an example to create a group GROUP1 with RUN and SLEEP states for
SS1 and SS2 signals:
#Creating power state ON for SS1
add_power_state -supply SS1 \
-state ON {-supply_expr {(power == {FULL_ON 0.8}) && (ground == {FULL_ON
0})}}
#Creating power states ON and OFF for SS2
add_power_state -supply SS2 \
-state ON {-supply_expr {(power == {FULL_ON 0.8}) && (ground == {FULL_ON
0})}}
add_power_state -supply SS2 \
-state OFF {-supply_expr {(power == {OFF}) && (ground == {FULL_ON 0})}}
#Creating group for power states
create_group GROUP1
add_power_state -group GROUP1
-state RUN {-logic_expr {SS1 == ON && SS2 == ON}}
-state SLEEP {-logic_expr {SS1 == ON && SS2 == ON}}
The following table shows the power states for GROUP1 group created
for SS1 and SS2 signals:

Supported Features
For each power state group, the member list is displayed in the Power State Table frame.
The following features are supported for Power State Group List:
* Dynamic debug functions (like active annotation, drag-and-drop power state group
to waveform, or to debug value) are supported for power state group objects and the
member object list.
* Drag and drop action is supported for power state group object and its member object
list.
* Create Power State Group List by UPF scope, similar to creating Power State Table
List in Power Domain tree is supported. Drag-and-drop action for power state group in
power domain tree is also supported.
* Double clicking the Power State Group node highlights the related power state group
object in Power State Table frame and syncs the UPF source code to its declaration.
* Double clicking the group object syncs the source code to its declaration in the UPF
source code, and highlights the group object node in the Power Domain tree.
* Double clicking the state object syncs the source code to the declaration of its related
group in the UPF source code.
* Double clicking the member of Power State Group syncs the source code to its
reference in related Power State Group.
* In Power State Table frame, as Power State Group can be used as a member of other
Power State Group, so, for each sub power state group/table object, right-click menu is
supported as Show Definition to sync source codes to its declaration and highlight the
related power state group/table item of definition in the Power State Table frame.
* Drag and drop action for Power State Group is supported in the UPF source code view
and nWave frame.

text:
Dumping Low Power Debug DB XML File During Compilation In
UFE Flow
Verdi allows you to debug low power objects instrumented by VCS NLP. You can
use the low power debug DB, an XML format file, dumped by VCS NLP to handle all
instrumentation scenarios.
You can use the -kdb option at compile time to dump low power debug DB file in the UFE
flow.
Following are the benefits of this feature:
* Allows you to dump low power instrument scenarios/objects with specific XML format
for every partition and reuse same information from same partition.
* Reduces the memory usage, thereby improving the compile-time performance.

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Use Model
The following is the syntax to dump DB XML file for single compile:
% vcs <design file> -upf <upf file> -kdb -debug_access+all <compile
options>

The following is the syntax to dump DB XML file for partition compile:
% vcs <design file> -upf <upf file> -partcomp -kdb -debug_access+all
<compile options>

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
% vlogan dut.v testbench.v design.v -sverilog -kdb
% vcs topcfg -q -upf top.upf -partcomp -kdb -lca -debug_access+all
-power=dumplpconnect

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Demo
The following demo illustrates how to import a UPF power file into the Verdi platform and
to use power-related panes to browse the power intent.
1. Copy the upf_demo folder located at the following path to your local directory:
$VERDI_HOME/demo/power/upf_demo

2. Load the design and the FSDB dump file into the Verdi platform using the following
command:
verdi -f run.f -ssf rtl.fsdb &

3. Load the UPF power file into the Verdi platform by invoking the File -> Import CPF/
UPF Files option to open the Import CPF/UPF Files form. Select UPF1.0 in the
Language field, double-click the demo.upf file, and click the OK button. After loading
is complete, power-related panes are opened and docked in the main window.
4. The Power Domain List pane shows all power domains with every domain marked with
a different color. All power definitions are shown under the power domain hierarchically.
The Power State/Mode Table pane is added to the middle pane. A power tab is added
to the source code pane. When you double-click on different items in the left pane, the
content in the power tab changes accordingly.
5. Double-click the PD_FSM node in the Power Domain List pane. Browse the components
of the PD_FSM power domain.
The Verdi platform with the Power-Aware Debug support can automatically extract power
state tables defined in the UPF and show the states in a table format.

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
1. In the Power State Table pane, double-click VDD and the source code jumps to VDD in
the Power Source Code pane.
2. Search capability for Power-Aware Debug
a. In the main window, invoke the Source -> Find String option. The PDML-Find form
is displayed.

b. Select String in the Find Type field, and type in isolation. Click the Find All button.
c. Search results are listed in the Search tab of the Message pane. Double-click any
line to jump to the corresponding source code in the source code pane.
3. Trace driver/load of a signal
a. In the Power Domain Hierarchy pane, double-click the PD_MEM node. The cursor
jumps to the respective line in the source code in the Power Source Code pane.
b. In the Power Source Code pane, right-click the VDD_MEM signal and select the Trace
Power Driver option. Power drivers are listed in the Trace tab of the Message
pane.

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
4. Report Impacted Signals by invoking the Power -> Report Impacted Signals by
Scope option to open the Scope Lists form. Use the Add button to add the scopes.
The Report Power Impacted Signals form opens up, as illustrated in the following

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
a. Select the Schematic button to open an nSchema pane displaying the connection
of the selected signal.
b. Select the Control Signals tab to browse the control signals of retention and
isolation rules.

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
You can bring up a schematic view of the power design in the Power Map pane using the
following steps:
1. From the main menu, select Power -> New Power Map -> Full Power Map to invoke
the Power Map pane.
2. Observe that all power domains are shown as rectangles. Drag and drop a domain to
the Power Source Code pane to browse its definition.
3. Observe that the power switch, isolation and retention rules are presented as cells
connecting to the related power domains. Drag and drop an isolation rule to the Power
Source Code pane to browse its definition.

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
4. Select the red dotted line between the domains. The red dotted line represents a noncovered isolation net.
5. To view the non-covered isolation net signals, select Schematic -> Report Selected
Impacted Signals. These signals are suggested by the Verdi platform to be guarded
with an isolation rule for protection.

Go to the nTrace window and perform the following steps to practice visualizing power
information in the window:
1. In the Design Browser pane, the instances have different colors. These colors are
assigned based on the power domain specified in the UPF. You can change the color
by performing the following steps:
a. Invoke the Power -> Highlight Power Domain option to display the Highlight
Power Domain form.
b. Select PD_TOP and change it to a different color, and then press the OK button.
A tip window is displayed for showing power information. This helps you to quickly
understand the power intent of any module or signal.
2. Put the mouse cursor on i_ALUB (under system/i_cpu) in the design hierarchy pane
to view the power domain and state condition.
3. Double-click i_ALUB to view the source code which has retention annotation on some
of the signals.
4. Double-click i_CCU (under system/i_cpu) to view more retention annotation on the
signals.
5. Put the mouse cursor on one of the retention signals to view the tip with save/restore,
and shut-off condition.
6. Select i_pram (under system) to view level shifter and isolation annotation.
7. Put the mouse cursor on one of the signals to view the tip window with isolation and
level-shifter rules.
The power content can be cross probed between panes by performing the following
steps:
8. Select i_pram in the Design Browser pane and drag-and-drop to the Power Source
Code pane.
9. Go to the Power Source Code pane to view the source code of i_pram power intent.
10. To view the rules of level shifter of this domain, double-click the ls_CPU_to_MEM node
under the Level Shifter node in the Power Domain Details pane.
11. The level shifter rule is applied to the inputs of the memory. Therefore, the source code
in nTrace has an "l" annotation on all the inputs of i_pram.

Go to the nSchema window and perform the following steps to practice visualizing power
information in the schematic window:
1. In the Design Browser pane, double-click the system node and select the New
Schematic

icon.

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
In the created nSchema window, blocks are highlighted with different power domain
colors to indicate to which power domain each block belongs to. It is a quick way to see
the number of power domains at the top-level view.
2. Double-click the CPU block and see that each of the three blocks below it belong to a
different power domain.
3. Select the ALUB block to view the Power Domain information on the toolbar.
4. Double-click the ALUB block to highlight the instances below. All the instances have
the same power domain as their parent scope. The signals highlighted in red are
retention signals.

shown on the toolbar. If the Show Tip option in the Schematics -> Select page of the
Preferences form is turned on, hovering the mouse cursor on that information displays
a tip for Restore and Save conditions.
6. Turn on the Schematic -> Active Annotation option; to see that the power state is
annotated on schematic symbols.
7. Type in 6850 in the Cursor Time field on the toolbar, the schematic symbol with state
off is grayed out.
8. To change the highlight color for power objects in the Preferences form, invoke the
Preferences form using the Tools -> Preferences option. Select the Power Aware
folder in the left pane to view the configuration page for Power Aware Objects. Select
the Retention Object, set the color to green, and click the Apply button.
9. Toggle off the Highlight Power Aware Design Object(s) option in the Preferences
form and click the Apply button. Then, the color highlight for retention signals in
the nSchema/nTrace window is removed. Similarly, toggle off the Highlight Power
Domain option to remove the color highlight for the power domains in all panes. Now,
toggle on both Highlight Power Aware Design Object(s) and Highlight Power
Domain options and click the Apply button to resume the highlight. Alternatively, select
View -> Highlight Power Aware Object and toggle on and off the Power Domain

Go to the nWave window and perform the following steps to practice visualizing power
information in the waveform window.

1. Click the Get Signals icon to open the Get Signals form.
2. Click the system -> i_cpu -> i_CCU node, select the signals, and click the OK button.
The signal pane shows the selected signals.
3. Drag-and-drop a node from the Design Browser pane to the nWave window. In the
nWave signal pane, added Isolation/Level-shifted signals are highlighted in yellow and
are annotated with the Iso/Lvs postfix.
To practice with Active Trace and learn how power information is visualized in the active
trace results, perform the following steps:
1. Drag-and-drop the i_ALUB scope from the Design Browser pane to the nWave window.
Select the ALU[7:0]signal in the nWave signal pane. Click the transition 3 -> 55 at time
951.
2. Double-click the transition to show the active driver in the Design Source Code pane.
3. Turn on the active annotation (Source -> Active Annotation) in the main nTrace
window.
4. Do active trace on the signal, a, by double-clicking on it.
The Power Domain field on the toolbar shows the power domain name of the signal a.
In the Message pane, each trace result is added with its corresponding power domain
name and the name is highlighted with the relevant power domain color.
Go to the Temporal Flow View pane and perform the following steps to see how power
information is visualized in the Temporal Flow View pane:
1. Select the ALU[7:0] signal in the nWave signal pane and click the transition f -> XX,
time 3900. Choose the Temporal Flow Window -> New Temporal Flow Window
option from the right click menu and click the OK button in the Create Temporal Flow
View form.
2. In the created Temporal Flow View pane, select the out[7:0] signal and select Trace
This Value (Trace -> Trace This Value) in the invoked TFV window to unroll the path.
The unrolled path shows that the cause of the value change is power isolation.

3. Drag-and-drop any pin of the power switch cell to the Power Source Code pane to
show the related power rule.
To debug power sequences, perform the following steps:
1. Go to the nWave window and zoom 100%.
Observe that there are some unknowns (X's) in the waveform.
2. Select View -> Power -> Mask Power Off to enable Verdi to automatically identify the
Xs caused by power off and mark them in a shade mask.
3. Drag and drop i_pram and i_ALUB scopes from the Design Browser
pane to the nWave window. See the waveform around time 3900ns, the
system.i_pram.data[7:0] signal has X, but does not have mask as it is not caused
by power off.
4. Right-click system.i_pram.data[7:0] in the nWave signal pane to invoke the Power
-> Add Power Domain option. This option traces the power domain and adds it under
the data[7:0] signal. As the power is on, X is not caused by power off.
Trace the active driver of X to find out why data[7:0] is X.
5. Select data[7:0]and invoke the Tools -> List X option to open the Source File to
List X form. Select the Use Current Simulation Results option in the Source File
Selection field. The other two options do not contain power information. Select the
Selected SignalsPD option in the List field.
After pressing the Next button in the Source File to List X form, the List X form displays
all unknowns.

the Trace Active X button. Click Yes, OK and Trace buttons in the following three
forms, the Trace Active X Results pane is displayed.

7. In the pane, it shows X is caused by power off. Select the Action -> Show source
code on nTrace option in the form to continue tracing.

text:
Appendix A: Power Map Validation
Currently, the Power Map analyzes the power mode (or state table) definition in UPF to
determine if a possibility exists that the from domain (the domain from where a signal is
coming from) is off while the to domain (the domain the signal is going to) is not. If this is
the case, unexpected results could propagate through such signals from the from domain
to the to domain.
For example, there are three power domains A, B, and C; two power modes: 1 and 2 in
total.
Domain A

Domain B

Domain C

Mode 1

On

On

Off

Mode 2

On

Off

Off

When domain B is off, domain C is always off (both in mode 1 and mode 2). When domain
C is off, domain B could be on (mode 1) or off (mode 2). So, from domain C to domain
B, it is required to insert an isolation cell. However, from domain B to domain C, it is not
necessary to insert an isolation cell.
To skip analyze power mode, turn off the Check Power Mode option (default: on) in the
Preferences form.

title: Appendix 351
text:
Data Structure 351

Preface
The Python-Based NPI Coverage Model User Guide provides information to let you
access coverage database generated by verification tools such as VCS simulator.

Customer Support
Customer support is available through SolvNetPlus.

Accessing SolvNetPlus
The SolvNetPlus site includes a knowledge base of technical articles and answers to
frequently asked questions about Synopsys tools. The SolvNetPlus site also gives you
access to a wide range of Synopsys online services including software downloads,
documentation, and technical support.
To access the SolvNetPlus site, go to the following address:
https://solvnetplus.synopsys.com
If prompted, enter your user name and password. If you do not have a Synopsys user
name and password, follow the instructions to sign up for an account.
If you need help using the SolvNetPlus site, click REGISTRATION HELP in the top-right
menu bar.

Contacting Customer Support
To contact Customer Support, go to https://solvnetplus.synopsys.com.

Synopsys Statement on Inclusivity and Diversity
Synopsys is committed to creating an inclusive environment where every employee,
customer, and partner feels welcomed. We are reviewing and removing exclusionary
language from our products and supporting customer-facing collateral. Our effort also
includes internal initiatives to remove biased language from our engineering and working
environment, including terms that are embedded in our software and IPs. At the same
time, we are working to ensure that our Web content and software applications are usable
to people of varying abilities. You might still find examples of non-inclusive language in our
software or documentation as our IPs implement industry-standard specifications that are
currently under review to remove exclusionary language.

Introduction to Python Based NPI
Python-Based NPI APIs support six models:
* Coverage
* Language
* Netlist
* Text
* Waveform
* Waveform Writer
Each model have their own APIs to let you be able to traverse data objects and obtain
objects' properties like the existing C-Based or Tcl-Based NPI APIs.
In this guide, the environment setting for using Python-Based NPI APIs for Coverage is
demonstrated.
* Package and Modules
* Module Functions and Class Objects
* User Interface and Use Flow

Package and Modules
Packages
The Python-based NPI package name is "pynpi", and it is placed at $VERDI_HOME/share/
NPI/python.

Chapter 1: Introduction to Python Based NPI
Module Functions and Class Objects

Modules
There are seven modules inside the "pynpi" package: npisys, lang, netlist, text, cov
waveform and waveformw. The first module, npisys, is the system model for initialization,
loading design and exit. The other modules represent language model, netlist model, text
model, coverage model, wave model and waveform writer model respectively

Module Functions and Class Objects
L0 Module Functions
Every module provides some L0 (level 0) functions to let you get the class objects. These
functions return a class object or a list of class objects, and they follow the specification of
the existing L0 APIs provided in C or Tcl.

L1 Module Functions
Similar to L0 module functions, every module also provides some L1 (level 1) functions to
let you get advanced information based on the results obtained by L0 module functions.
These functions follows the specification of the existing L1 APIs provided in C or Tcl.

The class object is similar to the so-called handle in NPI C APIs. The most difference is
that some basic L0 APIs in C and Tcl iscome class method function. These L0 APIs are
usually to get integer value, string value, one-to-one method to get a handle, and 1-tomany method to get handle iterator.

User Interface and Use Flow
Environment and Library Setting
The python library setting flow of using Python-Based NPI APIs contains four parts:
1. Check your Python's version:
Python-Based NPI APIs need the Python version greater than 3.6.0.
2. Environment setting for "VERDI_HOME" is required for Python-based NPI. Ensure that
you set it up before running program.

Chapter 1: Introduction to Python Based NPI
User Interface and Use Flow

3. Add the cross-platform Python library path to your code before loading the Pythonbased NPI by using the following commands:
import platform
arch = platform.machine()
if arch == "x86_64":
arch = "linux64"
sys.path.append(os.path.abspath(os.environ["VERDI_HOME"] + "/share/NPI/lib/" +
arch))

4. Import module "npisys" for using the function of NPI initialization and exit from pynpi
package.
from pynpi import npisys

5. Import the module you need from pynpi package. For example, if you want to use
Coverage model, you can import module like the following:
from pynpi import cov

6. Note that initialization function npisys.init() must be called before writing your code
by using any other modules. Also, you must call npisys.end() after finishing your
code. Following is a simple example to demonstrate how to use coverage model by
Python-Based NPI APIs.
Python program to use NPI models: (demo.py)
import sys
import os
import platform
arch = platform.machine()
if arch == "x86_64":
arch = "linux64"
sys.path.append(os.path.abspath(os.environ["VERDI_HOME"] + "/share/NPI/lib/"
+ arch))
from pynpi import npisys
from pynpi import cov
# Initialize NPI
if not npisys.init(sys.argv):
print("Error: Fail to initialize NPI")
assert 0
# Load design (if needed, depends on models)
if not npisys.load_design(sys.argv):
print("Error: Fail to load design")
assert 0
# Beginning of your code here -------------------#
# Example code can be found in later chapters
#
# End of your code ------------------------------# End NPI
npisys.end()

Chapter 1: Introduction to Python Based NPI
User Interface and Use Flow

C shell script example to setup environment and execute Python program: (run_demo)
#!/bin/csh -f
# Setup your $VERDI_HOME here
setenv VERDI_HOME [YOUR_VERDI_HOME_PATH]
# run the python program
# - Input arguments depend on your program design
# - If loading design is required, you can pass the options like
[YOUR_PYTHON]./demo.py -sv demo.v

To run the files, put the above files in the same directory and execute the run_demo C
shell script.
./run_demo

Module npisys
This chapter includes the following topics:
* Overview
* L0 APIs
* NPI General Options

Overview
Module npisys is for setting Python-based NPI. You must call npisys.init() before using
any other NPI modules and call npisys.end() after using any other NPI modules.

L0 APIs
Following are the public L0 APIs for system module:

npisys.init(pyArgvList)
System initialization for Python-Based NPI.
Parameters: pyArgList (str list) - input argument list, for example, sys.argv
Returns: Return 1 if successful. Otherwise, return 0.
>>>npisys.init(sys.argv)

npisys.load_design(pyArgvList)
Load design for Python-Based NPI.
Parameters: pyArgList (str list) - input argument list. For example, sys.argv
Returns: Return 1 if successful. Otherwise, return 0.

Overview
The NPI coverage model lets you access coverage databases generated by verification
tools such as the VCS simulator.
With the coverage model, you can create custom reports and tools to display and analyze
coverage data.

Quick Start
Example Code:
import sys
import os
rel_lib_path = os.environ['VERDI_HOME'] + '/share/NPI/python'
sys.path.append(os.path.abspath(rel_lib_path))
from pynpi import npisys
from pynpi import cov
# -- traverse coverage toggle info ------------------------------------def trv_toggle(hdl, indentCnt, test, fp_w):
childList = hdl.child_handles()
for child in childList:
for i in range(indentCnt):
fp_w.write(' ')
fp_w.write('# '+child.type()+': '+child.name()+'
cov:'+str(child.covered(test)))
fp_w.write('/'+str(child.coverable(test))+'\n')
trv_toggle(child, indentCnt+1, test, fp_w)
cov.release_handle(child)

Chapter 3: Python-Based NPI Coverage Model
Quick Start

# -- traverse coverage instances --------------------------------------def trv_cov_inst(hdl, indentCnt, test, fp_w):
instList = hdl.instance_handles()
for inst in instList:
for i in range(indentCnt):
fp_w.write(' ')
hdlType = inst.type()
fp_w.write(hdlType+': ')
if hdlType == 'npiCovDatabase':
fp_w.write(inst.name()+'\n')
else:
fp_w.write(inst.full_name()+'\n')
tm = inst.toggle_metric_handle()
if (tm):
trv_toggle(tm, indentCnt, test, fp_w)
trv_cov_inst(inst, indentCnt+1, test, fp_w)
cov.release_handle(inst)
# -- init -------------------------------------------------------------res = npisys.init(sys.argv)
if res != 1:
print('[Error] Failed to do npi init')
sys.exit(1)
# -- open log to write ------------------------------------------------fp_w = open('test.log', 'w')
vdbName = 'merged.vdb'
# -- traverse all the toggle bins and write their coverage info -------covDb = cov.open(vdbName)
if (covDb):
fp_w.write('load vdb: '+covDb.name()+'\n')
# -- merge tests --------------------------------------------------mergedTest = None
testList = covDb.test_handles()
for test in testList:
fp_w.write(test.name()+'\n')
if (mergedTest == None):
mergedTest = test
else:
mergedTest = cov.merge_test(mergedTest, test)
fp_w.write('mergedTest: '+mergedTest.name()+'\n')
trv_cov_inst(covDb, 1, mergedTest, fp_w)
covDb.close()
# -- close log and end ------------------------------------------------fp_w.close()
npisys.end()

In the coverage module, use the C/C++-Based NPI object diagrams to see how to use
Python-Based NPI class objects.
Follow these rules:
1. Every int or string property can be called as a class function.
The function name is that property after removing the prefix "npiCov" and converting
the rest to snake case.
Here is the mapping table:
C/C++-based NPI Usage

Python-based NPI Usage

npi_cov_get_str(npiCovName, hdl)

hdl.name()

npi_cov_get(npiCovLineNo, hdl)

hdl.line_no()

2. Every one-to-one method can be called as a class function.
The function name is that method plus "_method" after removing the prefix "npiCov"
and converting the rest to snake case.
For one-to-many methods, change "_method" to "_methods".
The C/C++ API returns an iterator for 1-to-many methods. Python returns a list.

Manipulate coverage database handles, tests, instances, and bins using the Python NPI
coverage class API to programmatically query and manage verification coverage data.
Key class categories include functional coverage (covergroups, coverpoints, crosses),
code coverage (branch, condition, toggle, FSM, line), assertion coverage (cover properties
and sequences), and power-domain coverage. Requires a loaded NPI coverage database.
Supports batch scripting and Verdi interactive sessions.

Introduction to Python Based NPI
Python-Based NPI APIs support six models:
* Coverage
* Language
* Netlist
* Text
* Waveform
* Waveform Writer
Each model have their own APIs to let you be able to traverse data objects and obtain
objects' properties like the existing C-Based or Tcl-Based NPI APIs.
In this guide, the environment setting for using Python-Based NPI APIs for Coverage is
demonstrated.
* Package and Modules
* Module Functions and Class Objects
* User Interface and Use Flow

Package and Modules
Packages
The Python-based NPI package name is "pynpi", and it is placed at $VERDI_HOME/share/
NPI/python.

Chapter 1: Introduction to Python Based NPI
Module Functions and Class Objects

Modules
There are seven modules inside the "pynpi" package: npisys, lang, netlist, text, cov
waveform and waveformw. The first module, npisys, is the system model for initialization,
loading design and exit. The other modules represent language model, netlist model, text
model, coverage model, wave model and waveform writer model respectively

Module Functions and Class Objects
L0 Module Functions
Every module provides some L0 (level 0) functions to let you get the class objects. These
functions return a class object or a list of class objects, and they follow the specification of
the existing L0 APIs provided in C or Tcl.

L1 Module Functions
Similar to L0 module functions, every module also provides some L1 (level 1) functions to
let you get advanced information based on the results obtained by L0 module functions.
These functions follows the specification of the existing L1 APIs provided in C or Tcl.

The class object is similar to the so-called handle in NPI C APIs. The most difference is
that some basic L0 APIs in C and Tcl iscome class method function. These L0 APIs are
usually to get integer value, string value, one-to-one method to get a handle, and 1-tomany method to get handle iterator.

Environment and Library Setting
The python library setting flow of using Python-Based NPI APIs contains four parts:
1. Check your Python's version:
Python-Based NPI APIs need the Python version greater than 3.6.0.
2. Environment setting for "VERDI_HOME" is required for Python-based NPI. Ensure that
you set it up before running program.

3. Add the cross-platform Python library path to your code before loading the Pythonbased NPI by using the following commands:
import platform
arch = platform.machine()
if arch == "x86_64":
arch = "linux64"
sys.path.append(os.path.abspath(os.environ["VERDI_HOME"] + "/share/NPI/lib/" +
arch))

4. Import module "npisys" for using the function of NPI initialization and exit from pynpi
package.
from pynpi import npisys

5. Import the module you need from pynpi package. For example, if you want to use
Coverage model, you can import module like the following:
from pynpi import cov

6. Note that initialization function npisys.init() must be called before writing your code
by using any other modules. Also, you must call npisys.end() after finishing your
code. Following is a simple example to demonstrate how to use coverage model by
Python-Based NPI APIs.

Python-Based NPI Coverage Model
This chapter includes the following topics:
* Overview
* Quick Start
* Class Objects

Overview
The NPI coverage model lets you access coverage databases generated by verification
tools such as the VCS simulator.
With the coverage model, you can create custom reports and tools to display and analyze
coverage data.

Quick Start
Example Code:
import sys
import os
rel_lib_path = os.environ['VERDI_HOME'] + '/share/NPI/python'
sys.path.append(os.path.abspath(rel_lib_path))
from pynpi import npisys
from pynpi import cov
# -- traverse coverage toggle info ------------------------------------def trv_toggle(hdl, indentCnt, test, fp_w):
childList = hdl.child_handles()
for child in childList:
for i in range(indentCnt):
fp_w.write(' ')
fp_w.write('# '+child.type()+': '+child.name()+'
cov:'+str(child.covered(test)))
fp_w.write('/'+str(child.coverable(test))+'\n')
trv_toggle(child, indentCnt+1, test, fp_w)
cov.release_handle(child)

Chapter 3: Python-Based NPI Coverage Model
Quick Start

# -- traverse coverage instances --------------------------------------def trv_cov_inst(hdl, indentCnt, test, fp_w):
instList = hdl.instance_handles()
for inst in instList:
for i in range(indentCnt):
fp_w.write(' ')
hdlType = inst.type()
fp_w.write(hdlType+': ')
if hdlType == 'npiCovDatabase':
fp_w.write(inst.name()+'\n')
else:
fp_w.write(inst.full_name()+'\n')
tm = inst.toggle_metric_handle()
if (tm):
trv_toggle(tm, indentCnt, test, fp_w)
trv_cov_inst(inst, indentCnt+1, test, fp_w)
cov.release_handle(inst)
# -- init -------------------------------------------------------------res = npisys.init(sys.argv)
if res != 1:
print('[Error] Failed to do npi init')
sys.exit(1)
# -- open log to write ------------------------------------------------fp_w = open('test.log', 'w')
vdbName = 'merged.vdb'
# -- traverse all the toggle bins and write their coverage info -------covDb = cov.open(vdbName)
if (covDb):
fp_w.write('load vdb: '+covDb.name()+'\n')
# -- merge tests --------------------------------------------------mergedTest = None
testList = covDb.test_handles()
for test in testList:
fp_w.write(test.name()+'\n')
if (mergedTest == None):
mergedTest = test
else:
mergedTest = cov.merge_test(mergedTest, test)
fp_w.write('mergedTest: '+mergedTest.name()+'\n')
trv_cov_inst(covDb, 1, mergedTest, fp_w)
covDb.close()
# -- close log and end ------------------------------------------------fp_w.close()
npisys.end()

Introduction to Python Based NPI
Python-Based NPI APIs support eight models. They are as follows:
* Language
* Netlist
* Waveform
* Text
* Coverage
* Waveform Writer
* UPF
* CRDB
Each model have their own APIs to let you be able to traverse data objects and obtain
objects' properties.
In this guide, the environment setting for using Python-Based NPI APIs for CRDB is
demonstrated.
This chapter includes the following topics:
* Packages and Modules
* User Interface and Use Flow

Packages and Modules
Packages
The Python-based NPI package name is "pynpi", and it is placed at $VERDI_HOME/share/
NPI/python.

Chapter 1: Introduction to Python Based NPI
User Interface and Use Flow

Modules
There are nine modules inside the "pynpi" package: npisys, lang, netlist, text, cov
waveform, waveformw, upf, and crdb. The first module, npisys, is the system model for
initialization, loading design and exit.
The other modules represent language model, netlist model, text model, coverage model,
wave model, waveform writer model, UPF model, and CRDB respectively.

Environment and Library Setting
The python library setting flow of using Python-Based NPI APIs contains four parts:
1. Check your Python's version:
Python-Based NPI APIs need the Python version greater than 3.6.0.
2. Environment setting for "VERDI_HOME" is required for Python-based NPI. Ensure that
you set it up before running program.
3. Add the cross-platform Python library path to your code before loading the Pythonbased NPI by using the following commands:
import platform
arch = platform.machine()
if arch == "x86_64":
arch = "linux64"
sys.path.append(os.path.abspath(os.environ["VERDI_HOME"] + "/share/NPI/lib/" +
arch))

4. Import module "npisys" for using the function of NPI initialization and exit from pynpi
package.
from pynpi import npisys

5. Import the module you need from pynpi package. For example, if you want to use
CRDB model, you can import the module as follows:
from pynpi import crdb

6. Note that initialization function npisys.init() must be called before writing your code
by using any other modules. Besides, npisys.end() should be called after finishing
your code. Following is a simple example to demonstrate how to use CRDB model by
Python-Based NPI APIs.

import sys
import os

+ arch))
from pynpi import npisys
from pynpi import crdb

assert 0

# End of your code ------------------------------# End NPI
npisys.end()

# Setup your $VERDI_HOME here
setenv VERDI_HOME [YOUR_VERDI_HOME_PATH]
# run the python program
[YOUR_PYTHON] ./demo.py

script run_demo.
./run_demo

Python-Based NPI CRDB Model
The Python-Based NPI Correlation Database (CRDB) Model helps you to check and query
how scopes and signals are mapped between RTL and gate-level designs. This feature
makes it easier to understand the relationship between different design levels.
This section describes about the following topics:
* Abstract
* Quick Start
* Classes
* Public Functions

Abstract
This model enables you to open a CRDB. You can explore the design hierarchy and view
the correlation results.

An example of how to generate a CRDB and use pyNPI crdb APIs is as follows:

Environment and Library Setting
To set the environment and library variables, follow the given steps:
1. Set the LD_LIBRARY_PATH environment variable so that your system can find the NPI
shared library included in the Verdi release package.
If you see an error such as "cannot open shared object file", add the shared
library path to the LD_LIBRARY_PATH environment variable before running your PythonBased NPI program.
For example, you can set the following environment variable in a 64-bit Linux machine
by a C shell (csh) script:
setenv LD_LIBRARY_PATH
$VERDI_HOME/share/NPI/lib/linux64:$LD_LIBRARY_PATH
setenv LD_LIBRARY_PATH
$VERDI_HOME/platform/linux64/bin:$LD_LIBRARY_PATH

2. Set the Python library path as follows:

Design
rtl.sv:
typedef struct packed {
reg [3:2][1:0] f1;
reg f2;
} ST;
module top(clk, i_st, o_st);
input clk;
input ST [1:0] i_st;
output ST [1:0] o_st;
generate
for(genvar i = 2; i <= 3 ; i = i + 1) begin : geni

for(genvar j = 0; j <= 1 ; j = j + 1) begin : genj
dut inst0(o_st[0].f1[i][j], i_st[0].f1[i][j], clk);
end
end
endgenerate
dut inst1(o_st[0].f2, i_st[0].f2, clk);
always@(posedge clk) begin
o_st[1] <= i_st[1];
end
endmodule
module dut(Q, D, clk);
output reg Q;
input D, clk;
always @(posedge clk) begin
Q <= D;
end
endmodule

import sys
from pynpi import npisys
from pynpi import crdb

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
def iter_sig_corr(signal):
corr_list = []
corr_iter = signal.get_corr_iter()
for (corr_sig, polarity) in corr_iter:
corr_list.append((corr_sig.get_full_name(), polarity))
if len(corr_list) == 0:
return;
print(f"---{signal.get_full_name()} correlation results---")
for (corr_name, polarity) in corr_list:
print(f"{corr_name}, Polarity: {polarity}")
print("")
callback_dict = {
crdb.ObjType_e.Signal: iter_sig_corr
}
if __name__ == '__main__':
# Initialize NPI
npisys.init(sys.argv)
# Start to develop your code ------------------------------orig_stdout = sys.stdout
f = open("g2r_mapping.txt", "w")
sys.stdout = f
database = crdb.open("demo.crdb")
opt = crdb.CrdbOpt(rtl=False)
crdb.hier_tree_trv(database, None, opt, callback_dict)
database.close()
sys.stdout = orig_stdout
f.close()
# End of your code ------------------------------# End NPI
npisys.end()

CrdbOpt
class crdb.CrdbOpt(**kwargs)
This class allows you to specify various options for filtering the results when traversing the
CRDB hierarchy.

reg_cell_only()
bool - If True, only return register cells. Default is False.

lib_cell_only()
bool - If True, only return library cells. Default is False.

sym_cell_only()
bool - If True, only return symbol library cells. Default is False.

reg_sig_only()
bool - If True, only return register signals. Default is False.

ignore_mapping_stats()
bool - If True, ignore mapping statistics. Default is False.

report_based_mapping()
bool - If True, use report-based mapping. Default is False.

corr_only()
bool - If True, only return correlated handles. Default is False.

uncorr_only()
bool - If True, only return uncorrelated handles. Default is False.

rtl()
bool - If True, include RTL-level objects. Default is True.

gate()
bool - If True, include Gate-level objects. Default is True.

depth()
int - The depth of the hierarchy to traverse. Default is 0 for all levels.

Synopsys is committed to creating an inclusive environment where every employee,

Introduction to Python Based NPI
Python-Based NPI APIs support the following six models:
* Language
* Netlist
* Waveform
* Text
* Coverage
* Waveform Writer
All models have their own APIs. These APIs enable you to traverse data objects and
obtain objects' properties such as the existing C-Based or Tcl-Based NPI APIs.
The following topics in this guide demonstrate the environment settings for using PythonBased NPI APIs for Language:
* Packages and Modules
* Module Functions and Class Objects
* User Interface and Use Flow

Packages and Modules
Packages
The Python-based NPI package name is "pynpi". It is placed at $VERDI_HOME/share/NPI/
python.

Chapter 1: Introduction to Python Based NPI
Module Functions and Class Objects

Modules
The following are the seven modules inside the pynpi package:
* npisys
* lang
* netlist
* text
* cov waveform
* waveformw
The first module, npisys, is the system model for initialization, loading design, and exit.
The others represent the language, netlist, text, coverage wave, and waveform writer
models respectively.

Module Functions and Class Objects
L0 Module Functions
Every module provides some L0 (level 0) functions to let you get the class objects.
These functions return a class object or a list of class objects. These functions follow the
specification of the existing L0 APIs provided in C or Tcl.

L1 Module Functions
Similar to L0 module functions, each module also provides some L1 (level 1) functions.
These functions enable you to get advanced information based on the results obtained
by L0 module functions. These functions follow the specification of the existing L1 APIs
provided in C or Tcl.

Class Objects
The class object is similar to the so-called handle in NPI C APIs. The main difference is
that some basic L0 APIs in C and Tcl become class methods. These L0 APIs help you
get integer values, string values, one-to-one methods for a single handle, or 1-to-many
methods for multiple handles.

Chapter 1: Introduction to Python Based NPI
User Interface and Use Flow

User Interface and Use Flow
This chapter describes the user interface and use flow for Python-Based NPI APIs.

Environment and Library Setting
The python library setting flow of using Python-Based NPI APIs contains four parts:
1. Verify the version of Python you are using.
Python-Based NPI APIs need the Python version greater than 3.6.0.
2. Configure the VERDI_HOME environment variable before you run any program that uses
the Python-based NPI.
3. Add the cross-platform Python library path to your code before loading the Pythonbased NPI by using the following commands:
import platform
arch = platform.machine()
if arch == "x86_64":
arch = "linux64"
sys.path.append(os.path.abspath(os.environ["VERDI_HOME"] + "/share/NPI/lib/" +
arch))

4. Import the module "npisys" from the package pynpi for using the NPI initialization and
exit functions.

5. Import the module you need from the "pynpi" package. For example, if you want to use
the language model, import the module as follows:

6. Call the initialization function npisys.init() before writing your code by using any
other modules. Call npisys.end() after finishing your code. The following is a simple
example to demonstrate how to use Python-Based NPI APIs.
The following is a Python program to use the NPI models (demo.py)

import os

arch))

Module npisys
This chapter contains the following topics:
* Overview
* L0 APIs
* NPI General Options

Overview
Module npisys is for setting Python-based NPI. You must call npisys.init() before using
any other NPI modules and call npisys.end() after using any other NPI modules.

L0 APIs
Following are the public L0 APIs for system module:
* npisys.init(pyArgvList)
* npisys.load_design(pyArgvList)
* npisys.end()

npisys.init(pyArgvList)
System initialization for Python-Based NPI.
Parameters: pyArgList (str list) - input argument list, for example, sys.argv
Returns: Return 1 if successful. Otherwise, return 0.
Example:
>>>npisys.init(sys.argv)

Chapter 2: Module npisys
NPI General Options

npisys.load_design(pyArgvList)
Load design for Python-Based NPI.
Parameters: pyArgList (str list) - input argument list, for example, sys.argv
Returns: Return 1 if successful. Otherwise, return 0.
Example:
>>>npisys.load_design(sys.argv)

Clean NPI-related settings and data.
Parameters: none
Returns: Return 1 if successful. Otherwise, return 0.
Example:
>>>npisys.end()

Python-Based NPI Language Model
This chapter contains the following topics:
* Overview
* Quick Start

Overview
NPI Language Model contains three language models:
* SystemVerilog Model
* VHDL Model
* SystemC Model
It lets users traverse designs from the HDL language perspective. Every construct in the
language is regarded as an object.
For NPI Language - SystemVerilog Model, the IEEE Std 1800 -2009 SystemVerilog
Language Reference Manual (LRM) is applied as the foundation of it. Most of the
SystemVerilog object model diagrams are similar to VPI Object Model Diagram in LRM
Chapter 37. For NPI Language - VHDL Model, the IEEE Std1076 -2008 VHDL Language
Reference Manual (LRM) is applied as the foundation of it. However, the style of the VHDL
object model diagrams follows NPI Language - SystemVerilog Model.
Refer to API Reference to see all the APIs that are used in the Language Model. Refer to
supported properties and methods of each object type to understand the HDL language
structure and to learn how to traverse designs via the Language Model.

Quick Start
Environment and library setting:
1. Use Python version greater than 3.6.0.
2. Update LD_LIBRARY_PATH to access NPI shared library put in Verdi release package.

Class Objects
This chapter contains the following topics:
* Supported Properties and Methods
* Mixed Design Objects
* SystemVerilog Objects
* VHDL Objects
* SystemC Objects

Supported Properties and Methods
All possible relationships and properties that an object might have are documented in
the form of object diagrams, which use enclosures to represent objects and arrows to
represent the type of relationship.
The 1-1 relationship is named "tag_handle()", for example, "hdl.scope_handle()" returns
the Scope handle of hdl.
The 1-m relationship is named "tag_handles()", for example,
"hdl.internal_scope_handles()" returns a list of all internal scopes of hdl.
A property might return an integer or a string. If the property supports both integer and
string, the option "is_get_enum" is used to control the output format. For example, the
property "Type" supports both integer and string, the propery is defined by the following
syntax:
def type(self, is_get_enum=False)

Default value of "is_get_enum" is False. "hdl.type()" returns object type in a string and
"hdl.type(True)" returns object type in an integer.
All objects have three common properties:
1. LangType: It shows the language type, and the returned property type is
CommonUseLang (for every language model could be used in mixed design), SvLang
(for SystemVerilog Model), VhdlLang (for VHDL Model) or ScLang (for SystemC
Model).

2. BelongToHierObj: It shows if the object belongs to hierarchy scope. If this object
is non scope object (for example, constant and vh literal)., the return value of this
property is always 0. Refer to Vh Design Unit and UDP.
3. Instrumented: If the object is instrumented by VCS with MVSIM NLP (Native Low
Power) mode, the returned value is 1. Otherwise, the returned value is 0.

Mixed design objects include the SystemVerilog Model, VHDL Model, and SystemC
Model.

lang.handle_by_name(name, hdl)
Get a handle to an object with a specific name.
The NPI routine handle_by_name returns a handle to an object with a specific name.
This function can be applied to all objects with a fullname property. The name can be
hierarchical or simple. If scope is NULL (C/C++), empty string "" (Tcl), or None (Python)
then the name is searched for from the top level of hierarchy. If a scope object is provided,
then search within that scope only.
* name (string) - A character string or pointer to a string containing the name of an
object.
* scope (handle) - Handle to a SystemVerilog scope.
Returns: the handle to an object.
module Counter (input wire clock, resetN,
output logic [15:0] count);
always @(posedge clock, negedge resetN) begin : B1
if( !resetN ) count <= 0;
else count <= count + 1;
end
module TEST;
wire [15:0] count;
bit clock;
bit resetN = 1;
Counter dut (clock, resetN, count);
always #10 clock = ~clock;
resetN = 0;
#2 resetN = 1;
#1 $finish;

lang.release_handle(hdl)
Release a handle and its associated resources allocated by NPI routines.
The NPI routine release_handle frees memory allocated for NPI handles. NPI might
allocate memory when a handle to an object is obtained. One might safely ignore calling
release_handle when a handle is no longer needed, but it is always recommended to do
so, provided the handle is valid and does not automatically become invalid in the future. A
guideline for better memory usage is to release the created handles whenever they are no
longer needed. This avoids logical memory leaks.
release_handle might not be called on an invalid handle.
Parameters: hdl (handle) - Handle to an object.

release_handle

Returns: Returns 1 (true) if the NPI memory management system releases the memory
used by the object. Returns 0 (false) if NPI does not free the memory of the object
because there might be another application program using it.

lang.compare_objects(hdl1, hdl2)
Compare two handles to determine whether they refer to the same object.
The NPI routine compare_objects() returns 1 (TRUE) if the two handles refer to the same
object. Otherwise, 0 (FALSE) is returned. The only thing NPI can compare for variable is
whether the variable is a constant. For example:
reg arr [1:0];
parameter p = 0;
integer i = 0;
lang.compare_objects (arr[0], arr[p]) # return 1
lang.compare_objects (arr[0], arr[i]) # return 0; NPI cannot get i's
value (defined in simulation time)

The following is another example:
struct packed {
int a;
reg [0:7] b;
} ps;
lang.compare_objects (ps[0], ps.b[7]) # return 1

* hdl1 (handle) - Handle to an object.
* hdl2 (handle) - Handle to an object.
Returns: 1 (TRUE) if the two handles refer to the same object; otherwise, 0 (FALSE).

[2:0] sa;

initial begin: init_blk
parameter p1 = 1;
// left [1]; right [1]
regArr[1] = regArr[1];
regArr[idx0+1] = regArr[2'b01];
regArr[p0+p1] = regArr[p1];
regArr[p0+1] = regArr[p0+p1];
// left [0][0]; right [0][0]
regArr[0][0] = regArr[0][0];
regArr[0][idx0] = regArr[0][idx0];
regArr[idx0][0] = regArr[idx0][1-1];
regArr[p0][p1*0] = regArr[p0][idx0];

// left == right
st1.a[0] = st1[38];
st1.b = st1[37];

st1.c.sb = st1.c[33:2];

lang.objects_overlap(hdl1, hdl2)
Check if two handles overlap physically.
The NPI routine objects_overlap() returns 1 (TRUE) if the two handles overlap physically.
Otherwise, 0 (FALSE) is returned. The valid input handle for objects_overlap is the handle
that belongs to vh name, simple expression, part-select or indexed part-select. the valid
input handle belongs to If any input handle doesn't belong to vh name, simple expression,
part-select or indexed part-select, objects_overlap always returns 0 (FALSE). VIA treats
the variable as arbitrary value whether the variable is not a constant. For example,
reg [2:0] pr;
parameter p = 0;
integer i = 0;
lang.objects_overlap (pr[1:0], pr[p]) # return 1
lang.objects_overlap (pr[1:0], pr[i]) # return 1; It is possible to be
overlap because VIA cannot get i's value (defined in simulation time),
treat "i" as arbitrary value.
lang.objects_overlap (pr[i:1], pr[p]) # return 0; It is impossible to be
overlap even VIA treat "i" as arbitrary value.

The following is another example:
struct packed {
int a;
reg [0:7] b;

The following is the active_trace_driver signal:

lang.active_trace_driver(sig_hier_name, time, trc_opt=None)
Find the active drivers of a signal (simple expression except operation) by its full name
based on the NPI Language Model and a specified time.
The active driver signal and statement handles are obtained by the full name
sig_hier_name and the input timing string.
The NPI Language Model handles are collected into the returned ActTrcRes object.
* time (string) - Specify the start timing string. If target source signal is not active at this
Returns: Return the ActTrcRes object.
Return type: ActTrcRes
wire w2, w3, w4;
reg Q, clk;

clk = 0;
end
always
forever #1 clk = ~clk;
always@(posedge clk)
if(w2)
Q = w3;
end
else begin
Q = w4;
end
end

lang.get_signal_define_typespec_by_hdl(sig_hdl)
Get the typespec handle of a signal from the NPI Language Model.
A typespec is a Typespec class or a VhType class.
The function uses the full hierarchy name of the signal.
For npiPartSelect, npiIndexedPartSelect, npiVhSliceName, or npiVhIndexName, it returns
the parent typespec or type handle.
Parameters: sig_hdl (handle) - Specify the target signal handle.
Returns: The typespec or type handle of the target signal.
Returns NULL if the signal has no typespec or type.

Preface
The Python Based NPI Language Model User Guide helps you to traverse designs from
the HDL language perspective.

Customer Support
Customer support is available through SolvNetPlus.

Accessing SolvNetPlus
The SolvNetPlus site includes a knowledge base of technical articles and answers to
frequently asked questions about Synopsys tools. The SolvNetPlus site also gives you
access to a wide range of Synopsys online services including software downloads,
documentation, and technical support.
To access the SolvNetPlus site, go to the following address:
https://solvnetplus.synopsys.com
If prompted, enter your user name and password. If you do not have a Synopsys user
name and password, follow the instructions to sign up for an account.
If you need help using the SolvNetPlus site, click REGISTRATION HELP in the top-right
menu bar.

Contacting Customer Support
To contact Customer Support, go to https://solvnetplus.synopsys.com.

Synopsys Statement on Inclusivity and Diversity
Synopsys is committed to creating an inclusive environment where every employee,
customer, and partner feels welcomed. We are reviewing and removing exclusionary
language from our products and supporting customer-facing collateral. Our effort also
includes internal initiatives to remove biased language from our engineering and working
environment, including terms that are embedded in our software and IPs. At the same
time, we are working to ensure that our Web content and software applications are usable
to people of varying abilities. You might still find examples of non-inclusive language in our
software or documentation as our IPs implement industry-standard specifications that are
currently under review to remove exclusionary language.

Introduction to Python Based NPI
Python-Based NPI APIs support the following six models:
* Language
* Netlist
* Waveform
* Text
* Coverage
* Waveform Writer
All models have their own APIs. These APIs enable you to traverse data objects and
obtain objects' properties such as the existing C-Based or Tcl-Based NPI APIs.
The following topics in this guide demonstrate the environment settings for using PythonBased NPI APIs for Language:
* Packages and Modules
* Module Functions and Class Objects
* User Interface and Use Flow

Packages and Modules
Packages
The Python-based NPI package name is "pynpi". It is placed at $VERDI_HOME/share/NPI/
python.

Chapter 1: Introduction to Python Based NPI
Module Functions and Class Objects

Modules
The following are the seven modules inside the pynpi package:
* npisys
* lang
* netlist
* text
* cov waveform
* waveformw
The first module, npisys, is the system model for initialization, loading design, and exit.
The others represent the language, netlist, text, coverage wave, and waveform writer
models respectively.

Module Functions and Class Objects
L0 Module Functions
Every module provides some L0 (level 0) functions to let you get the class objects.
These functions return a class object or a list of class objects. These functions follow the
specification of the existing L0 APIs provided in C or Tcl.

L1 Module Functions
Similar to L0 module functions, each module also provides some L1 (level 1) functions.
These functions enable you to get advanced information based on the results obtained
by L0 module functions. These functions follow the specification of the existing L1 APIs
provided in C or Tcl.

Class Objects
The class object is similar to the so-called handle in NPI C APIs. The main difference is
that some basic L0 APIs in C and Tcl become class methods. These L0 APIs help you
get integer values, string values, one-to-one methods for a single handle, or 1-to-many
methods for multiple handles.

Environment and Library Setting
The python library setting flow of using Python-Based NPI APIs contains four parts:
1. Verify the version of Python you are using.
Python-Based NPI APIs need the Python version greater than 3.6.0.
2. Configure the VERDI_HOME environment variable before you run any program that uses
the Python-based NPI.
3. Add the cross-platform Python library path to your code before loading the Pythonbased NPI by using the following commands:
import platform
arch = platform.machine()
if arch == "x86_64":
arch = "linux64"
sys.path.append(os.path.abspath(os.environ["VERDI_HOME"] + "/share/NPI/lib/" +
arch))

4. Import the module "npisys" from the package pynpi for using the NPI initialization and
exit functions.

5. Import the module you need from the "pynpi" package. For example, if you want to use
the language model, import the module as follows:

Module npisys
This chapter contains the following topics:
* Overview
* L0 APIs
* NPI General Options

Overview
Module npisys is for setting Python-based NPI. You must call npisys.init() before using
any other NPI modules and call npisys.end() after using any other NPI modules.

L0 APIs
Following are the public L0 APIs for system module:
* npisys.init(pyArgvList)
* npisys.load_design(pyArgvList)
* npisys.end()

npisys.init(pyArgvList)
System initialization for Python-Based NPI.
Parameters: pyArgList (str list) - input argument list, for example, sys.argv
Returns: Return 1 if successful. Otherwise, return 0.
Example:
>>>npisys.init(sys.argv)

Chapter 2: Module npisys
NPI General Options

npisys.load_design(pyArgvList)
Load design for Python-Based NPI.
Parameters: pyArgList (str list) - input argument list, for example, sys.argv
Returns: Return 1 if successful. Otherwise, return 0.
Example:
>>>npisys.load_design(sys.argv)

Clean NPI-related settings and data.
Parameters: none
Returns: Return 1 if successful. Otherwise, return 0.
Example:
>>>npisys.end()

Python-Based NPI Language Model
This chapter contains the following topics:
* Overview
* Quick Start

Overview
NPI Language Model contains three language models:
* SystemVerilog Model
* VHDL Model
* SystemC Model
It lets users traverse designs from the HDL language perspective. Every construct in the
language is regarded as an object.
For NPI Language - SystemVerilog Model, the IEEE Std 1800 -2009 SystemVerilog
Language Reference Manual (LRM) is applied as the foundation of it. Most of the
SystemVerilog object model diagrams are similar to VPI Object Model Diagram in LRM
Chapter 37. For NPI Language - VHDL Model, the IEEE Std1076 -2008 VHDL Language
Reference Manual (LRM) is applied as the foundation of it. However, the style of the VHDL
object model diagrams follows NPI Language - SystemVerilog Model.
Refer to API Reference to see all the APIs that are used in the Language Model. Refer to
supported properties and methods of each object type to understand the HDL language
structure and to learn how to traverse designs via the Language Model.

Quick Start
Environment and library setting:
1. Use Python version greater than 3.6.0.
2. Update LD_LIBRARY_PATH to access NPI shared library put in Verdi release package.

Class Objects
This chapter contains the following topics:
* Supported Properties and Methods
* Mixed Design Objects
* SystemVerilog Objects
* VHDL Objects
* SystemC Objects

Supported Properties and Methods
All possible relationships and properties that an object might have are documented in
the form of object diagrams, which use enclosures to represent objects and arrows to
represent the type of relationship.
The 1-1 relationship is named "tag_handle()", for example, "hdl.scope_handle()" returns
the Scope handle of hdl.
The 1-m relationship is named "tag_handles()", for example,
"hdl.internal_scope_handles()" returns a list of all internal scopes of hdl.
A property might return an integer or a string. If the property supports both integer and
string, the option "is_get_enum" is used to control the output format. For example, the
property "Type" supports both integer and string, the propery is defined by the following
syntax:
def type(self, is_get_enum=False)

Default value of "is_get_enum" is False. "hdl.type()" returns object type in a string and
"hdl.type(True)" returns object type in an integer.
All objects have three common properties:
1. LangType: It shows the language type, and the returned property type is
CommonUseLang (for every language model could be used in mixed design), SvLang
(for SystemVerilog Model), VhdlLang (for VHDL Model) or ScLang (for SystemC
Model).

2. BelongToHierObj: It shows if the object belongs to hierarchy scope. If this object
is non scope object (for example, constant and vh literal)., the return value of this
property is always 0. Refer to Vh Design Unit and UDP.
3. Instrumented: If the object is instrumented by VCS with MVSIM NLP (Native Low
Power) mode, the returned value is 1. Otherwise, the returned value is 0.

Mixed design objects include the SystemVerilog Model, VHDL Model, and SystemC
Model.

handle_by_name
lang.handle_by_name(name, hdl)
Get a handle to an object with a specific name.
The NPI routine handle_by_name returns a handle to an object with a specific name.
This function can be applied to all objects with a fullname property. The name can be
hierarchical or simple. If scope is NULL (C/C++), empty string "" (Tcl), or None (Python)
then the name is searched for from the top level of hierarchy. If a scope object is provided,
then search within that scope only.
* name (string) - A character string or pointer to a string containing the name of an
object.
* scope (handle) - Handle to a SystemVerilog scope.
Returns: the handle to an object.
module Counter (input wire clock, resetN,
output logic [15:0] count);
always @(posedge clock, negedge resetN) begin : B1
if( !resetN ) count <= 0;
else count <= count + 1;
end
module TEST;
wire [15:0] count;
bit clock;
bit resetN = 1;
Counter dut (clock, resetN, count);
always #10 clock = ~clock;
resetN = 0;
#2 resetN = 1;
#1 $finish;

handle_by_name

end

to all objects that can be sliced by left and right range, for example getting a partselect from a bit-var. If the input left range is equal to the right range, the functionality of

lang.release_handle(hdl)
Release a handle and its associated resources allocated by NPI routines.
The NPI routine release_handle frees memory allocated for NPI handles. NPI might
allocate memory when a handle to an object is obtained. One might safely ignore calling
release_handle when a handle is no longer needed, but it is always recommended to do
so, provided the handle is valid and does not automatically become invalid in the future. A
guideline for better memory usage is to release the created handles whenever they are no
longer needed. This avoids logical memory leaks.
release_handle might not be called on an invalid handle.
Parameters: hdl (handle) - Handle to an object.

release_handle

Returns: Returns 1 (true) if the NPI memory management system releases the memory
used by the object. Returns 0 (false) if NPI does not free the memory of the object
because there might be another application program using it.

hier_tree_dump_txt
lang.hier_tree_dump_txt(root_scope, file)
Dump the hierarchical tree view of a scope.
The hierarchical tree view of a scope, specified by its name root_scope, is dumped into a
text file. If root_scope is NULL, the hierarchy tree from the SV top modules, VHDL root or
SC top instance in the design is dumped.
* root_scope (string) - Specify the name of the target scope.
* file (file()) - Specify the pointer to the output file.
Returns: Return 0 if the corresponding scope cannot be found; otherwise, return 1.

generate
genvar i;

end
endgenerate

MOD inst1();

hier_tree_trv_register_cb
lang.hier_tree_trv_register_cb(obj_type, cb_func, cb_data)
Register a callback function for hier_tree_trv.
The API hier_tree_trv_register_cb links a user callback and its data to hier_tree_trv.
You can register callbacks for object types that you can iterate from a scope.
hier_tree_trv calls the callback when it visits the matching object type.
Also see hier_tree_trv and hier_tree_trv_reset_cb.
Note: the callback receives the object handle as an argument.
NPI releases the handle when the callback returns.

To keep the object, call set_permanent to mark it as "permanent".

The API scope_explore_register_cb links a user callback and its data to scope_explore.
You can register callbacks for object types that you can iterate from a scope.

Introduction to Python Based NPI
Python-Based NPI APIs support the following six models:
* Language
* Netlist
* Waveform
* Text
* Coverage
* Waveform Writer
All models have their own APIs.
These APIs let you traverse data objects and get object properties.
They work like the existing C-Based and Tcl-Based NPI APIs.
* Packages and Modules
* Module Functions and Class Objects
* User Interface and Use Flow

Packages and Modules
Packages
The Python-based NPI package name is "pynpi". It is placed at $VERDI_HOME/share/NPI/
python.

Chapter 1: Introduction to Python Based NPI
Module Functions and Class Objects

Modules
The following are the seven modules inside the pynpi package:
* npisys
* lang
* netlist
* text
* cov waveform
* waveformw
The first module, npisys, is the system model for initialization, loading design, and exit.
The others represent the language, netlist, text, coverage wave, and waveform writer
models respectively.

Module Functions and Class Objects

L0 Module Functions
Every module provides some L0 (level 0) functions to let you get the class objects.
These functions return a class object or a list of class objects. These functions follow the
specification of the existing L0 APIs provided in C or Tcl.

L1 Module Functions
Similar to L0 module functions, each module also provides some L1 (level 1) functions.
These functions enable you to get advanced information based on the results obtained
by L0 module functions. These functions follow the specification of the existing L1 APIs
provided in C or Tcl.

Class Objects
The class object is similar to the so-called handle in NPI C APIs. The main difference is
that some basic L0 APIs in C and Tcl become class methods. These L0 APIs help you get
integer values, string values, one-to-one methods to get a handle, and 1-to-many methods
to get a handle iterator.

User Interface and Use Flow
This chapter describes the user interface and use flow for Python-Based NPI APIs.

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Environment and Library Setting
The python library setting flow of using Python-Based NPI APIs contains four parts:
1. Verify the version of Python you are using.
Python-Based NPI APIs need the Python version greater than 3.6.0.
2. Configure the VERDI_HOME environment variable before you run any program that uses
the Python-based NPI.
3. Add the cross-platform Python library path to your code before loading the Pythonbased NPI by using the following commands:
import platform
arch = platform.machine()
if arch == "x86_64":
arch = "linux64"
sys.path.append(os.path.abspath(os.environ["VERDI_HOME"] + "/share/NPI/lib/" +
arch))

4. Import the module "npisys" from the package pynpi for using the NPI initialization and
exit functions.
from pynpi import npisys

5. Import the module you need from the "pynpi" package. For example, if you want to use
netlist model, import the module as follows:
from pynpi importnetlist

6. Note that initialization function npisys.init() must be called before writing your code
by using any other modules. Besides,npisys.end() should be called after finishing
your code. Following is a simple example to demonstrate how to use the netlist model
by Python-Based NPI APIs.
The following is a Python program to use NPI netlist model: (demo.py)
import sys
import os
import platform
arch = platform.machine()
if arch == "x86_64":
arch = "linux64"
sys.path.append(os.path.abspath(os.environ["VERDI_HOME"] + "/share/NPI/lib/"
+ arch))
from pynpi import npisys
from pynpi import netlist

Module npisys
Module npisys is for setting Python-based NPI. You have to call npisys.init() before
using any other NPI modules and call npisys.end() after using any other NPI modules.
* L0 APIs

L0 APIs
Following are the public L0 APIs for system module:
* npisys.init(pyArgvList)
* npisys.load_design(pyArgvList)
* npisys.end()

npisys.init(pyArgvList)
System initialization for Python-Based NPI.
Parameters: pyArgList (str list) - input argument list, for example, sys.argv
Returns: Return 1 if successful. Otherwise, return 0.
Example:
>>>npisys.init(sys.argv)

npisys.load_design(pyArgvList)
Load design for Python-Based NPI.
Parameters: pyArgList (str list) - input argument list. For example, sys.argv

>>>npisys.end()

Abstract
This module allows you to traverse designs from netlist perspective. The netlist is obtained
from the Verdi inference database, which can be regarded as the results of technologyindependent non optimized synthesis results.
In netlist model, a design only consists of four kinds of objects: instance, port, instance
port, and net.
Figure 1

Netlist Instance

RTL Configurations

If you import design with symbol libraries, then there is three other kinds of objects: library,
cell, and cell pin. The connectivity relationship is provided along with Classes.

RTL Configurations
The following table lists NPI options and their descriptions:
NPI Options

Description

DetailRTL

If set, instances are inferred in detailed view.

DetailMux

If set, unintended latches is extracted as MUX. This works only
when DetailRTL is set.

RecogFSM

If set, FSM recognition applies to the inferred objects.

GenBlock

If set, the generate block at the architecture level is expanded.
Therefore, the individual instances ise inferred.

InferenceLibCell

If set, cells with celldefine/endcelldesign, or imported with the
-v or -y options, is recognized as modules. Works only when the
symbol libraries does not exist.

RecogMem

If set, the memory block at the architecture level is expanded.
Individual instances are inferred.
There is no effect when the block is at the RTL level.

Properties and Enum
All objects have the following common properties:
1. type: It shows the type of the netlist handle.
A InstHdl object's type is ObjectType.INST.

A PinHdl object's type can be [ ObjectType.PORT, ObjectType.INSTPORT ] based on
its role, or [ ObjectType.PSEUDO_PORT, ObjectType.PSEUDO_INSTPORT] when it's
part-selected.
A NetHdl object's type can be [ ObjectType.DECL_NET, ObjectType.CONCAT_NET,
ObjectType.SLICE_NET] based on its declaration in design, or
ObjectType.PSEUDO_NETwhen it's part-selected.
A LibHdl object's type is ObjectType.LIB ObjectType.LIB.
A CellHdl object's type is ObjectType.CELL.
A CellPinHdl object's type is ObjectType.CELLPIN.
2. name and full_name: the short name and full hierarchical name for the handle.
3. info: The information string of a InstHdl in style "type, full_name, src_info." And "type,
full_name" for handle of other classes.
A property of handle might return an integer or a string. If the property supports both
integer and string, the option get_enum is used to control the output format.
For example, property lang_type defined by the following syntax:
def lang_type(self, get_enum=False)

An exception is the property type, it returns an IntEnum of class netlist. ObjectType when
get_enum set True.
All the property strings and integer are listed in: Property, Strings, and Integers.

class netlist. InstHdl(cps_obj)
InstHdl includes two types: module instance and primitive instance.
* Module Instance:
A module reference in the design that serves as a container for sub instance, port,
instance port, and net objects.
* Primitive Instance:
Denotes the minimum design unit. It is used to represent low-level logic gates and
switches with specific cell functions. For example, npiNlAndCell, npiNlFSMCell, and
npiNlBufCell.
You can query a InstHdl by public functions, either by get_inst(), or traverse by
get_top_inst_list()get_top_inst_list(), and InstHdl.inst_list().

class netlist.PinHdl(cps_obj)
PinHdl includes two types: port and instance port.
Port:
A port object represents the port defined in a module instance. It is used to communicate
between instance port and net objects belonging to the module instance.
Instance Port:
An instance port object represents the port instance along with the instance object. It is
used to communicate between instance and net objects connected outside the instance.
You can query a PinHdl by public functions, either by get_port(), get_instport(), or traverse
by InstHdl.port_list(), InstHdl.instport_list().

class netlist.NetHdl(cps_obj)
A net object represents physical connections between PinHdl objects.

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
NetHdl includes three types: decl net, slice net, and concat net.
Decl net:
Represents the full bus of a declared net.
Slice net:
Represents a variable slice in the source code.
Concat net:
An object concatenated with decl net and slice net objects.
Following is an example:
module top;
wire [3:0] a, b;
wire [5:0] c = {a[2:0],b[1:0]};

Where a[3:0] and b[3:0] are decl nets; a[2:0] and b[1:0] are slice nets; And a[2:0],b[1:0] is
a concat net.
You can query a NetHdl by public functions or traversed by get_net() or traversed by
InstHdl.net_list().

Tracing Callback Function
netlist.register_cb(func_type, cb_func, cb_data)
Register callback function as it creates the association between user-defined callback
function/data and specific connection functions.
* func_type (FuncType) - Function type to be registered.
* cb_func (function) - The callback function is called when each handle is traversed. If
the function returns False, the tracing is stopped on that handle.
* cb_data (object) - The callback data.
Returns: Returns 1 if the callback function is valid to be registered; otherwise, returns 0.

This code registers a callback function to collect AND cells when tracing. Besides, it stops
trace while encounter the OR cell.
>>> def cb_func(hdl, cb):
inst = hdl.scope_inst()
cellType = inst.cell_type()
if cellType == 'npiNlOrCell':
return False
if cellType == 'npiNlAndCell':
cb.append(inst)
return True
