Introduction to Python Based NPI
Python-Based NPI APIs support six models. They are as follows:
* Text
* Language
* Netlist
* Coverage
* Waveform
* Waveform Writer
Each model have their own APIs to let you be able to traverse data objects and obtain
objects' properties like the existing C-Based or Tcl-Based NPI APIs.
In this guide, the environment setting for using Python-Based NPI APIs for Text is
demonstrated.
* Packages and Modules
* Module Functions and Class Objects
* User Interface and Use Flow

Packages and Modules
This section describes the packages and modules.

Packages
The Python-based NPI package name is "pynpi", and it is placed at $VERDI_HOME/share/
NPI/python location.

Chapter 1: Introduction to Python Based NPI
Module Functions and Class Objects

Modules
There are seven modules inside the "pynpi" package: npisys, lang, netlist, text, cov
waveform, and waveformw. The first module, npisys, is the system model for initialization,
loading design and exit. The other modules represent language model, netlist model, text
model, coverage model, wave model, and waveform writer model respectively.

Module Functions and Class Objects
This section describes the module functions and class objects.

L0 Module Functions
Every module provides some L0 (level 0) functions to let you get the class objects. These
functions return a class object or a list of class objects, and they follow the specification of
the existing L0 APIs provided in C or Tcl.

L1 Module Functions
Similar to L0 module functions, every module also provides some L1 (level 1) functions to
let you get advanced information based on the results obtained by L0 module functions.
These functions follows the specification of the existing L1 APIs provided in C or Tcl.

The class object is similar to the so-called handle in NPI C APIs. The most difference is
that some basic L0 APIs in C and Tcl becomes class method function. These L0 APIs are
usually to get integer value, string value, one-to-one method to get a handle, and 1-tomany method to get handle iterator.

Environment and Library Setting:
The python library setting flow of using Python-Based NPI APIs contains four parts:
1. Check your Python's version:
Python-Based NPI APIs need the Python version greater than 3.6.0.
2. Environment setting for "VERDI_HOME" is required for Python-based NPI. Ensure that
you set it before running the program.
3. Add the cross-platform Python library path to your code before loading the Pythonbased NPI by using the following commands:
import platform
arch = platform.machine()
if arch == "x86_64":
arch = "linux64"
sys.path.append(os.path.abspath(os.environ["VERDI_HOME"] + "/share/NPI/lib/" +
arch))

4. Import "npisys" module for using the function of NPI initialization and exit from pynpi
package.
from pynpi import npisys

5. Import the module you need from pynpi package. For example, to import text module,
use the following command:
from pynpi import text

6. Note that initialization function npisys.init() must be called before writing your code
by using any other modules. Also, you must call npisys.end() after finishing your
code. Following is a simple example to demonstrate how to use text model by PythonBased NPI APIs.

Module npisys is for setting Python-based NPI. You must call npisys.init() before using
any other NPI modules and call npisys.end() after using any other NPI modules.

Python-Based NPI Text Model
This chapter includes the following topics:
* Overview
* Quick Start
* Class Objects
* L0 APIs

Overview
The NPI Text Model helps you to traverse or manipulate design source codes from a text
perspective. Every file, line, and word is regarded as an object and the traversing and
manipulative APIs are provided.
In addition to the basic insert, delete, and replace capabilities, you can also access the
attribute of each word from the design analysis results of the Verdi system.

Quick Start
This section describes the design, example code, and result as follows:
* Design (inc.v)
* Example Code:
* Execution Result

Design (inc.v)
define TOP(a,b) a + b - 1
module top (input clk);
initial
$display( TOP( TOP(2,3), TOP(22,33) ) );
endmodule

Quick Start

title: Verification ContinuumTM

import sys
import os
rel_lib_path = os.environ['VERDI_HOME'] + '/share/NPI/python'
sys.path.append(os.path.abspath(rel_lib_path))
from pynpi import npisys
from pynpi import text
# -- init -------------------------------------------------------------res = npisys.init(sys.argv)
if res != 1:
print('[Error] Failed to do npi init')
sys.exit(1)
# -- load design ------------------------------------------------------res = npisys.load_design(sys.argv)
if res != 1:
print('[Error] Failed to do npi load design')
sys.exit(1)
# -- get file list ----------------------------------------------------textFileList = text.get_file_list()
if len(textFileList) <= 0:
print('[Error] Failed to get file hdl')
sys.exit(1)
# -- traverse all files and words and expand macro and show macro
information after $display -----for file in textFileList:
lineList = file.line_handles()
for line in lineList:
if (line.line_content().find('$display') > 0):
print(line.line_content())
wordList = line.word_handles()
for word in wordList:
if (word.word_attribute() == 'npiTextMacroName'):
macro = word.text_macro()
print("** macro name: %s" %(word.word_name()));
print("** macro is ok: %d" %(macro.ok()))
print("** macro arg num: %d" %(macro.arg_num()))
print("** macro value: %s" %(macro.value()))
for i in range(macro.arg_num()):
print("** macro arg (%d): %s" %(i, macro.arg(i)))
print("** macro def file: %s" %(macro.def_file()))
print("** macro def line: %d" %(macro.def_line()))
print("** macro def value: %s" %(macro.def_value()))
for i in range(macro.arg_num()):
print("** macro def arg (%d): %s" %(i, macro.def_arg(i)))
if (word.expand_macro() == 1):
print(' ===> expand macro test ok!')
print(line.line_content())
# -- end --------------------------------------------------------------npisys.end()

Note:

Introduction to Python-Based NPI
Python-Based NPI APIs support seven models:
* Coverage
* Language
* Netlist
* Text
* Transaction Waveform Model
* Waveform
* Waveform Writer
Each model have their own APIs to let you be able to traverse data objects and obtain
objects' properties like the existing C-Based or Tcl-Based NPI APIs.
In this guide, the environment setting for using Python-Based NPI Transaction
Waveform Model is demonstrated.
* Packages and Modules
* Module Functions and Class Objects
* User Interface and Use Flow

Packages and Modules
Packages
The Python-based NPI package name is "pynpi", and it is placed at $VERDI_HOME/share/
NPI/python.

Chapter 1: Introduction to Python-Based NPI
Module Functions and Class Objects

Modules
There are seven modules inside the "pynpi" package: npisys, lang, netlist, text, cov
waveform and waveformw. The first module, npisys, is the system model for initialization,
loading design and exit. The other modules represent language model, netlist model, text
model, coverage model, wave model and waveform writer model respectively

Module Functions and Class Objects
L0 Module Functions
Every module provides some L0 (level 0) functions to let you get the class objects. These
functions return a class object or a list of class objects, and they follow the specification of
the existing L0 APIs provided in C or Tcl.

L1 Module Functions
Similar to L0 module functions, every module also provides some L1 (level 1) functions to
let you get advanced information based on the results obtained by L0 module functions.
These functions follows the specification of the existing L1 APIs provided in C or Tcl.

Class Objects
The class object is similar to the so-called handle in NPI C APIs. The most difference is
that some basic L0 APIs in C and Tcl becomes class method function. These L0 APIs are
usually to get integer value, string value, one-to-one method to get a handle, and 1-tomany method to get handle iterator.

User Interface and Use Flow
Environment and Library Setting
The python library setting flow of using Python-Based NPI APIs contains four parts:
1. Check your Python's version:
Python-Based NPI APIs need the Python version greater than 3.6.0.
2. Environment setting for "VERDI_HOME" is required for Python-based NPI. Ensure that
you set it up before running program.

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Chapter 1: Introduction to Python-Based NPI
User Interface and Use Flow

3. Add the cross-platform Python library path to your code before loading the Pythonbased NPI by using the following commands:
import platform
arch = platform.machine()
if arch == "x86_64":
arch = "linux64"
sys.path.append(os.path.abspath(os.environ["VERDI_HOME"] + "/share/NPI/lib/" +
arch))

4. Import module "npisys" for using the function of NPI initialization and exit from pynpi
package.

5. Import the module you need from pynpi package. For example, if you want to use
Coverage model, you can import module like the following:
from pynpi import cov

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
6. Note that initialization functionnpisys.init() must be called before writing your code
by using any other modules. Also, you must call npisys.end() after finishing your
code. Following is a simple example to demonstrate how to use coverage model by
Python-Based NPI APIs.
Python program to use NPI models: (demo.py)
import platform
arch = platform.machine()
if arch == "x86_64":
arch = "linux64"
sys.path.append(os.path.abspath(os.environ["VERDI_HOME"] + "/share/NPI/lib/"
+ arch))
from pynpi import cov
# Initialize NPI
if not npisys.init(sys.argv):
print("Error: Fail to initialize NPI")
assert 0
# Load design (if needed, depends on models)
if not npisys.load_design(sys.argv):
print("Error: Fail to load design")
assert 0
# Beginning of your code here -------------------#
# Example code can be found in later chapters
#
# End of your code ------------------------------# End NPI

def stream_trt_info( trt ):

print("\nstream_trt_info.")
if trt.goto_first():
while True:
print("trt name: ", trt.name(), "trt id: ", trt.id(), "trt time:
", trt.time() )
num = trt.attr_count()
if 36 < num: #use the 36th's attr as example
print("trt attr name: ", trt.attr_name(36), " attr value is : ",
trt.attr_value(36))
print("Property: Hidden? ", trt.attr_is_hidden(36), " Tag? " ,
trt.attr_is_tag(36), " default format: " , trt.attr_value_format(36) )
exnum = trt.expected_attr(36)
if exnum:
print("trt expected attr name: ", trt.attr_name(exnum), "
expected attr value is : ", trt.attr_value(exnum))
ret = trt.goto_next()
if not ret:
break
def trt_related_info( trt , rel_list ):
print("\ntrt_related_info.")
if trt.goto_time(5500000):
while True:
for rel in rel_list:
trt_list = trt.related_trt_list( rel ,
waveform.RelationDirType_e.Master)
for rtrt in trt_list:
print( "Dir Master" , trt.name()," related_trt is ", rtrt.name(),
" relation: " , rel.name() )
trt_list = trt.related_trt_list( rel ,
waveform.RelationDirType_e.Slave)
for rtrt in trt_list:
print( "Dir Slave" , trt.name()," related_trt is ", rtrt.name(),
" relation: " , rel.name() )
ret = trt.goto_prev()
if not ret:
break
def dump_tr_call_stack( trt ):
print("\ndump_tr_call_stack.")
type_name = ["Message","Transaction","Action","Group"]
if trt.goto_time(28000000):
while True:
type = trt.type()
if type != None:
print("trt type: ", type_name[type] )
print("time: ", trt.time() ," unfinished? ",
trt.is_unfinished() )
num = trt.call_stack_count()
if num: # use num-1 as example
print("call stack(begin): ", trt.call_stack(num-1) )
num = trt.call_stack_count(waveform.CallStackType_e.End)
if num: # use num-1 as example
print("call stack(end): ", trt.call_stack(num-1,
waveform.CallStackType_e.End) )

ret = trt.goto_next()
if not ret:
break
if __name__ == '__main__':
orig_stdout = sys.stdout
f = open('trt.log', 'w')
sys.stdout = f
fileHandle = waveform.open("tr_wave/begin_end_call_stack.fsdb")
if fileHandle is None:
print(" open waveform fail." )
quit()
rel_list = fileHandle.relation_list()
trt = fileHandle.trt_by_id( 998 ) #use trt's id: 998 as example.
stream = trt.stream()
fileHandle.load_trans()
print("trt stream name:" , stream.name())
stream_trt_info(trt)
trt_related_info(trt, rel_list)
dump_tr_call_stack(trt)
trt.release()
fileHandle.unload_trans()
fileHandle.reset_stream_list()

def stream_trt_info( trt ):

print("\nstream_trt_info.")
if trt.goto_first():
while True:
print("trt name: ", trt.name(), "trt id: ", trt.id(), "trt time:
", trt.time() )
num = trt.attr_count()
if 36 < num: #use the 36th's attr as example
print("trt attr name: ", trt.attr_name(36), " attr value is : ",
trt.attr_value(36))
print("Property: Hidden? ", trt.attr_is_hidden(36), " Tag? " ,
trt.attr_is_tag(36), " default format: " , trt.attr_value_format(36) )
exnum = trt.expected_attr(36)
if exnum:
print("trt expected attr name: ", trt.attr_name(exnum), "
expected attr value is : ", trt.attr_value(exnum))
ret = trt.goto_next()
if not ret:
break
def trt_related_info( trt , rel_list ):
print("\ntrt_related_info.")
if trt.goto_time(5500000):
while True:
for rel in rel_list:
trt_list = trt.related_trt_list( rel ,
waveform.RelationDirType_e.Master)
for rtrt in trt_list:
print( "Dir Master" , trt.name()," related_trt is ", rtrt.name(),
" relation: " , rel.name() )
trt_list = trt.related_trt_list( rel ,
waveform.RelationDirType_e.Slave)
for rtrt in trt_list:
print( "Dir Slave" , trt.name()," related_trt is ", rtrt.name(),
" relation: " , rel.name() )
ret = trt.goto_prev()
if not ret:
break

Introduction to Python Based NPI
Python-Based NPI APIs support seven models. They are as follows:
* Waveform Writer
* Waveform
* Transaction Waveform Writer
* Netlist
* Text
* Coverage
* Language
Each model have their own APIs to let you be able to traverse data objects and obtain
objects' properties like the existing C-Based or Tcl-Based NPI APIs.
In this guide, the environment setting for using Python-Based NPI APIs for Transaction
Waveform Writer is demonstrated.
* Packages and Modules
* Module Functions and Class Objects
* User Interface and Use Flow

Packages and Modules
Packages
The Python-based NPI package name is "pynpi", and it is placed at $VERDI_HOME/share/
NPI/python.

Chapter 1: Introduction to Python Based NPI
Module Functions and Class Objects

Modules
There are seven modules inside the "pynpi" package: npisys, lang, netlist, text, cov
waveform, and waveformw. The first module, npisys, is the system model for initialization,
loading design and exit. The other modules represent language model, netlist model, text
model, coverage model, wave model, and waveform writer model respectively

Module Functions and Class Objects
L0 Module Functions
Every module provides some L0 (level 0) functions to let you get the class objects. These
functions return a class object or a list of class objects, and they follow the specification of
the existing L0 APIs provided in C or Tcl.

L1 Module Functions
Similar to L0 module functions, every module also provides some L1 (level 1) functions to
let you get advanced information based on the results obtained by L0 module functions.
These functions follows the specification of the existing L1 APIs provided in C or Tcl.

Class Objects
The class object is similar to the so-called handle in NPI C APIs. The most difference is
that some basic L0 APIs in C and Tcl iscome class method function. These L0 APIs are
usually to get integer value, string value, one-to-one method to get a handle, and 1-tomany method to get handle iterator.

Environment and Library Setting
The python library setting flow of using Python-Based NPI APIs contains four parts:
1. Check your Python's version:
Python-Based NPI APIs need the Python version greater than 3.6.0.
2. Environment setting for "VERDI_HOME" is required for Python-based NPI. Remember to
set it well before running program.
3. Add the cross-platform Python library path to your code before loading the Pythonbased NPI by using the following commands:
import platform
arch = platform.machine()
if arch == "x86_64":
arch = "linux64"
sys.path.append(os.path.abspath(os.environ["VERDI_HOME"] + "/share/NPI/lib/" +
arch))

4. Import module "npisys" for using the function of NPI initialization and exit from pynpi
package.

5. Import the module you need from pynpi package. For example, if you want to use
waveform writer model, you can import the module as follows:
from pynpi import waveformw

6. Note that initialization function npisys.init() must be called before writing your code
by using any other modules. Also, npisys.end() must be called after finishing your
code. Following is a simple example to demonstrate how to use waveform writer model
by Python-Based NPI APIs.
Python program to use NPI waveform writer model: (demo.py)
import sys
import os
import platform
arch = platform.machine()
if arch == "x86_64":
arch = "linux64"
sys.path.append(os.path.abspath(os.environ["VERDI_HOME"] + "/share/NPI/lib/"
+ arch))
from pynpi import waveformw
# Initialize NPI
if not npisys.init(sys.argv):
print("Error: Fail to initialize NPI")
assert 0
# Load design (if needed, depends on models)
if not npisys.load_design(sys.argv):
print("Error: Fail to load design")

Illegal Cases of Different Handles
To ensure the given handle is valid, most of the APIs checks the handle validation and
returns the error message, if invalid. There are some possible reasons for causing the
failure.
* Use the handle which is not created by calling the corresponding API. The API for
creating the handle is as following:
1. Transaction FileHandle: create_tr().
2. Stream Handle: TrFileHandle.stream_begin().
3. Transaction Handle: StreamHandle.trans_begin().
* Use the handle which is already closed. The API for closing the handle is as following:
1. Transaction FileHandle: close().
2. Stream Handle: StreamHandle.end().
3. Transaction Handle: TransHandle.end().
* For few APIs, the given handles should be closed before used; else, the error is issued.
The APIs are as listed in the following:
1. StreamHandle.trans_begin(): The given stream handle should be
closed(StreamHandle.end()) in advance.
2. TransHandle.add_relation(): The given transaction handles - master (self) and
slave should be closed (TransHandle.end()) in advance.

Data Types of Attributes
This section summarizes the Verdi transaction data type categories and their definitions
including Transaction, Stream, Attribute, and Transaction Relation.

Illegal Cases of Different Handles

* Transaction: Transaction is a one entry of data input by user code (for example,
an UVM message) and it contains attributes of different data types. For maximum
flexibility, transactions can be in different types. The predefined transaction types are
as following:
1. TransType_e.Message: Regular transactions for printf-like logging purpose. The
transaction in this type is set as a 0-time transaction automatically, which means the
end time of this transaction is set equal to the begin time of the transaction.
2. TransType_e.Action: A zero time transaction for recording few Actions (for
example, read, write, interrupt). The transaction whose type is Action is set as
zero time automatically. Several Action transactions can be formed into a Group
transaction by adding the Rel_e.BelongTo between the Action transaction and the
Group transaction.
3. TransType_e.Transaction: A general transaction with a begin time and an end
time. Transaction can be set as zero time manually by setting the end time and the
begin time with same value.
4. TransType_e.Group: A Group contains several transactions (usually of Action
type). The begin time of this transaction is set as the begin time of its first member
transaction. Also, the end time of this transaction is set as the end time of its last
member transaction.
* Stream: A Stream is used to organize (or record as a Group in the FSDB file) a
temporal sequence of transactions grouped by some criteria, for example, transactions
originating from the same UVM component can be put into one stream. Different
streams cannot share the same transaction. Some streams have hierarchies (for
example, following the UVM component hierarchy), some do not (for example, UVM
phases, objections). Streams might form different hierarchies (for example, UVM
component hierarchy and sequence hierarchy).
* Attribute: An Attribute is a characteristic or property of a specific scope, stream, or
transaction.
* Transaction Relation: A Relation is a link between two transactions. It can be defined
using the API TransHandle.add_relation(). The parameter relation can be as
following:
1. Rel_e.BelongTo: It indicates the belong relation between two transactions, that
is, first transaction Master belongs to second transaction Slave. The transaction
Slave can only be in TransType_e.Group type and the transaction Master
cannot be in TransType_e.Group type. In practical terms, Master is always in
TransType_e.Action type and Slave has several transactions belonging to it.
2. Rel_e.AnnotateTo: It indicates the annotative relation between two transactions,
that is, first transaction Master (annotator) annotates to second transaction Slave
(annotate). Master can only be in TransType_e.Message type.

Enums

3. Rel_e.ParentChild: It indicates the layering relation between two
transactions, that is, first transaction Master is a parent and second transaction
Slave is a child. This relation is valid only if both Master and Slave are in
TransType_e.Transaction type. Master (parent) and Slave (child) in different
streams are allowable for this relation.
4. Rel_e.PredSucc: It indicates the ordering/triggering relation between two
transactions, that is, first transaction Master is a predecessor and transaction Slave
is a successor. The begin time of the transaction Master should be less than the
begin time of the transaction Slave.
5. User-defined string: It means the user can define the relation between two
transactions.

Create a Transaction waveform file with a given file name in current working directory.
* name - Name of the waveform file to be opened for writing. If name is omitted, the
default value is novas.fsdb.
* unit - The scale unit of this file. If unit is omitted, the default value is "1ns". If the scale
unit should be set as 10ns,user can give a string "10ns" as a unit for this API. Scale
unit should be set as [1, 10, 100][s, ms, us, ns, ps, fs]. It is set as 1 ns, if other value is
given.
* beginTime - The begin time of simulation for this Waveform file. If beginTime is
omitted, the begin time of this file is set as 0.

class waveformw.AttrFactory(name=None, val=None, type=None,
expectVal=None, radix=None, afDict=None)
AttrFactory helps users to create the attribute dictionary in spec.

name - Name of an attribute. Default value is None.
val - Attribute Value. Default value is None.
type - The AttrType_e type of Attribute Value and Expect Attribute Value. Default value is
AttrType_e.String.
expectVal - Expect Attribute Value. Default value is None.
radix - The radix Radix_e of the integer data type being used. Default value is
Radix_e.Dec.
afDict - The attribute info with dictionary type. Default value is None.

Introduction to Python Based NPI
Python-Based NPI APIs support seven models. They are as follows:
* Language
* Netlist
* Waveform
* Text
* Coverage
* Waveform Writer
* UPF
Each model have their own APIs to let you be able to traverse data objects and obtain
objects' properties.
In this guide, the environment setting for using Python-Based NPI APIs for UPF is
demonstrated.
* Packages and Modules

Packages and Modules
Packages
The Python-based NPI package name is "pynpi", and it is placed at $VERDI_HOME/share/
NPI/python.

Chapter 1: Introduction to Python Based NPI
User Interface and Use Flow

waveform, waveformw, and upf. The first module, npisys, is the system model for
initialization, loading design and exit. The other modules represent language model, netlist
model, text model, coverage model, wave model, waveform writer model, and UPF model
respectively

User Interface and Use Flow
This chapter describes the user interface and use flow for Python-Based NPI APIs.

text:
Environment and Library Setting
The python library setting flow of using Python-Based NPI APIs contains four parts:
1. Check your Python's version:
Python-Based NPI APIs need the Python version greater than 3.6.0.
2. Environment setting for "VERDI_HOME" is required for Python-based NPI. Ensure that
you set it up before running program.
3. Add the cross-platform Python library path to your code before loading the Pythonbased NPI by using the following commands:
import platform
arch = platform.machine()
if arch == "x86_64":
arch = "linux64"
sys.path.append(os.path.abspath(os.environ["VERDI_HOME"] + "/share/NPI/lib/" +
arch))

4. Import module "npisys" for using the function of NPI initialization and exit from pynpi
package.
from pynpi import npisys

5. Import the module you need from pynpi package. For example, if you want to use UPF
model, you can import the module as follows:
from pynpi import upf

6. Note that initialization function npisys.init() must be called before writing your code
by using any other modules. Besides, npisys.end() should be called after finishing
your code. Following is a simple example to demonstrate how to use UPF model by
Python-Based NPI APIs.

Chapter 1: Introduction to Python Based NPI
User Interface and Use Flow

Python program to use NPI UPF model: (demo.py)
import sys
import os
import platform
arch = platform.machine()
if arch == "x86_64":
arch = "linux64"
sys.path.append(os.path.abspath(os.environ["VERDI_HOME"] + "/share/NPI/lib/"
+ arch))
from pynpi import npisys
from pynpi import upf
# Initialize NPI
if not npisys.init(sys.argv):
print("Error: Fail to initialize NPI")
assert 0
# Beginning of your code here -------------------#
# Example code can be found in later chapters
#
# End of your code ------------------------------# End NPI
npisys.end()

Module npisys
This chapter contains the following topics:
* Overview
* L0 APIs
* NPI General Options

Overview
Module npisys is for setting Python-based NPI. You must call npisys.init() before using
any other NPI modules and call npisys.end() after using any other NPI modules.

Following are the public L0 APIs for system module:
* npisys.init(pyArgvList)
* npisys.load_design(pyArgvList)
* npisys.end()

npisys.init(pyArgvList)
System initialization for Python-Based NPI.
Parameters: pyArgList (str list) - input argument list, for example, sys.argv
Returns: Return 1 if successful. Otherwise, return 0.
Example:
>>>npisys.init(sys.argv)

Chapter 2: Module npisys
NPI General Options

npisys.load_design(pyArgvList)
Load design for Python-Based NPI.
Parameters: pyArgList (str list) - input argument list, for example, sys.argv
Returns: Return 1 if successful. Otherwise, return 0.
Example:
>>>npisys.load_design(sys.argv)

npisys.end()
Clean NPI-related settings and data.
Parameters: none
Returns: Return 1 if successful. Otherwise, return 0.
Example:
>>>npisys.end()

NPI General Options
The following table lists the NPI general options for npisys.init(). If not specified, NPI
uses the default setting:
-quiet If specified, the banner, errors, and warnings not be shown on the

console.

Python Based NPI UPF Model
Python-Based NPI Upf Model is used to provide APIs for external users getting their UPF
design information. This section describes about the following topics:
* Abstract
* Quick Start
* Properties and Enum
* Classes
* L0 APIs

Abstract
This model lets users get the power-management information from the Unified Power
Format (UPF) language perspective. For NPI Upf Model, the IEEE Standard 1801-2015
UPF Language Reference Manual (LRM) is applied as the foundation of it. Most of the
object diagrams are similar to the tables in LRM Section 10.6.
Refer to L0 APIs to see all the APIs that are used in the Upf Model. Refer to Classes to
understand the properties and relationships of each object.

An example of how to run a pyNPI Upf APIs is as follows:
* Quick Start

This topic describes the following sections:
* Environment and library setting
* Example

* Execution
* Result

Environment and library setting
1. Update LD_LIBRARY_PATH to access NPI shared library put in Verdi release package. If
there exists any error like "cannot open shared object file", add the shared library path
to LD_LIBRARY_PATH before running your Python-Based NPI program.
For example, you can set the following environment under 64-bit Linux machine by a C
shell (csh) script:
setenv LD_LIBRARY_PATH
$VERDI_HOME/share/NPI/lib/linux64:$LD_LIBRARY_PATH
setenv LD_LIBRARY_PATH
$VERDI_HOME/platform/linux64/bin:$LD_LIBRARY_PATH

2. Add python library path by the following commands:
rel_lib_path = os.environ["VERDI_HOME"] + "/share/NPI/python"
sys.path.append(os.path.abspath(rel_lib_path))

3. Import "npisys" to use the function of NPI initialization and exit.
Import "upf" to use the APIs of Upf Model.
Import libraries as follows:
from pynpi import npisys
from pynpi import upf

Each model have their own APIs to let you be able to traverse data objects and obtain
objects' properties like the existing C-Based or Tcl-Based NPI APIs.
In this guide, the environment setting for using Python-Based NPI APIs for Waveform is
demonstrated.
This chapter includes the following topics:
* Packages and Modules
* Module Functions and Class Objects
* User Interface and Use Flow

Packages and Modules
Packages
The Python-based NPI package name is "pynpi", and it is placed at $VERDI_HOME/share/
NPI/python.

Chapter 1: Introduction to Python Based NPI
Module Functions and Class Objects

Modules
There are seven modules inside the "pynpi" package: npisys, lang, netlist, text, cov
waveform and waveformw. The first module, npisys, is the system model for initialization,
loading design and exit. The other modules represent language model, netlist model, text
model, coverage model, wave model and waveform writer model respectively

Module Functions and Class Objects
L0 Module Functions
Every module provides some L0 (level 0) functions to let you get the class objects. These
functions return a class object or a list of class objects, and they follow the specification of
the existing L0 APIs provided in C or Tcl.

L1 Module Functions
Similar to L0 module functions, every module also provides some L1 (level 1) functions to
let you get advanced information based on the results obtained by L0 module functions.
These functions follows the specification of the existing L1 APIs provided in C or Tcl.

Class Objects
The class object is similar to the so-called handle in NPI C APIs. The most difference is
that some basic L0 APIs in C and Tcl iscome class method function. These L0 APIs are
usually to get integer value, string value, one-to-one method to get a handle, and 1-tomany method to get handle iterator.

Environment and Library Setting
The python library setting flow of using Python-Based NPI APIs contains four parts:
1. Check your Python's version:
Python-Based NPI APIs need the Python version greater than 3.6.0.
2. Environment setting for "VERDI_HOME" is required for Python-based NPI. Remember to
set it well before running program.

Chapter 1: Introduction to Python Based NPI
User Interface and Use Flow

3. Add the cross-platform Python library path to your code before loading the Pythonbased NPI by using the following commands:
import platform
arch = platform.machine()
if arch == "x86_64":
arch = "linux64"
sys.path.append(os.path.abspath(os.environ["VERDI_HOME"] + "/share/NPI/lib/" +
arch))

4. Import module "npisys" for using the function of NPI initialization and exit from pynpi
package.

5. Import the module you need from pynpi package. For example, if you want to use
waveform model, you can import the module as follows:

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
6. Note that initialization function npisys.init() must be called before writing your code
by using any other modules. Also, npisys.end() must be called after finishing your
code. Following is a simple example to demonstrate how to use waveform model by
Python-Based NPI APIs.
Python program to use NPI waveform model: (demo.py)
import platform
arch = platform.machine()
if arch == "x86_64":
arch = "linux64"
sys.path.append(os.path.abspath(os.environ["VERDI_HOME"] +
"/share/NPI/lib/"
+ arch))
# Initialize NPI
if not npisys.init(sys.argv):
print("Error: Fail to initialize NPI")
assert 0
# Load design (if needed, depends on models)
if not npisys.load_design(sys.argv):
print("Error: Fail to load design")
assert 0
# Beginning of your code here -------------------#
# Example code can be found in later chapters
#
# End of your code ------------------------------Verdi(R) Python-Based NPI Waveform Model

Module npisys
This chapter includes the following topics:
* Overview
* L0 APIs
* NPI General Options

Overview
Module npisys is for setting Python-based NPI. You must call npisys.init()before using
any other NPI modules and call npisys.end() after using any other NPI modules.

Following are the public L0 APIs for system module:

npisys.init(pyArgvList)
System initialization for Python-Based NPI.
Parameters: pyArgList (str list) - input argument list, for example, sys.argv
Returns: Return 1 if successful. Otherwise, return 0.
>>>npisys.init(sys.argv)

npisys.load_design(pyArgvList)
Load design for Python-Based NPI.
Parameters: pyArgList (str list) - input argument list. For example, sys.argv
Returns: Return 1 if successful. Otherwise, return 0.

Chapter 2: Module npisys
NPI General Options

>>>npisys.load_design(sys.argv)

Clean NPI-related settings and data.
Parameters: none
Returns: Return 1 if successful. Otherwise, return 0.
>>>npisys.end()

NPI General Options
The following table lists the NPI general options for npisys.init(). If not specified, NPI
uses the default setting:
-quiet If specified, the banner, errors, and warnings are not shown on the

Overview
This model provides convenient APIs to access a waveform. Performance of database
access and the programming usability are both considered in this model.

Quick Start
Following are the Environment and library setting:

rel_lib_path = os.environ["VERDI_HOME"] + "/share/NPI/
python"

Import waveform to use the APIs of Waveform Model.

linux64" and "$VERDI_HOME/platform/linux64/bin" to LD_LIBRARY_PATH:
os.environ['LD_LIBRARY_PATH'] =
os.environ['VERDI_HOME']+'/share/NPI/lib/
linux64:'+os.environ['VERDI_HOME']+'/platform/linux64/

WaveL1RC_e is an enum to identify the status of evaluation result.

SUCCESS: Successful evaluation.
FILE_DOES_NOT_EXIST: Waveform/FSDB file handle does not exist.

NO_WAVEFORM_TIMEINFO: Failed to get waveform's min or max time.
UNSUTIABLE_TIMERANGE: Invalid input time range. ( start_time > end_time or
start_time > waveform's max time..)
NO_IDENTIFIED_SIGNAME: Failed to find any signal name (use "." as delimiter) in given
expression.
EVALUATOR_ERROR: Failed to get evaluation result with the given expression.
SIG_NOT_FOUND: Failed to find at least one signal in the waveform.
SIG_HAS_MEMBER: Find a composite signal.
SIG_NO_SIZE: Find a zero-sized signal.
SIG_IS_REAL_OR_STR: Find a real or string typed signal.
NO_SIG_VALUE: Failed to get signal values.
OTHERS: Other unknown errors.
SUCCESS = 0
FILE_DOES_NOT_EXIST = 10
NO_WAVEFORM_TIMEINFO = 20
UNSUTIABLE_TIMERANGE = 21
NO_IDENTIFIED_SIGNAME = 30
EVALUATOR_ERROR = 31
SIG_NOT_FOUND = 40
SIG_HAS_MEMBER = 41
SIG_NO_SIZE = 42
SIG_IS_REAL_OR_STR = 43
NO_SIG_VALUE = 50
OTHERS = 99

Signal Value Evaluator
class waveform.SigValueEval

* Signal Value Evaluator
SigValueEval can calculate SystemVerilog expressions considering waveform values.
Currently, it supports the signal values that can be read with VctFormat_e format.
* Limitation:
Expressions contain any string/real/composite signal.

* Example:
sve.py:
def test():
# open a FSDB

fileHandle = waveform.open("novas.FSDB")
# User defined expression with the signal fullname.
expr = "top.sigA + top.sigB"
# Create a Signal Value Evaluator object
sve = waveform.SigValueEval()
# set the expression, waveform handle and time range.
sve.set_expr(expr)
sve.set_wave(fileHandle)
sve.reset_time()
sve.set_time ( 1000 , 2000 )
# Get the identifier signal name list from the given expression.
sigList = sve.get_identifier_sig_list()
for sigName in sigList:
print("sig name: ", sigName )
# evaluate to get true and false time stamp list
rc, trueL, falseL = sve.evaluate()
for mem in trueL:
print("true time: ", mem)
for mem in falseL:
print("false time: ", mem)
# evaluate to get tuple (time,value) list
rc, tvL = sve.evaluate(True)
for mem in tvL:
print("time, value: ", mem[0], " ", mem[1])
# Get posedge and negedge time stamp list
rc, posE, negE = sve.get_edge(False)
for mem in posE:
print("posedge time: ", mem)
for mem in negE:
print("negedge time: ", mem)
# Get dualedge time stamp list
rc, edge = sve.get_edge()
for mem in edge:
print("edge time: ", mem)
# Get posedge time stamp list
rc, edge = sve.get_posedge()

for mem in edge:
print("posedge time: ", mem)
# Get negedge time stamp list
rc, edge = sve.get_negedge()
for mem in edge:
print("negedge time: ", mem)
if __name__ == '__main__':
orig_stdout = sys.stdout
f = open('sig_value_eval.log', 'w')
sys.stdout = f
test()
sys.stdout = orig_stdout
f.close()

add(signal, filterEq=False)
Add a signal to the iterator.
All the signals added to iterator must be from the same waveform file object.
* signal - A waveform signal object SigHandle which is traversed later in this iterator.
* filterEq - Indicate if filtering out equivalent signals (False: not filter, True: filter).
* On success, return a number greater than 0. (Note: when filterEq is 1, the return
number for equivalent signals is the same).
* On failure, return 0.

iter_start(beginTime, endTime)
Specify the time range to iterate value changes. (All interesting signals should be added
before calling this API).
* beginTime - The begin time of vc iteration.
* endTime - The end time of vc iteration.

Iterate value changes between begin time and end time in a signal-based way.
* [signal_id, time], if success.
* [signal_id, time], if fail.
Return type: [int,int]

Stop iteration.

class waveform.SigValueEval

* Signal Value Evaluator
SigValueEval can calculate SystemVerilog expressions considering waveform values.
Currently, it supports the signal values that can be read with VctFormat_e format.
* Limitation:
Expressions contain any string/real/composite signal.

sve.py:
def test():
# open a FSDB

fileHandle = waveform.open("novas.FSDB")
# User defined expression with the signal fullname.
expr = "top.sigA + top.sigB"
# Create a Signal Value Evaluator object
sve = waveform.SigValueEval()
# set the expression, waveform handle and time range.
sve.set_expr(expr)
sve.set_wave(fileHandle)
sve.reset_time()
sve.set_time ( 1000 , 2000 )
# Get the identifier signal name list from the given expression.
sigList = sve.get_identifier_sig_list()
for sigName in sigList:
print("sig name: ", sigName )
# evaluate to get true and false time stamp list
rc, trueL, falseL = sve.evaluate()
for mem in trueL:
print("true time: ", mem)
for mem in falseL:
print("false time: ", mem)
# evaluate to get tuple (time,value) list
rc, tvL = sve.evaluate(True)
for mem in tvL:
print("time, value: ", mem[0], " ", mem[1])
# Get posedge and negedge time stamp list
rc, posE, negE = sve.get_edge(False)
for mem in posE:
print("posedge time: ", mem)
for mem in negE:
print("negedge time: ", mem)
# Get dualedge time stamp list
rc, edge = sve.get_edge()
for mem in edge:
print("edge time: ", mem)
# Get posedge time stamp list
rc, edge = sve.get_posedge()

for mem in edge:
print("posedge time: ", mem)
# Get negedge time stamp list
rc, edge = sve.get_negedge()
for mem in edge:
print("negedge time: ", mem)

test()

f.close()

reset_time()
Reset the time range (default time range is waveform's min time to max time).

set_time(begin,end)
Set time range.

* begin - Signal Value Evaluator begin time.
* end - Signal Value Evaluator end time.

set_wave(wave)
Set waveform handle.
Parameters: wave - File

set_expr(expr)
Set expression string.
Parameters: expr - Expression string.

reset_sig_map()
Reset the user-defined signal map.
>>> As sve_with_map.py shown

set_sig_map_ele(tag, sig)

* sig - SigHandle

get_sig_map_ele(tag)

Parameters: tag - Signal tag string.

get_identifier_sig_list()
Get the identifier signal name vector from the given expression.
Returns: - Signal name string list.
Return type: - list.

evaluate(timeValueMode=False)
Get the evaluation results based on the waveform and time range.
For example, the following table shows the time and value of sigA and sigB, and set
the expression as "sigA+sigB". The last row of the table shows the results according to
SystemVerilog expression definition.
time

sigA+sigB X 1 0 1 0 0 1 1 0

User can also get the ( time, value with VctFormat_e format ) results in
TimeValueTupleList.
The true (given expression function is true) / false (given expression function is false) time
stamp in TrueTimeStampList and FalseTimeStampList.

With the same example in the aforementioned table, you can get the lists as following:
* TrueTimeStampList = [10, 30, 60]

Protocol Extractor
classwaveform.ProtocolExtractor(protocol)
Protocol Extractor is an advanced API to extract the protocol from the waveform file. You
can use the protocol enum or self-defined protocol dict to get the protocol signals from the
waveform file.
The protocol extractor groups the signals based on the protocol and returns the
signal dicts for each protocol channel. The rule of grouping is based on the signal
name. Each group of signals has the same prefix name and the postfix name ("prefix
+protocol_signame+postfix") in the same scope.
For example, if the protocol is AHB, the signal name list is ["haddr", "hwrite", "htrans",
"hsize", "hburst", "hwdata", "hresp", "hready", "hrdata"]. You can get the following signal
groups:
* Group1's signal name list is ["haddr_o", "hwrite_o", "htrans_o", "hsize_o", "hburst_o",
"hwdata_o", "hresp_o", "hready_o", "hrdata_o"]
* Group2's signal name list is ["i_haddr", "i_hwrite", "i_htrans", "i_hsize", "i_hburst",
"i_hwdata", "i_hresp", "i_hready", "i_hrdata"]
Also, some of the signals can be leakage, which means the signals are not in the group.
* Group3's signal name list is ["haddr_l", "hwrite_l", "htrans_l", "hwdata_l", "hresp_l",
"hready_l", "hrdata_l"]

Additionally, ProtocolExtractor helps you to filter the signal group with essential signals,
and specify master or slave (MasterSlave_e) for each group.
VERDI APEX license is required.
Parameters: protocol -
Specify the protocol to be extracted as following:
* Protocol_e: Enum for built-in protocols.
* dict: User-defined protocol dict whose key or value pairs are:
Key(str): Protocol channel name.
Value(list(str)): Signal name list.

Message Extractor
classwaveform.MessageExtractor
MessageExtractor is an advanced API to extract the "Message" from the waveform file.
You can provide a clock signal, or a condition signal to extract the "Message".
A "Message" is a group of signals' values that is extracted from an "event". If there is a
clock signal, the "event" means the "Message" at the clock edge. If there is no clock signal,
the "Message" is extracted when one of the signal in the group has value change. The
condition signal is used to filter the "Message" when the condition signal is true.
* The clock signal is optional. You can provide the edge type of the clock
signal with keyword "posedge", "negedge" and "edge".
* The condition signal and the clock signal can be an expression with the
signal Key in the signal dict or the signal full name.
* Refer to the SigValueEval API for the expression syntax.
* VERDI APEX license is required.

classwaveform.ProtocolExtractor(protocol)
Protocol Extractor is an advanced API to extract the protocol from the waveform file. You
can use the protocol enum or self-defined protocol dict to get the protocol signals from the
waveform file.
The protocol extractor groups the signals based on the protocol and returns the
signal dicts for each protocol channel. The rule of grouping is based on the signal
name. Each group of signals has the same prefix name and the postfix name ("prefix
+protocol_signame+postfix") in the same scope.
For example, if the protocol is AHB, the signal name list is ["haddr", "hwrite", "htrans",
"hsize", "hburst", "hwdata", "hresp", "hready", "hrdata"]. You can get the following signal
groups:
* Group1's signal name list is ["haddr_o", "hwrite_o", "htrans_o", "hsize_o", "hburst_o",
"hwdata_o", "hresp_o", "hready_o", "hrdata_o"]
* Group2's signal name list is ["i_haddr", "i_hwrite", "i_htrans", "i_hsize", "i_hburst",
"i_hwdata", "i_hresp", "i_hready", "i_hrdata"]
Also, some of the signals can be leakage, which means the signals are not in the group.
* Group3's signal name list is ["haddr_l", "hwrite_l", "htrans_l", "hwdata_l", "hresp_l",
"hready_l", "hrdata_l"]

Additionally, ProtocolExtractor helps you to filter the signal group with essential signals,
and specify master or slave (MasterSlave_e) for each group.
VERDI APEX license is required.
Parameters: protocol -
Specify the protocol to be extracted as following:
* Protocol_e: Enum for built-in protocols.
* dict: User-defined protocol dict whose key or value pairs are:
Key(str): Protocol channel name.
Value(list(str)): Signal name list.
* ProtocolExtractor Function list:

Message Extractor
classwaveform.MessageExtractor
MessageExtractor is an advanced API to extract the "Message" from the waveform file.
You can provide a clock signal, or a condition signal to extract the "Message".
A "Message" is a group of signals' values that is extracted from an "event". If there is a
clock signal, the "event" means the "Message" at the clock edge. If there is no clock signal,
the "Message" is extracted when one of the signal in the group has value change. The
condition signal is used to filter the "Message" when the condition signal is true.
* The clock signal is optional. You can provide the edge type of the clock
signal with keyword "posedge", "negedge" and "edge".

condition signal is used to filter the "Message" when the condition signal is true.

* The condition signal and the clock signal can be an expression with the
signal Key in the signal dict or the signal full name.
* Refer to the SigValueEval API for the expression syntax.

import sys, os, json
waveName = "test_top.FSDB"
fileHandle = waveform.open(waveName)
if fileHandle == None:
print("Error: Fail to open the waveform file ", waveName)
exit(0)
# Create waveform.MessageExtractor Object
ME = waveform.MessageExtractor()
# Use iterator to get the time and sigvalue for each event
if ME.iter_start(fileHandle, "sig.json", bt = None, et
= None, format = waveform.VctFormat_e.HexStrVal) !=
waveform.WaveL1RC_e.SUCCESS:
print("Error: Fail to start the MessageExtractor.")
exit(0)
time, sigValue = ME.iter_next()
if time == -1:
break
print( "Time: ", time )
print( "SigValue: ", sigValue )
ME.iter_stop()
# Use extract to get timeList and the signal value List
TimeList, SigValueList = ME.extract(fileHandle, "sig.json", bt =
None, et = None, format = waveform.VctFormat_e.HexStrVal)
print( "TimeList: ", TimeList )
print( "SigValueList: ", SigValueList )
# Use extract to get timeList and the signal value List by given the
clock signal and condition signal.

TimeList, SigValueList = ME.extract(fileHandle, "sig.json" , clock =
"posedge hclk", condition = " ( hresetn != 0 ) && ( hwrite == 1 )
&& ( hready == 1 ) " )
print( "TimeList: ", TimeList )
print( "SigValueList: ", SigValueList )
# Use extract to get timeList and the signal value List by given the
channel name "AHB".
TimeList, SigValueList = ME.extract(fileHandle, "sig.json" , channel
= "AHB" )
print( "TimeList: ", TimeList )
print( "SigValueList: ", SigValueList )
# Close waveform and end NPI

* et - Specify the end time. (Default is None to wave max time)

* clock - Specify the clock signal. (Default is None)
* condition - Specify the condition signal. (Default is None)
* channel - Specify the channel name. (Default is None)
If channel is not None, clock and condition are ignored.
WaveL1RC_e.SUCCESS if success.

Introduction to Python Based NPI
Python-Based NPI APIs support six models. They are as follows:
* Waveform Writer
* Waveform
* Netlist
* Text
* Coverage
* Language
Each model have their own APIs to let you be able to traverse data objects and obtain
objects' properties like the existing C-Based or Tcl-Based NPI APIs.
In this guide, the environment setting for using Python-Based NPI APIs for Waveform
Writer is demonstrated.
* Packages and Modules
* Module Functions and Class Objects
* User Interface and Use Flow

Packages and Modules
Packages
The Python-based NPI package name is "pynpi", and it is placed at $VERDI_HOME/share/
NPI/python.

Chapter 1: Introduction to Python Based NPI
Module Functions and Class Objects

Modules
There are seven modules inside the "pynpi" package: npisys, lang, netlist, text, cov
waveform, and waveformw. The first module, npisys, is the system model for initialization,
loading design and exit. The other modules represent language model, netlist model, text
model, coverage model, wave model, and waveform writer model respectively

Module Functions and Class Objects
L0 Module Functions
Every module provides some L0 (level 0) functions to let you get the class objects. These
functions return a class object or a list of class objects, and they follow the specification of
the existing L0 APIs provided in C or Tcl.

L1 Module Functions
Similar to L0 module functions, every module also provides some L1 (level 1) functions to
let you get advanced information based on the results obtained by L0 module functions.
These functions follows the specification of the existing L1 APIs provided in C or Tcl.

Class Objects
The class object is similar to the so-called handle in NPI C APIs. The most difference is
that some basic L0 APIs in C and Tcl becomes class method function. These L0 APIs are
usually to get integer value, string value, one-to-one method to get a handle, and 1-tomany method to get handle iterator.

Chapter 1: Introduction to Python Based NPI
User Interface and Use Flow

Environment and Library Setting
The python library setting flow of using Python-Based NPI APIs contains four parts:
1. Check your Python's version:
Python-Based NPI APIs need the Python version greater than 3.6.0.
2. Environment setting for "VERDI_HOME" is required for Python-based NPI. Remember to
set it well before running program.
3. Add the cross-platform Python library path to your code before loading the Pythonbased NPI by using the following commands:
import platform
arch = platform.machine()
if arch == "x86_64":
arch = "linux64"
sys.path.append(os.path.abspath(os.environ["VERDI_HOME"] + "/share/NPI/lib/" +
arch))

4. Import module "npisys" for using the function of NPI initialization and exit from pynpi
package.
from pynpi import npisys

5. Import the module you need from pynpi package. For example, if you want to use
waveform writer model, you can import the module as follows:
from pynpi import waveformw

6. Note that initialization function npisys.init() must be called before writing your code
by using any other modules. Also, npisys.end() must be called after finishing your
code. Following is a simple example to demonstrate how to use waveform writer model
by Python-Based NPI APIs.
Python program to use NPI waveform writer model: (demo.py)
import sys
import os
import platform
arch = platform.machine()
if arch == "x86_64":
arch = "linux64"
sys.path.append(os.path.abspath(os.environ["VERDI_HOME"] + "/share/NPI/lib/"
+ arch))
from pynpi import npisys
from pynpi import waveformw
# Initialize NPI
if not npisys.init(sys.argv):
print("Error: Fail to initialize NPI")
assert 0
# Load design (if needed, depends on models)
if not npisys.load_design(sys.argv):
print("Error: Fail to load design")

User Interface and Use Flow
The flow of using Waveform writer APIs contains four parts:
* Waveform File
* Create Hierarchy
* Add value to Signals
* Close Waveform File
1. Create Waveform File: Obtain a Waveform writer object from API create() .
2. Create Hierarchy: describe the scope and signal hierarchy of the Waveform.
This phase is between the two APIs:
FileObj.begin_hierarchy()
FileObj.end_heirarchy()
3. Add value to signals: After calling FileObj.begin_hierarchy(), you can add value to
signals.
They can also increase time using API FileObj.incr_time().
4. Close Waveform File: close the FSDB writer object and free related memory with API
close().

waveform writer function
waveformw.create(name='novas.fsdb', unit='1ns', beginTime=0)
Create a Waveform file with a given file name in current working directory.
Parameters
* name - Name of the waveform file to be opened for writing. If name is omitted, the
default value is novas.fsdb.
* unit - The scale unit of this file. If unit is omitted, the default value is "1ns". If the scale
unit should be set as 10ns,user can give a string "10ns" as a unit for this API. Scale
unit should be as [1, 10, 100][s, ms, us, ns, ps, fs].
* beginTime - The begin time of simulation for this Waveform file. If beginTime is
omitted, the begin time of this file is set as 0.
* File object, is success.

create_scope(scopeType, name, defName=None)
Create a sub scope under current scope, and then set the new added scope as current
scope.
Note:
The following scope types cannot be created:
* ScopeType_e.ScModule
* ScopeType_e.Unknown
(For information on enum ScopeType_e, see the Python-Based NPI Waveform
Model guide. )

* scopeType - The scope type. ( Refer to the PyNPI Waveform Model's enum
ScopeType_e)
* name - The scope name. (this field cannot be NULL)
* defName - The scope define name. (for example, module name) (default is NULL)
* 1, if success.
* 0, if fail.
if
file.create_scope(waveformw.waveform.ScopeType_e.SvModule,"Module_tes
t" ) is 1:
print("Scope full name is ", file.scope_name())
Scope full name is Module_test

up_scope()
Make current scope go to its parent scope.
If no parent scope exits, it stays at current scope.
* 1, if success.
* 0, if fail or no parent scope
file.create_scope(waveformw.waveform.ScopeType_e.SvModule,"Module_test_
2" )
if file.up_scope() is 1:
print("Scope full name is ", file.scope_name())
Scope full name is Module_test

Get predefined scalar data type.
dtType - Basic scalar data type ScalarDtType_e.
leftRange - Left range of vector data type. The default value is None.
rightRange - Right range of vector data type. The default value is None.
* A data type object, if success.
Return type: dt object

* A new data type object, if success.
Return type: dt object
nameList = ["group_name_1","group_name_2"]
dtList =
[file.dt(waveformw.ScalarDtType_e.SvLogic),file.dt(waveformw.ScalarDtTyp

create_array_dt(baseDt, leftRange, rightRange)
Use a base data type to create an array data type.
baseDt - Base data type.
leftRange - Left-hand-side range.
rightRange - Right-hand-side range.
* A new data type object, if success.
Return type: dt object
arrayDt = file.create_array_dt(dt1, 0, 5)

create_enum_dt(label)
Create an enum data type. Users need to provide a Label List or a Label OrderedDict with
enum information.
* label - Label List or Label OrderedDict with enum information.
* List (Label) - The string type of label elements' name. ["name1", "name2",
,"nameN"], and the name should be unique. The value of the label increases
automatically (start from 0).
* OrderedDict (Label) - The OrderedDict keys represent the label elements' name
(string type), and the name should be unique. The OrderedDict keys represent the
label elements' value, the valid value type are None, "", bitString(01XZ), and positive
integer. The value of the label increases automatically (start from 0 or previous
countable value), when previous value contains x/z, deduction fails.
* A new enum data type object, if success.
Return type: dt object

>>> from pynpi import waveformw as writer
from collections import OrderedDict
file = writer.create("test_enum.fsdb", "10ns", 10)
file.create_scope(writer.waveform.ScopeType_e.SvModule,"SvModule_sig_enu
m" )
# creat an enum data type by OrderedDict
labelDict =
OrderedDict({"RED":"011","GREEN":None,"BLUE":"101","YELLOW":"","GRAY":"Z
x", "PINK":2 })
enumDtOD = file.create_enum_dt(labelDict)
sig_enum_OD = file.create_sig_by_dt_obj(enumDtOD, "sig_enum_OD",
writer.waveform.DirType_e.DirInput)
# creat an enum data type by List
labelList = ["Apple", "Banana", "Cat", "Dog","Zoo"]
enumDtLI = file.create_enum_dt(labelList)
sig_enum_LI = file.create_sig_by_dt_obj(enumDtLI, "sig_enum_LI",
writer.waveform.DirType_e.DirInput)
sig_enum_OD[0].add_value("GREEN",
writer.waveform.VctFormat_e.EnumStrVal)
sig_enum_LI[0].add_value("Zoo",
writer.waveform.VctFormat_e.EnumStrVal)
file.incr_time(10)
sig_enum_OD[0].add_value("3", writer.waveform.VctFormat_e.UintVal)
sig_enum_LI[0].add_value("2", writer.waveform.VctFormat_e.UintVal)
file.incr_time(10)
sig_enum_OD[0].add_value("110",
writer.waveform.VctFormat_e.BinStrVal)
sig_enum_LI[0].add_value("100",
writer.waveform.VctFormat_e.BinStrVal)
file.incr_time(10)
sig_enum_OD[0].add_value("Zx", writer.waveform.VctFormat_e.BinStrVal)
file.incr_time(10)
sig_enum_OD[0].add_value("10", writer.waveform.VctFormat_e.BinStrVal)
sig_enum_LI[0].add_value("1", writer.waveform.VctFormat_e.BinStrVal)
file.incr_time(10)
writer.close(file)

Preface
The Regression Debug Automation (RDA) User Guide explains the purpose of RDA,
its working principles, the technology it uses, and the process for automatic binning
of regression failure cases. The guide also describes how RDA automates root cause
analysis and tracing.

Customer Support
Customer support is available through SolvNetPlus.

Accessing SolvNetPlus
The SolvNetPlus site includes a knowledge base of technical articles and answers to
frequently asked questions about Synopsys tools. The SolvNetPlus site also gives you
access to a wide range of Synopsys online services including software downloads,
documentation, and technical support.
To access the SolvNetPlus site, go to the following address:
https://solvnetplus.synopsys.com
If prompted, enter your user name and password. If you do not have a Synopsys user
name and password, follow the instructions to sign up for an account.
If you need help using the SolvNetPlus site, click REGISTRATION HELP in the top-right
menu bar.

Contacting Customer Support
To contact Customer Support, go to https://solvnetplus.synopsys.com

Synopsys Statement on Inclusivity and Diversity
Synopsys is committed to creating an inclusive environment where every employee,

language from our products and supporting customer-facing collateral. Our effort also

Chapter 1: Preface
Synopsys Statement on Inclusivity and Diversity

includes internal initiatives to remove biased language from our engineering and working
environment, including terms that are embedded in our software and IPs. At the same
time, we are working to ensure that our web content and software applications are usable
to people of varying abilities. You may still find examples of non-inclusive language in our
software or documentation as our IPs implement industry-standard specifications that are
currently under review to remove exclusionary language.

Introduction
Synopsys Regression Debug Automation (RDA) is a solution that uses machine learning,
AI, and auto-trace technology to automate regression debug tasks. RDA automatically
groups failure cases (binning), finds root causes, and traces errors. It is designed for
complex System-on-Chip (SoC) and IP designs. Traditional regression debug flows need
engineers to spend a lot of time on manual binning, triaging, debugging, and tracing.
These tasks often start with many possible suspects and error points.
RDA automates the process of handling failed regression tests. It groups large numbers
of failed test cases, finds the root causes of failures, and identifies and isolates problem
areas. RDA also prepares debugging facilitators, completing these tasks much faster than
manual methods. By removing the need to compare waveforms, source code, and log files
manually, RDA reduces engineering effort and saves time--from days to just hours.
The following figure shows the effort distribution in the traditional regression debugging
process:
Figure 1

Engineer Efforts on Manual but Replaceable Tasks

Chapter 2: Introduction

With RDA automation, engineers can use their time more efficiently, as shown in the
Figure 2

Engineer Effort on Really Manual Task While Adopting RDA

Adopting RDA maximizes the efficiency and productivity of engineers, reduces cost,
improves turnaround time, and accelerates the debugging process.
The following topic provides an overview of the RDA technology: Technology Overview.

RDA uses computing resources to automate the machine-replaceable tasks. It
automatically traces the design and analyzes root causes of the regression test failures.
After regression, RDA runs in batch mode and generates analysis reports to review and
check the failure analysis. The following figure provides an overview of the RDA flow:
Figure 3

RDA Flow Overview

The RDA solution comes with the following key features:
* Regression Binning
RDA automates the tedious process of regression binning. It uses computing resources
and a machine learning database to analyze failed regression test cases. RDA then
sorts and groups cases with the same failure type into one bucket.
* Debug Facilitator

Chapter 2: Introduction

RDA uses the Debug Facilitator to create the database and debugging environments
you need. This helps you debug each binning bucket in different debug modes.
Debug Facilitator uses a build script and a run-simulation script to rebuild and
rerun simulations after regression. This speeds up the process by reducing manual
preparation efforts. Furthermore, you can use the same scripts for future regressions.
Debug Facilitator includes reverse debug in interactive mode. This feature allows
you to control simulation execution both forward and backward. You can also enable
transaction recording to debug at the protocol level.
* DUT Root Cause Analysis
RDA provides a DUT Root Cause Analysis (DUTRCA) solution. This feature compares
a failed simulation with a previously passed simulation. It analyzes all suspect points
that might lead to regression failure and helps find the possible root causes. DUTRCA
automatically identifies and analyzes the possible causes by tracing back all error
points at the same time.
* Testbench Root Cause Analysis
RDA provides a Testbench Root Cause Analysis (TBRCA) solution that identifies the
testbench component with which the error is associated. It also identifies the region
within that component where the error is located.
The TBRCA Transaction Difference analysis flow analyzes and compares the reference
simulation log file with the failing simulation log file. It identifies the differences between
the transactions recorded during both simulations. The TBRCA Message Analysis
flow analyzes a message and identifies transactions and signals associated with that
message. Automatic detection of transaction differences helps you debug testbench
errors faster. This feature saves time during the debugging process.
* X Root Cause Analysis
All unknown X signals are automatically scanned and traced to their root causes. This
process saves manual effort. By managing and tracing many X signals automatically,
you spend less time repeating the same debugging steps.
* Multiple Cycle Path Root Cause Analysis
RDA provides a Multiple Cycle Path Root Cause Analysis (MCPRCA) solution. This
feature automatically groups violations detected by VCS-SDC into fewer groups. It
uses Verdi to debug each group by viewing waveform, source code, and simulation
logs.

Chapter 2: Introduction

* FaultRCA: Fault Analysis
The FaultRCA utility helps in detecting the blocking points between the fault-injected
point and the observation or detection point. This overcomes the limitation of excessive
manual effort and time consumption required to debug general faults.
RDA uses an easy-to-use GUI reporter, RCA Manager, to view reports in different ways.
You can sort, group, and search all regression cleanup results directly in RCA Manager.
Debugging environments set up by Debug Facilitator can be started from RCA Manager.
You can also view traced paths from the analysis report in Temporal Flow View (TFV).
The RDA user guide consists of the following chapters to help you understand the key
features in detail:
* Regression Binning
* Debug Facilitator and Verdi VMS Integration
* Debug Facilitator Without Verdi VMS
* DUT Root Cause Analysis (DUTRCA)
* Testbench Root Cause Analysis (TBRCA)
* X Root Cause Analysis (XRCA)
* Multiple Cycle Path Root Cause Analysis (MCPRCA)
* FaultRCA: Fault Analysis

Regression Binning
* Regression Binning Application
* Regression Binning Usage

The first step after a regression failure is to process many failed cases. Manually checking,
analyzing, and organizing these cases can be very time-consuming and requires
significant manual work.
RDA offers Regression Binning, an automated process that uses machine learning and
data mining techniques to analyze failures and group those with the same issue type
together. The automation reduces engineer manual efforts and saves time.
The difference between the Manual Binning and Triaging, and the Automated Binning and
Triaging is shown in the following figure:
Figure 4

Manual Regression Binning Versus Automated Regression Binning

With a user-provided list of simulation log files of failure cases, Regression Binning mines
log files and conducts similarity checking which performs failure clustering based on the
similarity of log files.
The resulting groups are called buckets, where each bucket represents a failure type
that can be reviewed, analyzed, and debugged later. The following figure shows the
Regression Binning Technology:
Figure 5

Regression Binning Technology

Regression Binning Application
The Regression Binning application is an easy setup suitable for the Universal Verification
Methodology (UVM) regression environment and the SoC/IP level designs. Regression
Binning provides the following key features:
* Categorizes the simulation log files into different buckets, where each bucket
represents a failure type.
* Requires only simulation log files of the failed test cases.
* Provides a specific solution for the UVM-based error messages using unsupervised
machine learning based algorithm.
The Regression Binning application also supports the following advanced binning features:
* Extend binning capability by the user-defined rule of errors.
* Waive specific error patterns for binning.
* Group failed test cases without error messages but with a customized pass pattern,
recognized as Pass by RDA, in a Pass bucket.
* Replace or remove the unwanted parts of the specific error patterns.

Regression Binning Application

* Disable RCA and/or Debug Facilitator for the specific error patterns.
* Customize the priority of the specific error messages for binning.

Regression Binning Reports With Verdi
Through Regression Binning, failed tests are grouped into buckets and the binning reports
are generated. RDA provides the GUI interface, RCA Manager, to review each bucket for
each type of failure.
The Verdi SmartLog engine loads the selected log file for further reviewing and
debugging. The following figure shows the regression binning reports in Verdi:
Figure 6

Regression Binning Reports in Verdi

The following are the requirements for the Regression Binning setup:
* Simulation log files of the regression tests.
* User-defined rule file; this file is required when you have user-defined error messages,
waiving error messages, or prioritizing messages.

This section provides steps for performing Regression Binning, generating reports,
reviewing reports in Verdi, and configuring advanced user-defined rules to extend
Regression Binning capability.
* Performing Regression Binning Steps
* Showing Binning Reports in RCA Manager
* Reviewing and Debugging a Log in Verdi SmartLog From RDA Reports
* Multiple-Error Binning
* Binning User-Defined Rule
* Adding Rules, Usage, and Syntax

Performing Regression Binning Steps
The steps to perform Regression Binning with the autorca command are as follows:
1. Prepare a YAML configuration file for Regression Binning.
The configuration file configures RDA for the required Regression Binning engine and
the corresponding required data. You can reuse the same configuration file for the
future regressions.
You can use the autorca -gen_cfg_template <cfg_file_name> -gen_mode
<engine> command to auto generate an easy and ready-to-go template configuration
file, %> autorca -gen_cfg_template binning.yaml -gen_mode binning
For more information on how to generate a RDA configuration file for Regression
Binning, click the following video link:
This video focuses on generating a configuration file for RDA components, such
as Regression Binning, DUTRCA, Debug Facilitator, XRCA, and TBRCA.

The generation of the template file is shown in the following figure:
Figure 7

Template of Regression Binning Configuration File

2. In the latest_fail_list field, specify the path of the file that contains a list of log files
that have failures. The following figure shows an example of the contents in the list file:

3. This step is optional. Single-error binning uses a machine learning algorithm that
groups log files based on the similarity of their first error message. The algorithm
compares the first error in each log file and places files with similar first errors into the
same bucket.
However, the multiple_error_binning option enables a machine learning algorithm.
This algorithm groups similar multiple errors from one log file with errors from
other log files into the same bucket. Enable multiple-error binning by setting the
multiple_error_binning option to true. Refer to the Multiple-Error Binning section
for more details.
4. This is an optional step. For advanced usage, you can add a rule file in the
user_defined_rule field to add user-defined error message. You can waive or
prioritize them. Refer to the Binning User-Defined Rule section for details.
5. Perform Regression Binning by invoking the autorca -cfg <config_file> command
with the following updated Binning configuration file:
%> autorca -cfg binning.yaml

The Regression Binning generates the results report of the binning buckets, report.json.

A binning bucket list file is also generated. It lists the base simulation log files belonging
to each bucket. You can use RCA Manager to review the results. Refer to the following
section for details.

Showing Binning Reports in RCA Manager
To load the RDA reports into the RCA Manager, use the following command:
autorca -load_report <report_file>

For example, %> autorca -load_report report.json
This command allows you to use the related features in the RCA Manager.
The following figure shows the report when it is loaded in the RCA Manager:
Figure 8

Regression Binning Reports (Bucket list)

Each bucket contains the simulation log file of the major case, the error message, and
other cases that belong to the same bucket.
You can assign these buckets to the enrolled users and track their status.
For more details on the bucket assignment and management and icons available on RCA
manager, refer to the following sections:
* Assigning And Managing Bucket
* RCA Manager for Regression Binning

Assigning And Managing Bucket
To enhance collaboration and streamline debugging, buckets need status tracking and
clear ownership. The tool offers the following three key features:
* Status management that allows buckets to be marked with different working statuses.
* Bucket assignment enables each bucket to be assigned to a specific user from a
managed list. This ensures accountability and ownership.

Multiple-Error Binning
Multiple-error binning is based on the Natural Language Processing (NLP) algorithm to
calculate the similarities among the failed simulation logs. The simulation logs with similar
error message distributions are grouped into the same bucket using the Multiple-Error
Binning feature.
For example, a log file containing two UVM errors and one assertion error differs from a
log file containing only one UVM error. Even when both the log files have the same UVM
error, the two log files are grouped into different buckets.
The Multiple-Error Binning feature works in the following way:
* Collects all the error messages for each log file.
* Calculates the error distribution of each log file with the NLP algorithm based on all the
errors available in the logs.
* Groups log files into buckets with the error distribution of each log file.
Executing Multiple-Error Binning
By default, the machine learning single-error similarity binning is enabled. To enable
machine learning multiple-error binning, set the following option to true when you run
autorca -cfg run.yaml:
multiple_error_binning: true

By default, the multiple_error_binning option is set to false. After you enable the
multiple-error binning feature, run regression binning and load the report in the RCA
Manager.
In the RCA Manager, the Error Message section groups error message distributions in
each bucket. This section displays only the message part of the error message and the
error distribution of each log file. Variant parts of the messages are replaced with <*>.

The following figure displays the error message distributions in buckets in the
report.json file:
Figure 27

The Figure 27 displays two buckets. The first bucket contains one failing log file with 100%
of the similar UVM error type. The second bucket consists of three failing log files. Each
of these files contains 33.33% of the similar assertion error type, 33.33% of a similar UVM
error type, and 33.33% of another similar UVM error type; each displaying the content
of the error messages. The error distributions of each log file in a bucket might have
differences and the distribution percentage of the error messages might be common
with the remaining log files. Therefore, the sum of the error distributions can be less than
100%.
Consider the following three failing log files, each with similar error types grouped in the
same bucket:
* Failing log file 1: 99% UVM errors and 1% assertion errors.
* Failing log file 2: 99% UVM errors and 1% user-defined errors.
* Failing log file 3: 100% UVM errors.
After refining, the error distribution is 99% UVM errors.
Therefore, the error distributions for these log files are refined to display the similar error
type common across all log files. In this example, 99% of the errors are UVM errors. This
is called the refined error distribution.

Binning User-Defined Rule
RDA performs Regression Binning based on the predefined errors that include UVM
Errors, OVM Errors, SVA failures, Unsatisfied SystemVerilog constraints, and VCS
predefined errors.
However, when user-defined error messages in log files do not match predefined errors, or
when predefined errors do not meet the needs of your custom binning policy, Regression
Binning allows you to define your own rules. This feature allows Regression Binning to
operate according to your customized rules.
Add the required rules in a file, and specify the file in the user_defined_rule field of the
Regression Binning configuration file. To extend the Regression Binning capability, the
customizable rules are as follows:
* Waive rule: When you find negligible errors, you can specify the error patterns in the
Waive Rule, and then Regression Binning waives them from binning.
* User-defined errors rule:If your log files contain error messages that are not
predefined, specify the error patterns in the User-defined Errors Rule. Regression
Binning then considers these patterns as error messages.
* Pass rule: For the tests listed in the regression list without any error messages, you
can instruct Regression Binning to mark specific messages as pass tests.
* Replace rule: If failed tests fall into different groups based on error messages that
you consider the same, use the Replace Rule to remove or replace unwanted parts of
specific error patterns. Regression Binning uses the replaced error message to perform
similarity checking.
The following figure shows an example for the syntax of user_defined_rule. It consists
of two types of basic blocks, Filter and Waive, representing the specific error pattern to be
considered or waived.

Figure 30

User-Defined Rule Syntax

The priority of applying rules when an error matches more than one rule is as follows:
1. Waive rule
The error messages which match any waive rules have the highest priority and are not
shown in the binning report.
2. Predefined error rule
The priority of a predefined error rule is higher than a user-defined error rule if both the
rules have the same priority.
3. User-defined error rule
The error messages that match with any one of the filter blocks.
4. Pass rule
When the predefined and user-defined errors are not found and a message matches
with any of the pass rules, the test case categorizes into a Pass bucket.

Regression Binning With User-Defined Rules
The following steps describe how Regression Binning works with the user-defined rules:
* For each regression fail log, Regression Binning engine adopts waive rules to filter out
error messages that you want to ignore.
* Regression Binning engine adopts machine-learning based algorithm to classify the
target error message. It identifies all error messages that match the predefined and
user-defined error rules and follows the following criteria:
When all errors have the same priority, the first identified error message is the target
error message.
When errors have different priorities, the error message with the highest priority is
the target error message.
When errors have different priorities and the error message with the highest priority
matches both, a predefined error rule and a user-defined error rule with the same
priority, the error message is still the target error message, and the predefined error
rule is applied.
When the predefined and user-defined errors are not found and the message matches
with any pass rules, the test case categorizes into a Pass bucket.

Adding Rules, Usage, and Syntax
This section discusses the following topics:
