Regression Binning With User-Defined Errors
In addition to UVM/OVM error messages, SVA assertion failures, and VCS predefined
errors, you can extend binning capability to other error messages. Add new error patterns
to the user_define_rule file to extend the binning capability.
When a block contains a filter field, the regular expression inside it informs Regression
Binning which error messages to include. These selected error messages are then used
for grouping in the binning process.

Regression Binning recognizes the error patterns as a part of target analysis. It uses
machine learning to check how similar the errors are. Then, it automatically groups related
errors together.
Figure 31

Blocks to Set Filter in for Test cases

The block displays the following fields:
* filter: A regular expression enclosed by "//" to filter in.
* field: A keyword to capture the specified information. It is a regular expression
enclosed by the slash (/) symbol.
@Time@ (Optional): A special keyword to specify the position of the time
information. It supports the format of digits and digits+timeunit.
@Scope@ (Optional): A special keyword to specify the position of the scope
information.
The @Time@ and @Scope@ keywords are available only when you add
the field expression.
* testcase (Optional): You can specify names of the test cases separated by comma in
each block. The error patterns defined in filter of a block only affect the specified test
cases. When the test case is not specified, the error patterns affect all the test cases.
* desc (Optional): You can describe the block.
The messages of successfully capturing the user-specified fields are printed in
binning_output.log available at the following location:
<rcaWorkdir>/binning/binning_output.log

Example 1
Error message: FAILED, error content, 478124 ns
Binning rule:

filter=/FAILED/
field=/FAILED, .+ @TIME@/

Example 2
Error message: [478124 ns] UVM_ERROR (test) uvm_test_top.env.sb, error
content
Binning rule
filter=/UVM_ERROR /
field =/\[@TIME@\] UVM_ERROR \(.+\) @SCOPE@ .+/

Example 3
Error message: 478124: [FAIL][TEST] error content
Binning rule
filter=/\[FAIL\]/
field=/^@TIME@: \[FAIL\].+/

The grouped buckets in the Regression Binning reports can be used directly for the Root
Cause Analysis (RCA) and Debug Facilitator solutions. If you do not want RDA to perform
actions of RCA and Debug Facilitator for the specific error patterns, you can disable the
action with the disable option.
The syntax is as follows:
disable=[action][, action]

where [action] can be
DF: disable later Debug Facilitator action
RCA: disable later Root Cause Analysis (RCA) action

Example
filter=/error_pattern*/
priority=0
disable=DF

Regression Binning With Waive Rules
A block with a waive field explains that the described regular expression informs
Regression Binning to ignore the error patterns as error messages.
The block displays the following fields:
* waive: A regular expression inside "//" is used to filter out.
* testcase (Optional): Specify names of the test cases separated by comma in each
block. The error patterns defined in waive of this block only affect the specified test
cases. When the test case is not specified, the error patterns affect all test cases.
* desc (Optional): Add a description for the block.

Figure 32

Blocks to Set Waive for Test cases

Regression Binning With Priority Rules
When the priority is not mentioned, Regression Binning engine takes the first identified
error message in the simulation log as the target error message.
Priority rules allow you to specify the priority of the specific error message. After you
set priorities, the error message with the highest priority becomes the main target error
message.
Figure 33

Set Priority for a Specific Block

Additionally, the user_defined_rule_priority field sets the priority for all blocks in the
user_defined_rule file.
The predefined_rule_priority field sets the priority of all predefined rules.

The following figure displays that a user-defined error with a priority value of 3 has a
higher priority than all predefined errors and any other user-defined errors with a priority
value greater than 3:
Figure 34

Set Priority for a Specific Block and All Rules

Priority Rules
The following priority rules are defined for several conditions:
* A lower priority value means higher priority. If you do not set a priority, the default
priority number for the predefined and user-defined error message is 1.
* If multiple error messages have the same priority, Regression Binning selects the first
identified message as the target error message.
* If an error message matches both a predefined and a user-defined rule with the same
priority, the predefined error rule overrides the user-defined error rule.

Regression Binning With Pass Rules
Test cases that do not show any error messages and where the simulation stops without
errors are placed in unknown buckets.
Regression Binning considers these test cases as passed tests by adding a Pass rule with
specific pass patterns. Tests that match this rule are binned into Pass buckets. All other
cases that do not match are binned into unknown buckets.
Syntax
pass=/<pass_pattern1>/
testcase= [case1][, case2]//optional
desc= [descriptions1] //optional
pass=/<pass_pattern2>/
testcase= [case3]//optional
desc= [descriptions2] //optional

Regression Binning With Replace Rules
When you have different error messages of the same kind or of the same error group, use
Replace rule. This rule informs Regression Binning to preprocess in the background and
replace the error messages.
Regression Binning preprocesses the line of error message with the replacement patterns.
It then uses the new replaced error message to perform similarity checking and binning.
Syntax:
replace_src=/<replace source >/
replace_dest=/<replace destination>/
desc=[replace description]

For example:
replace_src=/__VC\d+\//
replace_dest=/\//
desc=replace config pattern

Regression Binning replaces the replace_source pattern in the error message with the
replace_destination pattern and returns a new error message for binning.
If there are multiple replace_source patterns, the patterns are applied in the order they
appear in the user-defined rule file.

Debug Facilitator and Verdi VMS Integration
* Application
* Usage

After regression, traditional debugging needs manual steps, such as rebuilding designs for
executable files that are deleted after regression. You also need to rerun simulations and
create Fast Signal Database (FSDB) files. Debugging is then performed in Verdi, either in
post-processing or interactive mode. For each failed test case, you must run the simulation
for the specific test pattern again. This process takes a lot of time.
RDA offers a solution for users who use Verdi VMS as their regression system. This
solution integrates Debug Facilitator with Verdi VMS. The integration uses Verdi VMS
configurations to perform Regression Binning (refer to the Regression Binning chapter for
more details). It facilitates the required database and debugging environments needed to
debug each bucket in different modes in Verdi.
After you add the RDA environment variables to the Verdi VMS .emc configuration file,
Debug Facilitator and Verdi VMS integrate directly. This integration rebuilds and reruns
simulations after regression runs in Verdi VMS. This integration makes the process faster.
It reduces the need to prepare scripts manually and removes the manual steps needed to
rerun simulations for each error case.

Figure 35

Overview of Debug Facilitator With Verdi VMS Flow

The Debug Facilitator and Verdi VMS integration selects the best failed test case from
each bucket to run the simulation. It saves the UVM error point, so you can quickly restore
the simulation status during debugging. The integration also provides a Reverse Debug
feature in interactive mode. This feature allows you to control forward and backward
simulation execution and enables transaction recording for protocol-level debugging.
A well-built Debug Facilitator can enable the Verdi GUI in different debugging modes. The
Verdi GUI displays the analysis results generated by AI-based Error Message Analysis as
the starting point of the debugging process.
The following figure displays the Verdi GUI for Debug Facilitator:

With a slight manual change in the Verdi VMS .emc configuration file, the RDA Debug
Facilitator reduces manual efforts required for setting up the debugging environment. You
do not need to create complex rebuild and rerun scripts. The Debug Facilitator features
and one-click Verdi launch help you identify and display the starting point for debugging.
This improves debugging turnaround time.
The usages provided in this chapter are applied to Debug Facilitator with
regressions in Verdi VMS. However, if you do not use Verdi VMS as your

The Error Message Analysis technology of Debug Facilitator automatically analyzes all the

Debug Facilitator includes all the features of Regression Binning (refer to the Regression

Update Verdi VMS .emc Configuration File
The following steps are required to update the Verdi VMS .emc configuration file for
performing Debug Facilitator with Verdi VMS:
1. Change the default values of the existing environment variables to "" in the env group
of the .emc file if the original default value is null. Otherwise, Verdi VMS errors out if
null is supplied to the environment variables in the RDA flow. For example:
env:
- VMS_HOME: ""
- VCS_HOME: ""
- VERDI_HOME: ""

2. Assign the following RDA specific environment variables to the corresponding variables
integrated in Verdi VMS:
Environment Variable

SNPS_RCA_COMP_OPT

Passes compilation options to VCS. RDA sets
necessary options to this environment variable
during compilation.

SNPS_RCA_RUN_OPT

Passes runtime options to simv. RDA sets
necessary options to the environment variable
when performs simulation.

SNPS_RCA_BUILD_DIR

Passes a certain version of design source code
(that is, change list) to the regression scripts
and the build directory gets generated by RDA.
RDA uses this path to build and run simulation.

SNPS_RCA_SEED

Passes test case seed to simv to rerun the
failing test case with the same seed. RDA
queries about it from the Verdi VMS database.

The following example adds RDA variables into the .emc file:
#Verdi VMS runs only if all exist or are set here
# - Blank values mean check the existence of the
variable first
# - Value after mean set to this
env:
- VMS_HOME: ""
- VCS_HOME: ""
- VERDI_HOME: ""
- SNPS_RCA_COMP_OPT: $SNPS_RCA_COMP_OPT
- SNPS_RCA_RUN_OPT: $SNPS_RCA_RUN_OPT
- SNPS_RCA_BUILD_DIR: $SNPS_RCA_BUILD_DIR
- SNPS_RCA_SEED: $SNPS_RCA_SEED
# end of env setting

Update Makefile Used Inside .emc Configuration File
During the rebuild and rerun process in the RDA flow, the following actions are required:
* Add RDA-specific environment variables to the scripts or makefile which are used
with Verdi VMS to perform build and run simulation:
$SNPS_RCA_COMP_OPT to VCS compilation command.
$SNPS_RCA_RUN_OPT to simv simulation runtime command.
If the build and run processes are inseparable, add them to your regression scripts.
* You must enable FSDB dumping in the VCS and simv commands.
The following example adds RDA variables into makefile:
#Build command in makefile
vcs_comp_reg:
vcs ${COMP_ARGS}${SNPS_RCA_COMP_OPT} \
+define+<DIRECTIVE_TO_ENABLE_FSDB> \
${TOP_SRC} ${COMP_CMDLINE_ARGS} ${INCLUDES} \
${DEFINES} ${COMP_REG_OUT}
# Run command for builds in Makefile
vcs_run_reg:
mkdir -p ${SIM_DIR}/${test}_${seed}; \
cd ${SIM_DIR}/${test}_${seed}; \
${COMP_DIR}/reg_simv ${COMMON_RUN_ARGS} \
${RUN_CMDLINE_ARGS} ${SNPS_RCA_RUN_OPT} \
-l reg_vcs_sim.log;

Debug Facilitator Without Verdi VMS
* Debug Facilitator Application
* Debug Facilitator Usage

After regression, traditional debugging needs manual steps, such as rebuilding designs for
executable files that are deleted after regression. You also need to rerun simulations and
create Fast Signal Database (FSDB) files. Debugging is then performed in Verdi, either in
post-processing or interactive mode. For each failed test case, you must run the simulation
for the specific test pattern again. This process takes a lot of time.
RDA provides Debug Facilitator to simplify the process. Debug Facilitator performs
Regression Binning (refer to the Regression Binning chapter for more details) and
facilitates the required database and debugging environments for debugging each binning
bucket in different modes in Verdi.
Debug Facilitator uses build and run-simulation scripts to rebuild and rerun simulations
after regression. This speeds up the process and reduces manual effort and time required
to perform the simulation for each error case. You can reuse these scripts for future
regressions.

Figure 52

Overview of Debug Facilitator Flow

Debug Facilitator automatically selects the most suitable failed test case of each bucket,
runs the simulation, and saves the UVM error point. You can restore the simulation
status to this point during debugging. The Reverse Debug feature in the interactive mode
controls forward and backward simulation execution. You can also enable transaction
recording to debug at the protocol level.
A well-built Debug Facilitator can enable the Verdi GUI for a test case in different
debugging modes. The Verdi GUI displays the analysis results generated by AI-based
Error Message Analysis to help you start the debugging process.
The following figure displays the Verdi GUI for Debug Facilitator:
Figure 53

Verdi GUI for Debug Facilitator

Debug Facilitator generates reusable scripts for the debugging environment, reducing
manual effort. The features supported by Debug Facilitator and easy access to Verdi help
you identify and display the starting point for debugging, improving turnaround time.

This chapter describes usages that are applied to Debug Facilitator without
Verdi VMS.

RDA Debug Facilitator completes regression binning before generating debugging data.
Based on the build and run scripts you specify, Debug Facilitator rebuilds the design and
testbench. It reruns simulations for each bucket in the bucket list created by regression
binning. For each bucket, Debug Facilitator selects the most suitable case and generates
debugging data. This data includes KDB files, waveforms, and transaction dumping data.
Figure 54

Debug Facilitator Creates Debug Point During Rerun and Applications in Verdi

During compilation, Verdi enables the Reverse Debug feature automatically. Debug
Facilitator reruns each case to the UVM error point and saves the current simulation status
in a session. This feature allows you to start future debugging sessions directly from where
the error occurred.
Debug Facilitator uses Error Message Analysis technology to automatically analyze all
related interfaces and transactions. The tool provides analysis details as the starting point
for debugging.

After you generate the debugging data, RDA provides Verdi GUI to review each bucket
and the corresponding debugging solutions.
The Verdi SmartLog engine loads the selected log file for further review and debugging.
Refer to the Reviewing and Debugging a Log in Verdi SmartLog From RDA Reports
section for more details.

Debug Facilitator Application
Debug Facilitator provides all features of Regression Binning (refer to the Regression
Binning Application section for more details). It also offers the following key features:
* Automatically select and auto rerun the suitable cases and dump necessary FSDB files
for each bucket.
* Apply Message Analysis to automatically analyze relative interfaces or transactions
and generate debugging suggestions for the DUT and the testbench.
Debug Facilitator supports the following features in interactive mode in Verdi GUI:
* Run simulation in Verdi GUI. This process is similar to software debugging and helps
with testbench debugging.
* Support Reverse Debug capability for the nightly saved checkpoints. This feature
allows you to trace back without rerunning the simulation.

RDA Debug Facilitator functions best for the UVM regression environment and SoC/IP
level design.

The following are the requirements for the Debug Facilitator setup:
* VCS simulation.
* Configuration file to instruct RDA how to perform Debug Facilitator.
* Two user-defined scripts; one for recompiling the latest design and another for
rerunning failed cases.

This section provides steps for performing Debug Facilitator, generating reports, reviewing
reports, and invoking Verdi in different debugging modes.
It contains the following topics:

Setting and Performing Debug Facilitator
The steps to perform Debug Facilitator are as follows:
1. Prepare a configuration file for RDA for Regression Binning and Debug Facilitator.
2. Prepare a file that lists failure cases.
3. Prepare two script files for rebuilding simv and resimulating respectively.
4. Perform Debug Facilitator by invoking the autorca -cfg <config_file> command
with the updated configuration file and prepared files,
%> autorca -cfg facilitator.yaml

Refer to the following sections for more details on performing Debug Facilitator:
* Prepare RDA Configuration File for Debug Facilitator
* User Implemented Scripts for Debug Facilitator
* Prepare Rebuild Script for Debug Facilitator Configuration File
* Prepare Rerun Script for Debug Facilitator Configuration File
* Perform RDA Debug Facilitator

Prepare RDA Configuration File for Debug Facilitator
The configuration file configures RDA for the required Debug Facilitator engine and
the corresponding required data. You can reuse the same configuration file for future
regressions.
You can use the following command to automatically generate a template configuration
file:
autorca -gen_cfg_template <config_file_name> -gen_mode <engine>

For example, %> autorca -gen_cfg_template debug_facilitator.yaml -gen_mode
facilitator

The generation of the template file is shown in the following figure:
Figure 56

Automatically Generated Template of Debug Facilitator Configuration File

The following files are generated:

Debug Automation to run Debug Facilitator. It specifies where to the required data is
saved and explains how to rebuild or rerun simulations.
* autorca_build_facilitator.sh: The script file is created in your local directory.
Debug Facilitator uses this file to execute rebuild simulations in your regression
environment for the cases selected automatically.

* autorca_rerun_facilitator.sh: The script file resides in your local directory. Debug
Facilitator uses this file to execute rerun simulations in your regression environment for
cases that are automatically selected.
* binning_rule.txt: The template file for the field, user_defined_rule of the binning
setting in the <template_df.yaml> file.
Refer to the Prepare Rebuild Script for Debug Facilitator Configuration File and Prepare
Rerun Script for Debug Facilitator Configuration File sections for more details on the two
scripts.
Refer to the Group Configurations in the RDA Configuration File section for descriptions
of the environment, regression, builds, rerun, binning, and message analysis configuration
groups.
Group Configurations in the RDA Configuration File
This section specifies the names of the group configurations available in the configuration
file and also describes how each configuration is specified in each group:
* environment
It is optional. You can specify environment variables, VCS_HOME and VERDI_HOME here.
If Verdi needs to be launched into a server farm, specify the submit job command in the
verdi_launch_command field, as shown in the following figure:

* regression
Specify the path of the latest file that lists failure cases in the latest_fail_list field.
This is used as an input of Regression Binning. The following example shows the
contents in the list file:

* builds

Specify the path of the rebuild script file that describes how to rebuild the design and
the testbench in the build_version field. After updating with debugging options in the
template file, autorca_build_facilitator.sh, you can use it as the rebuild script.
Alternatively, you can create your own script in the preferred script language. Currently,
Shell, Python, and Perl are supported. Refer to the Prepare Rebuild Script for Debug
Facilitator Configuration File section for more details on the rebuild script.
* rerun
Specify the path of the rerun script file that describes how to rerun failed cases for
generating the debugging data in the rerun_testcase field. After updating the
template file, autorca_rerun_facilitator.sh, you can use it as the rerun script.
Alternatively, you can create your own script in the preferred script language. Currently,
Shell, Python, and Perl are supported. Refer to the Prepare Rerun Script for Debug
Facilitator Configuration File section for more details on the rerun script.
The max_parallel_processes field is used to set maximum processes to rerun failed
cases in parallel. The higher the value, the greater the number of processes to rerun
failed cases.
* binning
It is optional. You can extend the specific binning rule by specifying a rule file in
the user_defined_rule. Refer to the Binning User-Defined Rule section of the
Regression Binning chapter for more details on syntax and usage.
* message analysis
It is optional. You can enable or disable the enable_message_analysis field. When
this setting is enabled, it enables the Message Analysis feature and shows the
analysis results in the invoked Verdi post-processing and interactive modes. The
enable_message_analysis field is enabled by default.

User Implemented Scripts for Debug Facilitator
The Debug Facilitator uses two scripts to call the simulator to rebuild and rerun simulations
in the regression environment. You must implement these scripts with information specific
to your regression environment. During Debug Facilitator operation, RDA automatically
selects a suitable failed test case from each bucket. Debug Facilitator rebuilds and reruns
these selected test cases in parallel, calling the two scripts as required at different stages
of the process.

Add RDA-specific environment variables in the scripts which store the following

Add $SNPS_RCA_COMP_OPT to VCS compilation command
Add $SNPS_RCA_RUN_OPT to simv simulation runtime command
If the build and run processes are inseparable, add them to your regression
scripts.
You need to always dump FSDB files.

Appendix A: Rebuild and Rerun Scripts in Shell Example
This appendix provides an example of Debug Facilitator rebuild and rerun scripts in Shell.
autorca_build_facilitator.sh:
#!/bin/sh
#Inputs: $1 is <full path of "rda_bucket_list.txt" which contains
all bucket-case>
#Outputs: print "<status>", on second last line
# " <simv full path>", on the last line

#<status> can be the following:
# SUCCESS => build success, need also output <simv full path>
# FAIL => build failed; stop recompilation flow
# NO_SIMV: if build simv only in run-phase, output this status,
and output "EMPTY_PATH"
# for <simv full path>
BUCKET_CASE_FILE=$1 #if need to check bucket
cases to build multi-simv, use this variable
LOCAL_DIR_TOP="/regression" #set regression top dir,
create sub-local-dir under it
make_local_dir $LOCAL_DIR_TOP #make new local directory and
chdir into; To build new sim. Use DATE as directory name, ex: "/
regression/20210219", and then chdir into.
link_cfg_files_here #link necessary cfg or design
files to compile
compile_simv $SNPS_RCA_COMP_OPT #compile design with RCA
predefined VCS compile option "$SNPS_RCA_COMP_OPT". This
compile_simv need to be blocking (don't return until it finishes)
status=$? #get compiler returned status
case $status in
"0")
echo " " #make new line
echo "SUCCESS"
echo "$(pwd)/simv"
exit 0
;;
*)
echo " " #make new line
echo "FAIL" #other error
echo ""
exit 0
;;
esac

#!/bin/sh
# Inputs: $1 is <full path of "rda_bucket_list.txt" which contains
all bucket-case>
# $2 is <testcase simv log>,
# $3 is <simv full path>
#Outputs: print 3 lines for "<work-directory>", "<testcase simv log
name>" and "<fsdb name>" on the last line of stdout. Ex:
/root/d1/regression/tmp/20210219
sim.log
dump.fsdb
# ps: rerun_testcase also is for Verdi interactive mode (GUI,
$SNPS_RCA_RUN_OPT contain "-verd"), "DISPLAY" is needed. This
script also use in post-sim, if need to setup regression variables,

we provide $SNPS_RCA_REVERSE_DEBUG to indicate status.
TESTCASE=$2
SIMV_PATH=$3
DATE=$(date +"%d-%m-%Y-%H-%M-%S") #for working dir name, change
it as you want
LOCAL_DIR_TOP="/regression" #set regression top dir, create
sub-local-dir under it
if [ ! -z $SNPS_RCA_REVERSE_DEBUG ]; then #env-var exists when
click "GUI {interactive mode} button". If another user does not
have permission to write regression directory, set another TOP
directory to save running data
source regression_env.csh #source your regression
environment setting if need
LOCAL_DIR_TOP="~/rca_rerun" #set local top "~/rerun" to
save personal data for different user
fi
get_seed_from_testcase $TESTCASE #get seed from testcase log,
set to $CASE_SEED
make_local_dir $LOCAL_DIR_TOP $TESTCASE $DATE #make local subdirectory
(Ex: $LOCAL_DIR_TOP/{$TESTCASE+$DATE} as name, Verdi
need individual dir to run interactive mode), and then chdir into.
link_case_or_simv_here $TESTCASE $SIMV_PATH #link or copy
necessary files to run
run_case_to_error $SIMV_PATH $TESTCASE $CASE_SEED
$SNPS_RCA_RUN_OPT
#1. Get testcase name by $TESTCASE; use simv in $SIMV_PATH (Which
is compiled by builds.build_version) to run testcase in local
directory with $CASE_SEED and "RCA predefined option
$SNPS_RCA_RUN_OPT"
#2. run_case_to_error only run to hit 1st UVM_ERROR and then exit;
to save running time
#Note:
# Turn on fsdb dumping in this script. AutoRCA auto disable dumping
if it is unnecessary.
# run_case_to_error don't return until it finishes, ex: qsub -I q o_vcs_32G <rerun_script>

DUT Root Cause Analysis (DUTRCA)
* DUTRCA Application
* DUTRCA Usage
* Low-Power Debug for DUTRCA

Traditionally, comparing a failed test case in regression with a passed test case from a
previous regression takes a lot of time. This process includes checking waveforms, log
files, and source code. The reasons for a test case to fail might include changes in RTL,
enabling Xprop, changes in testbench, or any simulation migration. In complex designs,
finding where to start debugging and locating the root cause requires much manual work
and can be very time-consuming
RDA provides a DUT Root Cause Analysis (DUTRCA) solution. It automatically compares
a currently failed simulation with a previously passed simulation. It analyzes all suspect
points that could have caused the regression to fail and finds the possible root causes.
Using DUTRCA, Verdi automatically traces and compares the previously passed and
currently failed designs and waveforms. It traces all error points together to help you find
and analyze possible root causes of the failure.
DUTRCA automation helps you find out why a simulation that passed before is now failing.
It does this by automatically searching for possible root causes using design changes and
both passing and failing FSDB files.

Figure 62

Overview of DUT Root Cause Analysis

After DUTRCA analysis, RDA provides the Verdi GUI that includes several debugging
tools. You can use these tools to review the analysis results, as well as the loaded design
and simulation results.
The DUTRCA solution helps you quickly find the root cause of failures. It automatically
analyzes differences between designs and simulation results. With DUTRCA, you do not
need to compare waveforms, source code, or log files manually. This saves engineering
time and effort, reducing debug time from days to hours.

DUTRCA uses Simulation Failure Analyzer, Design Change Analyzer, and TraceDiff to
review the failed simulation log file. It uses reference KDB and FSDB files and target KDB
and FSDB files to automatically find the root cause due to design changes.
DUTRCA analyzes the log file to find the debug entries. It then compares these entries
in the waveform with the reference model to find signals with value differences. DUTRCA
traces how the difference signals move through the design. It then matches these signals
to the points where the design has changed.
Additionally, you can specify particular signals or scopes that need tracing, such as those
with errors. DUTRCA also helps trace differences when migrating to a new VCS version or
changing VCS options.

Figure 63

Overview of DUT Root Cause Analysis

Key Engines of DUTRCA
The key engines of DUTRCA are as follows:
* Log analysis: DUTRCA uses log analysis to automatically analyze log files and
get debug entries to trace the root cause. Log Analysis includes the following three
technologies to perform error message analysis:
Assertion fail analysis: It detects the first assertion error message in the
simulation log file. It then uses the signals related to the assertion property as
debug entries, ensuring high accuracy.
Signal match: It takes the key name from a UVM error or a user-defined error
message. It then maps with the tree-top design hierarchy. If the user-defined error
messages have high correlation with the design scope name, it finds the possible
candidate for the debug entry scope.
Message analysis: It identifies the scoreboard that printed the message based on
the UVM error message. It then identifies the interface suitable for the debug entry
using the transaction dump information.
* Design difference analysis: DUTRCA automatically compares two simv.daidir files
and finds design changes between the two versions of the source codes. Additionally,
DUTRCA traces the root-causes based on the comparison and results.
* Waveform compare and value difference tracing: Through the Waveform
Comparison technology of Verdi nCompare, DUTRCA compares different types of
simulation results at different design phases. It uses the Waveform Value Difference
Tracing technology to trace back all caught error ports and identify and analyze the
possible root causes simultaneously.

The DUTRCA automatic value difference tracing is shown in the following figure:
Figure 64

DUTRCA Automatic Value Difference Tracing

The Waveform Value Difference Tracing technology also detects the waveform shift
between the reference and the target signals. It scans the ports in the target waveform
and estimates the reset time to eliminate the possibility of causing errors.
* DUT boundary difference detect: DUTRCA provides "RCA on Boundary" solution and
generates a report that helps you judge if the issue results from testbench changes or
DUT changes. The DUTRCA report helps in finding the source of the behavior change,
whether it occurs within the DUT scope or at the interface.
Figure 65

DUTRCA on Boundary Flow

Refer to the DUTRCA Reports With Verdi section for details on reviewing DUTRCA reports
with Verdi.

DUTRCA Reports With Verdi
RDA provides Verdi GUI to review DUTRCA reports generated after analyzing simulation
log, performing root cause analysis, comparing designs, and tracing signals. The
functions, such as filtering, searching, sorting, and showing source code differences are
also provided to help find the target source code or signal.
Verdi TFV shows the propagation paths of the root cause.

If the root cause is from the testbench or other IP, the report view provides enough
information to help you start debugging. The following figure shows the DUTRCA reports
in Verdi:
Figure 66

Waveform Similarity Analysis
Waveform Similarity Analysis is a built-in feature in the DUTRCA flow. This feature is
available when generating the RCA report. It identifies the most likely root cause to debug
first.
It judges the most suspicious root cause by analyzing the waveform dissimilarity while
performing DUTRCA. The root cause signal with the most dissimilar waveform is sorted to
the top-most position in the RCA report. The root cause with the most similar waveform is
sorted to the bottom-most position in the RCA report.
Consider the following root-cause signals along with their waveform comparisons:
* /system/i_cpu/i_ALUB/n18#351000 (most dissimilar)
* /system/i_cpu/i_PCU/data[7:0]#50000 (second most dissimilar)
* /system/i_cpu/i_PCU/n113#1000 (slightly dissimilar)
* /system/i_cpu/i_ALUB/IXR[0]#85300 (very similar)

DUTRCA Application
The DUTRCA application provides the following key features:
* Automatically perform log analysis to get debug entries and then trace debug entries to
the root-cause.
* Allow user to specify the faulty signals or scope for tracing.
* Trace differences for VCS migration issue or VCS options change.
* Compare two design databases (simv.daidir/kdb) automatically to auto find design
changes between the two design versions, and trace root-causes based on the
comparison results.
DUTRCA also supports the following features in Verdi GUI:
* Provide functions such as filter, search, sort, and source code differences to find target
source code or signal in the reviewing report GUI.
* Support sorting by rank feature using Waveform Similarity Analysis and Signal Match.
* Support TFV to show root-cause propagation paths.
* Generate report indicating if the root-cause is due to the testbench or the other IP.

DUTRCA functions best when

* There is no or minimal change in the testbench
* There is same seed for the testbench
* The root-cause is in the DUT
The following are the requirements for the DUTRCA setup:
* The passed and failed test case waveform FSDB files. DUTRCA supports the thirdparty simulator FSDB files. The .fsdb, .vf, .fsdb.gz, .fsdb.bz2, .slvf, .fsdb.zst,
and .zwd files are also supported as compressed input FSDB file types.
* The database, simv.daidir, generated by VCS unified compile flow and VCS with
-kdb option, and the simulation log file of the failed case.
* The database, simv.daidir, and the simulation log file of the passed case; these files
are required only when Design Change Analysis is needed.
* The DUTRCA configuration file with the required configurations.

The DUTRCA process identifies the target scope and time, taken from the specified log

Types of Mode
The dutrca configuration file setting consists of the mode field specifying a value that
determines the policy for the debug entries, as shown in the following table:
Mode Value

Mode

The following modes are specified in the dutrca configuration file:
* Auto mode
* Manual mode
* Auto + Manual mode
Auto mode
When auto mode is selected, autorca analyzes the error messages in the simulation log
file to identify the scope information.
If any suspicious scope is identified, DUTRCA performs tracing by the identified scope.
If the scope is not found, DUTRCA adopts the specified information, target_scope and
target_time, from the configuration file to perform tracing.

If the target_scope field is not specified, autorca exits the process. If the target_time
field is not specified, autorca takes the maximum time in the target waveform as the
target time.
Manual mode
The Auto + Manual mode is a default mode, and it combines the flow of both the modes.
When the tracing results are not found in the log file, DUTRCA continues performing
tracing with the scope specified in the configuration file.

DUTRCA:

The Auto + Manual mode is a default mode, and it combines the flow of both the modes.

Set tracing configurations
target_scope

When autorca cannot get a DUT scope or signal
from the log file, autorca uses this specified scope
to perform the search for the debug entries. It is
recommended to specify your DUT top as the scope.
This is a required field without default value. You
need to specify the demanded target scope.

max_signal_depth

Specify what depths to search from the target scope.
It is the number of hierarchy levels to search for the
subsequent scopes. If autorca cannot get results
from the specified target_scope, autorca tries
to search in the child scopes depth to the level
<max_signal_depth>. The default is 3.
When you set max_signal_depth to 0 (zero), DUTRCA

Setting max_signal_depth to 0 (zero) might affect
the DUTRCA performance.

max_mismatch_entry

In RDA, a mismatch entry is also called a debug entry.
After performing autorca, one mismatched point of the
searched out results is called a mismatch entry. The
autorca command stops the tracing when the number
of found debug entries equals to this value. The default

Slack time is the time range for scanning the debug
entry, as shown in the following figure.

DUTRCA supports the Percentage and Relative

Signal Match for Correlative Root Causes
After the root cause is sorted based on the waveform similarity analysis, signal match is
used to correlate root causes with the simulation log. Signal match identifies whether the
signal name relates to an error log. If the signal name relates to an error log, then that
signal name is listed at the highest rank in sorting.
Considering the root cause and its debug entries as a group, the related score can also
be calculated on the debug entry signal and root cause signal. It uses the highest score as
the root cause score. If a root cause is identified as a Correlative root cause, then it gets
the highest rank in sorting.

The feature is applied for the report with both the formats (signal-based root cause and
design-change-based root cause). However, only on signal-based root cause format, a
note indicates that a signal-based root cause is a correlative root cause.
Signal match for Correlative Root Causes is applied only when the simulation
log exists.

RTL+UPF to RTL+UPF
In the RTL+UPF to RTL+UPF scenario, there is a stable RTL+UPF design, but some
changes in the UPF configuration cause a mismatch. Changes in the UPF configuration,
such as the isolation difference, retention register difference, or Set Related Supply
Net (SRSN) difference can cause regression to fail. The following diagram displays the
DUTRCA flow in the RTL+UPF to RTL+UPF scenario:
Figure 96

DUTRCA Flow in RTL+UPF to RTL+UPF Scenario

You must send the following files to DUTRCA:
* One simulation log file
* One failed RTL design or waveform with UPF as the target
* One passed RTL design or waveform with UPF as the reference
To dump UPF into simv.daidir, you must add the -upf option in the VCS compile
command. Use the following command:
$vcs -full64 -kdb -debug_acc+all -sverilog -lca <design.sv> -upf
<upf_tcl.upf>

To dump UPF signals to the waveform, use the +fsdb+power=on simulation option.
The RTL+UPF to RTL+UPF scenario focuses on how to identify the UPF difference
between the two sets of UPF elaboration results. The Design Difference Analysis flow
includes the UPF elaboration results and compares the differences between the target and
reference UPF elaboration results. DUTRCA finds out the root cause including the UPF
differences, and the total design change concludes the UPF change in the RCA report.

Testbench Root Cause Analysis (TBRCA)
* TBRCA Application
* Transaction Difference Analysis
* Message Analysis

In a complex design environment, you construct the testbench with different components.
When an error occurs in a testbench component, finding the root cause can be difficult
and time-consuming. Testbench RCA identifies the root cause of testbench errors.
This includes identifying the specific testbench component and the region within that
component where the error occurs.
When you introduce an error into a design environment, the error can occur in the DUT
or the testbench. Testbench RCA focuses on errors in the testbench. If the tool does not
identify the root cause, Testbench RCA reports these as "items of interest" to help you to
debug.
If a design that was previously operating correctly begins to fail, it can be challenging
to identify and locate the cause of the error. This error can spread quickly through the
entire environment. Further, the error might not be reported at the simulation time where
the error occurs. You might not be able to detect and report the error immediately during
simulation. By the time the error gets detected and reported, it involves many testbench

variables and DUT signals. The following diagram shows an example for the time
difference between the cause of the error and the detection of the error:
Figure 108

Error Occurs Versus Errors Detected

Testbench RCA (TBRCA) is a component of the Regression RCA solutions. You can
choose to run TBRCA automatically as a part of the overall flow, or run TBRCA in the
standalone mode. The following figure illustrates running TBRCA in the standalone mode:
Figure 109

Testbench RCA in Standalone Mode

Testbench RCA Overall Flow

TBRCA supports the following two approaches to simplify the debug process:
Transaction Difference Analysis: The first approach involves the following steps:
1. Identify the reference and target simulations that can be compared.
2. Compare the reference and target simulations to identify when and where the
transactions of the target and reference results differ.
3. Report and analyze the differing transactions to locate the cause of differences.

Message Analysis: Message analysis is the second approach which requires only the
target FSDB file and the log file. It involves the following steps:
1. Analyze the first error message from the log file.
2. Identify transactions, signals, and source code related to the error message.

TBRCA Application
Testbench RCA operates on the design environments that use UVM or OVM testbenches.
Testbench RCA provides the following key features:
* Automatically performs Transaction Difference Analysis
Compares and analyzes the interface signals that are found in the target and
reference test cases.
Compares UVM hierarchy of the target and reference designs.
Compares the recorded transactions, both UVM transactions and Synopsys VIP
transactions.

TBRCA Application

* When the transaction differences are not found between the reference and target
simulations, TBRCA automatically performs Message Analysis.
* Message Analysis attempts to identify transactions that might be related to the first
error message to aid the debugging of the error.
* Generates report indicating whether the root-cause is due to the testbench or the other
IP. The report can be reviewed with Verdi and the related features.

You must enable recording of the following information:
* UVM (or OVM) hierarchy and structure (that is, connectivity)
* Sequencer and TLM port activity
* Signal activity of the interfaces that are used to connect the testbench and DUT
* KDB, the structure of the design
You must record the UVM (or OVM) hierarchy, structure, and transactions using the
following options:
Compilation option:
+define+UVM_VERDI_PORT_RECORDING -lca -kdb -debug_acc+all

Runtime options:
+UVM_TR_RECORD
+UVM_VERDI_TRACE=HIER+TLM

The KDB file can be created using the unified compilation flow, -kdb.
If you are using your own UVM/OVM library, then you must instrument the
libraries for recording. TBRCA supports only VCS simulator.

The TBRCA Transaction Difference Analysis flow analyzes two FSDB files - one from a
passing case and another from a related failing case. It identifies the differences between
the transactions recorded in two simulations. You can view and analyze the resulting
transaction differences and associated interface signals in the Verdi GUI.
The following are the requirements for Target and Reference Simulations and FSDB:
* Enable recording of all items associated with the UVM or OVM testbench.
* Use the same seed for both the passing and failing test cases. This avoids transaction
or sequence differences related to randomization.

The following figure displays the Transaction Difference Analysis flow:
Figure 111

Transaction Difference Analysis Flow

The Transaction Difference Analysis flow consists of the following major operations:
1. Interface analysis: The interface signals in both the passing and failing test cases are
analyzed and compared. These signals connect the testbench with the RTL code. For
more details on interface analysis, refer to Interface Analysis.
2. UVM/OVM characteristics analysis: The UVM or OVM hierarchy is compared
between the passing and failing designs. This comparison checks the basic structure
of the hierarchy, that includes comparing the number of components and their
connections. It also looks at activity of certain operations associated with the hierarchy,
such as when objections are raised and lowered. For more details on UVM/OVM
characteristics analysis, refer to UVM/OVM Characteristics Analysis.
3. Transaction comparison: Transactions recorded during the simulation of the passing
and failing tests are compared. The UVM or OVM transactions are compared. If the
design includes Synopsys VIPs that support Protocol Analyzer, these transactions are
compared and reported separately. For more details on transaction comparison, refer
to Transaction Comparison.
4. Debugging in Verdi GUI: You can view and analyze the results of comparing passing
and failing tests in the Verdi environment. Use the following command: autorca
-load_report <report_path>. For more details on debugging in Verdi GUI, refer to
Debugging in Verdi GUI.
Message Analysis is used only when the differences are not found between transactions in
the passing and failing tests. TBRCA uses message analysis to identify transactions that
might be related to the first error message. This helps in debugging the error.

Interface Analysis
Interface analysis determines which signal on the testbench/RTL boundary is the first
to differ and in which direction. When the UVM/OVM information is recorded during
simulation, details about the interfaces that are connected to the testbench are also
recorded. These interfaces are analyzed by TBRCA.
Scenarios to Perform Interface Analysis
You can come across the following scenarios while performing interface analysis:
1. When you find differences while comparing interface signals, first determine the
direction of each signal. TBRCA attempts to identify whether the interface signal is
driven by RTL code or by testbench code.
As SystemVerilog interface signals do not have an explicit direction
associated with them, TBRCA analyzes the SystemVerilog source code to
determine the direction.
2. When the first difference involves an interface signal driven from the RTL to the
testbench, the error likely exists in the RTL code (DUT). When the first difference is
associated with an interface signal driven from the testbench to the RTL, the error likely
exists in the testbench code.
3. When you find no differences while comparing the interface signals, but an error still
occurs, the error most likely exists in an internal testbench component.
4. When differences appear in both testbench inputs and outputs, and the first differences
occur at the same time, the error might exist in the DUT or the testbench. This situation
occurs because a feedback loop connects the testbench code and the RTL code.
The following figure explains all the four scenarios:

TBRCA reports differences when any of these conditions are true:
* Interface signals exist in the reference test but do not appear in the error test.
* Interface signals exist in the error test but do not appear in the reference test.
To view the interface analysis results and compare the differing signals in Verdi GUI, refer
to the Transaction Difference Analysis Review With Verdi section.
Interface analysis provides insight into the source of error. However, it might not
always provide a definitive answer for the source of the error.

UVM/OVM Characteristics Analysis
The second major operation is UVM/OVM Characteristics or Hierarchy Analysis where
the following characteristics of the target testbench are compared with the reference
testbench:
* Component hierarchy
* Component connections
* UVM/OVM objections
* UVM/OVM phases
* Resources
The following figure illustrates the characteristics comparison:
Figure 114

Reference Testbench Versus Target Testbench

TBRCA displays every difference between the target and reference testbench. You can
analyze these differences to assess how they might affect simulation results.

TBRCA reports differences due to addition or removal of a component from the testbench
hierarchy. For example, consider adding new components to the error test environment
in a system. When these new components are not use in the test case that is being
examined by TBRCA, such differences might not affect the simulation results.
You can view the UVM/OVM Hierarchy Analysis report files in Verdi.

The Testbench RCA Message Analysis flow analyzes messages using a Natural
Language Processing (NLP) algorithm. It identifies transactions and signals closely
associated with that message. The resulting transactions and signals can then be
analyzed in the Verdi GUI.
The message to be analyzed can be selected based on the options specified to TBRCA.
When you provide an error log file, TBRCA analyzes the first UVM (or OVM) error that it
finds. If you specify a particular error message, TBRCA analyzes that message instead.
The message analysis results depend on the quality of the error message. The message
analysis algorithm identifies transactions linked to a message. It parses and analyzes the
message contents, then searches for transactions with similar characteristics, such as
attribute names, signal names, and values.

Analyzing Log Message From the Extracted Log File
The simulation log file contains different types of log messages, and you can extract the

analyze_extract_msg_file option. This is shown in the following figure:
Figure 134

Analyzing the Extracted Message File

TBRCA always picks the first valid log message irrespective of the type (Fatal, Error,
Warning, or Information) from the extracted file for analysis. If the first character of a line

The extracted log file must contain the line number and its associated log message.

each line. It takes the left hand side of the colon as the line number of the log message
and the right-hand side of the colon as the log message.

and you must specify the original log file from which the log messages are

Time Out Related Cases Support
Simulation can be timed out with or without generating a UVM_ERROR. When the
simulation generates a UVM_ERROR even after it is timed out, analyzing UVM_ERROR is
not useful. Therefore, Message Analysis provides a solution of collecting thread details to
analyze the time-out related cases.
Collecting Thread Details
To collect the thread details, you must set the time-out time when the simulation stops
responding and update the VCS runtime arguments.
Setting time-out time
To collect the thread details at a particular time, set the simulation time-out or the time
when the simulation stops responding using the following environment variable:
setenv TBRCA_COLLECT_THREAD_TIME <simulation time>

For example, setenv TBRCA_COLLECT_THREAD_TIME 20000
Consider a simulation that runs from time 0 to 100000 and the time-out starts from the
time 20000, then you can set any time between 20000 to 100000 to collect the thread
details. The time-out value helps Message Analysis to stop simulation at the given time
and collect the thread details.
Updating VCS Runtime Arguments
In addition to the setting time-out, you can also add the following VCS runtime arguments
to collect the required details:
-ucli -i <$VERDI_HOME>/etc/tbAutoRCA/scripts/log_analysis/analyzers/
tbrca_timeout_analysis.tcl

After the simulation is completed, Message Analysis collects all the active thread details
which include Running, Waiting, and Blocking.
You can run the Message Analysis and open the report to view, navigate, and search the
thread details to identify the suspicious thread causing the simulation time-out.

The following figure displays the thread details in the report:
Figure 141

Displaying Collected Thread Details

The collected threads provide the file path, line number details, and the active status about
each thread. When you double-click each thread, it points you to the source code of that
thread.

X Root Cause Analysis (XRCA)
* What is XRCA?
* XRCA Application
* XRCA Usage
* XRCA Root Cause Reasons

Traditionally, unknown values (Xs) typically propagate through the design over multiple
statements. There are many root causes of unknown values. For example, if there is an
X in the input of a logic gate, if memory is not initialized, or if there is a setup or hold time
violation.
Usually, multiple Xs occur together. When you have multiple unknowns, select one X as
the startpoint for debugging, even if it is in your log or signal list. Then, trace backward
through the driver or fan-in signals of your chosen signal until you find the earliest X. If
the signal you selected is not the only cause of unknowns, pick another X from the group
and repeat the process. This cycle involves several small, repeated steps that can be
organized and automated.
XRCA automatically scans X signals in FSDB files and traces each X signal to its root
cause. It can process many X signals together, which reduces debugging time. XRCA also
creates clear, organized reports of the root causes. You can load these reports in Verdi to
view the tracing paths.
XRCA is a useful tool for debugging X signals during the start of gate-level simulation
and for finding X signal issues during regression. XRCA supports tracing at the gatelevel netlist, RTL, and VCS X propagation. It also helps trace X signals from low power
components and can detect X-pessimism.

What is XRCA?

What is XRCA?
XRCA is a highly effective tool that helps you quickly trace the path from an unknown
signal at an observation point to the root cause signal. This saves significant manual effort.
Using the input design and FSDB, XRCA with the tracing technology automatically traces
groups of X signals to their root causes. It also has built-in knowledge of how X values are
generated. With the analyzing technology, XRCA analyzes the root causes and generates
categorized reports. These reports are text files, and you can also use the capability for
further debugging in Verdi Apex mode. After the design and FSDB are ready, all tracings
and analysis steps run automatically, as shown in the following figure:
Figure 150

XRCA Methodology

Figure 151 shows that XRCA uses the dumped waveform and design as inputs. You
can also specify a signal list to only focus on specific signals with X values. If you do not
provide a signal list, XRCA runs in auto-scan mode. In auto-scan mode, it scans and
traverses all signals of the FSDB and generates a list of signals with X values.

What is XRCA?

Figure 151

XRCA Inputs

With a signal list (provided by the user or generated in auto-scan mode), XRCA
automatically traces back step by step to the active driver of unknown values. This
process continues for each signal until the path reaches the unknown root cause or meets
the specified stop criteria
From scanning to tracing, XRCA builds a behavior model that represents the actual design
behaviors. This model enables automatic tracing of all nodes of the design based on the
behavior to guide which fan-in signals should be traced further. The following figure is an
example showing the backward path tracing of XRCA in the behavior model:
Figure 152

XRCA Behavior Model

What is XRCA?

After completing the tracing process, XRCA analyzes the tracing results and organizes the
identified root causes into distinct categories. The following figure shows scenarios before
and after XRCA analysis and categorization:

X-Pessimism Detection
XRCA helps you find out the root causes of X signals. However, some X signals might be
false alarms due to X-pessimism. To identify X, you need to check the false X manually.
This is a time-consuming process.
For example:

If A has an unknown value, the simulation value of the AND gate is X. However, you can
find out that the result of an AND gate must be 0 because A AND is always equal to 0
(zero), irrespective of the value of A.

XRCA Application

XRCA-XPESS Engine
XRCA provides an X-pessimism engine to analyze the unknown values and validate
whether an X signal is a real X, or it has a constant value. This feature first runs XRCAXPESS to find out false X, and then runs XRCA engine to analyze the remaining nonXPESS signals.
Figure 154

XRCA-XPESS Engine

The XRCA-XPESS engine has the following limitation:
* The XRCA-XPESS engine detects X-pessimism reliably only on gate-level simulation
(GLS) designs. This feature does not support RTL designs.

XRCA Application
The following are the key points that XRCA adheres to:
* With a given unknown value signal list, XRCA analyzes all these issues automatically.
* Without a given X value signal list, XRCA automatically generates a signal list with X
values, then analyzes them.
* Generates a report, which classifies unknown values of the signals to the same root
causes.
* Allows Verdi to load the report and shows the trace path in Verdi Apex mode.
* Speeds up the debug process significantly.

Tracing Specific Items at the Set Time in XRCA
The target_signal_list option of the YAML file of XRCA appends a file that lists all the
signals, scopes, and assertions that you want to trace.
You must categorize your inputs by specifying assertList, scopeList, and signalList
keywords for assertions, scopes, and signals, respectively in the following file format:
<keyword>
<full_signal_name>#<time><time_unit>

Where,
* <keyword> can be one of the following:
signalList specifies the following <full_signal_name> lines or is left empty for
debug entries.
assertList specifies the following <full_signal_name> lines for assertions.
scopeList specifies the following <full_signal_name> lines for design scopes.

* <time> specifies the time point from where the tracing starts for the specified item.
* <time_unit> specifies the units of the time point from where the tracing starts for the
specified item.
* You can specify scopeList and signalList without time using the
following file format:
<keyword>
<full_signal/scope_name>

* When the file is not specified, XRCA automatically scans the FSDB file for
signals that have X and traces Xs on those signals.

XRCA Timing-Violation Correlation
XRCA automatically identifies cases where an X root cause is driven by a timing violation
reported in the simulation log. After running XRCA, a post-processing module performs the
following tasks:
* Scans XRCA root causes.
* Correlates them with timingviolation messages in the simulation log (VCS or thirdparty formats).
* Annotates matching root causes as timing violation and records the exact
simulation log file and line in the XRCA report.
When you load xrca_report.xml,
* For root causes that correlate to a timing violation, XRCA updates the displayed reason
text to X from timing violation.
* When a timingviolation subsection is present for a root cause, the GUI adds a
timing violation tree widget under that root cause.
* Use Show Timing Violation on SmartLog in SmartLog to open the simulation log
and jump to the recorded line. Use Show Timing Violation on Source View in
Source View to navigate to the related source location.
The following are the key features of XRCA Timing-Violation Correlation:
* It acts purely as a post process.
* It runs only when timing_violation_check is enabled and target_sim_log
specifies a readable simulation log file. For details, see Enabling XRCA TimingViolation Correlation.
The XRCA Timing-Violation Correlation section consists of the following topics:
* Enabling XRCA Timing-Violation Correlation
* Post-Processing After XRCA Run
* Loading Report With XRCA Timing-Violation Correlation
* Limitations of XRCA Timing-Violation Correlation

Enabling XRCA Timing-Violation Correlation
The XRCA Timing-Violation Correlation feature is conditionally enabled. To use this
feature, all of the following must be true:
* The timing_violation_check option is enabled in the XRCA YAML template.
* A valid simulation log path, target_sim_log, is specified in the XRCA YAML template.
* The file at that path exists and can be opened for reading.
However, if timing_violation_check is set to false, if the target_sim_log field is
missing or empty, or if the simulation log file cannot be opened, then
* The timing-violation post process is skipped.
* No timing-violation annotation is applied.
* No change to root cause reasons.
* No additional navigation is enabled.

Post-Processing After XRCA Run
After the XRCA run completes, the tool performs the following postprocessing steps to
correlate root causes with timing violations:
1. Extracts root-cause information from the XRCA output
a. After XRCA finishes, the output file xrca_report.xml is available.
b. XRCA parses xrca_report.xml to identify all <rootCause> entries.
c. For each root cause, the tool extracts the full signal name and identifies the driven
scope instance. The tool considers cross-module references (XMRs) also.
d. XRCA builds an inmemory list of root-cause signals and scopes, to be used in
subsequent searches.
2. Correlates root causes with timing violations in the simulation log
a. The tool uses the root-cause list and the specified simulation-log file
(target_sim_log).
b. It searches the simulation log for candidate locations that match a root-cause
scope.
c. When several timing-violation candidates exist, the tool selects the violation with a
time closest to, but earlier than, the original root-cause time.
d. For each candidate location, the tool checks whether it forms a valid
timingviolation block, based on existing SmartLog rules.

It supports VCS and third-party timing-violation formats.
e. When a timing-violation block is matched, XRCA collects the following
timingviolation information:
Timing-violation type (for example, hold)
Source code file
Source code line
Simulation log file
Simulation log line
Timing-violation time
Load parse rule for the log type
3. For each root cause with a correlated timing-violation block, the tool creates a
timing-violation subsection under the related <rootCause> element in the enriched
xrca_report.xml file.
4. For each root cause, the tool performs the following:
Constructs a timing-violation subsection under root cause section.
Saves the updated xrca_report.xml (overwriting the report file).

Multiple Cycle Path Root Cause Analysis
(MCPRCA)
* MCPRCA Usage

During RTL simulation, Dynamic SDC Verification in VCS detects timing constraint bugs,
such as Multiple Cycle Path (MCP), FP, and clock group issues. SDC forms a key part of
RTL signoff. Teams use VCS with SDC (VCS-SDC) for signoff during verification. VCSSDC reduces project cycle time by several weeks.
Debugging violations detected by VCS-SDC can be difficult when MCP bugs affect many
signals. RDA offers a Multiple Cycle Path Root Cause Analysis (MCPRCA) solution. This
solution automatically groups violations into fewer categories. It provides connections to
further debug with waveform, source code, and simulation log, using Verdi.

MCPRCA helps you to debug the VCS-SDC detected violations using Verdi. After
completing simulation with VCS-SDC, MCPRCA checks the results of VCS-SDC and
helps in finding out the violations. MCPRCA uses the Violation Binning feature to group
violations from a simulation log and generate further debug entries.
RDA provides the Verdi GUI to review MCPRCA reports generated after analyzing
violations from the log file. You can also use the GUI to debug the source code, logs, and
waveform.

testbench.dut.mux.ff1.

{*}

Violation index with two FROM signals and one TO signal. This index can waive.
TO signal: top.sub1.ccc

FaultRCA: Fault Analysis
FaultRCA consists of the following sections:
* General Fault Analysis
* NC Analysis
* Limitation of FaultRCA

Debugging general faults, such as NO, NN, ND, and so on, means that you need to
trace the fanout from the fault location. Follow the path finding the blocking points in the
downstream circuits until you reach an observation or detection point. This is a timeconsuming process that requires manual efforts.
To overcome the limitation of excessive manual effort and time consumption, FaultRCA
provides utility that helps in detecting the blocking points between the fault-injected point
and the observation or detection point.
A path is created from the fault location to the observation point. Along this path, you can
identify and collect blocking points. This helps you focus on the path and attempt to make
the fault move from the injected point) to the observation point.
Blocking Points
Blocking points are the points through which a fault cannot propagate. For example, as
shown in Figure 209, assume A is the fault location where the fault SA1 (stuck-at-1) is
injected. The fault propagates to C. However, the fault cannot propagate to D.
As the value of B is constantly 0, the primitive AND gate never allows the fault at C to
propagate to D. Because the fault is not propagated to D, the AND cell is called the
blocking cell.

Figure 209

Blocking Cell

This section consists of the following topics:
* Fault Analysis Method
* Running Fault Analysis
* Configuration Fields in the Configuration File
* Generating and Loading Tracing Report in Verdi
* Viewing Tracing Report in Verdi
* Ranking Report

Fault Analysis Method
The fault analysis method provides the following two modes:
* Static Trace Mode
* Block Cell Detection Mode

Static Trace Mode
FaultRCA traces the path from the input fault to the destination point. You can either
extract the observation point from the fault database (FDB) or provide a list of signals to
the tool. You can run this mode in the following two ways:
* Target Signal Mode
* Auto Mode
Target Signal Mode
To analyze one or more signals, use target signal mode. In this mode, you must provide
one or multiple input signals. The information, such as observations list and signal type,
are extracted from the FDB. FaultRCA generates an XML report (.xml) and a text report
(.txt) containing the tracing path.

The format of the fault list file is <Signal Full hierarchy name>. For example,
top.a.b
top.c.d.e

Auto Mode
To analyze a list of critical location points available in the FDB, use auto mode. Auto
mode analyzes more than one signal, and it allows you to select the number of signals to
analyze. The FaultRCA utility automatically analyzes the most critical locations, that is, the
blocking points that cover highest number of NO fault from the FDB. It generates an XML
report and a text report containing tracing paths of all the signals. The information, such as
observation points, signal types, and a list of critical blocking points is extracted from the
FDB.

Block Cell Detection Mode
FaultRCA traces a path between the input fault to the destination point and finds any
blocking cell along the path. You can get the observation point from the FDB or provide
a list of signals to the tool. For this mode, you need the dumped waveform from either a
good machine or faulty machine (gm/fm). One input pin has the GM/FM annotation value.
All output pins have only the GM annotation values.
A block instance on a flip-flop checks the current status of the GM/FM annotation and the
incoming clock cycle. Specifically, it checks the input GM/FM status in the current clock
cycle and the output GM/FM status in the next clock cycle.
When the next clock cycle arrives at the signal connected to the register clock port, the
block checks the clock port. If the clock port is rising or falling, it finds the next rising or
falling time. Otherwise, it finds the next time the value changes.
This mode supports only Stuck@0 and Stuck@1. You can run it in the target signal mode.
Target Signal Mode
If you want to analyze one or multiple signals, use target signal mode. In this mode, you
must provide one or multiple input signals and the target signal list name.
The following is the format of the fault list:
<stuck@0>/<stuck@1>, <Signal full hierarchy name>

0, top.a.b
1, top.c.d.e

Running Fault Analysis
You can run fault analysis using autorca in the static trace mode and the block cell
detection mode.
To generate the configuration file template (run.yaml), use the following command:
autorca -gen_cfg_template <run.yaml> -gen_mode faultrca

When you run the command, the run.yaml file is generated.
The following are the requirements to run fault analysis:
* The simv.daidir directory
* The mode field must be set to 1 by default.
* The gm/fm waveform is required for the block cell detection mode.
For FDB, you must specify the following fields:
* FDB project name: Specify the name of the FDB project to be used.
* FDB path: Specify the full path of the FDB directory.
* Campaign name: Specify the campaign name that is used for dumping FDB.
* For the destination point, you can provide the text file or extract the observation or
detection point from the FDB.
For the target signal mode, you must specify the text file containing the name of the
signals. For more information on the format of the fault list file for the static trace mode
and the block cell detection mode, refer to the Static Trace Mode and Block Cell Detection
Mode sections, respectively.
For the auto mode, specify the number of top critical locations that you require.

Configuration Fields in the Configuration File
When you run the following command using autorca and gen_cfg_template, a
configuration file is generated:
autorca -gen_cfg_template <run.yaml> -gen_mode faultrca

You can use the autogenerated file to run FaultRCA. The following is the format of the file
in the FaultRCA mode:

field, mode 2: required field

Introduction
Synopsys Regression Debug Automation (RDA) is a solution that uses machine learning,
AI, and auto-trace technology to automate regression debug tasks. RDA automatically
groups failure cases (binning), finds root causes, and traces errors. It is designed for
complex System-on-Chip (SoC) and IP designs. Traditional regression debug flows need
engineers to spend a lot of time on manual binning, triaging, debugging, and tracing.
These tasks often start with many possible suspects and error points.
RDA automates the process of handling failed regression tests. It groups large numbers
of failed test cases, finds the root causes of failures, and identifies and isolates problem
areas. RDA also prepares debugging facilitators, completing these tasks much faster than
manual methods. By removing the need to compare waveforms, source code, and log files
manually, RDA reduces engineering effort and saves time--from days to just hours.
The following figure shows the effort distribution in the traditional regression debugging
process:
Figure 1

Engineer Efforts on Manual but Replaceable Tasks

Chapter 2: Introduction

With RDA automation, engineers can use their time more efficiently, as shown in the
Figure 2

Engineer Effort on Really Manual Task While Adopting RDA

Adopting RDA maximizes the efficiency and productivity of engineers, reduces cost,
improves turnaround time, and accelerates the debugging process.
The following topic provides an overview of the RDA technology: Technology Overview.

RDA uses computing resources to automate the machine-replaceable tasks. It
automatically traces the design and analyzes root causes of the regression test failures.
After regression, RDA runs in batch mode and generates analysis reports to review and
check the failure analysis. The following figure provides an overview of the RDA flow:
Figure 3

RDA Flow Overview

The RDA solution comes with the following key features:
* Regression Binning
RDA automates the tedious process of regression binning. It uses computing resources
and a machine learning database to analyze failed regression test cases. RDA then
sorts and groups cases with the same failure type into one bucket.
* Debug Facilitator

Chapter 2: Introduction

title: Appendix 257
text:
RDA uses the Debug Facilitator to create the database and debugging environments
you need. This helps you debug each binning bucket in different debug modes.
Debug Facilitator uses a build script and a run-simulation script to rebuild and
rerun simulations after regression. This speeds up the process by reducing manual
preparation efforts. Furthermore, you can use the same scripts for future regressions.
Debug Facilitator includes reverse debug in interactive mode. This feature allows
you to control simulation execution both forward and backward. You can also enable
transaction recording to debug at the protocol level.
* DUT Root Cause Analysis
RDA provides a DUT Root Cause Analysis (DUTRCA) solution. This feature compares
a failed simulation with a previously passed simulation. It analyzes all suspect points
that might lead to regression failure and helps find the possible root causes. DUTRCA
automatically identifies and analyzes the possible causes by tracing back all error
points at the same time.
* Testbench Root Cause Analysis
RDA provides a Testbench Root Cause Analysis (TBRCA) solution that identifies the
testbench component with which the error is associated. It also identifies the region
within that component where the error is located.
The TBRCA Transaction Difference analysis flow analyzes and compares the reference
simulation log file with the failing simulation log file. It identifies the differences between
the transactions recorded during both simulations. The TBRCA Message Analysis
flow analyzes a message and identifies transactions and signals associated with that
message. Automatic detection of transaction differences helps you debug testbench
errors faster. This feature saves time during the debugging process.
* X Root Cause Analysis
All unknown X signals are automatically scanned and traced to their root causes. This
process saves manual effort. By managing and tracing many X signals automatically,
you spend less time repeating the same debugging steps.
* Multiple Cycle Path Root Cause Analysis
RDA provides a Multiple Cycle Path Root Cause Analysis (MCPRCA) solution. This
feature automatically groups violations detected by VCS-SDC into fewer groups. It
uses Verdi to debug each group by viewing waveform, source code, and simulation
logs.

* FaultRCA: Fault Analysis
The FaultRCA utility helps in detecting the blocking points between the fault-injected
point and the observation or detection point. This overcomes the limitation of excessive
manual effort and time consumption required to debug general faults.
RDA uses an easy-to-use GUI reporter, RCA Manager, to view reports in different ways.
You can sort, group, and search all regression cleanup results directly in RCA Manager.
Debugging environments set up by Debug Facilitator can be started from RCA Manager.
You can also view traced paths from the analysis report in Temporal Flow View (TFV).

Regression Binning
* Regression Binning Application
* Regression Binning Usage

The first step after a regression failure is to process many failed cases. Manually checking,
analyzing, and organizing these cases can be very time-consuming and requires
significant manual work.
RDA offers Regression Binning, an automated process that uses machine learning and
data mining techniques to analyze failures and group those with the same issue type
together. The automation reduces engineer manual efforts and saves time.
The difference between the Manual Binning and Triaging, and the Automated Binning and
Triaging is shown in the following figure:
Figure 4

Manual Regression Binning Versus Automated Regression Binning

With a user-provided list of simulation log files of failure cases, Regression Binning mines
log files and conducts similarity checking which performs failure clustering based on the
similarity of log files.
The resulting groups are called buckets, where each bucket represents a failure type
that can be reviewed, analyzed, and debugged later. The following figure shows the
Regression Binning Technology:
Figure 5

Regression Binning Technology

Regression Binning Application
The Regression Binning application is an easy setup suitable for the Universal Verification
Methodology (UVM) regression environment and the SoC/IP level designs. Regression
Binning provides the following key features:
* Categorizes the simulation log files into different buckets, where each bucket
represents a failure type.
* Requires only simulation log files of the failed test cases.
* Provides a specific solution for the UVM-based error messages using unsupervised
machine learning based algorithm.
The Regression Binning application also supports the following advanced binning features:
* Extend binning capability by the user-defined rule of errors.
* Waive specific error patterns for binning.
* Group failed test cases without error messages but with a customized pass pattern,
recognized as Pass by RDA, in a Pass bucket.
* Replace or remove the unwanted parts of the specific error patterns.

Regression Binning Application

* Disable RCA and/or Debug Facilitator for the specific error patterns.
* Customize the priority of the specific error messages for binning.

Regression Binning Reports With Verdi
Through Regression Binning, failed tests are grouped into buckets and the binning reports
are generated. RDA provides the GUI interface, RCA Manager, to review each bucket for
each type of failure.
The Verdi SmartLog engine loads the selected log file for further reviewing and
debugging. The following figure shows the regression binning reports in Verdi:
Figure 6

Regression Binning Reports in Verdi

The following are the requirements for the Regression Binning setup:
* Simulation log files of the regression tests.
* User-defined rule file; this file is required when you have user-defined error messages,
waiving error messages, or prioritizing messages.

This section provides steps for performing Regression Binning, generating reports,
reviewing reports in Verdi, and configuring advanced user-defined rules to extend
Regression Binning capability.

Performing Regression Binning Steps
The steps to perform Regression Binning with the autorca command are as follows:
1. Prepare a YAML configuration file for Regression Binning.
The configuration file configures RDA for the required Regression Binning engine and
the corresponding required data. You can reuse the same configuration file for the
future regressions.
You can use the autorca -gen_cfg_template <cfg_file_name> -gen_mode
<engine> command to auto generate an easy and ready-to-go template configuration
file, %> autorca -gen_cfg_template binning.yaml -gen_mode binning
For more information on how to generate a RDA configuration file for Regression
Binning, click the following video link:
This video focuses on generating a configuration file for RDA components, such
as Regression Binning, DUTRCA, Debug Facilitator, XRCA, and TBRCA.

The generation of the template file is shown in the following figure:
Figure 7

Template of Regression Binning Configuration File

2. In the latest_fail_list field, specify the path of the file that contains a list of log files
that have failures. The following figure shows an example of the contents in the list file:

3. This step is optional. Single-error binning uses a machine learning algorithm that
groups log files based on the similarity of their first error message. The algorithm
compares the first error in each log file and places files with similar first errors into the
same bucket.
However, the multiple_error_binning option enables a machine learning algorithm.
