The following example shows how to debug the error starting with the error or differential
transaction shown on Transaction and Protocol Analyzer. As the error is reported in the
driver, you can investigate whether the error is associated with the driver-transfer
method. Double-click the method name, as shown in the following figure:

If the first interface signal difference is associated with the sig_data_out signal, it
means that the error is likely associated with the data phase of the transfer. Based on this
explanation, you can investigate the drive_data_phase method.

This method of identifying the source of an error is called Static Analysis. You must
investigate the read_byte and write_byte. This shows that the error most likely occurred
while reading or writing a byte.
The following figure shows that the error got injected in the read_byte method:
Figure 123

Error Injected in read_byte Method

The tracking of an error through static analysis shows that Transaction Difference
Analysis correctly identifies the component where the error is located. It also highlights the
transaction value to start the debugging process.

The Testbench RCA Message Analysis flow analyzes messages using a Natural
Language Processing (NLP) algorithm. It identifies transactions and signals closely
associated with that message. The resulting transactions and signals can then be
analyzed in the Verdi GUI.
The message to be analyzed can be selected based on the options specified to TBRCA.
When you provide an error log file, TBRCA analyzes the first UVM (or OVM) error that it
finds. If you specify a particular error message, TBRCA analyzes that message instead.
The message analysis results depend on the quality of the error message. The message
analysis algorithm identifies transactions linked to a message. It parses and analyzes the

Message Analysis highlights two attributes, addr and data[0], that might be associated
with the errors. You must check the driving of the address phase and data phase. Because

title: Appendix 257
text:
As per the static analysis, the error most likely occurred while reading or writing a byte, as
shown in the following figure:

Using static analysis, Message Analysis identifies the component where the error
happened. It also highlights the transaction of value to help you begin debugging.

Message Analysis Features
The Message Analysis approach uses log messages to identify the cause of error. The
following sections describe various features of Message Analysis:
* Log Message Callstack Details
* Matching Attributes And Values
* Matching Transaction Details
* Matching Interfaces
* Analyzing Log Message From the Extracted Log File
* Assertion Type Message Analysis
* Support for User-Defined Messages
* Time Out Related Cases Support
* Verdi Interactive Message Analysis Features
* Show All ERROR-Related Log Messages in SmartLog - Upward Track
* ERROR and GOLDEN Pattern Log Messages

Log Message Callstack Details
When the log message call stack details are not available in the simulation log file, then
you can dump the WARNING, ERROR, and FATAL messages call stack details into the
simulation log file using the following runtime options:
+UVM_STACKTRACE=warn +UVM_STACKTRACE=error +UVM_STACKTRACE=fatal

VCS dumps the log message call stack details into the log file above the ERROR/
WARNING/FATAL message. TBRCA can read these call stack details from the simulation
log file and show them to you.
The following figure displays the Message callstack details. The first column shows the
file name and the line number of each call stack, and the second column shows the scope
of the file to which the line number refers.
Figure 127

Log Message Call Stack Details

You can double-click the required call stack or use the RMB action Show in nTrace to
open the file path and the line number of the selected call stack details. The following
figure displays the Show in nTrace feature:
Figure 128

Displaying Selected Stack in the Source Window

Matching Attributes And Values
Message Analysis provides the final matching attributes and values in the RCA report.
These attributes and values are one of the criteria for the Message Analysis to find
transactions from FSDB.
Loading Search Expression Into the Transaction And Protocol Analyzer Search
Dialog Box
Select the RMB option Load Search Expression to load the attributes and values in the
expressions format into the Transaction and Protocol Analyzer (TNPA) Search dialog box.
Figure 129

Load Search Expression

You can double-click to choose the required expression and start defining to search for the
required transactions in the TNPA window.
For more details about the TNPA Search dialog box, refer to the Search Capability for
Transactions section of the Verdi Transaction and Protocol Debug User Guide.

Matching Transaction Details
The Matching Transaction Details section provides all the matching transactions
collected using different approaches for analysis. It consists of the following two groups:
* Analysis Based on Message Description
* Active Transactions at Error Time
The following figure displays the Matching Transaction Details section:
Figure 130

Matching Transaction Details

Each group contains the matching transactions. Each transaction contains the related port
or stream names and the related virtual interface.

Figure 131

Additional Details for Each Transaction

You can use the RMB option View All Transactions to add all the transactions in the
selected group.
You can use the RMB option View in nWave to add the selected interface into nWave.
Analysis Based on Message Description
The Analysis Based on Message Description group contains transactions found by
analyzing the message description. This group focuses on the listed attributes and their
values.
Figure 132

Displaying Matching Attribute and Values

Active Transactions at Error Time
The Active Transactions at Error Time section contains transactions that are active or
detected when the error occurs. This section captures transactions present at the exact
error time. The tool filters these transactions using the log message TB scope and the
ERROR message call stack.

Matching Interfaces
Matching analysis displays all the matching interfaces grouped by the sources. You can
review the matching interfaces and can get information required for debugging an issue. It
includes the following groups:
* Message Reported TB Interfaces
* Matching Transaction Related Interfaces
* Matching Interfaces by the Message Source File Name
Figure 133

Matching Interfaces

To add the interface and matching signals into nWave, click the RMB option View in
nWave. In the absence of the matching signals, TBRCA adds all the interface signals into
nWave.

Analyzing Log Message From the Extracted Log File
The simulation log file contains different types of log messages, and you can extract the
types of log messages needed for analysis into a separate file, as shown in the following
example:

With this feature, you can analyze the extracted log file using the Message Analysis
approach.
In the YAML configuration file, you can input the extracted log file to be analyzed using the
analyze_extract_msg_file option. This is shown in the following figure:
Figure 134

Analyzing the Extracted Message File

TBRCA always picks the first valid log message irrespective of the type (Fatal, Error,
Warning, or Information) from the extracted file for analysis. If the first character of a line
contains #, assuming it to be a comment, TBRCA picks the next line.
The extracted log file must contain the line number and its associated log message.
TBRCA considers colon (:) as a delimiter to differentiate line number and log message at
each line. It takes the left hand side of the colon as the line number of the log message
and the right-hand side of the colon as the log message.
In the YAML configuration file, the target_sim_log option is mandatory
and you must specify the original log file from which the log messages are
extracted.

Assertion Type Message Analysis
Message Analysis reports the number of assertion messages found from the simulation
log and analyzes the assertion message reported before the UVM_ERROR message.

Figure 135

Assertion Type Message Analysis

Before opening the RCA report, set the following environment variable to add the assertion
related signal into the nWave window:
setenv IMPST_DISABLE_MUST_EXIST_PATH 1

RCA report displays the analysis details of the assertion message under the Assertion
analysis details section, as shown in the following figure:
Figure 136

Assertion Analysis Details

The Assertion analysis details section displays details related to assertion name and the
matching interfaces.
Select the assertion name and click the RMB option Load Signals and View Source to
load the assertion property associated source into nTrace and signals into nWave. It also
adds the assertion_time marker at the assertion start time.

Figure 137

Loading Signals and Viewing Source

You can use the RMB option View in nWave to add matching interfaces and signals into
nWave as shown in the following figure:
Figure 138

Viewing Matching Interfaces into nWave

Support for User-Defined Messages
Simulation log file can contain user-defined messages along with the normal UVM/OVM
format log messages. In the following figure, the highlighted messages are dumped using
macros:

To enable TBRCA to interpret the format of user-defined log messages, create a rule file
and specify it in the YAML configuration file. Use the partition_rule_files option, as
shown in the following figure.
Figure 139

Creating the Rule File

The rule file contains details about the user-defined log messages.
The rules are provided as input to Verdi SmartLog as partition-rule files.
Therefore, it must follow the syntax and format of the Verdi SmartLog partition
rule file. Refer to the SmartLog Tutorial chapter of the Verdi User Guide and
Tutorial for more details.
You can input the user-defined log message details into the Pattern field. The Pattern
option accepts the regular expressions as shown in the following figure. TBRCA accepts
multiple rule files. To understand the user-defined message format, you must mention the
user_defined or UserDefined string as a part of the Type option. TBRCA allows the
string to be case-insensitive.
Figure 140

User-Defined Log Message Details in the Pattern Field

When TBRCA reads the simulation log files, it identifies the log message using the
rule files and collects the user-defined messages. After collecting all the user-defined

messages, TBRCA analyzes the first ERROR type message. If the first message is not an
ERROR type, then it analyzes WARNING or FATAL type user-defined message.
If TBRCA does not find any of the message types, it analyzes the log message using the
default approach.

Time Out Related Cases Support
Simulation can be timed out with or without generating a UVM_ERROR. When the
simulation generates a UVM_ERROR even after it is timed out, analyzing UVM_ERROR is
not useful. Therefore, Message Analysis provides a solution of collecting thread details to
analyze the time-out related cases.
Collecting Thread Details
To collect the thread details, you must set the time-out time when the simulation stops
responding and update the VCS runtime arguments.
Setting time-out time
To collect the thread details at a particular time, set the simulation time-out or the time
when the simulation stops responding using the following environment variable:
setenv TBRCA_COLLECT_THREAD_TIME <simulation time>

Verdi Interactive Message Analysis Features
Message analysis supports the source code analysis features using the Verdi interactive
debug mode.
During the interactive mode, you can further debug the issue using the following Verdi
interactive debug features:

* Analyze the runtime object information of the design.

You must have write access to the design location to identify the design
changes.
Analyze Attribute Value Changes
During the simulation run, the transaction attribute value gets updated and changed
multiple times and at multiple places.

Some of the designs might fail due to a value mismatch of a particular attribute. In such
cases, the feature of analyzing attribute value changes provides the following details:
* Different values assigned to the attribute.
* Time when each value gets changed.
* File path and line number of each value change.
When the message analysis report opens, select the required transactions for which you
need to analyze the value changes.

the selected attribute.

X Root Cause Analysis (XRCA)
* What is XRCA?
* XRCA Application
* XRCA Usage
* XRCA Root Cause Reasons

Traditionally, unknown values (Xs) typically propagate through the design over multiple
statements. There are many root causes of unknown values. For example, if there is an
X in the input of a logic gate, if memory is not initialized, or if there is a setup or hold time
violation.
Usually, multiple Xs occur together. When you have multiple unknowns, select one X as
the startpoint for debugging, even if it is in your log or signal list. Then, trace backward
through the driver or fan-in signals of your chosen signal until you find the earliest X. If
the signal you selected is not the only cause of unknowns, pick another X from the group
and repeat the process. This cycle involves several small, repeated steps that can be
organized and automated.
XRCA automatically scans X signals in FSDB files and traces each X signal to its root
cause. It can process many X signals together, which reduces debugging time. XRCA also
creates clear, organized reports of the root causes. You can load these reports in Verdi to
view the tracing paths.
XRCA is a useful tool for debugging X signals during the start of gate-level simulation
and for finding X signal issues during regression. XRCA supports tracing at the gatelevel netlist, RTL, and VCS X propagation. It also helps trace X signals from low power
components and can detect X-pessimism.

What is XRCA?

What is XRCA?

What is XRCA?
XRCA is a highly effective tool that helps you quickly trace the path from an unknown
signal at an observation point to the root cause signal. This saves significant manual effort.
Using the input design and FSDB, XRCA with the tracing technology automatically traces
groups of X signals to their root causes. It also has built-in knowledge of how X values are
generated. With the analyzing technology, XRCA analyzes the root causes and generates
categorized reports. These reports are text files, and you can also use the capability for
further debugging in Verdi Apex mode. After the design and FSDB are ready, all tracings
and analysis steps run automatically, as shown in the following figure:
Figure 150

XRCA Methodology

Figure 151 shows that XRCA uses the dumped waveform and design as inputs. You
can also specify a signal list to only focus on specific signals with X values. If you do not
provide a signal list, XRCA runs in auto-scan mode. In auto-scan mode, it scans and
traverses all signals of the FSDB and generates a list of signals with X values.

What is XRCA?

Figure 151

XRCA Inputs

With a signal list (provided by the user or generated in auto-scan mode), XRCA
automatically traces back step by step to the active driver of unknown values. This
process continues for each signal until the path reaches the unknown root cause or meets
the specified stop criteria
From scanning to tracing, XRCA builds a behavior model that represents the actual design
behaviors. This model enables automatic tracing of all nodes of the design based on the
behavior to guide which fan-in signals should be traced further. The following figure is an
example showing the backward path tracing of XRCA in the behavior model:
Figure 152

XRCA Behavior Model

What is XRCA?

After completing the tracing process, XRCA analyzes the tracing results and organizes the
identified root causes into distinct categories. The following figure shows scenarios before
and after XRCA analysis and categorization:
Figure 153

Found Root Cause Category After XRCA Analysis

For more information on the XRCA tool, click the following video link:
This video focuses on debugging unknown (X) values in DFT verification using
the automated X Root Cause Analysis (XRCA) feature of Verdi. Unknown
values can propagate through a design, which makes debugging more difficult.

X-Pessimism Detection
XRCA helps you find out the root causes of X signals. However, some X signals might be
false alarms due to X-pessimism. To identify X, you need to check the false X manually.
This is a time-consuming process.
For example:

If A has an unknown value, the simulation value of the AND gate is X. However, you can
find out that the result of an AND gate must be 0 because A AND is always equal to 0
(zero), irrespective of the value of A.

XRCA Application

XRCA-XPESS Engine
XRCA provides an X-pessimism engine to analyze the unknown values and validate
whether an X signal is a real X, or it has a constant value. This feature first runs XRCAXPESS to find out false X, and then runs XRCA engine to analyze the remaining nonXPESS signals.
Figure 154

XRCA-XPESS Engine

The XRCA-XPESS engine has the following limitation:
* The XRCA-XPESS engine detects X-pessimism reliably only on gate-level simulation
(GLS) designs. This feature does not support RTL designs.

XRCA Application
The following are the key points that XRCA adheres to:
* With a given unknown value signal list, XRCA analyzes all these issues automatically.
* Without a given X value signal list, XRCA automatically generates a signal list with X
values, then analyzes them.
* Generates a report, which classifies unknown values of the signals to the same root
causes.
* Allows Verdi to load the report and shows the trace path in Verdi Apex mode.
* Speeds up the debug process significantly.

XRCA Report With Verdi

* The design simv.daidir (compiled by vcs -kdb or vericom -usevcs=adv)
* Waveform file (generated by the Synopsys tool or any third-party tool)
For gate-level design, cells and libraries are suggested to be dumped in
waveform file.
* X signal list (optional)

sim_time_unit

[Optional] Specify the time unit for the
error message. You must specify a
positive time value with a unit, such as
2ns or 10ps.
The binning time unit is found in the
error message. If the time unit is not
found in the error message, you must
specify the sim_time_unit field in the
YAML file.
If this field is not specified, XRCA
checks for the binning-error type and
uses ns for the standard error type.
If this field is not specified and the
binning-error type is not standard, an
error occurs.
If the time units are not specified
in the YAML file or in the error
message, it affects the time tracing
for X.

target_signal_list

[Optional] Specify the signal list file for
XRCA tracing. If you do not specify
the file, XRCA scans all X signals for
tracing. For more details on this option,
refer to the Tracing Specific Items at the
Set Time in XRCA.

Stops tracing at the task boundary
when XRCA finds the traced signal
inside the task block. Set -task_stop
to true to enable the feature. By
default, it is false.

Advanced Option for Debug Entry Scanning
target_scope

[Optional] Specify the DUT hierarchy
in the target_scope option to enable
XRCA to scan for the X debug-entry
signals.

max_err_cnt

Specify the maximum count to scan X
debug entry. The default is 256. Set it to
0 for no limitation.

max_scan_level

Specify maximum scanning
level to scan X debug entry from
target_scope. The default is 3. Set it
to 0 to scan all the levels.

max_sample_per_signal

Specify maximum count of X debug
entry for each signal. The default is 1.
Set it to 0 for no limitation.

target_signal_type

Specify the type of signals to be
scanned:
* type: {boundary, register, all} or the
union of some of them.
* boundary: input/output/inout direction
signals.
* register: register type signals.
* all: all signals in the FSDB file.

begin_time [time[unit]]

Specify the begin time of scanning the
X debug entry signals in the waveform
file. The default is 1 and the default time
unit is FSDB time unit.

end_time [time[unit]]

Specify the end time of scanning the
X debug entry signals in the waveform
file. The default is waveform max time
and the default time unit is FSDB time
unit.

gen_list [true|false]

Dumps X debug entry signal list
scanned by XRCA and does not invoke
tracing. The default is false.

Tracing Specific Items at the Set Time in XRCA
The target_signal_list option of the YAML file of XRCA appends a file that lists all the
signals, scopes, and assertions that you want to trace.
You must categorize your inputs by specifying assertList, scopeList, and signalList
keywords for assertions, scopes, and signals, respectively in the following file format:
<keyword>
<full_signal_name>#<time><time_unit>

Where,
* <keyword> can be one of the following:
signalList specifies the following <full_signal_name> lines or is left empty for
debug entries.
assertList specifies the following <full_signal_name> lines for assertions.
scopeList specifies the following <full_signal_name> lines for design scopes.

* <time> specifies the time point from where the tracing starts for the specified item.
* <time_unit> specifies the units of the time point from where the tracing starts for the
specified item.
* You can specify scopeList and signalList without time using the
following file format:
<keyword>
<full_signal/scope_name>

* When the file is not specified, XRCA automatically scans the FSDB file for
signals that have X and traces Xs on those signals.
## Example 1: (debug entries)
##
system.CPU.output#100ns
##
system.CPU.output#100000ps
##
/system/CPU/output#100ns
## You can specify signals without time if the time is not available.
##
system.CPU.output
##
/system/CPU/output
## You must specify assertions with time.
## Example 2: (assertions with the same start and fail times)
##
assertList
##
system.CPU.check_reset#250ns
##
/system/CPU/check_clock#500000ps
## Example 3: (assertions with different start and fail times)
##
assertList
##
system.CPU.check_reset#200ns#250ns
##
/system/CPU/check_clock#400000ps#500000ps
## Example 4: (scopes)
##
scopeList
##
system.CPU.ALU#100ns
##
/system/CPU/PCU#20000ps
## You can specify scopes without time if the time is not available.
##
system.CPU.PCU
##
/system/CPU/PCU

Invoking XRCA and Reviewing XRCA Results in Verdi
To invoke XRCA, use the following command:
$ autorca -cfg <template_name.yaml>

While launching XRCA, XRCA finds the X signal for analysis by following the process
shown in Figure 159:
Figure 159

Flowchart to Find X Signal for Analysis

After successfully finding the X signal for analysis, XRCA performs X tracing to trace the
root cause of the found X signal. When the XRCA tracing finishes, the console displays
the following message to load the trace report:
[RCA] Load report with 'autorca -load_report xrca_report.xml'

title: Appendix 257

Load the XRCA report in Verdi using the following command:
$ autorca -load_report xrca_report.xml

XRCA GUI Report
XRCA GUI Report is integrated with the existing functions of SmartLog to help you browse
the whole XRCA report structure with a concise template. You can trace the XRCA results
using XRCA GUI Report that provides the following key features:
* Tree widget report layout
* Filtering/sorting/search function
* Four report types grouping
* Intuitive GUI interaction with TFV, nWave, and nTrace
* X-propagation flow of XRCA
The following figure displays the report loaded to Verdi:
Figure 160

GUI Window for XRCA Results

The following are the features of the XRCA GUI window:
* Loads XRCA results report to Verdi in a standalone window.
* Displays all the debug entries in one window.
* Supports collapse configuration by default.
* Adds and expands the X-pessimism Result section when there is an X-pessimism
signal in the report. However, you can collapse the merge nodes under x-pessimism
debug entry.

* The tree structure of XRCA Root Cause Results for each debug entry consists of the
following items:
Debug entry,
Root cause,
Hint (if analyzing X-propagation/NLP data)
Module, signal name (available in case of module grouping)
Reason (available in case of reason grouping)
* Allows single selection.
* Provides toolbar for interactive actions such as filtering, sorting, and searching.
Refer to the following sections for details on the XRCA GUI report layout and features:
* Tree Widget Report Layout
* Impact of X-pessimism on XRCA Report
* XRCA Report Debug View

Tree Widget Report Layout
XRCA results are displayed in a tree widget layout and provide details that include tracing
configuration, XRCA root cause results, related design, and related waveform based on
the XRCA trace result.
The following figure displays XRCA configuration, X-pessimism, and XRCA Root Cause
Results:
Figure 161

XRCA Tree Widget Report Layout

The Tree Widget view consists of the following sections:
* Configuration: The XRCA Configuration section of the Tree widget view displays the
following items:
XRCA version used to analysis
FSDB file
Time unit
Signal file (displayed when you specify the signal list)
Analysis X options (otherwise, XRCA performs auto-scan)
Trace Options
X-pessimism options (displayed for XRCA reports with the xpess:true
configuration X-Pessimism option)
* X-pessimism Result: The X-pessimism result is displayed only when XRCA has the
xpess:true configuration option. The report displays x-pessimism debug entry with its
merge nodes.
* XRCA Root Cause Results: All the debug entries and their root cause information are
displayed in the XRCA Root Cause Results section.
Hint
XRCA integrates the traditional Verdi flow for tracing X-propagation hint with the XRCA
GUI report as shown in the following figure:
Figure 162

X-Propagation Hint With XRCA GUI Report

In the report, the X-propagation signal is tagged with the prefix "hint" and has a reason
"Driven by X-propagation statement (t-merge/x-merge)."
You can check all the X-propagation signals on the path from the debug entry signal to its
root cause and can use the nTrace/nWave/TFV sync features to analyze them.

When you load the XRCA tracing report containing XPROP information, nTrace enables
the X-propagation instrument by default. An X red notation on the instance tree and a
green tag on the source view display the XPROP section.
Figure 163

X-Propagation Information

Moreover, you can double-click the X-propagation signal to open TFV to analyze the
tracing path. TFV displays the X-propagation signal with X-propagation notation (t-merge)/
(x-merge) as shown in the following figure:
Figure 164

TFV Displaying X-Propagation Signal

Impact of X-pessimism on XRCA Report
For describing the impact of X-pessimism on XRCA report, primarily the following parts of
the report are used:
* Root cause found signals
* X-pessimism signals
Following are the cases to demonstrate the XRCA report with X-pessimism included:
1. XRCA runs with X-pessimism disabled.
2. XRCA runs with X-pessimism enabled. X-pessimism signal is not specified.
3. XRCA runs with X-pessimism enabled. X-pessimism signal is specified.
Case1: XRCA runs with X-pessimism disabled
In this case, the original XRCA report is demonstrated. XRCA traces the specified signals
iteratively and arranges them by root cause. For example,
XRCA reports X at top.dut.e and top.dut.h is contributed from X at top.dut.a.

Root Cause Found:
#0 top.dut.a(X from un-initialized signal)
TM0C1 top.dut.e#3500
TM0C1 top.dut.h#3500
#0 top.dut.b(X from un-initialized signal)
TM0C1 top.dut.g#3500
TM0C1 top.dut.h#3500

Case2: XRCA runs with X-pessimism enabled
In this case, the X-pessimism signal is not specified in XRCA. If only top.dut.f signal is
verified as FalseX, XRCA removes top.dut.a as the root cause of top.dut.h because
signal top.dut.a is in the fan-in of signal top.dut.h.

Root Cause Found:
#0 top.dut.a(X from un-initialized signal)
TM0C1 top.dut.e#3500
#0 top.dut.b(X from un-initialized signal)
TM0C1 top.dut.g#3500
TM0C1 top.dut.h#3500

Case3: XRCA runs with X-pessimism enabled
In this case, the X-pessimism signal is specified in XRCA.
If three signals, top.dut.f, top.dut.g, top.dut.h, are verified as FalseX, XRCA
removes top.dut.a as the root cause of top.dut.h. All debug entries related to
top.dut.b are FalseX, so top.dut.b is removed from the root cause list. Two userdefined signals, top.dut.g and top.dut.h are verified as FalseX, so XRCA adds them in
the X-pessimism report.

Root Cause Found:
#0 top.dut.a(X from un-initialized signal)
TM0C1 top.dut.e#3500
X-pessimism:
top.dut.g#3500
top.dut.h#3500

* (Merge Node): It is present under debug entry and contains root X-pessimism signals

Click the signal hyper-link, it opens the GUI window to replay the tracing path with Xpess

Also, there is a pair of highlighted paths. A split signal merges at the OR gate with different

XRCA Timing-Violation Correlation
XRCA automatically identifies cases where an X root cause is driven by a timing violation
reported in the simulation log. After running XRCA, a post-processing module performs the
following tasks:
* Scans XRCA root causes.
* Correlates them with timingviolation messages in the simulation log (VCS or thirdparty formats).
* Annotates matching root causes as timing violation and records the exact
simulation log file and line in the XRCA report.
When you load xrca_report.xml,
* For root causes that correlate to a timing violation, XRCA updates the displayed reason
text to X from timing violation.
* When a timingviolation subsection is present for a root cause, the GUI adds a
timing violation tree widget under that root cause.
* Use Show Timing Violation on SmartLog in SmartLog to open the simulation log
and jump to the recorded line. Use Show Timing Violation on Source View in
Source View to navigate to the related source location.
The following are the key features of XRCA Timing-Violation Correlation:
* It acts purely as a post process.
* It runs only when timing_violation_check is enabled and target_sim_log
specifies a readable simulation log file. For details, see Enabling XRCA TimingViolation Correlation.
The XRCA Timing-Violation Correlation section consists of the following topics:
* Enabling XRCA Timing-Violation Correlation
* Post-Processing After XRCA Run
* Loading Report With XRCA Timing-Violation Correlation
* Limitations of XRCA Timing-Violation Correlation

Enabling XRCA Timing-Violation Correlation
The XRCA Timing-Violation Correlation feature is conditionally enabled. To use this
feature, all of the following must be true:
* The timing_violation_check option is enabled in the XRCA YAML template.
* A valid simulation log path, target_sim_log, is specified in the XRCA YAML template.
* The file at that path exists and can be opened for reading.
However, if timing_violation_check is set to false, if the target_sim_log field is
missing or empty, or if the simulation log file cannot be opened, then
* The timing-violation post process is skipped.
* No timing-violation annotation is applied.
* No change to root cause reasons.
* No additional navigation is enabled.

title: Appendix 257
text:
Post-Processing After XRCA Run
After the XRCA run completes, the tool performs the following postprocessing steps to
correlate root causes with timing violations:
1. Extracts root-cause information from the XRCA output
a. After XRCA finishes, the output file xrca_report.xml is available.
b. XRCA parses xrca_report.xml to identify all <rootCause> entries.
c. For each root cause, the tool extracts the full signal name and identifies the driven
scope instance. The tool considers cross-module references (XMRs) also.
d. XRCA builds an inmemory list of root-cause signals and scopes, to be used in
subsequent searches.
2. Correlates root causes with timing violations in the simulation log
a. The tool uses the root-cause list and the specified simulation-log file
(target_sim_log).
b. It searches the simulation log for candidate locations that match a root-cause
scope.
c. When several timing-violation candidates exist, the tool selects the violation with a
time closest to, but earlier than, the original root-cause time.
d. For each candidate location, the tool checks whether it forms a valid
timingviolation block, based on existing SmartLog rules.

title: Appendix 257
text:
It supports VCS and third-party timing-violation formats.
e. When a timing-violation block is matched, XRCA collects the following
timingviolation information:
Timing-violation type (for example, hold)
Source code file
Source code line
Simulation log file
Simulation log line
Timing-violation time
Load parse rule for the log type
3. For each root cause with a correlated timing-violation block, the tool creates a
timing-violation subsection under the related <rootCause> element in the enriched
xrca_report.xml file.
4. For each root cause, the tool performs the following:
Constructs a timing-violation subsection under root cause section.
Saves the updated xrca_report.xml (overwriting the report file).

Loading Report With XRCA Timing-Violation Correlation
When you load the enriched XRCA report (xrca_report.xml) in Verdi, the GUI interprets
timing-violation data stored during post-processing. XRCA displays the reason for each
root cause entry as follows:
* For each <rootCause> entry,
Check if corresponding timing-violation subsection exists.
If the timing-violation tree subsection exists, create timing-violation tree widget
using the following format:
Timing Violation: <Timing violation type>@<Source code file>:<Source
code line>[Simulation log file:Simulation log line]

Timing Violation: hold@star79337.v:896338[sim.log:908]

Remap or override the displayed reason text for this root cause to X from timing
violation.
If the root cause does not contain timingviolation information, the GUI displays
the original reason as provided in the XRCA report.
* When you select a timing-violation tree widget under a root cause and click Show
Timing Violation on SmartLog, XRCA uses SmartLog Tcl commands to:
Open SmartLog if it is not opened.
Open the simulation log file referenced in the timing-violation tree widget (if not
already open in SmartLog).
Load the appropriate parsing rule for the simulation log. For example, a rule specific
for VCS or third-party simulator timing violations.
Move the SmartLog view cursor to the line number associated with the timing
violation. This displays the exact timing violation message.
* When you choose Show Timing Violation on Source View, XRCA automatically
navigates to the source code pane. It highlights the relevant source code line
corresponding to the timing violation, as detailed in the timing violation tree widget.

Limitations of XRCA Timing-Violation Correlation
The XRCA Timing-Violation Correlation feature has the following limitations:
* It supports only VCS and third-party simulator log formats.
* It requires timing_violation_check to be enabled and a valid, readable simulation
log path (target_sim_log) from the RDA or autorca configuration.

Multiple Cycle Path Root Cause Analysis
(MCPRCA)
* MCPRCA Usage

During RTL simulation, Dynamic SDC Verification in VCS detects timing constraint bugs,
such as Multiple Cycle Path (MCP), FP, and clock group issues. SDC forms a key part of
RTL signoff. Teams use VCS with SDC (VCS-SDC) for signoff during verification. VCSSDC reduces project cycle time by several weeks.
Debugging violations detected by VCS-SDC can be difficult when MCP bugs affect many
signals. RDA offers a Multiple Cycle Path Root Cause Analysis (MCPRCA) solution. This
solution automatically groups violations into fewer categories. It provides connections to
further debug with waveform, source code, and simulation log, using Verdi.

MCPRCA helps you to debug the VCS-SDC detected violations using Verdi. After
completing simulation with VCS-SDC, MCPRCA checks the results of VCS-SDC and
helps in finding out the violations. MCPRCA uses the Violation Binning feature to group
violations from a simulation log and generate further debug entries.
RDA provides the Verdi GUI to review MCPRCA reports generated after analyzing
violations from the log file. You can also use the GUI to debug the source code, logs, and
waveform.

The following figure gives an overview of the MCPRCA debug flow:
Figure 187

MCPRCA Debug Flow

The following are the requirements for the MCPRCA setup:
* VCS compilation with SDC commands which contains MCP, FP, or clock group
property.
* Run simulation. The property can pass or fail.

The following steps are required to perform MCPRCA:
1. Prepare a configuration file for MCPRCA. Refer to the Preparing RDA Configuration
File for MCPRCA section for more details.
2. Invoke MCPRCA. Refer to the Invoking MCPRCA section for more details.
3. Review the MCPRCA results in Verdi. Refer to the Reviewing MCPRCA in Verdi GUI
section for more details.
The MCPRCA Usage section consists of the following topics:
* Preparing RDA Configuration File for MCPRCA
* Invoking MCPRCA
* Reviewing MCPRCA in Verdi GUI
* SDC Annotation
* Smart Waiver

Preparing RDA Configuration File for MCPRCA
You can generate an empty MCPRCA template for the VCS-SDC mode using the following
command:
> $VERDI_HOME/bin/autorca -gen_cfg_template <template_name.yaml>
-gen_mode mcprca

After generating the configuration file, you can see a template, <template_name.yaml>,

Invoking MCPRCA
You can invoke MCPRCA using the following autorca command:
> $VERDI_HOME/bin/autorca -cfg <template_name.yaml>

After MCPRCA, you can use Verdi to review and check the analysis results. Use
the following command to load the RDA tracing results into Verdi and enable the
corresponding features:
%> autorca -load_report <tracing_reports>

autorca -load_report mcprca_report.xml

After you load the MCPRCA report, Verdi displays the report results. Verdi also prepares
other debug entries, including SmartLog, Violation Waveform, Connection to SDC
command, and SDC clock annotation.

Verdi GUI Features
You can perform the following actions on Verdi GUI:
* Grouping
* Direct to Target Violation in SmartLog
* Invoking the Target Violation Waveform in nWave
* Directing to the Target Signal in nTrace
* Directing to the Target SDC Command in nTrace
Grouping
The Grouping feature is a key feature in MCPRCA. It reviews all violations grouped into
bins with different information. That is, violations grouped in the same bin might be caused

by the same bug. Click the Group by list and select any one of the grouping rules. The
following figure displays the Group by field:
Figure 191

Selecting Grouping Rules

You can use the following grouping rules for MCP to group violations into bins with
different aspects:
* signal_to: Group violations by the same signals (TO) names.
* signal_from: Group violations by the same signals (FROM) names.
* signal_both: Group violations by the same signals (TO) and same signals (FROM)
names.
* clock_to: Group violations by the same clock names of signals (TO).
* clock_from: Group violations by the same clock names of signals (FROM).
* sdc_command: Group violations by the same SDC command.
Using the Grouping feature, you can review the results of different grouping rules
immediately in the active report window.
Direct to Target Violation in SmartLog
You can view the original simulation log by opening the target violation in SmartLog. To do
this, click the SmartLog Entry in the Action column. Alternatively, right-click Recommend
Debug Index or All Violation Index and choose Open in SmartLog.

The following figure displays how to select the Open in SmartLog option:
Figure 192

Ways to Direct to the Target Violation Message

The activated SmartLog performs the following steps:
1. Goes to the line of the target violation message.
2. Highlights all keywords to group. For example, it highlights testbench.mult.ff2[1]
while grouping with signal(TO).
3. Lists all matching keywords. You can click these keywords to jump to other violations in
the same bin, shown in the right-hand side.
4. Reuses only one SmartLog window even when you view different indexes.
Figure 193

SmartLog View

Invoking the Target Violation Waveform in nWave
When VCS-SDC marks violation details in nWave, the violation waveform Tcl files are
saved. MCPRCA allows you to invoke them.

When you set the target_waveform configuration option in the MCPRCA configuration
in the Actions
file, you can activate nWave. To open in nWave, click nWave Entry
column. You can also right-click the Recommend Debug Index or All Violation Index
and select Open in nWave, as shown in the following figure:
Figure 194

Ways to Invoke the Target Violation Waveform

The corresponding waveform details such as violation index, FROM-TO signals, and their
value change are displayed. For more details, refer to the VCS-SDC function specification.
You can reuse the same nWave window. This means that after clearing the old
information, the window displays the new information.
Figure 195

The nWave View

Directing to the Target Signal in nTrace
MCPRCA provides the cross-reference of signals from the report to nTrace. You can use
any one of the following ways to use this feature:
* Click nTrace Entry

in the Actions column.

* Double-click Signal(TO) or Signal(FROM).
* Right-click Signal(TO) or Signal(FROM) and select Open in nTrace.
Figure 196

View of Directing the Target Signal

Directing to the Target SDC Command in nTrace
MCPRCA provides the cross-reference of SDC command from the report to nTrace. You
can use any one of the following ways to use this feature:
* Click nTrace Entry

in the Actions column.

* Double-click Clock or SDC Command Type.
* Right-click Clock or SDC Command Type and select Open in nTrace.
In nTrace, the SDC command file opens in a new tab. The command you want to see is
clearly highlighted. If you select a different SDC command, the same tab is used.

Figure 197

View of Directing SDC Command

title: Appendix 257
text:
SDC Annotation
An SDC command can create clocks to validate the SDC functionality. RDA provides a
connection between the clocks in the RTL code and the SDC commands for you to review
them easily.
Currently, only VCS-SDC flow supports SDC annotation.
The following describes the flow of SDC annotation where the VCS and MCPRCA parts
are the requirements to make SDC annotation available:
1. VCS Part: VCS needs to compile with the required option -sdc=debug:clock.
2. MCPRCA Part: For MCPRCA, fill the path of mcpLogs to mcp_logs_dir in the
configuration file.

title: Appendix 257
text:
3. Verdi GUI Part:
a. After loading MCPRCA report with Verdi, choose Source > SDC Annotation to turn
on the SDC annotation feature as shown in the following figure:
Figure 198

Invoking SDC Annotation

b. When you hover the mouse over the clock signal with the SDC annotation, the clock
information infotip appears as shown in the following figure:
Figure 199

SDC Annotation

c. Press the Shift key on your keyboard to invoke a Tooltip Viewer window containing
a link. When you click the link, it activates a new tab of nTrace directing to the target
SDC command.
For example, in the following figure when you click the link of SDC clock, sys_clk,
you are directed to the target SDC command:
Figure 200

Directing to the Target SDC Command

Smart Waiver
You can use the Smart Waiver feature to reduce noise by removing the violation indexes
that are not the real root cause from the report. You can use the waive rule to classify the
violation messages and move them to the waived folder. A waive rule consists of the rule
name, the FROM signal and the TO signal.
The following is the waive rule format of the content of the specified waiver files:
Waive violation index matches FROM signal and TO signal. Signal name is allowed to use
wildcard (* ?)
* waive -name $RuleName -to {<$ToSignalName>} -from {<$FromSignalName>}
To disable waive rule, rule names are separated with a space.
* waive -disable {$RuleName1 $RuleName2 $RuleName3}

* Waive violation index matches the FROM signal testbench.dut.mux.ff1 and to
signal testbench.dut.mux.out2.
waive -name rule1 -to {testbench.dut.mux.out2} -from
{testbench.dut.mux.ff1}

The rule1 waives index matched with the FROM signal and the TO signal.
* Waive violation index with TO signal testbench.dut.mux.out.
waive -name rule2 -to {testbench.dut.out}
waive -name rule3 -to {testbench.dut.out} -from {*}

The rule2 is equal to rule3; they waive indexes which are matched with the TO
signal.
* Waive violation index with the FROM signal testbench.dut.mux.ff1.
testbench.dut.mux.ff1.
waive -name rule4 -from {testbench.dut.mux.ff1}
waive -name rule5 -from {testbench.dut.mux.ff1} -to
{*}

The rule3 is equal to rule4; they waive indexes which are matched with the FROM
signal.
* Disable waive rule.
waive -disable {rule1 rule2 rule3}

This command disables rule1, rule2, and rule3 specified in the same file.
* Waive violation index with multiple FROM signals.
Violation index with two FROM signals and one TO signal. This index can waive.
TO signal: top.sub1.ccc
FROM signal: top.sub2.aaa
FROM signal: top.sub3.bbb
Waive with full signal specified.
waive -name rule6 -to {top.sub1.ccc} -from
{top.sub2.aaa}
waive -name rule7 -to {top.sub1.ccc} -from
{top.sub3.bbb}

Waive with TO signal specified. This rule waives other matched index.
waive -name rule8 -to {top.sub1.ccc}

FaultRCA: Fault Analysis
FaultRCA consists of the following sections:
* General Fault Analysis
* NC Analysis
* Limitation of FaultRCA

Debugging general faults, such as NO, NN, ND, and so on, means that you need to
trace the fanout from the fault location. Follow the path finding the blocking points in the
downstream circuits until you reach an observation or detection point. This is a timeconsuming process that requires manual efforts.
To overcome the limitation of excessive manual effort and time consumption, FaultRCA
provides utility that helps in detecting the blocking points between the fault-injected point
and the observation or detection point.
A path is created from the fault location to the observation point. Along this path, you can
identify and collect blocking points. This helps you focus on the path and attempt to make
the fault move from the injected point) to the observation point.
Blocking Points
Blocking points are the points through which a fault cannot propagate. For example, as
shown in Figure 209, assume A is the fault location where the fault SA1 (stuck-at-1) is
injected. The fault propagates to C. However, the fault cannot propagate to D.
As the value of B is constantly 0, the primitive AND gate never allows the fault at C to
propagate to D. Because the fault is not propagated to D, the AND cell is called the
blocking cell.

Figure 209

Blocking Cell

This section consists of the following topics:
* Fault Analysis Method
* Running Fault Analysis
* Configuration Fields in the Configuration File
* Generating and Loading Tracing Report in Verdi
* Viewing Tracing Report in Verdi
* Ranking Report

Fault Analysis Method
The fault analysis method provides the following two modes:
* Static Trace Mode
* Block Cell Detection Mode

Static Trace Mode
FaultRCA traces the path from the input fault to the destination point. You can either
extract the observation point from the fault database (FDB) or provide a list of signals to
the tool. You can run this mode in the following two ways:
* Target Signal Mode
* Auto Mode
Target Signal Mode
To analyze one or more signals, use target signal mode. In this mode, you must provide
one or multiple input signals. The information, such as observations list and signal type,
are extracted from the FDB. FaultRCA generates an XML report (.xml) and a text report
(.txt) containing the tracing path.

The format of the fault list file is <Signal Full hierarchy name>. For example,
top.a.b
top.c.d.e

Auto Mode
To analyze a list of critical location points available in the FDB, use auto mode. Auto
mode analyzes more than one signal, and it allows you to select the number of signals to
analyze. The FaultRCA utility automatically analyzes the most critical locations, that is, the
blocking points that cover highest number of NO fault from the FDB. It generates an XML
report and a text report containing tracing paths of all the signals. The information, such as
observation points, signal types, and a list of critical blocking points is extracted from the
FDB.

Block Cell Detection Mode
FaultRCA traces a path between the input fault to the destination point and finds any
blocking cell along the path. You can get the observation point from the FDB or provide
a list of signals to the tool. For this mode, you need the dumped waveform from either a
good machine or faulty machine (gm/fm). One input pin has the GM/FM annotation value.
All output pins have only the GM annotation values.
A block instance on a flip-flop checks the current status of the GM/FM annotation and the
incoming clock cycle. Specifically, it checks the input GM/FM status in the current clock
cycle and the output GM/FM status in the next clock cycle.
When the next clock cycle arrives at the signal connected to the register clock port, the
block checks the clock port. If the clock port is rising or falling, it finds the next rising or
falling time. Otherwise, it finds the next time the value changes.
This mode supports only Stuck@0 and Stuck@1. You can run it in the target signal mode.
Target Signal Mode
If you want to analyze one or multiple signals, use target signal mode. In this mode, you
must provide one or multiple input signals and the target signal list name.
The following is the format of the fault list:
<stuck@0>/<stuck@1>, <Signal full hierarchy name>

0, top.a.b
1, top.c.d.e

Running Fault Analysis
You can run fault analysis using autorca in the static trace mode and the block cell
detection mode.
To generate the configuration file template (run.yaml), use the following command:
autorca -gen_cfg_template <run.yaml> -gen_mode faultrca

When you run the command, the run.yaml file is generated.
The following are the requirements to run fault analysis:
* The simv.daidir directory
* The mode field must be set to 1 by default.
* The gm/fm waveform is required for the block cell detection mode.
For FDB, you must specify the following fields:
* FDB project name: Specify the name of the FDB project to be used.
* FDB path: Specify the full path of the FDB directory.
* Campaign name: Specify the campaign name that is used for dumping FDB.
* For the destination point, you can provide the text file or extract the observation or
detection point from the FDB.
For the target signal mode, you must specify the text file containing the name of the
signals. For more information on the format of the fault list file for the static trace mode
and the block cell detection mode, refer to the Static Trace Mode and Block Cell Detection
Mode sections, respectively.
For the auto mode, specify the number of top critical locations that you require.

Generating and Loading Tracing Report in Verdi
You can generate the tracing report in the .xml and .txt formats using the following

autorca command:

autorca -cfg run.yaml

FaultRCA generates the following types of reports:
* Faultrca_report.xml
* Faultrca_report.txt
* Faultrca_block.xml
* Faultrca_block.txt
You can load the generated report in Verdi using the following command:
autorca -load_report <report_name>.xml

You can view the XML report in Verdi. However, you cannot view the text report
in Verdi.

Ranking Report
The block cell detection mode generates reports in the text and XML formats, for example,
faultrca_block.txt and faultrca_block.xml. In the generated reports, the input
faults are grouped based on the same blocking points. The ranking report is a feature that
prioritizes blocking points with the highest number of input faults and positions them at the
top, as shown in the following figure:
Figure 223

Ranking Report

In Figure 223, the blocking point

or1200_testbench.or1200_top_i.or1200_or1200_sprs(@1):SigOp4:242:242:Combo

groups three input faults, which is more than the input faults grouped under the other
blocking point. Therefore, the blocking point with three input faults is placed at the top.

The Not Controllable (NC) analysis provides a method to reduce manual efforts while
cleaning up the NC faults. NC faults occur in unselected signals during fault simulation.
An NC fault happens when the fanin value stays constant, which makes the fault
uncontrollable.
The existing FDB consists of multiple critical locations, and each critical location consists
of multiple faults. The faults are categorized with common location points to determine
which location point has the maximum number of NC faults. To find the root cause, you
must trace through the NC locations to find the faults where the fanin value remains
constant. This is a time-consuming process.
The NC analysis automates tracing and scans for every NC location, and traces its fanin
cone. The tracing continues until no fanin or all fanin are found with the changed values.
This ensures that the root cause is found. The root cause with the highest number of
critical locations and faults is the top root cause. The report displays the root-cause bucket
containing all the root causes, critical locations, and faults grouped inside the blocking
points.
NC Faults
NC faults are faults that stay constant during simulation. These faults occur when a signal,
which is the input to the fault, does not change its value. That is, the value stays at zero
or one throughout the simulation. The 0-X-0 or 1-X-1 state does not count as switching
states. You must run the fault manager with testability enabled to generate NC faults. The
following figure displays how a not controlled input affects the output:
Figure 224

This section consists of the following topics:
* NC Analysis Method
* Running NC Analysis
* Configuration Fields in the Configuration File
* Generating and Loading Tracing Report in Verdi

NC Analysis Method
The current FDB organizes NC faults by their shared locations. You can further trace the
critical locations with NC faults to find the root cause that does not change value. This

manual debugging process is time-consuming and inefficient. The following figure displays
the unselected report that contains the blocking points with NC faults:
Figure 225

Unselected Report Format

Fault Ranking
The Fault Ranking utility automates to streamline debugging efforts. It focuses on blocking
points in the FDB that are caused from the same root cause, where the value does not
change. The automation reduces the redundant debugging.
The NC Fault Ranking utility scans all the critical locations with NC faults, It traces its fanin
cone until it finds no fanin or all fanin pins with changed values. In the NC Fault Ranking
report, a signal with no fanin or all fanin pins with the changed values is categorized as the
NC root cause. Critical locations are grouped based on the same root cause. The FDB NC
faults are grouped by the same critical location, and the critical locations are grouped by
the same root cause. All root causes that are formed by the same signal and module are
grouped together.
This automation minimizes manual debugging and traces NC signals directly to their root
causes, saving significant time and effort.
The following figure displays the NC fault ranking report:
Figure 226

NC Fault Ranking report

Tracing Behavior of NC Signal
The following are the rules to continue tracing the signals for NC critical locations:
* The input pins that are active (contributing to the output) and have a constant value are
circle.
marked with the red
* The input pins that are non-active (not contributing to the output) and have a constant
value are marked with the gray

circle.

* If all the input pins have

circle, expand the fanin pins.

* If a combination gate, for example, register and sequential gate, does not have an
active fanin value change, expand the non-active fanin pins.
The following rules, also called as the stop criteria, provide the exact root cause for NC
faults:
* If all fanin pin values change, tracing stops. The output is then marked as the root
cause.
* If the input signal has no driver, the signal is marked as the root cause.
* If all fanin pins of the non-combinational gates are non-active, the tracing stops. The
output is marked as the root cause.
The following figure displays the unselected report:
Figure 227

Example Showing Tracing Behavior of the NC Signal

In Figure 227, consider the location, test.a123.u0.us23.n238, for the root cause,
aes.test_se. Click the test.a123.u0.us23.n238 location in the report to see the tracing
result in Temporal Flow View (TFV).

In the TFV tracing result, the n26 and n87 signals are marked with the
circle. It
means that these signals are active fanins and they do not have any value change.
Therefore, the tracing of signals can be continued until it satisfies the stop criteria.
The following are the results of three paths as shown in Figure 227:
* Path 1: n238 > n87 > n21 > n389 > a[1] > test_se (root cause)
* Path 2: n238 > n26 > n43 > n402 > n409 > a[6] > N56 (root cause)
* Path 3: n238 > n43 > n373 > a[5:4] > test_se (root cause)
This shows that Figure 227 has two root causes, test_se and N56, which are indicated as

R in TFV.

For more information on the report, refer to the Report Format section.

Report Format
The FDB unselected report provides details about the traced location signals and their

Running NC Analysis
You can run the NC analysis using autorca.

To generate the configuration file template (run.yaml), use the following command:
autorca -gen_cfg_template <run.yaml> -gen_mode faultrca

When you run the command, the run.yaml file is generated.
The following are the requirements:
* The simv.daidir directory (required)
* The mode field must be set to 2 by default.
* The waveform is required for the NC Analysis.
For FDB, you must specify the following:
* FDB project name: Specify the name of the FDB project to be used.
* FDB path: Specify the full path of the FDB directory.
* Campaign name: Specify the campaign name that is used for dumping FDB.

The Not Controllable (NC) analysis provides a method to reduce manual efforts while
cleaning up the NC faults. NC faults occur in unselected signals during fault simulation.
An NC fault happens when the fanin value stays constant, which makes the fault
uncontrollable.
The existing FDB consists of multiple critical locations, and each critical location consists
of multiple faults. The faults are categorized with common location points to determine
which location point has the maximum number of NC faults. To find the root cause, you

NC Faults
NC faults are faults that stay constant during simulation. These faults occur when a signal,
which is the input to the fault, does not change its value. That is, the value stays at zero
or one throughout the simulation. The 0-X-0 or 1-X-1 state does not count as switching
states. You must run the fault manager with testability enabled to generate NC faults. The
following figure displays how a not controlled input affects the output:

NC Analysis Method
The current FDB organizes NC faults by their shared locations. You can further trace the
critical locations with NC faults to find the root cause that does not change value. This

manual debugging process is time-consuming and inefficient. The following figure displays
the unselected report that contains the blocking points with NC faults:
Figure 225

Unselected Report Format

Fault Ranking
The Fault Ranking utility automates to streamline debugging efforts. It focuses on blocking
points in the FDB that are caused from the same root cause, where the value does not
change. The automation reduces the redundant debugging.
The NC Fault Ranking utility scans all the critical locations with NC faults, It traces its fanin
cone until it finds no fanin or all fanin pins with changed values. In the NC Fault Ranking
report, a signal with no fanin or all fanin pins with the changed values is categorized as the
NC root cause. Critical locations are grouped based on the same root cause. The FDB NC
faults are grouped by the same critical location, and the critical locations are grouped by
the same root cause. All root causes that are formed by the same signal and module are
grouped together.
This automation minimizes manual debugging and traces NC signals directly to their root
causes, saving significant time and effort.

In Figure 227, consider the location, test.a123.u0.us23.n238, for the root cause,
aes.test_se. Click the test.a123.u0.us23.n238 location in the report to see the tracing
result in Temporal Flow View (TFV).

In the TFV tracing result, the n26 and n87 signals are marked with the
circle. It
means that these signals are active fanins and they do not have any value change.
Therefore, the tracing of signals can be continued until it satisfies the stop criteria.
The following are the results of three paths as shown in Figure 227:
* Path 1: n238 > n87 > n21 > n389 > a[1] > test_se (root cause)
* Path 2: n238 > n26 > n43 > n402 > n409 > a[6] > N56 (root cause)
* Path 3: n238 > n43 > n373 > a[5:4] > test_se (root cause)
This shows that Figure 227 has two root causes, test_se and N56, which are indicated as

R in TFV.

For more information on the report, refer to the Report Format section.

Report Format
The FDB unselected report provides details about the traced location signals and their
associated faults. The report consists of the root causes, and each root cause has its
associated faults. The root causes are sorted based on the number of faults. You must
focus on the root causes to resolve the blocking points.

Running NC Analysis
You can run the NC analysis using autorca.

To generate the configuration file template (run.yaml), use the following command:
autorca -gen_cfg_template <run.yaml> -gen_mode faultrca

When you run the command, the run.yaml file is generated.
The following are the requirements:
* The simv.daidir directory (required)
* The mode field must be set to 2 by default.
* The waveform is required for the NC Analysis.
For FDB, you must specify the following:
* FDB project name: Specify the name of the FDB project to be used.
* FDB path: Specify the full path of the FDB directory.
* Campaign name: Specify the campaign name that is used for dumping FDB.

Configuration Fields in the Configuration File
When you run the following command using autorca and gen_cfg_template, a
configuration file is generated:
autorca -gen_cfg_template <run.yaml> -gen_mode faultrca

You can use the autogenerated file (faultrca_report.xml) to run FaultRCA. For the
format of the file in the FaultRCA mode, refer to the Configuration File Format in FaultRCA
section.
The following table describes the required fields in the configuration file:

Specify the Debug Mode
mode

Specify the debug mode. Set this field to 1
for the Fault Analysis mode and 2 for the NC
Fault Auto Ranking mode.
The default is 1.

Design/Waveform Setting
target_simv_daidir

Specify the path of the target debugging
database, simv.daidir.

target_waveform

Specify the target waveform file. It is a
required field for the Block Cell Detection
mode.

Fault Database Setting
fdb_project

Specify the name of the FDB project to be
used.

fdb_path

Specify the full path of the FDB directory.

campaign

Specify the fault campaign name.

For details about the other available fields, refer to the Configuration Fields in the
Configuration File section.

Generating and Loading Tracing Report in Verdi
You can generate the tracing report using the following autorca command:
autorca -cfg run.yaml

You can load the generated report in Verdi using the following command:
autorca -load_report faultrca_report.xml

When you load a report using the -load_report option, the following three icons are
displayed on the toolbar:
Figure 229

Icons of the Right-Click Options

*

: When you select a signal and click this icon, the signal is displayed in nTrace.

*

: When you select a signal and click this icon, the signal is displayed in nWave.

*

: When you select a signal and click this icon, the signal is displayed in nSchema.

The following figure displays the report loaded in Verdi:
Figure 230

NC Report in Verdi

You can right-click Location/Root cause:Signal and then click Show in TFV to
display the selected signal in the TFV window. When you click a signal, the Tcl command
tfgFusaAutoTrace -sig xxx is generated that opens the TFV window.
Similarly, you can click Show in nTrace and Show in waveform to see your signal in the
source code and waveform windows, respectively.
In the TFV window, the signals are indicated with nt (red and gray) and R, where
*

contributors.

Limitation of FaultRCA

Limitation of FaultRCA
FaultRCA has the following limitation:
* FaultRCA does not support point-to-point trace in the nSchema feature for the symbollibrary setting mode.

* tbrca: Specifies the TBRCA mode.

* xrca: Specifies the XRCA mode.

Introduction
The Verdi(R) Automated Debug Platform and the Siloti(R) Visibility Automation System are
advanced solutions for debugging digital designs that increase design productivity with
complex System-on-Chip (SoC), ASIC, and FPGA designs.
The Verdi platform provides powerful technology to help you comprehend complex and
unfamiliar design behavior, automate difficult and tedious debug processes, unify diverse
and complicated design environments, and infer the dynamic behavior of a design over
time.
In addition to the standard features of a source code browser, schematics, waveforms,
state-machine diagrams, and waveform comparison (for comparing simulation results
in FSDB format), the Verdi platform includes advanced features for automatic tracing of
signal activity using temporal flow views, assertion-based debug, power-aware debug, and
debug and analysis of transaction and message data. All of this is available in a graphical
user interface using the Qt platform that supports multi-window docking and is easily
customizable.
The Siloti system speeds up the simulation by eliminating the overhead associated with
recording signal values and by enabling full visibility of the design activity based on a
relatively small amount of signal data captured during full-chip simulation, regression
simulation, and hardware emulation/ acceleration. The Siloti system is fully integrated with
the Verdi platform so that users can leverage the benefits of full visibility for gate or RTL
debug.
Synopsys also provides the following two modules that complement the Verdi platform:
* The nAnalyzer Design Analysis module is for debugging the implementation aspects of
the design, such as clock trees and static timing failures.
* The nECO Automated Netlist Modification module is for solving problems associated
with manual netlist changes.
The Verdi and Siloti systems and the additional nAnalyzer and nECO modules enable
engineers to locate, isolate, understand, and resolve bugs in a fraction of the time
of traditional solutions. This maximizes the efficiency and productivity of expensive
engineering resources, significantly reduces costs, and dramatically accelerates the
process of getting silicon to the market.

For detailed platform support information, see the Release Specific Support page on the
Synopsys Qualified System Configuration website at the following address:
http://www.synopsys.com/qsc
This Web page provides release-specific information about the supported hardware,
operating systems, and required operating system patches. If the required patch described
on this page is not available from the platform vendor, install the most recent patch
instead.

RHEL (Redhat) Platform Support Notes
* The 32-bit and 64-bit platforms support both the AMD Opteron and Intel EM64T
architectures.
* RHEL versions 7.3+ and 8+ are supported in the binary compatibility mode.
* RHEL v4 is not supported.

For information about using the correct glibc version for the SWIFT interface on
RHEL v4, send an e-mail to support_center@synopsys.com.

SLES (SUSE) Platform Support Notes
* The 32-bit and 64-bit platforms both support the AMD Opteron and Intel EM64T
architectures.
* SLES 12-SP5+ and 15-SP2+ are supported in the binary compatibility mode.

CentOS Platform Support Notes
* The 32-bit and 64-bit platforms both support the AMD Opteron and Intel EM64T
architectures.
* CentOS version 7.3.1611 is supported in the binary compatibility mode.

aarch64 Platform Support Notes

Availability of Verdi as a Single Linux Executable
Verdi is released as a Single Linux Executable (SLE). You can install Verdi only on Red
Hat Enterprise Linux (RHEL) platform and Verdi can run on SUSE operating system as a
binary compatible platform.
This change in the availability of Verdi as a SLE provides the following advantages:
* SLE is simple to install and use.
* Works with only one installation on Linux.

* Available as a single executable that works on various qualified Linux OS distributions.
* SLE ensures consistent product behavior on any Linux OS distribution.
You must install Verdi in an empty directory using the latest version of the Synopsys
Installer. Do not install this release over an existing release of a Synopsys tool.
Verdi uses the Synopsys Installer, which allows you to install the product using either
a text script or a graphical user interface (GUI). For information about downloading the
Synopsys Installer, see the Synopsys Installer section at the following address:
http://www.synopsys.com/install
To install Verdi, follow the procedures described in the Installing Synopsys Tools section.

Ubuntu Platform Support Notes
Ubuntu 14.04 is supported in binary compatibility mode. It requires GCC 4.8.4 and linker
version 2.24.
The following packages are required to run Verdi on Ubuntu. Ubuntu provides separate
packages for 64-bit and 32-bit systems. Packages marked with :i386 are for 32-bit
systems.
* libc6, gdb
* dc
* libncurses5-dev
* libncurses5-dev:i386
* g++
* pstack
* libelf1:i386
* libgcc-4.8-dev:i386
* libstdc++6:i386
* gcc-multilib
* g++-multilib
* libc6-dbg
* libc6-dbg:i386
* libexpat-dev

* libexpat-dev:i386libxss-dev

* libXft-dev:i386
* libSM
* libSM:i386
* libpng3
* libpng3:i386
* libxi6
* libxi6:i386
NOTE: Allocate 30 GB of free disk space before installing these packages. You also need
superuser access. Install the packages using the following command:
<% aptitude install <package name>
NOTE: For more information about the Ubuntu platform support, send an e-mail to
support_center@synopsys.com.

Verdi Support on AA Platform
Starting with the U-2023.03 release, Verdi supports AA platform for all features in Verdi
Base, Verdi Elite, Verdi Apex, PowerReplay, and also for the following items:
* Coverage and Planner
* IDX, RDA
* NPI and VC App
* PowerReplay
* HWSW Debug
* Siloti Correlation (part of Apex)
* VMS/VC ExecMan
* FSDB Dumpers for third-party simulators
* UPFA
For stand-alone nWave, Linux64 and Aarch64 platforms will use Verdi license. Linux64
uses Verdi license by setting the VERDI_WAVE_CKOUT_VERDI_LIC environment
variable.

Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL) Support for Verdi
Starting with the U-2023.03-SP2 release, you can run Verdi Base on Ubuntu 22.04 LTS
on Windows 10 through WSL1 and WSL2 with Linux64 library. The Verdi Base feature is
qualified on the 16 GB memory WSL/Windows 10 machines. The following packages are
required for Ubuntu 22.04 LTS:
* libfreetype.so.6
* libXss.so.1
* libXft.so.2
* libXt.so.6
* libXmuk.so.6
* libpng12.so.0
* libncurses.so.5

Installation and Licensing Information

Installation and Licensing Information
The Y-2026.03-SP2 release of the Verdi platform is a standalone release. It must be
installed in an empty directory. For installation instructions, see the installation.pdf file in
the product download directory.
Do not install this release over an existing release of Verdi or any Synopsys
tool.
Before running the Synopsys Tools, you must have installed and configured the Synopsys
Common Licensing (SCL) software, retrieved your license key file, and defined the license
file environment variable.
For detailed information about the SCL installation and setup, see the Synopsys Common
Licensing Quickstart Guide at the following address:
http://www.synopsys.com/licensing
This release of the product is based on Synopsys Common Licensing. You
must use the latest version of the SCL server (snpslmd daemon) and the
latest SCL license key file to use the product. For more information, see the
SCL Release Notes and Administration Guide. You can find a copy of the
documentation at the following address: http://www.synopsys.com/licensing

License Updates in S-2021.09 Release
Starting with the S-2021.09 release, Verdi capabilities are enabled with new license
features comprising of VERDI-BASE, VERDI-ELITE, VERDI-APEX, VERDI-APEX-AN, and
VERDI-APEX-RT.
The license features and corresponding use-model of releases prior to S-2021.09
continues to support without any changes required in the existing tool setup.
The license file in S-2021.09 makes use of the FLEXLM "PACKAGE" feature to support
the new license features and also allows backward compatibility for older releases. To
enable support of these new features, an upgrade to SCL version 2020.06-* is required.

What's New in This Release

Interactive Debug Feature
Starting with this release, Verdi supports the following Interactive Debug feature:
* Support for Virtual Interface Handles in Non-Component Class Objects

Support for Virtual Interface Handles in Non-Component Class
Objects
Starting with this release, Verdi introduces enhanced visibility for virtual interface handles
(VIFs) in the UVM Hierarchy Tree View. Verdi displays the VIFs that are direct members of
non-component class objects residing one level below the UVM components. This feature
is activated by enabling the +VERDI_DHIER_COMP_MEMBER_VIF simulation runtime option.
For more information, see "Interface Mapping Node in the OVM/UVM Hierarchy Tree" in
Verdi(R) UVM Debug User Guide.

What's New in This Release

Coverage Debug Features
Starting with this release, Verdi supports the following Coverage Debug features:
* Covergroup Instance HVP Source Name Format Improvement
* Conversion Between XML Report and HVP
* Enhanced Plan Review
* Modifier Usability Enhancements
* Tcl Hook for Post-Recalculate Automation

Covergroup Instance HVP Source Name Format Improvement
Starting with this release, Verdi improves the source name format for covergroup
instances in the Hierarchical Verification Plan (HVP). When you define a covergroup
in a package, Verdi now uses only the full hierarchy path of the instance as the HVP
source name. The package name is no longer included as a prefix. This change ensures
unique and clear source names. It also simplifies source pattern definitions and improves
readability.
If you reuse the existing plans, Verdi maintains backward compatibility. You can still use
the previous source name format for matching.
For more information, see "HVP Source Name Format for Covergroup Instances" in the
Verdi Coverage User Guide and Tutorial.

Conversion Between XML Report and HVP
Starting with this release, Verdi supports converting between XML report and Hierarchical
Verification Plan (HVP) formats. You can save and load expanded XML reports in both file
mode and VMS mode, making integration with HVP and Verdi coverage seamless. This
enhancement improves report readability and enables round-trip usage between Verdi
coverage and HVP flows.
For more information, see "Generating the HVP Excel XML Plan With Report" in the Verdi
Coverage User Guide and Tutorial.

Enhanced Plan Review
Starting with this release, Verdi improves plan review usability in the GUI. Plans now
open in an expanded state by default, showing first-level features and subplans for faster
navigation. You can use new and enhanced context menu options and keyboard shortcuts
to expand or collapse plan nodes by feature, measure, or source level. The Plan view
adds an optional Source Patterns column to display source information at the measure
level, supporting multiline and wrapped text. These changes make plan review more
efficient and configurable.

What's New in This Release

For more information, see "Using the HVP Planner" in the Verdi Coverage User Guide and
Tutorial.

Modifier Usability Enhancements
Starting with this release, Verdi displays clear indicators when modifiers are applied to a
plan, even if the modifier window is closed. You can also view invalid operands in modifier
expressions and see the applied status, including matched counts and modified item
names. You can also activate or deactivate all child modifiers at once using the master
check box for a modifier file. These enhancements simplify modifier management and
improve workflow transparency.
For more information, see "Using Modifiers" in the Verdi Coverage User Guide and
Tutorial.

Tcl Hook for Post-Recalculate Automation
Starting with this release, Verdi supports a Tcl hook framework that allows you to register
Tcl procs to run automatically after each Hierarchical Verification Plan (HVP) recalculate.
This feature enables seamless automation and custom workflows triggered by recalculate
completion. Use the bundled reference proc or create your own to streamline verification
plan management and improve efficiency.
For more information, see "Post-Recalculate Hook Framework" in the Verdi Coverage
User Guide and Tutorial and the "Coverage Debug" chapter in the Verdi and Siloti Tcl
Reference.

VIA Feature
Starting with this release, Verdi supports the following VIA feature:
* Module Parameter Insight Report

Module Parameter Insight Report
Get Module Parameter is a design-comprehension feature used to report module
parameter values across the design hierarchy, helping users quickly understand how
parameterized instances are configured during debug, analysis, and review.
In earlier releases, mode supported only default, local, type, and other. In Y-2026.03SP-1, a new mode, non-local, is added to report only the non-local parameters.
The updated mode definitions are as follows:
default: dump all kinds of parameters
local: only dump local parameters

Available Features in the Y-2026.03-SP1 Release

type: only dump type parameters
other: only dump non-local and non-type parameters
non-local: only dump non-local parameters

Coverage Features
Starting with this release, Verdi supports the following Coverage features:
* Auto-Export of Sub-Plans When Syncing Top Plan
* RM Link Synchronization Through a CLI Option

Auto-Export of Sub-Plans When Syncing Top Plan
Starting with this release, the Verdi tool supports automatic export of all sub-plans when
you export a top plan to Jama. You no longer need to export each sub-plan manually.
This feature reduces errors and saves time, especially for large plans. Control autoexport using the ENABLE_NEW_RM_MANAGER and AUTO_SYNC_SUBPLAN_MODE environment
variables. The tool always syncs sub-plans automatically on the first export. For
incremental syncs, you must select the Accept SubPlan checkbox in the RM Review
Window.

RM Link Synchronization Through a CLI Option
Starting with this release, Verdi supports the -sync_rm_link <0|1> command-line option.
This option allows you to force the RM Link Synchronization preference on or off for the
current session, overriding the value in novas.rc. Use this feature to ensure consistent
behavior in automated and batch flows, regardless of user or host settings.
