Log Annotation
You can annotate the time and the severity of log messages in the Transaction pane with
the Transaction -> Add Log Annotation command. When this command is enabled, the
Log Annotation form is invoked. In this form, you can select the types of log messages to
be annotated in the Transaction pane. One or more of the following message types can be
selected: Fatal, Error, Warning, and Info.
For example, for the annotation of an Info message, a black line is drawn based on the
time associated with the message. You can click on the line to invoke and view the log
message. The message is displayed in a dialog that is drawn over the objects in the
Transaction pane.
A log file must be loaded before invoking the Add Log Annotation command.
Figure 119

Log Annotation and Message Display in Transaction Pane

To view the complete simulation log, you can invoke the Smart Log pane by selecting the
Smart Log
icon in the Verdi pane. Click the
icon to synchronize the Protocol
Analyzer pane with the Smart Log pane. Protocol analyzer marks the log position in the
Smart Log pane for the selected transaction.

Figure 120

Synchronization with Smart Log Pane

Detail Pane
You can see Details and Call Stack tabs in the Detail pane.

Details
The Details tab displays the field and the value for the selected object.
Figure 121

Details Tab

You can select an object and use the right-click command to see the document for the
particular field.

Figure 122

View Selected Field in Protocol Document Window

You can specify the format to display the value of the attribute from the Value Radix pulldown menu. The options include: Binary, Decimal, Unsigned, Octal, and Hexadecimal.
If the selected attribute is a string or time that is presented in a fixed way, the
Value Radix pull-down menu is disabled.
Figure 123

Specify Radix Value

Call Stack
The complete call stack for the selected object is displayed in the Call Stack tab. You can
check the call hierarchy. If the class design is loaded into nTrace, you can double-click a
particular line in the call stack to view the corresponding code in the Source Code pane.

Figure 124

Call Stack Tab

The Call Stack tab lists the path and the line number of all the source code files that were
traversed up to the recording of the selected transaction. Double-click an item in the call
stack to highlight the corresponding line in the Source Code pane.
Figure 125

Call Stack for Selected Transaction

Search Results
The Search Results tab displays all objects that match the search criteria that were
specified using the Protocol Analyzer advanced search feature. You can traverse
through the list of matching objects and select an object to view the object details. During
interactive debug, the search results are updated with the objects that match the latest
search criteria when the simulator stops.

To specify the transaction search criteria, use the Transaction -> Search Transaction
command to invoke the Set Search Attribute form. If you plan to use the search
criteria again, click the Save button to save the current search criteria as a .list file.
Click the Search button to highlight transactions that match the search criteria in the
Transaction pane. These transactions are displayed and stored in the Search Results tab
simultaneously.
While the quick filter feature filters the object based on the AND condition, with the
advanced search feature, you can define customized search criteria and save the criteria
for future debug purposes.
Figure 126

Search Results Displayed in Search Results Tab

All the operations mentioned above can be used during interactive mode.

B
Appendix B: Automatically Record SCV
Transactions
Verdi provides an FSDB transaction back-end for SystemC designs that uses SCV to
capture transactions. This is useful for designs that have already been instrumented with
SCV scv_tr_ statements to record transactions. You just need to activate the FSDB
transaction back-end provided by Verdi which is described in this appendix.
* The supported usage is available since Verdi 2014.12 in combination with
VCS, VCS+Virtualizer, or IUS.
* If your SystemC design has not yet been instrumented for transaction
recording, use the SystemC transaction API. See the VC APPS Native
Programming Interface User Guide.

Use Model
The following is the use model of the SCV transaction recording feature:
1. The $VERDI_HOME/share/fsdbTrans_API/inc/scv_fsdbTrans_API.h header file
needs to be included and the snps_scv::scv_fsdbTrans_init function needs to be
called in your SCV-code. For example:

#include scv_fsdbTrans_API.h

int sc_main(int argc, char* argv[])
{
scv_tr_cwrdb_init();
snps_scv::scv_fsdbTrans_init(argc, argv);

}

The following environment variables also need to be set to enable SystemC dumping
feature in Verdi:
%> setenv VERDI3_SC_BETA 1
%> setenv FSDB_DUMP_RIDB 1

Appendix B: Appendix B: Automatically Record SCV Transactions

2. Include the directory of the header file:
%> g++ <g++ options> -I$VERDI_HOME/share/fsdbTrans_API/inc

3. Always link this Verdi library:
$VERDI_HOME/share/fsdbTrans_API/lib/$(FTAPI_PLATFORM)/libFTAPI.so

4. Also link the simulator-specific libraries:
$VERDI_HOME/share/PLI/<simulator>/<platform>/libsscore_<simulator_vers
ion>*_scv_fsdbTrans_*.so

Limitations
The following are the limitations of the SCV transaction recording feature:
* This feature is not available for standalone Virtualizer. it is available only for Virtualizer
with VCS co-simulation.
* Dumping of TLM ports is not supported.

SCProfiler, SNPS_PAM

C
Appendix C: Dumping Transaction Data Using
SC-API
The functions of the SC-API have almost a one-to-one correspondence to the functions
of the C-API. You can use this API in your SystemC-model to dump transactions
conveniently to the FSDB file and observe the results in the Verdi platform.
The SC-API uses the C-API to implement its functionality and provides the following
features by overloading some of the functions:
* All functions are prefixed with sc_fsdbTrans.
* SystemC time, SystemC scope, and the C call stack are automatically added as
attributes to the recorded transactions and are displayed in the Verdi platform.
The following sections describe how you can use the SC-API and the environment settings
for compilation and execution.
For more information on SC-API description, see the $VERDI_HOME/share/
fsdbTrans_API/inc/sc_fsdbTrans_API.h header file.
* The SC-API can be used with the C-API. Both SC-API and C-API write
the same FSDB file. All file, stream, and transaction handles are valid
for both SC-API and C-API. This combined usage, although possible,
is not recommended. It is recommended to use each API in its domain
consistently, the SC-API within the SystemC code. This is easy because
all C-API functions have a corresponding function in the SC-API. You can
therefore use all C-API functions by adding the sc_ prefix with the function
name.
* When the Verdi dumper (using the $fsdbDumpvars command) and C-API
or SC-API are used simultaneously to generate FSDB files, the FSDB file
name for the Verdi dumper cannot be the same as the one for C-API and
SC-API.

SC-API Descriptions

SC-API Descriptions
This section introduces the usage of the SC-API functions that are new or different
from the C-API functions. Refer to the $VERDI_HOME/share/fsdbTrans_API/inc/
sc_fsdbTrans_API.h header file for other one-to-one corresponding API functions.
fsdbTrans_file_id sc_fsdbTrans_file_open

sc_fsdbTrans_file_open (const char* file_name);

Firstly, the fsdbTrans_set_time_unit() function is called to set the
unit returned by the sc_get_time_resolution() SystemC function.
Then the fsdbTrans_file_open(filename) function is called and the
result is returned.

file_name

Name of the FSDB file to be opened.

fsdbTrans_file
_id

Unique file id: If no error occurs.
0: If an error occurs while opening the FSDB file.

fsdbTrans_stream_id sc_fsdbTrans_create_stream_begin

sc_fsdbTrans_create_stream_begin(fsdbTrans_file_id file_id [, const char*
scope[, char delimiter]]);

If scope is omitted (which is the suggested usage), it is determined as the hierarchical path to
transaction stream from the SystemC context. Then fsdbTrans_create_stream_begin is call
to create a stream and return it's result as stream_id.

file_id

The return value from the call to sc_fsdbTrans_file_open()

scope

The hierarchical path to the transaction stream; per default determined automatically from the
SystemC context if omitted.

delimiter

The hierarchical path delimiter, `.' per default if not specified otherwise.

fsdbTrans_ret_va
lue_e

Unique stream id: If no error occurs.
0: If an error occurred while opening the transaction stream.

SC-API Descriptions

fsdbTrans_trans_id sc_fsdbTrans_begin

sc_fsdbTrans_begin(fsdbTrans_stream_id sid,
fsdbTrans_trans_type_e trans_type);

Firstly, the fsdbTrans_set_time_stamp() function is called with
the time stamp from the sc_core::sc_time_stamp() SystemC
function.
Then, the fsdbTrans_begin(sid, type) function is called to create
the transaction, and add the current "C" call stack as a $backtrace
attribute.
Then, return the transaction ID. Use the transaction_id to create
transaction details or add relationship between transactions. If the
returned value is `0', it indicates that something is wrong and the
transaction cannot be created.

sid

Specifies the stream ID it belongs to.

trans_type

Specifies the transaction type. The Transaction Debug windows
use different representations (GUI symbols) for each type. The
trans_type attribute is one of the following: fsdbTrans_MESSAGE,
fsdbTrans_ACTION, fsdbTrans_TRANSACTION or fsdbTrans_GROUP.

fsdbTrans_trans
_id

Unique transaction ID: If no error occurs.
0: If an error occurs while opening the transaction.

fsdbTrans_ret_value_e sc_fsdbTrans_end

sc_fsdbTrans_end (fsdbTrans_trans_id tid);

Firstly, the fsdbTrans_set_time_stamp() function is called with the
time stamp from the SystemC function sc_core::sc_time_stamp().
Then, the fsdbTrans_end(tid) function is called to close the
transaction and return its return value.

tid

Specifies the transaction ID to be closed.

fsdbTrans_ret_val fsdbTrans_RET_SUCCESS: If no error occurs.
ue_e

SC-API Descriptions

fsdbTrans_ret_value_e sc_fsdbTrans_add_attribute

sc_fsdbTrans_add_attribute (fsdbTrans_trans_id tid, T
attr)

Add an attribute of any data type into the tid transaction, which is the
first argument.
The second argument is an expression of an arbitrary type T, value
attr and a readable representation #attr, that is, the variable name,
or the literal expression (such as, counter + 1).

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
ta type into the tid transaction, which is the
first argument.
The second argument is an expression of an arbitrary type T, value
attr and a readable representation #attr, that is, the variable name,
or the literal expression (such as, counter + 1).
This function creates an attribute with attrname equal to #attr and
the value equal to attr.
The type of the FSDB attribute depends on the type of the attr
expression.
The conversion rules are:
* If the value is an integer type with 64 bits or less, an integer
attribute of a matching width (8, 16, 32, or 64 bit) with decimal
representation is created.
* If the value is a pointer type, a matching 32 or 64bit integer
attribute with hexadecimal representation is created.
* If the value is a size limited SystemC integer type (sc_int,
sc_uint, sc_int_base, sc_uint_base), a matching width (8,
16, 32, or 64 bit) integer attribute with decimal representation is
created.
* If the value is an unlimited SystemC integer type (sc_signed,
sc_unsigned, sc_bigint, sc_biguint), and the length is > 64
bit, a string attribute is created; if the length is 64 bits or less, a
matching width (8, 16, 32, or 64 bit) integer attribute with decimal
representation is created.
* If the value is of a floating or fixed point type that fits a float or a
double, a float or double attribute is created.
* For SystemC fast fixed point types (sc_fixed_fast,
sc_ufixed_fast, sc_fix_fast, sc_ufix_fast, sc_fxval_fast),
a double attribute is created.
* All other data types are stored as string attributes, converted by the
string stream operator of the data type (as required by all SystemC
data types).

tid

Specifies the transaction.
An error is issued if this is not a valid transaction id (obtained from the
sc_fsdbTrans_begin() API).
An error is issued if sc_fsdbTrans_end() is already called for tid,
and this call has no effect.

attrname

Specifies the name of the attribute being added. A warning is issued if
attrname exceeds the maximum length and attrname is truncated.

attr

Specifies the value of the attribute being added. The data type of this
value determines the FSDB attribute type (refer to the conversion
rules in the Description field).

Example Using VCS
Use the following steps and the example to use SC-API for transaction dumping.
1. Change the current directory to the example path:
%> cd <Verdi install path>/demo/transaction/systemc_api

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
2. Use the source file to set the environment variables and VCS setting:
%> source sourceMeVCS

3. Use the following command to compile, link the main.cpp example file, and execute
the simulation:
%> syscan -cflags -g main.cpp \
-cflags -I$VERDI_HOME/share/fsdbTrans_API/inc
%> vcs -full64 -sysc sc_main -debug_access+r -lca \
-timescale=1ns/1ps \
$VERDI_HOME/share/fsdbTrans_API/lib/LINUX64/libFTAPI.so \
%> ./simv -ucli -do dump.ucli

The default.ridb, novas.fsdb, and sc_trans.fsdb files are generated in the
current working directory. The SystemC signals are dumped into the novas.fsdb file
and SystemC transactions are dumped into the sc_trans.fsdb file.
4. Invoke the Verdi platform with the verdi_cmd.tcl Tcl file and start debugging at both
signal and transaction levels:
%> verdi -ridb default.ridb -ssf novas.fsdb -play verdi_cmd.tcl
-nologo &

5. You can also use the runMeVCS script to go through step 3 to step 4:
%> source runMeVCS

Example Using IUS
Use the following steps and the example to use the SC-API for transaction dumping.

-nologo &

Appendix D: Automatically Recording OVM
Transactions and Messages
Use the following simple methods to enable automatic OVM transaction and message
recording:
* Compiling and Linking a Design
* Support for UVM Aware Debug
* Recording Transactions for Non-Sequencer Components

Compiling and Linking a Design
For the VCS simulator:
1. The FSDB dumper needs to be specified at the beginning. For example:
%> setenv tab $VERDI_HOME/share/PLI/VCS/LINUXAMD64/novas.tab
%> setenv pli $VERDI_HOME/share/PLI/VCS/LINUXAMD64/pli.a

2. Specify the following environment variable before compilation:
%> setenv VCS_OVM_HOME $VERDI_HOME/share/vmlib/ovm/ovm/lib/src

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
3. Add the -ntb_opts ovm compile option for OVM library. For example:
%> vcs -full64 -debug_access+all -sverilog -P $tab $pli \
-l compile.log -ntb_opts ovm \
-assert dve -assert api +memcbk +vcs+lic+wait ./xbus_tb_top.sv
+incdir+. +incdir+../sv +incdir+../../../src \

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
4. Add the +OVM_TR_RECORD run time option to dump transactions. For example:
%>./simv +OVM_TESTNAME=test_read_modify_xbus_tb_top
+fsdb+trans_begin_callstack +OVM_TR_RECORD

Appendix D: Appendix D: Automatically Recording OVM Transactions and Messages
Support for UVM Aware Debug

For other simulators:
1. Compile the design with the Verdi OVM library. For example:
%> vlog +incdir+../sv
+incdir+$OVM_HOME/src $OVM_HOME/src/ovm_pkg.sv xbus_tb_top.sv

2. Add the +OVM_TR_RECORD run time option to dump transactions. For example:
%> vsim +OVM_TR_RECORD +OVM_TESTNAME=test_read_modify_write -pli
novas_fli.so -do vsim.do -c -suppress 3829 xbus_tb_top

Support for UVM Aware Debug
Two runtime options are available to dump information for UVM Aware Debug. You can
use them to debug the OVM design with the UVM Aware Debug application.
The runtime options +UVM_VERDI_TRACE or +OVM_VERDI_TRACE enable specific Verdi
features. These include component level transaction recording, port level transaction
recording, factory dumping, and dynamic hierarchy tree dumping.
Both options dump the same information for UVM Aware Debug. They display identical
behavior.
The following table lists the format and details.
Table 4

UVM_VERDI_TRACE/OVM_VERDI_TRACE Arguments

+UVM_VERDI_TRACE
Usage

+UVM_VERDI_TRACE = UVM_AWARE| FAC|TLM|HIER
+OVM_VERDI_TRACE = UVM_AWARE| FAC|TLM|HIER

UVM_AWARE

If this argument is specified, similar to UVM_CONFIG_DB_TRACE,
configuration information is dumped.
Factory override trace messages are also enabled.
Dynamic hierarchy tree dumping are enabled.

TLM

Port level transaction recording is enabled.
The +OVM_TR_RECORD option is automatically enabled to record
transactions into the FSDB file.

TLM+IMP

Both port and implementation port level transaction recording is enabled.
Note that IMP must be used with TLM.
The +OVM_TR_RECORD option is automatically enabled to record
transactions into the FSDB file.

HIER

Dynamic hierarchy tree dumping is enabled.

Appendix D: Appendix D: Automatically Recording OVM Transactions and Messages
Recording Transactions for Non-Sequencer Components

Table 4

UVM_VERDI_TRACE/OVM_VERDI_TRACE Arguments (Continued)

FAC

Factory dumping is enabled.

* +define+OVM_VERDI_NO_FACTORY_RECORDING: Add this compile option to
disable the compilation of instrumented codes for factory recording.
* +OVM_VERDI_TRACE=FAC: Add this runtime option to enable factory recording.
Multiple features can be enabled with the "|" operator.
For example:
You can enable port level transaction recording and message dumping with the
+OVM_VERDI_TRACE=TLM|HIER compound argument:
>./simv +OVM_VERBOSITY=OVM_LOW +OVM_TESTNAME=test_read_modify_write
+OVM_VERDI_TRACE="TLM|HIER"

Use the Transaction Debug features described in previous chapters. They help
you recognize transactions and messages in the novas.fsdb transaction-based
FSDB file.

Recording Transactions for Non-Sequencer Components
If automatic recording for non-sequencer components (for example, drivers or
monitors) is required, you need to modify the code of the components to explicitly call
void'(this.begin_tr()) and void'(this.end_tr())to trigger the recording hooks.
You need to make sure begin_tr() and end_tr() are called in pairs.
Here is an example to explicitly call void'(this.begin_tr()) and
void'(this.end_tr()) in a wishbone monitor:
class uart_base_monitor extends ovm_monitor;
function void detect_bus_event(uart_bus_transaction bus_trans);
m_bus_port.write(bus_trans);
this.end_tr(bus_trans); // By Synopsys
endfunction : detect_bus_event
endclass : uart_base_monitor
class uart_wishbone_monitor extends uart_base_monitor;
//@ run related
task run();
//@ detect and put transaction

Appendix E: Using the Old Transaction Table
View
The content in this chapter describes the previous behavior of the tool. This
behavior is planned to phase out. Refer to the Verdi Migration Guide or contact
Synopsys Support Center to roll back to the old function.
The Transaction Table View window displays streams in the FSDB file as a spreadsheet
view of transaction types. The contents are based on data-mining (during loading) or
other operations. Examples include drag and drop streams from other windows or created
virtual streams. You can read and analyze the streams by the tabular highlight form.
The relationship between transactions can also be shown in the Transaction Table View

Transaction Table View Window
After importing an FSDB file, invoke the Show Quick Filter command by clicking the
button or selecting the View -> Show Quick Filter command. The Transaction Table View
window is illustrated in Figure: Invoke the Hierarchy Tree/Quick Filter Pane, with the Quick
Filter pane added to the left side. The Quick Filter pane shows the selected transaction
information inline from the spreadsheet pane. See the next sections for details about the
Transaction Table View window functions.

Transaction Table View Window

Figure 128

Invoke the Hierarchy Tree/Quick Filter Pane

As shown in Figure: Transaction Table View Window Overview, the spreadsheet pane
displays all imported streams in each tab and all transactions of the stream per tab. Each
tab contains one stream. A row shows a transaction and the columns show all normal
attributes and visible predefined attributes prefixed with the dollar ($) character. When
the number of rows reaches a pre-defined number, the contents of this tab are shown
by page and the page buttons are provided to change pages easily. The predefined
number is 30000 currently and you can change the default value in the Transaction Table
View page under the Transaction Debug folder in the Preferences form opened by the
Tools -> Preferences command. The selected transaction is displayed in yellow color
and the marked row is displayed in red color. The transaction time is also shown in the
Cursor Time and Marker Time fields. The Quick Filter pane shows the attributes of the
selected transaction inline (see Figure: Transaction Table View Window Overview). Tabs
are divided into two categories: non-editable and editable:
* Non-editable tab (with the
icon before the tag name): These tabs cannot be
edited after adding the streams. A stream is the same as the stream displayed in the
Transaction and Protocol Analyzer window and is shown by a tabular view in the tab.
* Editable tab (with the
icon before the tag name): A container for data mining.
Transactions can be added from different streams, can be deleted, and then can be
referenced for creating a virtual stream.

Column (Attribute) Operations
By default, after creating the tabs, the visible predefined attributes, including streams,
begin_Time, end_Time, label, and tag, and all the normal attributes are listed by
columns in one tab.
The same type of VIP transactions (from the same top-level channel) are grouped into
one tab with the tab naming convention: instance_name:column_name. If the transactions
come from different channels, these are grouped into different tabs with the tab naming
convention: instance_name:column_name:channel_name.

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
For VIP transactions, all the attributes are displayed based on the pre-defined order
decided by the VIP. The ordering of the VIP attributes displayed in the tab is as follows:
* Firstly, the predefined attributes in the XML file with the field_order keyword are
displayed.
* Other attributes' order follows the current column configuration defined using the View
-> Configure Columns command (as described below).
You can use the View -> Configure Columns command to design the tab format in the
Configure Columns form, that is, hide/show some attributes or pack some attributes into
one column. The string entered in the Find field finds the partial matched attributes in
both lists and the results are highlighted. The Configure Columns form displays attributes
in the Invisible Column and Visible Column fields so you can easily understand which
attributes are visible or not. The following paragraphs describe the operations applied in
columns.
* Visible/Invisible Columns: Use the arrow buttons in the Configure Columns form to
decide the visibility of columns in the spreadsheet pane.
* Pack/Unpack Attributes: Attributes can be combined to one column. Select the
attributes and click the Pack Selected button in the Configure Columns form (see
Figure: Pack the Attributes). The names of packed attributes are added with the
(PackNumber) suffix. After clicking the Apply button, the columns are combined to one
column with the concatenated names (for example (addr;read_write)). Click the
Unpack Selected button to unpack these attributes.
Figure 139

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Pack the Attributes

* Column Order: The column order of the spreadsheet pane can be changed using the
Up and the Down buttons (see Figure: Pack the Attributes) in the Configure Columns
form.

* Column Value Radix: The attribute value radix can be changed by right-clicking on the
attribute name and selecting the radix from the menu. This is disabled when used in
the predefined attributes and packed columns.
Figure 140

Change Value Radix

You can save or restore the configuration by clicking Save or Restore buttons.

Row (Transaction) Operations
The sorting of the rows (transactions) is based on increasing begin_time by default.
When moving the cursor to the row and left-clicking on the row, the row is highlighted in
yellow. Multiple row selection is also provided. The row is marked in red by middle-clicking.
Only one marked transaction is supported in a tab. The following paragraphs describe the
operations applied in rows.
* Sort: The transactions (rows) can be sorted based on the selected attribute (column).
The sorting is applied in this page when you directly click on the attribute name (Figure:
Sorting in a Page). Click on the attribute name again to switch the ascending and
descending sorting direction.
Figure 141

Sorting in a Page

The global sorting action is also provided to sort all the transactions of all pages.
Right-click on the attribute name and select the Global Sort command (refer to
Figure: Sorting all Transactions in All Pages) to sort the transactions in ascending or
descending direction.

Figure 142

Sorting all Transactions in All Pages

* Search: The transactions (attributes) can be searched using the Search commands
for analyzing the stream. The Search -> Go To commands can be used to search the
first transaction, last transaction, or marker transaction in this tab. The Search -> Go
To -> Time command can be used to find the previous and closest transaction that has
the begin_time attribute as a time value. You can use the Search -> Find command
to find the entry of the first transaction that contains partial matching of the string value.
If the All Tabs option is enabled, the searching is through all the tabs (see Figure: Find
String).
Figure 143

The Search -> Search by Attributes command is used to search in the current
tab using the rule displayed in the Expression field. The usage is the same as the
description in the Creating Virtual Streams section. If the All Tabs option is enabled,
the searching is through all tabs. You can save or append the searching conditions to a
list file by clicking Save or Append buttons.
* Editable/Non-editable Tab: The included transactions are allowed to come from
different streams and can be added or deleted (use the Delete Transactions
command in the right-click command menu) in editable tabs. The transaction cannot be
added or deleted in non-editable tabs.
* Highlight Relation: The relationship between transactions can be highlighted by
right-clicking on the spreadsheet pane or selecting the View -> Highlight Relation
command. For example, invoke the View -> Highlight Relation -> Child command.
The child/children of the selected transaction are highlighted in light red (see Figure:
Highlight Relation Command) and the Status Message is updated with the highlighted
relationship of the transaction. If there are other related transactions in other tab(s), the
related tab(s) text changes color too and you can see them after switching to that tab
(see Figure: Highlight Relation with Related Tab Text Color Changing).

Support for Transaction Comparison
The comparing feature is enabled in the transaction window. The tTableView is the
transaction analysis window and you can provide comparison in this window. Choose
the Tools -> Compare Menu/Toolbar command from the main window as shown in the
following figure. The Compare command is enabled when FSDB is opened in tTableView.
Figure 149

tTableView Compare Command

To invoke Compare command from the stream tab, click the right mouse button as shown
in the following figure. The stream is specified as the base stream by default. If you invoke
Compare command from the virtual stream or editable tab, the base stream needs to be
specified.
Figure 150

Compare Command From Stream Tab

Compare Options
After invoking the Compare command, Compare Options window opens as shown in the
following figure:
Figure 151

Compare Options Window

The Streams option includes the following fields:
* Base Stream: This text field specifies the base stream name in the FSDB file. The
base stream name can be specified by either typing directly in the text field or by
clicking the Browse button and selecting the stream name in the Select Stream form.
This feature is not supported in the virtual stream.
* Compared Stream: This text field specifies the stream name to be compared in the
FSDB file. The stream name can be specified by either typing directly in the text field or
clicking the Browse button and selecting the stream name in the Select Stream form.
This feature is not supported in the virtual stream.
When you browse the Compared Stream field, it shows streams in all tTableView/
tBrowser FSDBs. It also allows you to specify the stream from new FSDB by Load button.

When you browse the Base Stream field, it shows streams only in the current tTableView
opened FSDB and the Load button is disabled. The following figure shows the Select
Stream window:

Trans. Attributes Tab
The following fields and buttons are available in the Trans. Attributes tab.
Compare
This tab specifies which attributes in the base stream is compared.
Figure 153

Compare Tab

* Deselected Attributes: This column lists the attributes that are not compared.
* Selected Attributes: This column lists the attributes that are compared. The
$beginTime and $endTime attributes are listed by default. Use the
and
buttons to move the selected attributes to compare from Deselected Attributes to

Selected Attributes, and vice versa. Only one attribute can be selected at a time.
Use the
and
buttons to move all the selected attributes to compare from
Deselected Attributes to Selected Attributes, and vice versa.
Name Mapping
This tab is used to rearrange name mapping of each attribute in the compared stream to
the attribute in the base stream.
Figure 154

Name Mapping Tab

* Mapping Attributes: This column lists the attributes that are mapped. Select the
attribute in the white cells and use the
and
buttons to move the selected
attributes from Mapping Attributes to Unmapping Attributes, and vice versa. The
gray cells cannot be selected.
* Unmapping Attributes: This column lists the attributes without mapping. You can use
the
and
buttons to move the selected attributes from Unmapping Attributes
to Mapping Attributes, and vice versa. Click the Default button to reset all attributes
back to the default name mapping. If a base attribute is selected to compare, but there
is no compared attribute to map it, a warning pops up.
Time Tab
The Time Range section includes the Time Range and Time Tolerance options as shown
in the following figure.

Figure 155

Time Tab

Time Range
Only one of the following options can be selected at a time.
* Full Range: When this option is turned on, the full transaction time range is used for
comparison. The default is on.
* Specific Range: When this option is turned on, the partial transaction time range in the
stream is used for comparison. The default is off.
* Base Stream: Specifies the base stream time range used for comparison in the From
and To text fields. The time unit is the file time unit of the base stream.
* Compare Stream: When this option is turned on, it specifies a different time range to
use for the stream that is compared in the From and To text fields. When this option
is turned off, the compared stream uses the same time range as the base stream. The
time unit is the file time unit of the base stream.
An information pops-up if the base and compared stream have different time
units.
Time Tolerance
* Tolerance of Begin Time: Specifies the time tolerance for the comparison begin time.
The default value is 0. This text field is available only when the BeginTime attribute is
selected to be compared. The time unit is the file time unit of the base stream.
* Tolerance of End Time: Specifies the time tolerance for the comparison end time.
The default value is 0. This text field is available only when the EndTime attribute is
selected to be compared.
General Tab

The General tab is shown in the following figure:
Figure 156

General Tab

The General tab includes the following options:
* Case Sensitive: When this option is turned on, attributes are compared with casesensitivity. When this option is turned off, the attributes are compared without casesensitivity. The default value is off.
* Stop Criteria: When this option is turned on, the maximum number of errors allowed
before stopping the comparison are specified. The default value is on, and the default
difference count is 500.
After specifying the compare options, click Ok to save the settings and close the Compare
Options window, then perform the comparison, or click the Cancel button to close the
Compare Options window without making any changes.

Comparison Results
The comparison result is shown in the Comparison tab, which is none-editable. There is a
toolbar to indicate Base and Compared Stream, and provide buttons to find first/previous/
next/last different row in the current page.

Preface
This book is designed to allow you to quickly become proficient in the Verdi platform.
This manual focuses on the most commonly used commands without going into detail
on everything. For detailed descriptions of individual commands, refer to the appropriate
chapter of the Verdi and Siloti Command Reference Manual.
The manual should be read from beginning to end, although you may skip any sections
with which you are already familiar.
* If you are new to the Verdi platform, begin with the User Interface, Launching
Techniques and various Tutorials chapters. After you are familiar with the individual
modules, review the Application Tutorials chapter.
* If you are familiar with the Verdi platform but want to learn new ways to apply it, review
the Application Tutorials chapter.

Audience
The audience for this manual includes engineers who are familiar with languages
and tools used in design and verification such as Verilog, VHDL, SystemVerilog,
simulators, timing analyzers, and transactions. The application of these languages may
be for System-on-Chip (SoC), Application Specific Integrated Circuit (ASIC), and Field

This document assumes that you have a basic knowledge of the platform on which your

Synopsys is committed to creating an inclusive environment where every employee,

Introduction to Verdi
* Technology Overview

(R)

The Verdi Automated Debug Platform is a sophisticated tool designed to enhance
the debugging of digital designs, thereby boosting productivity for complex System-onChip (SoC), ASIC, and FPGA projects. Unlike traditional debug tools that depend solely
on structural information and the engineer's ability to deduce design behavior from its
structure, the Verdi platform offers advanced technology to help users understand intricate
and unfamiliar design behaviors. It automates challenging and monotonous debugging
tasks, integrates various complex design environments, and deduces the dynamic
behavior of a design over time.
The Verdi platform offers a comprehensive suite of features beyond the basics of a
source code browser, schematics, waveforms, state machine diagrams, and waveform
comparison for FSDB (Fast Signal Database) format simulation results. It includes
advanced capabilities such as automatic signal activity tracing with temporal flow views,
assertion-based debugging, power aware debugging, and the analysis of transaction
and message data. These features are accessible through a customizable graphical user
interface built on the Qt platform, which supports multi-window docking.
The Verdi platform helps engineers to swiftly identify, isolate, comprehend, and fix bugs,
thereby boosting the efficiency and productivity of engineering resources, cutting costs,
and accelerating the time-to-market for silicon products.

Technology Overview
A technology base is constructed that is optimized for design exploration, understanding,
and debugging. The Verdi platform's unique architecture features powerful compilers,
interfaces, databases, analysis engines and visualization tools in an integrated system for
complete debugging.

Compilers, Interfaces and Interoperability
The Verdi platform has compilers for the most common design/verification languages and
provides several interfaces for standard simulators.
* Compilers: The Verdi platform provides compilers for the languages used in most
design and verification environments, such as Verilog, VHDL, SystemVerilog (both
design and verification code), and power code (CPF or UPF). As the code is analyzed
and compiled, it is checked for syntax and semantic errors.
* Interfaces: The Verdi platform's readers import industry-standard VCD and SDF data
from all simulators and timing tools. The results are read from the detection tool and
stored in the Fast Signal Database (FSDB). Direct dumping to FSDB through the object
files linked to a verification tool (simulator) results in smaller waveform files and flexible
access to post- simulation data.
* Interoperability: The Verdi platform provides extensive, well-documented, and
supported interfaces that ensure interoperability with all leading logic simulators and
a variety of formal verification and timing analysis tools. These interfaces also enable
the integration of other verification applications through Tcl (Tool Command Language)
and C language APIs. Synopsys has partnered with many design and verification
companies to integrate their tools with the Verdi platform, which helps save time
and reduce costs by offering a unified view across the entire verification and debug
workflow.

Technology Overview

Databases
The Verdi platform provides two databases. All analysis engines and visualization tools
use these databases.
* Knowledge Database (KDB): The Verdi platform employs its internal synthesis
technology during the design compilation process to identify and extract detailed
structural, logical, and functional information about the design. This comprehensive
design data is subsequently stored in the Knowledge Database (KDB).
* Fast Signal Database (FSDB): The FSDB (Fast Signal Database) is designed to
efficiently store simulation results, including transaction data and logged messages
from SystemVerilog Testbench (SVTB) or other supported languages, in a compact
format that allows for rapid data access. Synopsys provides object files that can be
linked with popular simulators to directly save simulation results in FSDB format. You
can create FSDB files either from the provided routines or by converting VCD (Value
Change Dump) files. Additionally, FSDB read/write API routines are available for
customers and partners to use.

Analysis Engines
Using the information from the KDB and FSDB, the Verdi platform provides a set of
analysis engines for different applications, including:
* Structure Analysis: analyze design structure to show how components are
connected.
* Behavior Analysis: analyze design and simulation results to display design operation
over time.
* Assertion Evaluation: answer questions and search for details about design operation
from a previous simulation.
* Transaction/Message Analysis: analyze transaction and message (log) data in the
FSDB file and visualize in nWave and a spreadsheet view.
* Power State Evaluation: evaluate the power state based on the power intent
description in the CPF/UPF and the values of related signals in the FSDB file.

Graphical User Interface
The graphical user interface uses the Qt platform and provides the following functions:
* A Welcome page summarizing the available resources in a single location.
* History support enabling easy restoration of previous sessions.

Technology Overview

* Typical work modes with predefined window layouts making the debug content easy to
locate.
* A unique Spotlight function searches for a command without exhaustively searching
through all the drop-down menus.
* Several customization options:
System frames and toolbar icons can be undocked, moved to a new location, and
then docked again.
A pane can be maximized by double-clicking the pane banner so that the content is
more visible. You can double-click it again to shrink it to its original size.
The visible toolbar icons can be selected through a menu option.
Bindkey values, drop-down menu names, and locations can be customized through
the customization form.

Visualization
The Verdi platform delivers outstanding temporal visualization features with its Temporal
Flow View. This cutting-edge tool extracts and displays multicycle temporal behavior from
design data and simulation results. .
The Verdi platform offers sophisticated structure visualization and analysis tools such as
nTrace for source code, nWave for waveforms, nSchema for schematic/logic diagrams,
and nState for finite state machines (FSMs). These tools are intended to analyze
the structure of the design in the form of the signal relationships in the RTL, physical
connections in schematic/logic diagrams, states and transitions in FSM bubble diagrams,
and value changes in waveforms.
The Property Tools window in the Verdi platform provides integrated support for assertions
and enables quick traversal from an assertion failure to the related design activity. While
the Transaction/Message Analyzer enables debug and analysis at higher levels of
abstraction from transaction or log information saved to the FSDB file, the Power Manager
window provides visualization of the power intent and supports cross-probing with other
Verdi platform windows.
The Verdi platform offers fully integrated views, enabling you to select any section of the
design source code and immediately generate corresponding hierarchical or flattened
logic diagrams. This allows for efficient exploration of a design and its verification results
by clicking on context-sensitive hyperlinked objects and signals within any view. This
seamless integration facilitates quick and easy switching between views to find and isolate
the specific information required to understand any part of the design and resolve any

The Verdi platform has many commands. Many are invoked through mouse clicks or drags
rather than pull-down menus at the top of each window. Read this chapter to learn the
interface conventions before proceeding further.

The features described are common to nWave, nTrace, nSchema, nState, and Flow View
components. Refer to the User Interface Overview section of the Introduction chapter in
the Verdi and Siloti Command Reference Manual for additional information.
* Frame Banner
* Pull-Down Menu Commands
* Hamburger Menu
* Mnemonic Keys
* BindKeys
* Toolbars

* Mouse Operation
* Right Mouse Button Menus
* Undock/Dock
* Online Help
* Feedback Button

* Quick Launcher
* Find
* Search
* Recently Used Commands

Frame Banner
The banner at the top of each pane identifies the application, frame number (such as
<nWave:2>), and file, unit, or scope displayed in that pane. The asterisk (*) character
appearing at the front of the banner indicates that the pane is the active one.
Double-click the pane banner bar to maximize a pane or to shrink the pane back to the
previous size as shown in the following figure.

Figure 4

Maximize the Source Code Pane

Right-click the banner of a dockable pane to display a configuration option menu that lists
all the available dockable panes and toolbar categories. Toggle the option to hide/show the
entire pull-down menu, dockable pane, or toolbar category.

Figure 5

Configuration Option Menu to Hide/Show Dock Panes/Toolbar Categories

You can hide banners in Verdi by clicking the Hide Banners
button at the bottomright corner. This action hides the docker banner and displays a down-arrow button at the
upper-right corner of each docker window, as shown in the following figure. To show the
banner again, click the down-arrow button.

Figure 6

Hide and Unhide Banner

Pull-Down Menu Commands
A pull-down menu bar is located just below the banner for panes that are also windows.
Each menu item contains several commands that display when the menu is selected.
The pull-down menu can be hidden or displayed by selecting the right-click Menu option
invoked from the window banner, menu bar, or toolbar.
When the Menu option is toggled off, the pull-down menu of the pane or window is hidden.
You can press the Alt key within the pane or window to display or hide the pull-down menu
again. Also, when the cursor is clicked elsewhere in the pane or window, the menu is
automatically hidden again.
When the Menu option is toggled on (the value on means always show the pull-down
menu), the pull-down menu cannot be shown/hidden by pressing the Alt key.
For each subwindow or window in the Verdi platform, custom commands can be added
using the Tools -> Customize Menu/Toolbar command.

Hamburger Menu
button located in the bottom-right corner of Verdi. When
Verdi provides a Hide Menus
you click this button, the menu bar disappears. A hamburger icon appears on the far left
side of the toolbar, as shown in the following figure. You can use this button to display the
menus again. Alternatively, use Ctrl+Shift+B to toggle the menu bar between the hidden
and visible states.
Figure 7

Hamburger Menu Button

Mnemonic Keys
The pull-down menus support Meta key invocation using mnemonics. The mnemonic for
each item is indicated by an underline. For example, to display the File -> Open menu
(meta -fo), press and hold the <Meta> key on your keyboard (the diamond key/<Alt> key
on Sun keyboards or the <Alt> key on Windows' keyboards) and press the "f" key, then
release the <Meta> key and press the letter "o" key.

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
BindKeys
A command can be bound to either a keystroke or a mouse button. After the bindkeys
are defined, commands can be invoked with a keystroke or mouse click. For example,
the Source -> Active Annotation command can be invoked using the "X" key (the
defined bindkey is the letter after the command in the menu). The bindkeys of the menu
commands can be customized using the Tools -> Customize Menu/Toolbar command.

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Toolbars
A row of icons appears beneath the pull-down menu bar on panes that are also windows.
These icons provide access to frequently used commands for the current window.

The available toolbar icons may be modified using one of the following methods:
* Enable/disable the icon category using the main window right-click option menu.
* Left-click to select the separator bar and then drag left or right to decrease or increase
the associated space. When the space is decreased such that some icons are no
longer visible, a double arrow (>>) symbol is displayed to the right of the category.
Clicking this symbol displays the hidden icons.
* Left-click to select the gray bar and then drag up or down to undock the category and
then move to a new location on the toolbar or to left/right/below the window. Available
slots are highlighted with a blue dashed line.
* Define/modify/add toolbar icons and categories using the Tools -> Customize Menu/
Toolbar command. Refer to the nTrace chapter of the Verdi and Siloti Command
Reference Manual for details.

Mouse Operation
The mouse is most often used to select objects by clicking the left mouse button. A range
of objects can be selected by dragging with the left mouse button over the objects or by
using the <Shift> key along with left-clicking. To add or remove individual objects to or
from the selection, use the <Ctrl> key along with the left-click.
The Verdi platform also makes use of drag-and-drop to move information from one pane/
window to another. Normally drag-and-drop is performed by pressing the middle mouse
button or left mouse button to select the object, holding the button as the mouse is moved
to a new location, and then releasing the button to "drop" the object into a new location.
The drag-and-drop operation can be performed between different pane types, for example,
dragging a signal from the nWave pane and dropping it to the source code pane executes
tracing connectivity of the selected signal. If the pane is in the background (displayed as
a tab), moving the dragged object to the tab name and dropping it changes the tab to the
foreground and drops the object. The resulting behavior is the same as if the object is
dropped directly in the pane.
The drag-and-drop operation depends on the center of the arrow cursor and not the tip
of this cursor. For example, if a signal is dragged from nWave then it is dropped to the
Source Code pane depending on the center of the arrow cursor as shown in the figure:
Figure 8

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Right Mouse Button Menus
Right-click an object to display a menu with commands appropriate for that object type.
These menus are described in detail in the Right-Click Commands sections of the Verdi
and Siloti Command Reference Manual.

Undock/Dock
The main window of the Verdi platform consists of dockable panes that can be released
(undocked) from the main window. The dockable panes can be docked to the main
window again.
Every dockable pane has its own banner or title bar. The dockable panes can be moved
from one dock area to another by dragging the pane banner. A dockable pane can attach
above, below, left, right or over another dockable pane. A tab is created when you dock a
pane over another dockable pane. Refer to the following figures for examples.
Figure 9

Undock Design Browser Pane from Main Window

Figure 10

Redock Design Browser Pane to Main Window

Figure 11

Dock nWave to the Right of the Design Browser Pane

Figure 12

Dock nWave above the Design Source Code Pane

Figure 13

Online Help
The nTrace main window and the standalone nWave/nSchema windows provide online
help, which can be accessed through the Help menu.

Feedback Button
In each window (including undocked windows), you can invoke the feedback dialog by the
menu command Help -> Feedback. You can fill the entries and the feedback is sent to
verdi_feedback@synopsys.com, by default.
To disable this feature, set the environment variable VERDI_DISABLE_FEEDBACK using the
following command:
setenv VERDI_DISABLE_FEEDBACK 1

The following options are available on the Feedback Dialog window:
* Type: Specifies the type of feedback. The options are as follows:
I Like Something: Select this option if you have a positive feedback.
I Don't Like Something: Select this option if you have a negative feedback.
I Have a Suggestion: Select this option if you have a suggestion to provide.
* Feature: Specifies the feature you want to provide the feedback for. The options are as
follows:
Source View
Waveform View
Schematic View
AMS Debug
PowerAware Debug

Testbench Debug
HW/SW debug
Fault Analysis Debug
Coverage and Planner
Other
When you click the menu command Help -> Feedback from a specific
window, the feature name is autofilled based on where you click the
feedback menu command from. For example, Feature is set to Waveform
View automatically if the user clicks feedback menu command from nWave
* Input Your Feedback Here: You can specify your feedback in this field. There is
a placeholder "The more you tell us, the more we can help" in it. Input at least one
character in this field for the Send button to be enabled.
The following figure shows the behavior of this field. When nothing is specified, Send
button is disabled and when some text is entered, the Send button is enabled.
Figure 16

Input Your Text Here

* Include Product Release Version: Specifies that you agree to add the Verdi version
along with the feedback email content. The value of this option is on by default. Toggle
the option to off if you do not want to add the Verdi version along with the feedback
email content.

* Advanced>>: Click this option if you want to include a screen shot or an attachment to
be sent along with the feedback email content.
Include Screenshot
Preview
Attachment
The screen shot only captures the window under Verdi instead of the whole desktop.
If the check box Include Screenshot is toggled off, the Preview button is disabled.
Otherwise, it is enabled. When you click the Preview button, you can see the
screenshot image. The following figure depicts the behavior of Advanced>> option.
Figure 17

Advanced>> option

If the screenshot needs to exclude this Feedback Dialog window, the only
way is to hide this dialog, make screenshot and show it again.
Clicking Browse pops up a file dialog Choose Attached File for you to choose single
attachment, as shown in the following figure:
Figure 18

Choose Attached File

The selected file is shown in the Attachment label.

Figure 19

Attachment Label

Send: Click this option to send the feedback email to verdi_feedback@synopsys.com,,
by default.
To configure the destination address, set the environment variable
VERDI_FEEDBACK_EMAIL using the following command:
setenv VERDI_FEEDBACK_EMAIL [recipient_address]

* Close: Click this option to close the Feedback Dialog window.

Feedback Email Format
The type is specified in the mail body and the feature is added to the subject line. The
screenshot and attached file appears as attachments in the email. The version of Verdi (if
Include Product Release Version is on) and the message you enter in the Input Your
Feedback Here field are added as the mail content.

Verdi provides the Quick Launcher feature that enables quick access to integrated tools,
applications, and sessions quickly.
To open Quick Launcher, click the Quick Launcher icon located in the upper right corner

Search
Verdi provides search pane for the broader search. Search applies to all the windows of
the Verdi.
Perform the following steps to use the search feature:
1. Click search (magnifying glass) icon on the upper right corner of the window to open
the search pane, as shown in the following figure:

2. Enter any search key/text in the search pane.
3. Click search (magnifying glass) icon in the search pane.
4. Click on any searched result to go to the found result.
5. Search pane can be undocked as an individual pane, as shown in the following figure:
6. Search pane has the following tabs to search the results based on these categories:
GUI
Menu
DB/Log/Doc

7. You can choose the required tab and search the information.
Figure 29

Undocked Search Pane and Search Tabs

Following are the limitations of this feature:
* The correct behavior of searching when the editor is on editing and unsaved status is
not guaranteed. The result content may be wrong.
If line content was deleted or changed, although the current content does not match
with the search keyword, it may still show on the search pane when the previous
document matches the keyword before modified.
If line content was added, although the fresh new content matches with the
keyword, Verdi cannot read in the content and search pane does not show the fresh
matched line content.
* The correct behavior of the jumping when the editor is edited after searching is not
guaranteed. As a result items display with the line number of the matched line of the
old document. If document content changes, the line number of the new document
does not always reflect the match line number of the result. Any clicking on the result
item may lead to unpredictable behavior.
* GUI tab in new search pane apply blocking search which may cause user to wait for
the search results, therefore, a busy dialog is provided for the earlier abort.

* All window supported unified find has supported find bar, but not all the supported
search pane.
* Onesearch has its own special searching rule and non-blocking search and other tab in
search does not work.
* Original onesearch Tcl does not work.
* The following windows are not supported:
OVM/UVM Hierarchy tree view
Interactive Debug

Recently Used Commands
Verdi provides a button in the upper-right corner with a drop-down list of recently used
commands. The list depends on the active window. This button appears on demand (for
example, when at least one recently used command is available).
Verdi stores 10 recently used menu commands and toolbar commands of each window
type. Different windows with the same window type (for example, nWave2, nWave3,
nWave4 and so on) shares the same recently used commands. Each window type has
their own recently used command set.
The recently used commands are stored in novas.rc so that next time when user invoke
Verdi, recently command button restores the setting from novas.rc
Use the following environment variable to enable this feature:
setenv VERDI_RECENT_CMD 1

windows:

nTrace Source Code Pane
The source code pane appears on the right side of the nTrace main window. Multiple
source code files can be displayed as multiple tabs. If a module is described in multiple
source files, multiple tabs are opened to display the complete source code when the node
is set as an active scope. Each tab is undockable.
Figure 33

nTrace Multiple Source Code Tabs

The source code view displays the source code for the active unit in the design browser.
This window is divided into the following two areas:
* Source Code Area
* Indicator Area

Source Code Area
The source code area contains the HDL source code. The Verdi platform color-codes
the source code to differentiate syntax elements. You can set the syntax colors to your
preferences. Some colors change during debugging. For example, signals that are traced
are displayed in green to highlight the trace history. You can reset all the traced signals'
colors to their default settings using the Trace -> Reset Traced Signal's Color command.

nTrace User Interface

Indicator Area
The indicator area contains line numbers and graphical indicators that result from load
tracing, driver tracing, connectivity tracing, and bookmarking. The following table describes
the symbols used in the indicator area:
Symbol

Definition
Driver - result from last trace command. Multiple drivers are
possible.
Active driver - selected driver from last active trace
command or current Show command.
Load - result from last trace command. Multiple loads are
possible.
Possible driver - result from the possible analyzed traced
result.
Unanalyzed driver - result from the unanalyzed traced
result.
Bookmark - marks a selection for easy referral.
Pass through load - result from the pass-through driver
traced results.
Pass through driver - result from the pass-through load
traced results.
Pass through connectivity - result from the pass-through
connectivity traced results.

The indicator area also shows interactive simulation controls such as breakpoints and
current active statement arrows.

The nWave pane/standalone window consists of three resizable subwindows (also known
as panes):
* Signal pane
* Value pane
* Waveform pane

* nWave Signal Pane
* nWave Value Pane
* nWave Waveform Pane
* nWave Toolbar Icons
* Get Signals
* nWave Mouse Operations

nWave Signal Pane
The Signal pane displays signals and group names on the left side of the nWave display.
You can use the Signal pane to select and manipulate signals and groups of signals.
Three types of objects appear in the Signal pane:
* Signal name
* Signal cursor
signal cursor

* Group name

Signal Name
A signal name appears to the left of its waveform. In addition to identifying the waveforms,
the signal names are selectable areas; clicking on a signal name selects that signal for
manipulation. The signal name can be displayed as either a full hierarchical name or a
local name. By default, nWave right-justifies the signal name. However, you can change
the justification. If a name is too long, use the horizontal scroll bar or adjust the window
size to see the entire name.

Signal Cursor
The signal cursor marks the insertion point for signal commands: Add, Move, Paste,
Overlay Signals, and Create Bus. Middle-click to set the signal cursor.
create bus

Group Name
You can place similar signals in the same group. The group name can be changed from
the default of G1, G2, and so on.

nWave Value Pane
time

The Value pane is next to the Signal pane and displays the value of each signal at the
cursor time in the Waveform pane. You can select the display format for signals. For

cursor

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
example, they can be displayed as hex, octal, binary, decimal value, or user-defined alias
text.
Preferences for what is displayed (for example, leading zeros, marker value), can be set
through the Value pane menu or the Tools -> Preferences command.
For any value change of a signal, nWave displays the old value to the new value in the
Value pane indicating that the value is changed from 0 to 1 or 1 to 0. If the value (such as
the value change of the long bus value) is not fully visible due to the width of the Value
pane, move the cursor on top of that value in the Value pane, and the value is displayed in
the tip window.

nWave Waveform Pane
The Waveform pane appears to the right and displays the waveforms. In addition, the
Waveform pane contains the following objects:
waveform pane

* Cursor
* Marker
marker

* Zoom scale ruler
zoom-scale ruler

Full-scale Ruler

* Full scale ruler

Cursor
The cursor is used to show the current simulation time for all windows and to provide one
endpoint for delta time calculations. To set the cursor, left-click the mouse button. The
toolbar displays the cursor time.
delta time

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Note the following when setting the cursor:
* The setting affects the time display (and, therefore, the results) in all panes/windows
that display values.
* If you click inside the Waveform pane and choose the Waveform -> Snap Cursor to
Transitions command ("s" key), the cursor can only be set where there is a signal
transition.
* If you de-select the Waveform -> Snap Cursor to Transition command, you can set
the cursor to any location.

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Marker
The marker is used to provide the second point of a delta calculation. To set the marker,
click the middle mouse button. The toolbar displays the amount of time between the cursor
and the marker (the delta time).
delta time

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Note the following when setting the marker:
* If you click inside the Waveform pane and choose the Waveform -> Snap Cursor to
Transitions command ("s" key), the marker can only be set where there is a signal
transition.
* If you de-select the Waveform -> Snap Cursor to Transition command, you can set
the marker to any location.
* If you choose the Waveform -> Fix Cursor/Marker Delta Time command ("x" key),
cursor or marker is spaced at the same delta time.
* If you de-select the Waveform -> Fix Cursor/Marker Delta Time command, cursor or
marker is not spaced at the same delta time.
After you set the cursor time and the marker time, right-click to zoom and fit
the waveform display to the time range between the cursor and the marker
times.

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
time range

Zoom-Scale Ruler
The zoom-scale ruler appears at the top of the Waveform pane and displays the current
displayed time range.
zoom-scale ruler

Full-Scale Ruler
The full-scale ruler appears at the bottom of the Waveform pane. This ruler displays
the time range of all the results (not just the displayed portion) and indicates where the
cursor and marker positions are in this range. You can change cursor and marker times
by clicking on the full-scale ruler. Selecting a range (dragging with the left mouse button)
zooms the display so that the selected area zooms the display in the Waveform pane to
the selected area.
time range

Get Signals
The nWave window does not display any signals by default; signals are added by dragging
from other windows or by selection in the Get Signals form (using the Signal -> Get
get signals

Signals command). Signals are displayed hierarchically based on the design unit selected
in the design hierarchy box on the left side of the form.
Figure 37

nWave Get Signal Form

To select signals, navigate the design tree in the Design Hierarchy pane to find the
required signals, then either drag them to the mirror signal pane in the right-side pane
(which mirrors the signals in the Waveform pane) or select the signals and click Apply.
When you have selected all of the signals of interest, click OK.
The design hierarchy of the simulation files may not match that of the currently
opened design source. You can display waveform data independent of the
design that is loaded.
design hierarchy

The mirror signal pane allows you to manipulate the arrangement of the signals displayed
in the Get Signals form without immediately affecting the waveform pane. After finishing
the signal arrangement, click Apply to synchronize the waveform pane. Click OK to apply
the arrangement and close the form.
mirror signal window

get signals

Siloti Command Reference Manual for details.

You can open a new nSchema pane from the nTrace main window by clicking on the New

The schematic window displays the schematic generated from the corresponding HDL
source code and provides another design view for debugging. You can debug the design
using menu commands or mouse operations.
In nSchema, VDD, VCC, VEE, POWER and PWR net names are treated as supply nets
and VSS, GND and GROUND net names are treated as ground nets. These nets are case
insensitive. When a signal is treated as a power/ground global signal, trace actions are
skipped.

nCompare User Interface
The nCompare pane compares simulation results stored in FSDB dump files using flexible,
user-specified comparison criteria.
It is optimized for rapid comparison of large data sets and is seamlessly integrated with the
Verdi platform.

This integration allows you to easily identify and display differences between simulation
runs.
The nCompare pane can be accessed by selecting the Tools -> nCompare command
from the nWave pane.

Comparing Different Simulation Runs
The nCompare pane is used to identify mismatch simulation errors between various
simulation runs.
Examples include mismatches between pre-synthesis and post-synthesis stages, different
clock speeds of the same design, different technologies, or simulation files produced by
different simulators.

Rule File
The rule file is described using Tcl language.
TCL

The nCompare module uses Tcl language and nCompare-defined-Tcl-extended
comparison commands to describe the comparison rules and specify comparison options.
A basic rule file should have at least the following three parts:
1. Specification of golden and secondary simulation files.
2. Specification of compared signal pairs.
3. Start time-based comparison.

nECO User Interface

The following is a simple rule file that would compare all signals in 1.fsdb and 2.fsdb:
cmpOpenFsdbcmpOpenFsdb 1.fsdb 2.fsdb
cmpSetSignalPaircmpSetSignalPair top -level 0
cmpCompare

User Interface) or using the nCompare utility, the nCompare pane displays the mismatch
errors. These errors can be sorted by design hierarchy or time sequence, allowing for easy

Organizations increasingly pair on-premises EDA environments with public cloud capacity

Cloud Infrastructure and Synopsys Tools in the Cloud
Many organizations use public cloud infrastructure to handle peak demand and specific

Cloud Advantages
Public cloud environments offer the following advantages:
* Elastic scalability, providing access to gain unlimited compute and storage resources.
* Hardware-optimized environments, allowing the use of the latest high-performance
CPUs and GPUs for projects.
Synopsys Tool Advantages
Synopsys tools are designed to take full advantage of cloud infrastructure and offer the
following benefits:
* Run on cloud service providers, including Azure, AWS, GCP, OCI, and HPE
GreenLake.
* Access Pay-Per-Use (PPU) licensing for several products.
* Integrate with hybrid environments and scale compute resources as needed.
* Use cost-saving "Spot" instances with save-restore for long-running tools.
* Receive ongoing improvements in memory and IO optimization.
You can deploy and use Synopsys tools in a Hybrid Cloud environment. This enables
workflows that span both on-premises infrastructure and public cloud resources. For more

Chapter 4: Cloud Enablement for Verdi
Hybrid Cloud

Hybrid Cloud
A hybrid cloud setup lets you use both on-premises and public cloud resources. You can
extend compute capacity to the cloud while keeping access to your existing data and
environments. The hybrid cloud model supports flexible scaling, efficient resource use, and
consistent design flows.
A hybrid cloud setup allows you to run workloads on premises, in the cloud, or across
both, depending on resource availability. This approach helps you meet peak demand,
reduce turnaround time, and follow enterprise IT and security policies.
The two common hybrid cloud configurations are as follows:
* Lift-and-shift: Identify flows or design blocks to run in the cloud environment. Package
the required files, such as design files, scripts, and libraries. Move them to cloud
storage to run tools in the cloud.
* Data-synchronization service: Use a data-synchronization service to keep cloud
storage synchronized with on-premises data. The synchronization ensures data is
available for cloud jobs and that output data, such as logs and reports, is accessible on
premises.
Use the Synopsys Cloud Hybrid Solution for the data-synchronization service. Combine
the Synopsys Cloud Hybrid Solution with Pay-Per-Use licensing for flagship tools. This
option gives you access to many licenses for peak demand. These tools are billed per
minute with no commitment required.
For more information on the Hybrid solution and Pay-Per-Use licensing, visit Synopsys
Cloud Platform.

In earlier versions, Verdi performed design elaboration during runtime. This made loading
large designs slow and used a lot of memory. Now, Verdi can elaborate the design in batch
mode and save the elaboration database to disk. This new method makes loading faster
and uses less memory.
When you use the -kdb option, VCS invokes elabcom to elaborate the design and create
the resolved KDB. If you use the -kdb=common_elab option, VCS uses its common
elaboration engine to generate the resolved KDB in a single step.
You must also use the -kdb=common_elab option with vlogan. This is because vlogan
needs to dump extra files during the analysis stage.

generate the KDB. In case of VCS three-step flow, add the -kdb or -kdb=common_elab

argument with the -kdb/-kdb=common_elab option:
It is not recommended to use the -kdb=only and -kdb=postelab options along
with the VCS -simcopy option.
-kdb=postelab
Tells VCS elaboration process to skip kdb elaboration (running elabcom process) and

Following is the use model:

directory and runs the script directly without generating simulation database. Following is

It is not recommended to use the -kdb=only and -kdb=postelab options along
with the VCS -simcopy option.
-kdb=exec_postelab
VCS finds the -kdb=exec_postelab file in the current working directory and runs the
script directly without generating simulation database.
Following is the use model:
% vcs -kdb=postelab <compile_options> <source files>
% vcs -kdb=exec_postelab <compile_options> <source files>

-kdb=gatesrc
For gate-level designs, you usually rely on schematic view or waveform to debug.
Source codes are seldom used since the gate-netlists are usually generated by tools that
are not human-readable. In previous releases, during compilation, compiler used to spend
huge amount of resource (time/diskspace) dealing with the textDoc.
Following are the results:
* Dumping of textDocs to disk for Gate-Level designs does not happen.
* It is expected that the disk size for KDB would be much smaller (30% ~ 50%)
Following is the use model:
% vlogan -kdb=gatesrc [other options] <design files>

Verdi does not need any additional options while importing the design compiled
with -kdb=gatesrc.
Limitations:
* When a design containing vcs_vip protected content is compiled with the
-kdb=gatesrc option, only the encrypted content within protected blocks is visible.
* The option -kdb=gatesrc is used for gate level designs. If Verdi is launching with RTL
designs compiled with the -kdb=gatesrc option, then most of the nTrace features on
the source window does not work as expected. For example, the features requiring full
source code visibility may be unavailable or the source code bindings may be incorrect.

Using Multiple -kdb Switches
Use Model for Adding With Multiple KDBs

Use Model for Adding With Single KDB Separated by Comma ","

text:
Suppressing Inline PSL Errors During VHDL Compilation
The feature to suppress inline PSL (Property Specification Language) errors during VHDL
compilation addresses compatibility issues between the -kdb and -psl options in the
Unified Front-End (UFE) flow. When both options are used together, you may encounter
an error that blocks compilation. This feature introduces an environment variable to
demote the error to a warning. Compilation can then proceed. However, debugging inline
PSL parts in Verdi remains unsupported.
Benefits
* Enables compilation of VHDL designs with both -kdb and -psl options.
* Prevents job failures caused by the incompatibility of these options.
* Maintains transparency during the VCS elaboration stage.
To enable this feature, perform the following steps:
1. Set the SNPS_VCS_VERDI_IGNORE_PSL environment variable to 1 using the following
setenv SNPS_VCS_VERDI_IGNORE_PSL 1

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
This variable suppresses the error message and converts it into a warning.
2. Run the vhdlan command with both -kdb and -psl options. The environment variable
demotes the error to a warning.
vhdlan -kdb test.vhd -psl

Output
Warning-[KDB-OPT-IG] KDB Option Ignored
Option '-kdb' cannot work together with option '-psl', it is
ignored.
Remove this option and recompile the design.

Optimizing Disk Space Usage in KDB Files
The Knowledge Database (KDB) is a critical component in simulation workflows, storing
essential data for debugging and analysis. However, its size can grow significantly,

consuming excessive disk space. To address this, Verdi introduces a disk space
optimization feature that applies advanced compression techniques to reduce the size of
KDB files under the simv.daidir directory.
Benefits of Disk Space Optimization
* Reduced Disk Usage: Compresses textDoc and data model components, significantly
lowering storage requirements.
* Customizable Compression: Allows you to selectively enable compression for
textDoc and data model using two different options.
Enabling Disk Space Optimization
The disk space optimization is enabled by default. It can be overridden using the compiletime option -kdb=diskopt:<sub-option>, which can be used during the compilation
process. This can be applied in both the 3-step and 2-step compilation flows.
The <sub-option> parameter allows you to control the scope of compression. The
supported sub-options are all and none.
The default behavior is a balanced solution between compile-time overhead and file
space. If you need faster compilation, use -kdb=diskopt:none and if you need smaller
file, use -kdb=diskopt:all options respectively.
Example: 3-Step Compilation Flow
vlogan -kdb=diskopt:all <vlogan_options> <source_files>
vlogan -kdb=diskopt:all <vlogan_options> <source_files>
vcs -kdb=diskopt:all <vcs_options> <top_module>

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
After enabling the feature, the size of the simv.daidir directory should be significantly
reduced. Use standard disk usage commands (for example, du -sh simv.daidir) to
confirm the reduction.
* Backward Compatibility: Older versions of Verdi cannot load KDB files compiled
with compression enabled. Ensure you use the same major release of Verdi for
compatibility.
* Performance Impact: Enabling compression may increase compile, elaboration,
and import times due to the additional CPU effort required for compression and
decompression.
* Language Support: Currently, only Verilog is supported. VHDL and other languages
are supported in future stages.

Making Verdi KDB Elaboration Database Self-Contained Using
-kdb=selfcontained
The -kdb=selfcontained option in VCS helps you create a self-contained Verdi
Knowledge Database (KDB) during the 3-step compilation flow. By default, the KDB
directory contains symbolic links to files in physical libraries outside the KDB directory.
This can cause problems if you want to move or copy the KDB to another location, such
as a different server or cloud storage. Using this option, you can replace these links with
actual files, making the KDB directory fully portable.
To enable the self-contained KDB feature, run VCS with the -kdb=selfcontained option:
1. Make sure you are using the 3-step VCS compilation flow.
2. Ensure your synopsys_sim.setup file correctly maps logical to physical libraries.
3. Use the -kdb=selfcontained option during the VCS elaboration step.
Syntax:
vcs <top_level_module_name> -debug_access -kdb=selfcontained

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
This command creates the KDB elaboration database in simv.daidir/kdb.elab++ with
all required files included, not just symbolic links.

Loading Designs With Different Strategies
When you create a KDB using vcs -kdb, you have several ways to load your design into
Verdi.
To load the entire design, including all hierarchy and instances at once, use this command:
> verdi -dbdir <design.dbdir>

If your design is large or complex and may use a lot of memory, you can use Smart Load.
Smart Load loads only the first level of hierarchy at the start. When you access another
hierarchy, Verdi incrementally loads the hierarchy on demand. This saves time and
resources as they are not touched, so instances do not occupy them. Use this command:
> verdi -dbdir <design.dbdir> -smart_load_kdb

Refer to the -smart_load_kdb option description in the Verdi and Siloti Command
Reference Manual for details.
If you want to focus on specific parts of your design or exclude some modules, use
Preload. Preload lets you load selected scopes first. You can add more scopes later
without reloading everything. Use this command:
> verdi -dbdir <design.dbdir> -preload <preload_cfg_file>

For details, see the -preload option in the Verdi and Siloti Command Reference Manual.

Using Verdi Executable to Import Design From UFE
The Unified Compiler Flow (UFE) uses VCS with the -kdb option and the generated
simv.daidir includes the KDB information.
Verdi supports the following use models to import design from simv.daidir related files:
* "verdi -dbdir simv.daidir"
* "verdi -simBin simv"
* "verdi -ssf novas.fsdb"
The priority to import design from UFE is as following (from high to low):
1. Use the new -dbdir option to specify the simv.daidir directory
Similar to: dve -dbdir simv.daidir
2. Use the -simBin option to specify simv
Load simv.daidir from the same directory as simv and invoke Verdi if simv.daidir
is not available.
3. Use the -ssf option to specify FSDB file and the design is automatically loaded.

-kdb" with VCS K-2015.09-SP2 or later.
The FSDB or all FSDB files in virtual FSDB should be generated by the same
simv that is generated by VCS with the -kdb option. The import options -top,
-elab, -lib, -f, and -ridb cannot be specified for this usage.

The instance_item rule specifies that all the selected instances in the list is loaded.
When the level is 0, Verdi loads the instances recursively to all their sub-instances. When

Verdi takes the first instance in list as the beginning instance.
