The following sections describe the features and usage for the Resource View.

With the addition of the Verdi OVM library, the options available in the Resource
View for UVM are also available for OVM.
The following tasks are included:
* Viewing the Source Code and Accessor
* Applying Quick Filter in the Resource View

Viewing the Source Code and Accessor
Perform the following steps to view the source code of a resource or configuration:
1. Select a resource or configuration name in the Resource View pane, the history of the
corresponding item is displayed in the Access History pane as shown in Figure 37.
2. Click the Show Call in Source Window option in the right-click option menu and
double-click the history in the Access History pane to view the code where the set/get
function is called in the Source Code pane. You can select only one item at a time.
Figure 40

Viewing the History and Source Code

3. To view the accessor class or object of the selected function in the Class Browser
or Object Browser panes, use the Show Accessor in Class Browser or Show
Accessor in Object Browser options in the right-click menu, you can see the line of
the function-called location in the Source Code pane and the accessor of this function
in the Object Browser pane.
4. For virtual interface resources, select an item with the Virtual Interface option in the
Resource View pane and use the Show Source for Virtual Interface option in the
right-click option menu to view the definition code in the Source Code pane.

Verdi allows you to search the register hierarchy tree for a specific register or register field

Register Hierarchy pane.
For information on the usage of Unified Find feature, see the Using Unified Find section
in the Verdi User Guide and Tutorial guide.
Wildcards are supported in the Search text field. The case-sensitivity of the search string
entered in the Search text field depends on the Match case right-click option.
UVM Register View does not support full path search, such as regmodel.SESSION[1] or
regmodel.myclass. You can only search for the name of a register or register field item in
register hierarchy tree. For example, you can search register/field name that contains _ID
by specifying the search string as *_ID.

Displaying Warning Messages for Incomplete Register Hierarchy
The Register Hierarchy pane of the Register View is built by the data recorded in both
interactive and post-processing mode. However, it takes time to record the register
hierarchy data if the hierarchy tree is huge. Therefore, Verdi provides a default maximum
count for the recorded data. If the maximum count is exceeded, the recording process is
stopped. This makes the register hierarchy tree incomplete.
For incomplete register hierarchy, Verdi issues a warning message as follows:
Figure 90

Warning Message for Incomplete Register Hierarchy

The +UVM_REG_DUMP_LIMIT environment variable is used to limit the number of recorded
registers in the register hierarchy. The default value of +UVM_REG_DUMP_LIMIT is 5000.

Following is the use model:
+UVM_REG_DUMP_LIMIT=<number>

If +UVM_REG_DUMP_LIMIT=0, then there is no limitation and all the registers are recorded.

Displaying Register Access Status in the Register View
Verdi displays register access status of a register in the Register Access History pane
of the Register View. The register access status represents the operation result and is
displayed in the Status column of the Register Access History pane.
There are three register access status types:
* UVM_IS_OK
* UVM_NOT_OK
* UVM_HAS_X
The following table describes the status of the register operations:
UVM_IS_OK

Operation completed successfully

UVM_NOT_OK

Operation completed with error

UVM_HAS_X

Operation completed successfully, bit has
unknown bits

Figure 91

Register Access Status in the Register View

Key Points to Note
* If the access history of the selected register has no status information, the Status field
of the register is hidden in the Register Access History pane.
* The UVM_IS_OK status is displayed in black color.
* The UVM_NOT_OK status is displayed in dark red color, and shows the address
(hexadecimal) with it, as shown in the following figure.
* The UVM_HAS_X status is displayed in blue color, and shows the address (hexadecimal)
with it, as shown in the following figure.
Figure 92

Register Access Status Display in Register View

Verdi supports multitasking update in the UVM debug windows. That is, when UVM debug
windows are being updated with data, Verdi allows you to perform other operations without
blocking the GUI.
Verdi supports multitasking update for the following UVM debug windows:
* Register View

GUI Operations for Multitasking Update in UVM Debug Windows
During multitasking update, Verdi displays the Busy/Progressing bar on top right corner
of the view, and shows the Busy icon on the tab, as shown in the following figure.

UVM debug windows can have multiple multitasking updates processing at the same time.
Verdi displays Busy/Progressing bar for each update. You can hover the mouse pointer
on a Busy/Progressing bar to view its information in a tooltip.
Figure 93

GUI to Notify Data Update in UVM Debug Windows

You can click the Drop-down button, as shown in the following figure, to view all the
multitasking updates. You can use the Stop button on each bar to stop each update.
Figure 94

Viewing Busy/Progressing Bar for Each Multitasking Update Task

When a multitasking update is initiated, Verdi clears all the invalid data in the view. If the
data is already available during updating, Verdi performs incremental update of the data in
the view.

If you click the Stop button to stop a multitasking update, Verdi displays Data Incomplete
icon on the title bar of the current pane, as shown in the following figure, to notify that the
data update is incomplete. Also, Verdi displays the bar for UVM windows if the updating
of the data in the view is stopped. You can refresh the view by clicking the Refresh View
icon, as shown in the following figure, to reload or refresh its multitasking update.
Figure 95

Data Incomplete Icon

When a multitasking update is still happening, you can jump to or open another pane to
do other operations. You can see that the Busy icon on the tab is still active as the data
update still happens in the background. This icon disappears once the data update is
completed.
Figure 96

Switching to Another Pane

Applying New Settings for the Current View With multitasking
Update Tasks
You can perform the following operations on the current view with multitasking update
tasks:
* Change preference settings
* Perform right-click operations
* Apply new quick filter settings
When you apply new preference settings, Verdi reloads all the views in UVM aware
windows. If the current view has a multitasking update, Verdi restarts it to upload the new
data to the view.
You can apply new quick filter settings to the current view even when the multitasking
update is happening. When you apply new quick filter settings, Verdi stops the original
multitasking update and triggers a new update to get the new data for the view.
The following sections describe the status of quick filters and right-click options when
multitasking updates are processing data in the UVM Aware windows:
* Register View
* Resource View
* Phase View
* Sequence View

The search functionality is disabled in the Register Hierarchy pane.
For both the Register Attribute and Access History panes, when new quick filter
settings are applied, Verdi stops the current multitasking update task and triggers a new
multitasking update to get the new data for the view.

A register model in a UVM register layer typically contains hierarchy of blocks that map to
the design hierarchy. Register blocks can contain registers, register files, register maps,
memories, and other blocks.
Verdi allows you to debug UVM register information in the post-processing mode using the
UVM Register View. UVM Aware debug refers to the annotation FSBD file when running in
post-processing mode.
This feature allows you to perform the following:
* View the register hierarchy, register attribute values, and access history of an interface
FSDB.
* Add register objects to the waveform.
* Synchronize cursor time between Register View and waveform and display the register
attribute values according to the cursor time. You can also specify cursor time to
display the register attribute values.
* Select a hardware address signal in register map to create address alias table in
the waveform, so that the waveform can display the register alias names to replace
address on the signal.

Dumping UVM Register Information in Post-Processing Mode
This section describes the compile-time and runtime options required to dump the
necessary information for UVM Register View in the post-processing mode.

Dumping Register Hierarchy and Access History Information
For VCS:
Use the -ntb_opts uvm compile-time option to include Verdi UVM library. Following is the
syntax to generate simv with register post-processing data:
% vcs -kdb -sverilog -debug_access+all -ntb_opts uvm -lca filename.sv
%./simv +UVM_VERDI_TRACE=RAL +fsdbfile+<name>.fsdb -l sim.log

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Example:
% vcs -full64 -kdb -sverilog -debug_access+all -ntb_opts uvm -lca
-timescale=1ns/1ns +incdir+./apb +incdir+vip tb_top.sv test.sv
%./simv +UVM_VERDI_TRACE=RAL +fsdbfile+test.fsdb -l sim.log

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
For Third-Party Simulators:
Specify the following include paths for the UVM library:
* -incdir $VERDI_HOME/etc/uvm-1.1/verdi/
* $VERDI_HOME/etc/uvm-1.1/verdi/uvm_custom_install_verdi_recorder.sv
* $VERDI_HOME/etc/uvm-1.1/verdi/dpi/uvm_verdi_dpi.cpp

Dumping Class Objects for Register View Post-Processing in VCS
If you want to add registers to waveform and view both register hierarchy and access
history, use the +UVM_VERDI_TRACE=RALWAVE runtime option to enable register object,
register hierarchy, and register access history recording.
Following is an example to generate object dumping data for Register View postprocessing:
% vcs -kdb -sverilog -debug_access+all -ntb_opts_uvm -lca filename.sv
% ./simv +UVM_VERDI_TRACE=RALWAVE +fsdbfile+test.fsdb -l sim.log

To specify dumping level for UVM component object, you need to specify
+UVM_OBJ_DUMP_LEVEL=N.
The default value of N is 1. If N is specified as 0, all level of objects are dumped.

Simulation Options for Generating FSDB File With Register
Information in Post-Processing Mode
Table 1 shows the runtime options required to generate FSDB file with register information
in the post-processing mode.

Table 1

Runtime Options

+UVM_VERDI_TRACE=RAL

Dumps the register hierarchy and
access history data into the FSDB file.

+UVM_VERDI_TRACE=RALWAVE

Controls whether to load the
configuration file to dump all
register-related object data when
Verdi recorder is used. It also
dumps the register hierarchy and
access history data, so that the
+UVM_VERDI_TRACE=RAL option is not
required if you use this option. This
option is supported only in VCS.

Following is the example for VCS simulator to generate FSDB file with the register
hierarchy and access history data:
% ./simv +UVM_VERDI_TRACE=RAL +fsdbfile+<name>.fsdb -l sim.log

Following is the example for VCS simulator to generate FSDB file with register hierarchy,
register access history, and related object dumping:
% ./simv +UVM_VERDI_TRACE=RALWAVE +fsdbfile+<name>.fsdb -l sim.log

Invoking Verdi in Post-Processing mode
To open UVM Register View in post-processing mode, invoke Verdi with an FSDB file.
Following is the VCS example to run Verdi by importing the design and loading the FSDB
file:
% verdi -ssf <filename>.fsdb

Updating Register Attribute Values According to the Cursor Time
or Selected Access History in Post-Processing Mode
You can double-click an item in the Access History pane to set the cursor time as the
access time in the Time text box. Also, you can specify a valid cursor time in the Time text
box. When the cursor time is set, the Register Attribute pane updates the values according
to the cursor time.
This feature is supported for VCS and third party simulators in post-processing mode.
To view the attribute values of a specific access time:
Specify valid cursor time in the Time text box and press Enter. The default cursor time is 0.
Or,
Double-click an item in the Access History pane.
The values in the Register Attribute pane are updated according to the new cursor time, as
shown in Figure 100.
You can change the cursor time in the Time text box. If the time specified in the Time
text box does not match the time in the Access History pane, then Verdi searches for the
register with the time nearest to the time specified in the Time text box and displays its
values in the Register Attribute pane.
For example, in the following figure, if you enter time 3000 in the Time text box, the
Register Attribute pane displays the data of the register with time 2950.

Figure 100

Specifying Cursor Time in the Register View

Synchronizing Time Between nWave and Register View in
Post-Processing Mode
Verdi supports time synchronization between the Register View and the nWave in postprocessing mode.
If you select View-> Sync Time with Waveform option, you can synchronize time with the
nWave either by double-clicking an item in the Access History pane or by specifying cursor
time in Time text box as shown in Figure 101.
Also, any cursor time change in the nWave applies to the Register View, and the values of
the Register Attribute pane are updated according to the new cursor time.
This feature is supported for VCS and third-party simulators in post-processing mode.

Figure 101

Synchronizing Time Between nWave and Register View

Adding Register Items to the Waveform
You can use the Add to Waveform right-click option in the Register Hierarchy pane and
Register Attribute pane, as shown in Figure 102, to add register objects into any existing
or a new waveform.
Figure 102

Add to Waveform

If you select Add to Waveform option in the Trace menu, Verdi considers the items
selected in the Register Attribute pane.

Table 2 describes the operations of the Add to Waveform option for different types of
register objects.
Table 2

Operation of Add to Waveform Option for Register Objects

Register Type

Operation

Register Block/File

All register fields under the selected block/file
are added to the nWave.

Register

All register fields of the selected register are
added to the nWave.

Register Field

Only the selected register field are added to
the nWave.

Memory

The menu item should be disabled.

Register Map

The menu item should be disabled.

Array of
Registers/Blocks/Files

A dialog box should appear and allow you
to specify the ranges of the array. Only the
fields of the selected ranges are added to the
nWave.

Key Point to Note
If you perform Add to Waveform for a register object, the waveform displays the value
changes of the object being dumped.
For example, if the class uvm_reg_field is as follows:
class uvm_reg_field extends uvm_object;
rand uvm_reg_data_t value; // Mirrored after randomize()
local uvm_reg_data_t m_mirrored; // Present in the HW
local uvm_reg_data_t m_desired; // Mirrored after set()

When you perform Add to Waveform, the waveform displays the value changes of
variables value, m_desired and m_mirrored.
However, the value on Register View indicates the value when the register operation read,
write, peek, or poke is performed. The nature of values on the waveform and Register
View are different. It is inadequate to compare these values.

Adding Address Alias Table to nWave
You can use the Add Alias Table to Waveform right-click option in the Register Hierarchy
pane to add address alias table from Register View to any existing or a new nWave
window.
Perform the following steps to add address alias table to the nWave:

to Waveform right-click option.

Save/Restore Session Support for the Register View in
Post-Processing Mode
In post-processing mode, you can use the File -> Save Session command to save the
current debugging session, including the UVM Register View.
In the Register View, the following items are restored as they were before the save
session:
* Register View pane layout (Register Hierarchy/Register Attribute/Register Access
History pane on or off)
* Register hierarchy data and selected items if exist
* Register attribute data and selected items if exist

* Register access history of the selected register data and selected items if exist
* Quick Filter on/off status, the values inside it and the status of check boxes
* If you have performed the radix display change on some signals before save session,
those are restored too.

You can dump UVM component waveforms into FSDB using the Verdi UVM library. Verdi
Dynamic Object Dumping technology is used to enable the dumping. In addition, the UVM
component hierarchy is dumped as well.
You can use the Verdi OVM/UVM Hierarchy View to display the testbench hierarchy. You
can also choose a UVM component waveform and add it to nWave from the OVM/UVM
Hierarchy View.

Dumping UVM Component Waveforms
This section describes how you can enable UVM component waveform dumping during
the simulation and then how you can view this waveform in nWave in the following steps:
1. Use the UVM library shipped with either Verdi or VCS starting with 2015.09-SP2
release and later. If you do not want to use any extra UVM file options, use the ntb_opts option.
2. Add the -debug_access+all option at VCS compile command line before running
simulation for component object dumping.
3. Enable FSDB dumping either using the $fsdbDumpvars system task or the dump UCLI
command. Note that this step is optional.
4. Add the runtime option +UVM_VERDI_TRACE=COMPWAVE. You can stack this option on
other +UVM_VERDI_TRACE options. Since component waveform is triggered from OVM/
UVM Dynamic Hierarchy Tree, the +UVM_VERDI_TRACE=COMPWAVE option enables
+UVM_VERDI_TRACE=HIER also.
5. Launch Verdi.
The following is a sample Makefile:
all:
comp run verdi_pp
comp:
% vcs -full64 -sverilog -ntb_opts uvm \ +incdir+../sv -debug_access+all
-kdb ubus_tb_top.sv -l compile.log
run:
% simv -l vcs.log +UVM_TESTNAME=test_read_modify_write
+UVM_VERDI_TRACE=COMPWAVE
verdi_pp:
% verdi -simBin ./simv -ssf novas.fsdb -nologo

Limitations

This feature functions under the following limitations:
* Only VCS simulator is supported.
* Only uvm_component and uvm_port_base classes and classes extended from them
are supported.
* The following data types are not supported:
Char var
Dynamic array (Including queue, associate array)
* Only one level of members of the class is dumped. For example, the members of class
of uvm_component is not displayed in nWave.

Practice
The following practice example illustrates the following:
* How to generate the FSDB file that includes the Testbench Hierarchy Tree information,
and how to load this dynamic data into the Verdi platform for viewing the hierarchy and
the connection information.
* View the detailed call-stacks of this dynamic information.
* Correlate the dynamic recorded information with the source code.
* Understand the source of testbench objects generation from the source code.
The practice example uses the OVM UART example located in the $VERDI_HOME/share/
vmlib/ovm/ovm/lib/examples/ uart16550 directory. It demonstrates the use of the
Testbench Hierarchy tree to debug the connection of a port.
1. Copy the case to your local directory.
%> cp -r $VERDI_HOME/share/vmlib/ovm/ovm/lib/ .

2. Change directory to sv_latest.
%> cd lib/examples/uart16550/verif/testbench/sv_latest

3. Setup the environment variable for this practice.
%> setenv VERDI_HOME <Verdi_Install_Directory>
%> setenv OVM_HOME $VERDI_HOME/share/vmlib/ovm/ovm/lib

a. Setup the variable for your simulation machine:

b. Open the run_vcs file, modify the SNPSLMD_LICENSE_FILE and VCS_HOME variables
to match your simulation path.

Known Issues and Limitations
UVM Debug Limitations
The following known issues and limitations exist in the UVM Debug feature:
* Inactive sequence data (that is, data which is no longer inside the simulator) is
available only when the UVM default recorder is replaced by the Verdi recorder.
* A performance issue exists when retrieving sequence data from the simulator.
* Drag-and-drop operations are not supported.
* Time synchronization with other windows is not supported.
* The transaction data unrelated to sequence data may be displayed in the Sequence
View pane. You can add a stream attribute preventing this transaction data from being
displayed in the Sequence View pane.
* With Verdi 2013.09, if you let the simulator run to the end of simulation, the simulator
quits and the Verdi platform exits the interactive mode. At this time, simulator data is
not available. This is addressed starting Verdi 2014.03 release onwards.
* The number of phases is fixed for the usage of VMM/OVM libraries.
* Although the Sequence View pane is supported for OVM/UVM libraries, the menu and
the window is not disabled in VMM.
* For OVM recording flow, Verdi recorder may not record some parent-child relations.
As a result, the relations of these events are retrieved from the simulator. However, if
the simulation stops after these relations are cleared from simulator, the Verdi platform
cannot retrieve these relations.
* Virtual registers and memory management models are currently not supported.
* An array of registers in the hierarchy tree is either completely expanded or completely
collapsed. Partial array expansion in the hierarchy tree is not supported.

Chapter 6: Known Issues and Limitations
UVM Register View Debug in Post-Processing Mode: Limitations

* If two defined registers are referencing the same register object, only one register is
displayed on the hierarchy tree.
* If the history of configurations/resources cannot be retrieved from the FSDB, the
content of the history in the Resource History pane does not match the content of the
configuration/resource in the Resource pane.

UVM Register View Debug in Post-Processing Mode: Limitations
The following known issues and limitations exist in the UVM Register View debug in postprocessing mode feature:
* The Register View in interactive mode is supported in VCS only. The Register View in
post-processing mode is supported with VCS and third-party simulators.
* Since the object dumping is only supported in VCS, the Add to Waveform option is not
supported in third-party simulators. This option is not supported without the complete
register object dumping. To enable object dumping into FSDB file, you must use the
+UVM_VERDI_TRACE=RALWAVE VCS runtime option. You must also include Verdi UVM
library and recorder while compiling.
* The register memory may be big in size, so array or hierarchy view for memory items
are not created. Currently, the access history of the memory item are listed, but the
attribute values in any specific time for register or field data in memory type are not
updated.
* The register declaration name is available only in the interactive mode.
-> Register View option in the toolbar is available in the post* The UVM icon
processing mode if the FSDB file is loaded. However, if the design without the FSDB
file is imported, then this option is not available.
* Register View does not support virtual FSDB file.
* Verdi does not support "set" and "get" actions of a register from UVM post-processing
mode. Therefore, the desired and mirrored values are used only for reference.
* Register View in post-processing mode does not support time range access.
* If you write data to register field, UVM does not display the message with complete
information. Therefore, you cannot view the register field action in the Register View.
If you turn on the UVM compiler directive UVM_REG_NO_INDIVIDUAL_FIELD_ACCESS, the
register field action is reflected to register, so that you can view the register action in the
register Access History pane.

Chapter 6: Known Issues and Limitations
Testbench Hierarchy Limitations

Testbench Hierarchy Limitations
* For IUS, the call stack cannot be displayed. You can see only a single call in the callstack on the Creation and Connection tabs.
* For MTI, the Testbench Hierarchy tree is not supported.

This book is a reference manual for the VC Apps Help and provides detailed descriptions
and application example for each App. For advanced use of the Native Programming
Interface (NPI), refer to VC Apps - Verdi Native Programming Interface (NPI) manual and

Audience
The audience for this manual includes engineers who are familiar with languages and
tools used in design and verification such as Verilog, VHDL, and SystemVerilog.
This document assumes that you have a basic knowledge of the Verdi debug platform and
also the platform on which your version of the Verdi platform runs: UNIX or Linux and that
you are knowledgeable in C/C++ and Tcl.

Using Verdi Executable to Import Design from UFE
The Unified Compiler Flow (UFE) uses VCS with the -kdb option and the generated
simv.daidir includes the KDB information. Verdi supports the following use models to
import design from simv.daidir related files:
* verdi -dbdir simv.daidir
* verdi -simBin simv
* verdi -ssf novas.fsdb

Introduction
Commonly used VC Apps are pre-packaged in the installation package of the Verdi
platform. User can access these VC Apps from VC Apps Toolbox area from the GUI of
the Verdi Automated Debug Platform. The VC Apps in VC Apps Toolbox are developed
and tested by Synopsys. User can also access the original source code of some Apps in
the Toolbox and customize to fit different requirements. VC Apps toolbox also provides
flexibility that allow user to add in-house tools into VC Apps Toolbox and share within
design team by leveraging the manage.rc mechanism.
* VC Apps Overview

VC Apps Overview
VC Apps includes the following categories:
* Design Exploration
* Design Validation
* FSDB Investigation
* Utility
* Advanced VC Apps
The following sections provide the overview of these categories.
* Design Exploration
* Design Validation
* FSDB Investigation
* Utility
* Advanced VC Apps

Chapter 1: Introduction
VC Apps Overview

VC Apps in this category help users traverse design information from the Verdi Knowledge
Database (KDB).
They output the traversed information into a specific format for other purposes.
Refer to the Design Explorationchapter for details.

Design Validation
VC Apps in this category help users traverse design information from the Verdi Knowledge
Database (KDB).
They check whether the traversed information meets certain design rules.
Refer to the chapter for details Design Validation.

VC Apps in this category help users traverse information from Verdi Fast Signal Database
(FSDB).
They output the result into a specific format.
Refer to the chapter for details FSDB Investigation.

Utility
Apps in this category are Synopsys tools provided to help users leverage information in
Verdi for various purposes.
The utilities come in binary format. You cannot access the original source code of the
utilities.
Refer to the chapter for details Utility.

Advanced VC Apps
Advanced VC Apps includes advanced apps for Design Manipulation, Design Exploration,
and FSDB Investigation.
The advanced VC Apps are available in Verdi Apex mode.

Overview
The VC Apps Toolbox is an interface to execute VC applications (VC Apps) from the GUI
of the Verdi(R) Automated Debug Platform.
VC Apps are provided by Synopsys personnel. They are based on commonly used Verdi
NPI (Native Programming Interface) scripts and Verdi Tcl commands.
The VC Apps Toolbox further enriches the Verdi feature set with automated and
customized toolkits.
Examples include traversing the design or investigating an FSDB file in a fast and efficient
way.
Users can additionally use the toolkits to create customized applications on demand.
The VC Apps Toolbox mechanism includes the following features:
* Gives a platform to execute and organize VC Apps.
* Provides a general GUI Input Form to input the value of arguments.
* Supports specification of the output file and rule file to be opened by the SmartLog after
execution.
* Creates customized applications.
* Updates the latest VC Apps without re downloading.

This VC Apps Toolbox includes many NPI scripts.
The user interface to manage these scripts can be invoked from the Verdi platform's main
window.
The following sections describe how to invoke the VC Apps Toolbox and how to use the
features in the VC Apps Toolbox form.
Usage contains the following topics:
* Invoke the VC Apps Toolbox
* Manage Applications
* Execute Applications
* Find Applications
* Configure Applications
* Access Application Source Files
* Add Applications and Folders
* Get Help for Applications
* Update Applications

Invoke the VC Apps Toolbox
After invoking the Verdi platform, the VC Apps Toolbox icon appears in the upper right
corner of the main window.
Figure 1

VC Apps Toolbox Icon

Clicking the VC Apps Toolbox icon opens the VC Apps Toolbox form. This form can be
used to manage and execute all VC Apps. As shown below, the VC Apps Toolbox form is

composed of the Applications List View pane, Directory Path field, Find Tool field and the
Apps Organization icon by default.
Figure 2

VC Apps Toolbox Form

You can use the Find Tool field to locate VC Apps. The Directory Path field shows
the current directory path. The Applications List View pane displays all the folders and
Applications belonging to the current directory. Each VC App has its own unique icon.
In the Utility directory, there is a SmartLog application that can show the results of the VC
Apps execution with different rules.

Figure 3

Utility Directory

The details of the SmartLog frame is out of the scope of this document.

Manage Applications
Currently, VC Apps are categorized in the following folders: Design Exploration, Design
Manipulation, Design Validation, FSDB Investigation, and Utility. Double-clicking the
folder in the VC Apps Toolbox form pushes the view into the folder where all VC Apps
belonging to this folder are displayed.

Manipulation, Design Validation, FSDB Investigation, and Utility. Double-clicking the
folder in the VC Apps Toolbox form pushes the view into the folder where all VC Apps
belonging to this folder are displayed. Clicking the Apps Organization icon in the upper
left opens the hierarchy browser to view the organization of all VC Apps.

You can change the content of the folder by dragging and dropping the script to another

folder), and then drop the object by releasing the mouse button until the preview border
becomes a line under the required location. You can drag and drop objects from the main
window to the hierarchy browser, or move the objects from a location in the hierarchy
browser to another location in the same hierarchy browser.
You can delete folders and applications using the Delete command in the right-click
command menu.

generic Input form might be opened for users to input additional information, for example,

Configure Applications
Most VC Apps in the VC Apps Toolbox are open sourced, so the configuration of each
application can be modified. In the Applications List View pane of the VC Apps Toolbox

form, select a VC App icon and use the Config command in the right-click command
menu to open the Config App form. The following figure shows an example of the Config
App form from the Get Module Hierarchy App.
Figure 11

Config App Form

In this form, you can change the display name, file location, and icon in the following fields:
* Display Name: Specify the display name to be shown in the VC Apps Toolbox form
and as the naming for the Input form. In a directory, applications or folders with the
same display names are not allowed.
* Path: Specify the reference path to the location of the files. The recommendation is to
put all relative files into one directory.
* File Name: Specify the Tcl file for execution. All Tcl commands should be wrapped in
"proc".
* Help File: Specify the HTML file as the manual.
* Icon: Specify the icons to be shown in the VC Apps Toolbox form. The supported types
are *.bmp, *.gif, *.ico, *.jpeg, *.jpg. *.mng, *.pbm, *.pgm, *.png, *.ppm, *.svg, *.tif,
*.tiff, *.xbm, and *.xpm. The recommendation is to use the square icon with pixel
50x50 and bigger.

Click the OK button to apply the updated configuration.
If you are familiar with Tcl, you can even modify the Tcl script and then modify the
argument settings for the main procedure in the Arguments table. If the Arguments
table is empty, the execution application does not have an Input form. The following fields
compose the procedure:
* Argument Prompt: Specify the argument prompt in the Input form.
* Default Value: Specify the default value of the argument after displaying the Input
form. Refer to the Set Default Value for the Argument section for details.
* Browser Type: Specify the type of browser to invoke after clicking the
button in the
Input form. Specify each browser type in each Browser Type field. After executing the
App, the argument have a
button to select the content if the Browser Type field is
not None. You can see the corresponding browser after clicking each button.
Figure 12

Browser Types

* Display Log: Specify the argument as the output file that is opened in the SmartLog
frame after the App is executed.
* Log Rule: Specify the log rule file that is used by the SmartLog frame.

bracket characters. The command is executed by the Tcl interpreter and the return
value is obtained after invoking the Input form.
* Fixed default value: Specify a fixed value without the "[]" bracket characters.

menu. When double-clicking an App in the VC Apps Toolbox form, the Verdi platform
sources the Tcl script file and then call the specified procedure name to execute your

b. Relative path from current working directory
c. The Verdi installation path

and path in this field.
* Icon: You can click the arrow in the Icon field to specify the default icon, or click the
Browse button to select your own icon.

It gets the equivalent signals from the specified signals.

This App traces connectivities of the specified signals. The tracing passes through the
module ports and stops at the primitive cells. In the output file, for every input signal, it
reports the equivalent signals. The output file can be in the following formats:
* Default: A general log file with full hierarchical name.
* Elfile: An exclusion file, which can be loaded by VerdiCoverage or URG to exclude the
signals.
* Hier: A hierarchical configuration file, which can be used by VCS (-cm_hier
<hier_config_file>) to exclude the signals during the compile phase.
When the format is default, the tracing does not pass through the assignment
cell; it treats assignment cell as the primitive cell.
For example, for a given signal top.A.C.po, if the format is elfile or hier, this App passes
through the assignment, and the equivalent signals are top.A.po, top.A.H.po, top.w1,
top.G.pi, top.G.po, top.w2, top.B.pi1, top.B.D.pi1, top.B.D.E.p1, top.B.D.F.pi, top.B.D.F.po,
top.B.D.w, top.B.D.E.p2, top.B.pi2, top.B.D.pi2, and top.B.D.E.p3.

If the format is default, this App does not pass through the assignment. Thus, the
equivalent signals are top.A.po, top.A.H.po, top.w1, top.G.pi, top.B.pi, top.B.D.pi1,
top.B.D.F.pi, and top.B.D.E.p1.

The signal can be provided either by single full hierarchical name or full hierarchical
names listed in a file.
The other available options to filter the result or to control the tracing scopes are as
follows:
1. Report Port Signal: It only shows the equivalent signals representing a port.
In the previous example, top.w1 is an internal wire and is not shown when this option
is on.
2. Target Inst List: It specifies the file name, which contains the instance hierarchical
name per line, that filters the result to signals under the specified instances. Wildcard
for the last hierarchy like "top.B.D.*" is supported. It means all instances under top.B.D
are supported.
In the previous example, if the target instances are top.A and top.B.D.*, the result is
signals under top.A, top.B.D.E, and top.B.D.F, which are top.A.po, top.D.E.p1, and
top.D.F.pi.

3. Limit Trace Scope: It does limited tracing only under scopes of instances in the Target
Inst List.
In the previous example, the target instances are top.A and top.B.D.*, and theLimit Trace
Scope is set to on. The limited passing instances are top, top.A, top.B, top.B.D, top.B.D.E,
and top.B.D.F. This reduces the tracing effort in top.A.H and top.G, as the result remains
the same, which is top.A.po, top.D.E.p1, and top.D.F.pi.

Get the fanIn registers information of a specified signals.
This App traces the fan-in of the specified signals under a specified top scope. The tracing
stops at the registers and primary ports of the top scope. In the output file, for every

input signal, it reports information of the traced registers and ports. And for each register
instance, it also includes the information of its ports along with the role.
For example, by given signal and given top scope, the tracing does not cross through the
given top scope boundary. Thus, only the registers A and B (the blue ones) are listed in
the output log. If the user specifies the option to report primary ports, then the output port
of the given top scope (the blue port) is also listed.

The signal can be provided either by single full hierarchical name, or full hierarchical
names listed in a file.
If the top scope is not specified, the App reports all registers traced in the design, and by
default, it does not report the primary ports.
When symbol library is imported, it is suggested to add the option -use_symbol_lib.

This app does not support gate-level design that nSchema cannot recognize flip-flop or
other register type cells.

Get the fanOut registers information of the specified signals.
This App traces the fan-out of the specified signals under a specified top scope. The
tracing stops at registers and primary ports of the top scope. In the output file, for every
input signal, it reports information of the traced registers and ports. And for each register
instance, it includes the information of its ports along with the role.
For example, for the given signal and given top scope, the tracing does not cross through
the given top scope boundary. Thus, only the registers A and B (the blue ones) are listed
in the output log. If you specify the option to report the primary ports, then the output port
of the given top scope (the blue port) is also listed.

The signal can be provided either by single full hierarchical name or full hierarchical
names listed in a file.
If the top scope is not specified, the App reports all registers traced in the design, and by
default, it does not report the primary ports.
When symbol library is imported, it is suggested to add the option -use_symbol_lib.

This app does not support gate-level design that nSchema cannot recognize flip-flop or
other register type cells.

1. Open Verdi with design, select Tools > VC Apps Toolbox. Otherwise, you can click
the VC Apps Toolbox icon directly.

2. Go to Design Exploration.
3. Click Get FanOut Register icon.

Input Type: Specify the input type, Name or File.
Signals: Specify the signal full hierarchical name or file name according toInput
Type.

Top Scope: Specify the top scope full hierarchical name, which cannot be
traversed.
Report Port: Specify whether to list the primary ports of top scope traced in the
result.
Show Scope Module Name: Specify whether to show the scope module name of
the register in the result.
Mark Driven Port: Specify whether to mark the driven port in the result.
Show Connected Net: Specify whether to show the register connected net in the
report.
Use Symbol Library: Specify whether symbol library is imported.

getModParam.tcl

get_mod_param_main { target_scope target_scope_file depth modules modules_file
output_log {mode "default"} {dump_is_local "FALSE"} }

target_scope:
(Optional) Specify full name of target scope or a list of scopes.
If both target_scope and target_scope_file are not specified, all module instances are
handled.
target_scope_file:
(Optional) A file contains the list of target scopes.
If both target_scope and target_scope_file are not specified, all module instances are
handled.
depth:
(Optional) Specify depth to traverse.
If not specified or specifying 0, traverse without depth limitation.
modules:
(Optional) Specify the module name; default is empty string.
The name can be specified by exact one or wildcard.
The name can be module hierarchy name or module definition name.
If both modules and modules_file are not specified, all modules are handled.
Use space to specify more than one module; for example,
"system.i_cpu ALU PC* system.i_cpu.i_*.reg*"

modules_file:
(Optional) A file contains the list of modules.
If both modules and modules_file are not specified, all modules are handled.
mode:
Specify the mode, "default", "local", "type", or "other".
* default: Dump all kinds of parameters.
* local: Only dump local parameters.

* type: Only dump type parameters.
* other: Only dump non-local and non-type parameters.
dump_is_local:
Specify whether to dump parameters with local information.

Lists detail parameter information of specified scopes and NPI types.

The List Scope Parameter VC App reports detail parameter information, including
decompile string, final value, and default value.
1. Decompile: The RHS string of parameter definition.
2. Final Value: The parameter value after evaluating parameter assignment and
defparam.
3. Default Value: The RHS value of parameter definition.
The output format can be:
* default: General readable log file.
* XML: XML format file.
This VC App calculates parameter value if it is an operation, such as "1+2+3".

Report in default format:

"List Scope Parameter" also supports aggressive options to retrieve parameter information
such as target scope, depth, a list of NPI type, and mode.
You can specify a target scope to be traverse. If the target scope is not specified, the VC
App traverses design from root.
The option "depth" is accompanied by the target scope. depth is used to assign the
hierarchy to be traversed. If depth is not specified, the VC App traverses the whole design
without level limitation.
The VC App also provides support to report parameter within specified NPI types. For
example, you can specify "npiModule npiInterface" as the target NPI types, thus the VC
App only reports parameters under modules and interfaces. If the option is not specified,
the VC APP reports parameters in all possible scopes.
The option "mode" can be:
* default: Dump all kinds of parameters.
* local: Only dump local parameters.
* type: Only dump type parameters.
* other: Only dump non-local and non-type parameters.
To dump parameters with local information, add the option "-dump_is_local" or set "Report
Local Info" as TRUE.

To use the App in the Verdi GUI mode, perform the following steps:
1. Open Verdi with design, select Tools -> VC Apps Toolbox.

2. Go to Design Exploration, and click the List Scope Parameter icon.

3. Fill in the arguments:

Target Scope: The target scope to get parameters. If scope is not specified,
traverse from root.
Depth (Optional): Level to be traversed from the target scope. If depth is not
specified, traverse whole design without level limitation.
Target NPI Type (Optional): Only report parameters within target NPI types, for
example, npiModule, npiInterface. If NPI type is not specified, report parameters
within all possible scope types.
Output Log (Optional): Specify the output log file name. Default log name
islistScopeParam.log.
Output Format: Specify the output file format, "default", or "XML".
Mode: Specify the mode, "default", "local", "type", or "other".
Report Local Info: Specify whether to dump parameters with local information.

4. The output log reports the list of parameter value.

The following section describes the Signal Search:

Signal Search

1. a list of keywords separated by blanks,
For example, "TEST.TOP.CPU data rst".
2. target scope,
can be full hierarchical name or partial name
can be multiple scopes separated by blanks
empty string means the search of all design scopes

4. output log file name
* Report the signal's full hierarchical name which matches ALL the keywords; and those
signals should belong to ONE of the specified target scopes
* The search be case insensitive

proc signal_search_main { search_rule keyword_list target_scope output_log }

search_rule:

keyword_list:
A list of keywords; use spaces for multiple keywords. For example, "CPU data rst".

Signal Search

target_scope:
Specify the target scopes; the scope can be a complete string or a keyword with the
search rule; use spaces for multiple scopes. For example, "TEST.TOP.CPU TOP2".

Detect Dangling Port

Detect Dangling Port

This App detects dangling port which is connected to the specified module instance.
For example, by given module "tb.dd", you can find port "tb.dd.sk" is connected to
"tb.rr.sk". However, there is no load for "tb.rr.sk", which can be seen as dangling.
Therefore, it is defined that the port "tb.dd.sk" is "left dangling" at "tb.rr.sk". Although
"tb.dd.sk" seems having connections to other modules, but it is actually dangling at some
point. This App can help you find the dangling port and the dangling point.
On the other hand, "tb.rr.rk" is connected to a net "temp_rk" by assignment. Even the net
"temp_rk" is floating at its load, "tb.dd.rk" is not left dangling. If you want to treat a port,
with assignment connections to all floating nets, as dangling, set "Report port with floating
net" to True, or -float in perl.

None

Full Name
Hierarchy Manipulation

HierMan App is designed for users to change the design hierarchy and make all the
necessary modifications automatically.
For example, you can "group" several instances in the design and create a new scope for
them, or just "move" an existing instance from the current position to a specific scope.
Instead of making lots of modifications in the design source code manually, HierMan
handles all connection changes and make the necessary modifications in the design.
With this application, you can put more effort on planning the hierarchy and eliminate the
tedious and error prone modifications of all necessary changes in the design source code.

X Rectify

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Sometimes RTL IP contain "X" assignments in the development and simulation phase and
the "X" assignment might cause non-deterministic synthesized logic (0 or 1). Therefore,
using X rectify, an additional step is added before synthesis to remove explicit "X"
assignments and force them to a specific "0" or "1" value. Removal of "X" assignments
enables a deterministic synthesized logic that is compatible over multiple product
generations
Following is an RTL X Rectification Flow:

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
Syntax
npiXRectify <verdi_import_design_options> \
-default_value <0|1> \
-attribute "<attr>*" \
-skip "<filename>*" \
-af <attribute list filename> \
-sf <skip file list filename> \
-dir <target directory> \
-macro_restore_off \

-file_flatten_view \

Examples
To rectify x to 0, use the following option:
%> npiXRectify -dbdir ./simv.daidir -default_value 0

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
To rectify x to 0, while attribute my_attr follows the value to rectify x, use the following
option:
%> npiXRectify -dbdir ./simv.daidir -default_value 0 -attribute "my_attr"

To rectify multiple attributes, use the following option:
%> npiXRectify -dbdir ./simv.daidir -default_value 0 -attribute "my_attr1
my_attr2"

To rectify x to 0, while skip some files use the following option:
%> npiXRectify -f run.f -default_value 0 -attribute "my_attr1 my_attr2"
-skip "sub1.sv sub2.sv"

To write out the generated rectification files in directory out_dir with flatten view, use the
following option:
%> npiXRectify -dbdir ./simv.daidir -default_value 0 -dir out_dir
-file_flatten_view

To use a file attr_file.txt to list all attributes (one attribute per line), and to use a file
skip_file.txt to list all skip files (one file name per line), use the following option:
%> npiXRectify -dbdir ./simv.daidir -default_value 0 -af attr_file.txt
-sf skip_file.txt

Report Moving Average is an app for power profiling. The input file configuration options
are as follows:
* -fsdb power_fsdb/vf files
* -s signal_list
* -bt time
This is optional. It is default as fsdb's begin.
* -et time
This is optional. It is default as fsdb's end
* -ave_size <moving_average_window_size with timeunit>
* -ave_offset <time specifies the sliding delta> This is optional. Default as
10% of theave_size.
* -ave_dump_fsdb
This is optional. By default, this option is off.
* -slope_window <slope_window_size>
This is optional. Default is same as ave_offset.
* -threshold_slope <threshold of absolute slope value>
This is optional. It is default to disable max absolute slope searching. Set 0 to show all
data
* -threshold_peak <threshold of peak value> This is optional. Default is to disable
peak searching. Set 0 to show all data
* -show_top_data <number>
This is optional, The default value is 10. Set 0 to show all data with ranking.
* -o filename
This is optional. Default as <filename>.peak.log and<filename>.slope.log
The output files are as follows:
* <moving average output>.fsdb
* <filename>.slope.log
* <filename>.peak.log

Verdi supports a FSDB/Waveform utility tool called WaveCheck. It enables automatic
waveform checking according to users' requirements.
Starting with this release, Verdi provides a quick and easy way to check analog and digital
values of MSV (Mix Signal Verification) simulations.
You can do this without collateral modifications by using the WaveCheck utility.

WaveCheck also has a Graphical User Interface (GUI) to analyze and review checker
passes and failures. For faster analysis and debugging, it interfaces with Verdi's Waveform
viewer to:
* Draw the signals involved in the checker failure.
* Highlight the time and values of each failure.
Figure 40

WaveCheck Architecture

* WaveCheck Entry
* Checker Command Keywords
* GUI
* Example
* Limitations

WaveCheck Entry
To enable and use WaveCheck in Verdi, you need at least 2023.12-SP1 version and set
up following environment variables:

Environment
WaveCheck needs a minimum environment to run. In addition, these environment
variables are required to be set:
* VERDI_HOME
* SNPSLMD_LICENSE_FILE: Needs to point to a valid Synopsys license server for Verdi,
and requires VERDI APEX LICENSE.
* Entry for WaveCheck is in the folder: $VERDI_HOME/share/VIA/Apps/Bin

WaveCheck Usage
WaveCheck <input_name>|[-in <input_name>]
[-outdir <dir>] [-out <output_report>] [-log
<output_log>] [-show_full_path]
[-show_fsdb_name] [-nogui] [-help]

* <input_name>|[-in <input_name>]: input_name, it can be a checker file name or a
report folder's name. WaveCheck verifies user-defined checkers, if the input is a file or
invoke the GUI with previous results from the report folder.
* [-outdir <outdir>]: Specifies that outdir holds output and log files. Defaults to the
folder "waveCheckReport"
* [-out <output_report>]: Defaults to "wavecheck.rpt" in $outdir.
* [-log <output_log>]: Defaults to "wavecheck.log" in $outdir.
* [-show_full_path]: Shows signal full name in GUI. Defaults to only leaf signal
name.
* [-show_fsdb_name]: Shows waveform-defined names before signal names in GUI.
Defaults to off.
* [-nogui]: Runs WaveCheck without invoking GUI to view results.
* [-help]: Gets the usage message.

Entry in ToolBox
1. Open Verdi, select Tools ==> VC Apps Toolbox; or click VC Apps Toolbox icon
directly.

2. Go to Fsdb Investigation, click WaveCheck icon.

WaveCheck dialog box appears

3. Click Run Checkers to run a checker script file, or click Load Report to reload an
existing report.

Entry in Batch Mode
$VERDI_HOME/share/VIA/Apps/Bin/WaveCheck

/> WaveCheck <checker file>

Required input for different scenarios:
* Execute checkers and show the report on GUI.
$waveCheck <checker file>

* Execute checkers without showing the report on GUI
$waveCheck <checker file> -nogui

* Display the existing report on GUI
$waveCheck <report directory>
#<checker file>:The file contains the user-defined checkers to be verified on a given

waveform files that are also specified inside.

#<report directory>:The report folder is the output folder that is produced by the

previous execution of WaveCheck.

Setting Command

fsdb
Syntax: fsdb [logical_fsdb_name] <path_to_fsdb>
The command is used to establish the mapping between the <logical_fsdb_name> to the
waveform file.
The <logical_fsdb_name> is used as prefix of a signal, indicating the signal's source.
This allows WaveCheck to identify and analyze the targeted waveform.
A checker file must contain at least one fsdb specification command. Each
<logical_fsdb_name> within the file should be unique to avoid conflicts.
If a <logical_fsdb_name> is not explicitly provided, it is default set to "dflt". If a
<logical_fsdb_name> is duplicated, the subsequent command is disregarded.

fsdb
novas.fsdb
// the default fsdb file, has an
implicit label of "dflt".
fsdb ref
/folder/novas.fsdb
fsdb xa
xa.fsdb
fsdb no2
novas.fsdb
fsdb dflt dflt.fsdb
// Error, same logical_fsdb_name dflt
fsdb no2
novas.fsdb
fsdb no2
novas.fsdb
// Error, same logical_fsdb_name no2
checker -name check1 -signal ref:soc.addr
// signal fullname
"soc.addr" in the waveform(fsdb) "ref"
checker -name checkme -signal topdesign1.foo // signal fullname
"topdesign1.foo" in the dflt waveform(fsdb)

display
Syntax: display [-fsdb_names] [-full_paths]
The optional display command controls three options in the output file and the default GUI
display.
* [-fsdb_names]
Print the fsdb names in front of the signals, default set as off.
fsdb names are defined by fsdb command.
* [-full_paths]
Print the signal fullname, default set as off.
display -fsdb_names -full_paths

violations_count_limit

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
display.

violations_count_limit
Syntax: violations_count_limit <per-checker-limit> <global_limit>.
The limit command sets up a limit on how many times a checker reports a failure. You can
use this command to let WaveCheck know when to stop checking one checker or stop
running the WaveCheck.
The per-checker limit can also be set as an option on the checker command (by adding
-limit "n" switch).

* <per-checker-limit>
Set a per-checker limit.
Default set as 10
* <global_limit>
Set a global-checker limit.
Default set as 1000.
violations_count_limit 5 20

Checker Command
All the checker commands require a "-name" argument. The unique label is used in the
output reports and in the GUI to identify the checker.
The time range of each check can be specified by using the arguments "-tstart" for
start time and "-tstop" for stop time.
If the start time is missing, it uses the start time of the waveform, likewise if the stop time is
missing, it uses the end time of the waveform.
* value
* threshold_low
* threshold_high
* freq
* delay
* pulsewidth_low
* pulsewidth_high
* bandwidth_low
* bandwidth_high
* diff
* coverage

value
value -name <name> -signal <signal> -value <value> [-evtol <tolerance>]
[-tstart <time>] [-tstop <time>] [-logkey <label>] [-limit <max_errors>]
[-enable <enable_name>]

The value checker checks to ensure that the specified signal matches an expected value
throughout a given time range.
You can also specify a tolerance for ensuring the value stays in each value range. The
signal can be either analog, digital(non-composite), or a digital bus.
The value checker verifies that a specified signal aligns with an expected value over a
defined time range.
* -value <value>: Expected value.
* [-evtol <tolerance>]: Expected value tolerance. Defaults to 0.
* [-tstart <time>]: The start time of the check time window. Defaults to wave
mintime.

threshold_low
threshold_low -name <name> -signal <signal> -value <value> [-evtol
<tolerance>] [-tstart <time>] [-tstop <time>] [-logkey <label>] [-limit
<max_errors>] [-enable <enable_name>]

The threshold low checker checks to ensure that the specified signal is higher than an
expected value throughout a given time range.
You can also specify a tolerance for ensuring the value stays in a given value range. The
signal can be either analog, digital(non-composite), or a digital bus.
* -value <value>: Expected value.
* [-evtol <tolerance>]: Expected value tolerance. Defaults to 0.
* [-tstart <time>]: The start time of the check time window. Defaults to wave
mintime.

threshold_high
threshold_high -name <name> -signal <signal> -value <value> [-evtol
<tolerance>] [-tstart <time>] [-tstop <time>] [-logkey <label>] [-limit
<max_errors>] [-enable <enable_name>]

The threshold high checker checks to ensure that the specified signal is lower than an
expected value throughout a given time range.
You can also specify a tolerance for ensuring the value stays in each value range. The
signal can be either analog, digital(non-composite), or a digital bus.
* -value <value>: Expected value.
* [-evtol <tolerance>]: Expected value tolerance. Defaults to 0.
* [-tstart <time>]: The start time of the check time window. Defaults to wave
mintime.

freq
freq -name <name> -signal <signal> -period_r2r <period>|period_f2f
<period> [-sigth <value>] [-delaytol <tolerance>] [-tstart <time>]
[-tstop <time>] [-logkey <label>] [-limit <max_errors>] [-enable
<enable_name>]

The frequency checker checks to make sure a signal maintains its expected frequency for
the given time range.
The checker works on only analog signals. You can specify the checker to check the
period on rising-to-rising edges, falling-to-falling edges, or either.

* -period_r2r <period> | period_f2f <period>: Specify the period value for rising
to rising or falling to falling.
* [-sigth <value>]: Specify the threshold value. Default set as -1, it means use vc as
the event point (either).
* [-delaytol <tolerance>]: Specify the tolerance value. Default set as 0.

delay -name <name> -signal <signal> -signal2 <signal> -delay
<time>[-sig1th <value>] [-sig2th <value>] [-sig1edge rise|fall|either]
[-sig2edge rise|fall|either] [-delaytol <tolerance>] [-tstart <time>]
[-tstop <time>] [-logkey <label>] [-limit <max_errors>] [-enable
<enable_name>]

The delay checker measures the time delay with an expected tolerance from a transition of
a reference signal to another signal of interest that transitions later.
The checker works on both analog and digital (non-composite) signals and can even
accommodate scenarios where one signal is analog, and the other is digital (noncomposite).
The two signals can even come from different waveform files when using the logical fsdb
name in front of the signal name (see the fsdb command section earlier).
The threshold values for the signals are set as 0 by default.
The behavior of the edge can be described as follows:
* For analog signals
A rising edge means a transition from a lower value to the threshold value.
A falling edge means a transition from a higher value to the threshold value.
* For digital bus signals
The checker converts the signal value to a two-state 64-bit unsigned value.
A rising edge means a transition from a lower value to the threshold value.
A falling edge means a transition from a higher value to the threshold value.
* For digital bit signals
The checker ignores the threshold value.
A rising edge means a transition from 0 to x, z, or 1, and from x or z to 1.
A falling edge means a transition from 1 to x, z, or 0, and from x or z to 0.
Otherwise, no edge.
* -signal2 <signal>: Specify the observed signal name.
* -delay <time>: Specify the delay time.
* [-sig1th <value>]: Specify the threshold value for sig1. Default set as 0.

Check if the values of two signal values have any difference. The signal types to be
compared should be:
* Analog diff: Analog signal compared with Analog signal.
Signal1's value changes and time is golden to compare with signal2's value at that
time.

* Digital diff: Digital signal compared with Digital signal.

Report failure when signal1's value and signal2's value are different.

* -signal <signal>: Specify the signal1 name.
* -signal2 <signal>: Specify the signal2 name.
* [-evtol <tolerance>]: Value tolerance, only works on the analog diff checker.

coverage
coverage -name <name> -inst <instance_path> -analog_range <value> [-all]
[-signal <wildcardpattern>] [-tstart <time>] [-tstop <time>] [-logkey
<label>] [-limit <max_errors>]

The coverage checker examines all the analog signals in an instance of a design and
ensures that all the signals' highest value to lowest value have covered a specified target
range.
For example, if you set the analog range as 100 mV. Each of the signal's highest value
and its lowest value must be separated by at least 100mV. If the low value throughout the
waveform for a signal was 10mV and the high value was 109mV, that would be considered
a failure.
The coverage checker lists all the analog signals' results, whether the checker
passes or fails.

* -inst <instance_path>: Specify the observed instance path, also known as the
scope of the waveform.
* -analog_range <value>: Specify the analog signal range.
* [-all]: Specify all the signals recursively down the hierarchy below the given
instance, also known as all the subscopes below the given scope.
* [-signal <wildcardpattern>]: Specify the wildcard pattern to select only certain
signals. Default set as *.

Syntax: combination -name <name> -checknames
<checker_name>,<checker_name>

The combination checker performs a Boolean AND operation on any two or more existing
checkers that are already defined.
A combination checker only passes when all the contained checkers pass. This way you
can easily ensure a group of checkers passes without inspecting individually.
* -chekcnames: The name of the checkers defined earlier in this run.

MY_ERROR

combination -name comb_test -checknames test_b_0,test_c_10

enable
Syntax: enable -name <name> -expr "expression" [-delay <time>]
Enable command creates expression condition based on the default (dflt) waveform's
signals. The expression follows LRM express rules.
This can be used by the checker commands to "enable" the checker to be evaluated only
when the enable expression is true.
The supported operators for the expression are ~ , &, | , ^ , ~&, ~|, ~^ , ! , && , || , < , > ,+ ,
- ,* , << , >> , <<<, >>> , {}, ==, !=, <= ,>= , ().
* -expr "expression": Expression condition.
* [-delay <time>]: Specify a delay to the expression, the time unit followed by the "dflt"
waveform's time unit.

* The enable "my_enable" would be true when the address is masked and wr_en signal
is true.

Main Window
The following image presents the appearance of the main window of WaveCheck,
accompanied by visual guides.
WaveCheck runs checkers across specified waveforms and displays the results on GUI.
Concurrently, it generates the report and log files.
Users also have the option to load an existing report via the GUI.

Checker Summary
It displays the results and uses different colors to categorize them based on the checkers'
results.

Sort by Column
Users can sort the checker by different columns.

Filter
Users can adjust the displayed data in the checker summary table by modifying the filter
menus.
The filter menus are accessible via the filter buttons on the checker summary's header.

Original Checker Command and the Checker Result
* You can left-click with a mouse on the checker summary table to retrieve the
corresponding original checker command and its result.

* The results from the selected checker are displayed in the Checker Result View.

They are organized in chronological order, based on the timestamps of the failures.

Signal Name Display Option
* Select View to change the signal name display option.

Reload Existing Reports
* Select File > Load Report to load an existing report.

Viewing Specific Failure on nWave
From the list of checker failures, you can select one to examine by clicking on it.
The Verdi nWave window displays the related signals and highlights the failures with
markers.
A marker is a yellow triangle at the failure time point.
The keywords "START" and "STOP" are this checker's beginning and end times.
Some checkers have the keywords "e", "a", "t1" and "t2".
These represent the "expect timepoint", "actual timepoint", "tolerance start timepoint
(expect timepoint - tolerance time)" and "tolerance end timepoint (expect timepoint +
tolerance time)".

Checking Existing Marker
To check the existing marker on the nWave, follow the given steps:
1. Right-click with a mouse.
2. Select Marker > Goto Marker.

Preface
This book explains how to use the Native Programming Interface (NPI).
(R)

The NPI provides an interface layer to access the knowledge database in the Verdi
Automated Debug Platform.

You can use this interface to create customized utilities. Both Tcl commands and C APIs
are available.
NPI consists of two levels: NPI Models and NPI Libraries.

Audience
The audience for this manual includes engineers who are familiar with languages and
tools used in design and verification such as Verilog, VHDL, and SystemVerilog.
This document assumes basic knowledge of UNIX or Linux.
You should also be familiar with the Verdi platform and with C/C++ and Tcl.

Customer Support
Customer support is available through SolvNetPlus.

Accessing SolvNetPlus
The SolvNetPlus site includes a knowledge base of technical articles and FAQs about
Synopsys tools.
It also provides access to online services such as software downloads, documentation,
and technical support.

https://solvnetplus.synopsys.com

name and password, follow the instructions to sign up for an account.

menu bar.

Synopsys Statement on Inclusivity and Diversity
Synopsys is committed to creating an inclusive environment where every employee,
customer, and partner feels welcomed. We are reviewing and removing exclusionary
language from our products and supporting customer-facing collateral. Our effort also
includes internal initiatives to remove biased language from our engineering and working
environment, including terms that are embedded in our software and IPs. At the same
time, we are working to ensure that our Web content and software applications are usable
to people of varying abilities. You might still find examples of non-inclusive language in our
software or documentation as our IPs implement industry-standard specifications that are
currently under review to remove exclusionary language.

NPI Usage
Currently, users can work with the NPI models through two kinds of interfaces, one is
the Tcl command interface and the other is the C interface. Compared to the C interface,
Tcl commands provided by the NPI model can be played in both batch mode (through a
command file) and interactive mode (through the Tcl console) when the Verdi executable
is invoked. There is no need to compile an executable. In addition, users can hook
their existing application programs through the Tcl interface with the novas executable.
However, since Tcl is an interpreted language, the Tcl command interface has worse
performance due to the Tcl interpreter effort. It is recommended that you use the C
interface if the application has stringent performance requirements.

Creating VC Apps by NPI as an Executable
The following picture shows the flow of making C/C++ source codes as a VC Apps
executable:

You can make a standalone VC Apps executable by compiling and linking their C/C++
source codes with the NPI shared libraries.

Concept: Shared Library - libNPI.so and libnpiL1.so
NPI provides two shared library - libNPI.so and libnpiL1.so - for users to program
C/C++ VC Apps. The libraries is loaded by the setting of the environment variable
$LD_LIBRARY_PATH when the VC Apps executable starts.
libNPI.so is the shared library of NPI models (NPI L0), such as NPI Language model, NPI
Netlist model, NPI FSDB model, and so on.
libnpiL1.so is the shared library of NPI libraries (NPI L1). Refer the description of NPI
Libraries for details.

File Structure of the NPI C-API
The NPI C-API library is located under the Verdi release package: $(VERDI_HOME)/
share/NPI. The file structure of NPI directory is as follows:
NPI/

L1/
inc/
lib/

LINUX64/
LINUX/
SUSE64/
SUSE32/
SOLARIS_64/
SOLARIS_32/

The directory L1/ contains the source code of NPI Libraries. Refer to the descriptions of
NPI Libraries.
The directory lib/ contains the shared library - libNPI.so and libnpiL1.so - for each platform.
The directory inc/ contains the header files (*.h) of the NPI C-API. The file structure of inc/
is as follows:
inc/

npi.h(initialization and design import)
npi_type.h (basic type definition)
npi_hdl.h (C-API for NPI Language model)

npi_fsdb_trans.h (C-API for NPI FSDB model - transaction FSDB)
npi_util.h (C-API for NPI utility - used in NPI Libraries)

The files npi_hdl.h, npi_nl.h, npi_dm.h, npi_text.h, npi_fsdb.h, and npi_fsdb_trans.h
correspond to the NPI models. Refer to the descriptions of those models.

Following is an example that demonstrates the NPI C/C++ program as a VC Apps
executable:
my_program.cpp
include <cstdio>
include "npi_hdl.h" // use when you'd like to use NPI
Language model

npi_init()

{
// initialize NPI models
if( !npi_init(argc, argv) )
// the argc and argv might be different from those in

if( !npi_load_design(argc, argv) )
printf("\n Warning: There are some errors while
loading design\n");
printf("\n BEGIN my_program.exe \n");
// iterate top instances by NPI Language model
// npiHandle, npi_iterate, npi_scan, and npi_get_str
are defined in npi_hdl.h
npiHandle ref_hdl = NULL;
npiHandle itr = npi_iterate(npiInstance, ref_hdl); //
npiInstance is a defined symbol in npi_hdl.h
npiHandle top_hdl;
while(top_hdl = npi_scan(itr)) {
const char* topName = npi_get_str(npiName,
top_hdl); // npiName is a defined symbol in npi_hdl.h
printf("Top instance: %s\n", topName);
}
// end of NPI models
printf(" END my_program.exe \n");

}

The details of the above example are not going to be described. The example just shows
how to compile, make, and run the program.

Compile and Make
The following command shows how to compile my_program.cpp with NPI. Specify the
path to the NPI header files (npi.h and npi_hdl.h in this example) after -I option.
Assume $VERDI_HOME is the location of Verdi installation path.
%> g++ -c my_program.cpp -I$VERDI_HOME/share/NPI/inc

The following command shows how to make the VC Apps executable "my_program.exe".
Specify the path of the NPI shared library libNPI.so after -L. Assume the LINUX64 platform
is used.
%> g++ -o my_program.exe my_program.o -L$VERDI_HOME/share/NPI/lib/LINUX64
-lNPI -ldl -lpthread -lrt -lz

The library dllib, pthreadlib, rtlib, and zlib are necessary by using the option "-ldl
-lpthread -lrt -lz".
Sometimes, the compiler version ofg++ might not be compatible with the NPI libraries. If
above commands fail to pass the compilation due to g++ version, the vg_gnu package is
recommended to resolve the issue.
You can go to Synopsys ftp to get the latest vg_gnu package.
Assume the vg_gnu package is installed under $VG_GNU_HOME directory. The following
command shows how to make the VC Apps executable "my_program.exe" with vg_gnu g+
+ library:
%> g++ -o my_program.exe my_program.o -L$VERDI_HOME/share/NPI/lib/LINUX64
-L$VG_GNU_HOME/linux/gcc/lib64 -lNPI -ldl -lpthread -lrt -lz

For a well-organized compile and make process, it is better to have a Makefile, like the
example as follows:
Makefile

gcc compiler setup

CC = g++
CFLAGS = -Wall -g
LD = $(CC)
LDFLAGS =

Basic NPI Program Architecture
The following example shows the basic construct of an NPI program:
(include other header files)
// 1. include header files for NPI
include "npi.h" // a must-have for NPI programs
include "npi_hdl.h" // use when you'd like to use NPI
Language-SystemVerilog model
include "npi_nl.h" // use when you'd like to use NPI Netlist model
include "npi_dm.h" // use when you'd like to use NPI DM model
include "npi_text.h" // use when you'd like to use NPI Text model
include "npi_fsdb.h" // use when you'd like to use NPI FSDB model

{
// 2. parse the user-specific arguments for the program

int npi_argc;
char** npi_argv;
parse_arguments(argc, argv, npi_argc /*Output*/,
npi_argv /*Output*/);
// 3. initialize NPI models
if( !npi_init(npi_argc, npi_argv) )
// 4. if you'd like to use NPI Language/Netlist/DM/Text model,
npi_load_design is a must
if( using_npi_language_or_netlist_or_dm_or_text_model() )
npi_load_design(npi_argc, npi_argv);
(your NPI procedures)
// 5. end of NPI models
}

A typical NPI program contains the following 5 sections:
1. Include the NPI header files.
2. Separate the arguments for NPI from those for your program.
3. Initialize NPI.
4. Load the design if necessary.
5. End NPI.

Include Files
The header file: npi.h should always be included for an NPI program while including the
other NPI header files based on the models to be used.
Refer to the following for the mapping between the header files and the NPI models:
* npi_hdl.h: NPI Language model.
* npi_nl.h: NPI Netlist model.
* npi_dm.h: NPI Design Manipulation (DM) model.
* npi_text.h: NPI Text model.
* npi_fsdb.h: NPI FSDB model.
* npi_fsdb_trans.h: NPI FSDB model for transaction FSDB.

Parsing Arguments in the NPI Program
Typically, the usage of an NPI program is similar to the following:
%> my_NPI_program.exe <verdi import design options> <NPI options> <user
options>

where <novas import design options> might include the following common options. Other
<novas import design options> can be listed by "novas -h".
Table 1

Novas Import Design Options

-f filename

Specify the design file (for example, *.f) to be imported.

-lib libName

Specify the design library name (for example, work.lib++/).

-path pathname Specify the path of the design file (*.f) or design library
(work.lib++).
-top topModule Specify the top module of the design library.
-verilog

Specify the Verilog language type for the imported files (for
example, *.v).

-sv filename

Specify the SystemVerilog language type for the imported
files (for example, *.sv).

<NPI options> are for NPI models. Refer to the following section for details. You need to
separate user-defined arguments from <verdi import design options> and <NPI options>.
For example, pick up "-input_signal system.i_cpu.i_ALUB.carry_mode" in the following
command line:
%> my_program_arg.exe -lib work -top system -input_signal
"system.i_cpu.i_ALUB.carry_mode"

The following code snippet demonstrates how this can be achieved:

{
// 2. parse the user-specific arguments for the program
string input_signal; // use STL string
int npi_argc = 0;
char** npi_argv = (char**) malloc(sizeof(char*)*argc);
for(int i=0; i<argc; i++) {
if( strcmp(argv[i], "-input_signal") != 0 ) {
// record the arguments that are not user-defined

npi_argv[npi_argc] = argv[i];
npi_argc++;

}

}
// the argument "-input_signal"
// the next argument is the target string
i++;
input_signal = argv[i]; // record the target string
}

// now you can pass npi_argc and npi_argv to npi_init()
if( !npi_init(npi_argc, npi_argv) )
}

As a result, <verdi import design options> and <NPI options> is saved in npi_argv and the
user-defined option is saved in the "input_signal" variable.

npi_init() and npi_end() : Initialize and Close NPI
npi_init() and npi_end()are used to initialize and end an NPI program. They are required
for all NPI models.
The arguments (npi_argc and npi_argv) passed to npi_init() are call-by-reference,
npi_init() takes the NPI options and only leave the Verdi import design options.

npi_load_design() : Loading Designs in the NPI Program
If you want to use the NPI Language model, the NPI Netlist model, the NPI DM model,
or the NPI Text model, you must call npi_load_design() before using the APIs of those
models.

Use NPI Model in Tcl

following is the Verdi Tcl command that stops the Verdi executable

The program assumes the Verdi executable imports the design first. So playing
my_program.tcl can be executed as follows:
%> verdi -play my_program.tcl -f run.f -path ../Design

"-f run.f -path ../Design" represents the Verdi options for importing the design. Use "verdi
-h" for details. The program lists all the top module names in the design.

Passing Arguments in your NPI Program
Although the Verdi executable can act as a Tcl interpreter, it cannot pass any arguments
from the command line. That is, you cannot use the Tcl command $argv in your
program for the Verdi executable. For example, if you issue the following command
to run the program "my_program2.tcl", Verdi does not parse the argument: "-input
system.i_cpu.i_ALUB.carry_mode" and thus a runtime error is given.
%> verdi -play my_program2.tcl -f run.f -path ../Design -input
"system.i_cpu.i_ALUB.carry_mode"

Verdi cannot parse the argument: "-input system.i_cpu.i_ALUB.carry_mode". Therefore, if
you wrote the codes below in "my_program2.tcl"

the following code cannot be accepted by the Verdi executable
set my_arg [lindex $argv 7]

One of the solutions is to use a wrapper Tcl to take in the arguments and then pass them
to the NPI program using environment variables. This is illustrated with the following
example. The tclsh supports the usage of "$argv".
wrap.tcl
!/usr/local/bin/tclsh
set my_arg [lindex $argv 1]
set env(INPUT_SIG) $my_arg
exec verdi -play my_program2.tcl -f run.f
-path ../../demo_gate_design/Design/ &

my_program2.tcl
puts "==============================="
puts "Program Name : my_program2.tcl"

get input argument from the environment variable "INPUT_SIG"
set input_arg $env(INPUT_SIG)
puts "Input : $input_arg"
get the handle of INPUT_SIG, npi_handle_by_name is the NPI command
set hdl [npi_handle_by_name -name $input_arg -scope ""]
set file_name [npi_get_str -property "npiFile" -object $hdl]
set line_no [npi_get -property "npiLineNo" -object $hdl]
puts " File name : $file_name"
puts " Line no. : $line_no"
puts "=============================="
following is the Verdi Tcl command that stops the Verdi executable

Remember to change "wrap.tcl" as executable mode. The program can be run with the
following command. This program outputs the file and line number information for the
specified object in the design.
%> ./wrap.tcl -input "system.i_cpu.i_ALUB.carry_mode"

If you want to use the default NPI libraries without any customization, NPI provides the

1. In your C/C++ program, include the file "npi_L1.h".
#include "npi_L1.h"

// then your applications can use the APIs in NPI Libraries

The following shows an example that uses the NPI Libraries API,
npi_mod_define_dump_fileName_lineNo, to dump the file name and line number of a
specific module definition.

// header for NPI Models: npi_init,
npi_load_design, npi_end
include "npi_L1.h" // header for NPI Libraries
{
// initialize NPI and load design
// Novas loading design options are contained in argc, argv
// dump file name and line number for the module definition "MOD"
// into the file "output.log"
FILE* pFile = fopen("output.log", "w");
npi_mod_define_dump_fileName_lineNo("MOD", pFile);
fclose(pFile);
// leaving NPI
}
