npi_nl_trace_network_sig_2_sig
Report tracing result and the network between start nets and end nets based on NPI
Netlist model.
A general trace connection app is provided. The function starts tracing from the nets listed
in the startFile. When tracing to a module listed in the modMap, it does not go into the
module. Instead, it goes to the corresponding port and keeps tracing.
There are some conditions for the program to stop tracing:
1. It meets the floating ports/instports or constant-tied signal.
2. It meets the nets listed in the endFile.
3. It meets the instports of flip-flop cell.
4. It meets the instports of an instance whose npiNlCellType is not npiNlModule nor
listed in the passCellFile.
5. It meets ports of the top boundary module of the whole design.
6. It meets the instports of an instance whose module name is listed in the stopModFile.
7. Finally, if the tracing level exceed the depth user specified, it stops tracing. Then, the
tracing result of each ports is dumped to the resultFile.
The whole graph network of the points mentioned above (start points, jump points, end
points and stop points) are dumped to the networkFile.

resultFile
networkFile
{ passCellFile "" } { isPassCellPosList 1 }
{ mapFile "" } {linkFile "" }
{ isToBit 0 }
{ detailMode 0 } { networkStyle 0 } { depth 20 }

startFile

Specify the file name containing the full actual name / npiNlFullName of start nets, and the
trace direction of each net.

Format:
net_full_actual_name npiNlDriver/npiNlLoad Does not support wildcard.
endFile

Specify the file name containing the full actual name / npiNlFullName of end nets.
Wildcard supported. If one line has first character `#', it is treated as comment line.
resultFile

Specify the file name where the trace results of each start net is shown.
networkFile

Specify the file name where the network relationship is shown. To specify the complexity of
the network please refer to: detailMode.
passCellFile

Specify the file name containing the npiNlCellType that pass through and keep tracing. Nospecified type: tracing passes through module boundaries by default(npiNlCellType ==
npiNlModuleCell). If one line has first character `#', it is treated as comment line.
isPassCellPosList = 1, only the npiNlCellType listing in the file + npiNlModuleCell passes,

npi_nl_trace_network_sig_2_inst
Report tracing result and the network between start nets and end instances based
on NPI Netlist model.
A general trace connection app is provided. The function starts tracing from the nets listed
in the startFile. When tracing to a module listed in the modMap, it does not go into the
module. Instead, it goes to the corresponding port and keeps tracing.
There are some conditions for the program to stop tracing:
1. It meets the floating ports or instports or constant-tied signal.
2. It meets the ports of end instance listed in the endFile.
3. It meets the instports of flip-flop cell.
4. It meets the instports of an instance whose npiNlCellType is not npiNlModule nor
listed in the passCellFile.
5. It meets ports of the top boundary module of the whole design.
6. It meets the instports of an instance whose module name is listed in the stopModFile.
7. Finally, if the tracing level exceed the depth user specified, it stops tracing. Then, the
tracing result of each ports is dumped to the resultFile.
The whole graph network of the points mentioned above (start points, jump points, end
points and stop points) are dumped to the networkFile.

npiVanlBitValue_e defaultValue = NPI_VANL_X, npiVanlBeginType_e
beginType = npiVanlDefaultBegin);

scopeHierName

Specifies the full hierarchical name of the top boundary scope. When a specific scope is
set, any signal outside the scope is not considered. If it's NULL, all scopes are included.
defaultValue

Specifies the default value that would be assigned to a signal if no specific value is set.
Enum npiVanlBitValue_e is a four-state value set, especially used in NPI VANL Library.
NPI_VANL_0

Logical zero

NPI_VANL_1

NPI_VANL_X

Unknown logic value

High-impedance state

npiVanlBeginType_e is stated below:
npiVanlDefaultBegin

Default

Iterate whole design and search for literal nets
under top boundary scope, get their values and
call npi_vanl_set_value_by_hdl internally.

npi_nl_trace_network_port_2_inst
Report tracing result and the network between start ports and end instances based
on NPI Netlist model.
A general trace connection app is provided. The function starts tracing from the ports listed
in the startFile.
When tracing to a module listed in the modMap, it does not go into the module. Instead, it
jumps to the correspondent port and keep tracing.
There are some conditions for the program to stop tracing:
* First, it meets the floating ports/instports or constant-tied signal.
* Second, it meets the ports of end instance listed in the endFile.
* Third, it meets the instports of flip-flop cell.
* Fourth, it meets the instports of an instance whose npiNlCellType is not npiNlModule
nor listed in the passCellFile.
* Fifth, it meets ports of the top boundary module of the whole design.
* Sixth, it meets the instports of an instance whose module name is listed in the
stopModFile.
And last, if the tracing level exceed the depth user specified, it stops tracing.
In the end, the tracing result of each ports is dumped to the resultFile and the whole graph
network of the points mentioned above (start points, jump points, end points and stop
points) is dumped to the networkFile.

Tcl
proc ::npi_L1::npi_nl_trace_network_port_2_inst { startFile endFile
resultFile networkFile
{ passCellFile "" } { isPassCellPosList 1 }
{ mapFile "" } {linkFile "" }
{ isToBit 0 } { isEndAtModule 0 }
{ detailMode 0 } { networkStyle 0 } { depth 20 }
{ stopModFile "" } }

* startFile: Specify the file name containing the full actual name / npiNlFullName of
start ports, and the trace direction of each port.
Trace direction is optional. If trace direction is not specified, for output it traces load,
others trace the driver.
Format:
port_full_actual_name npiNlDriver/npiNlLoad

Wildcard supported for the ports' name for the following case:
- top.u1.p*
- top.u1.p*[1]
- top.u1.* // all ports under top.u1

* endFile: Specify the file name containing the end instances. It can be module
name, or the full actual name / npiNlFullName of end instances, according to the flag
isEndAtModule.
isEndAtModule = 0: full actual name / npiNlFullName of instances
isEndAtModule = 1: module name

Wildcard supported.
* resultFile: Specify the file name where the trace results of each start port is shown.
* networkFile: Specify the file name where the network relationship is shown. To
specify the complexity of the network, refer to detailMode.

* passCellFile: Specify the file name containing the npiNlCellType that passes through
and keep tracing. No-specified type: tracing only passes through module boundaries by
default. (npiNlCellType == npiNlModuleCell)
isPassCellPosList = 1, only the npiNlCellType listing in the file + npiNlModuleCell pass,
while others do not.
isPassCellPosList = 0, then npiNlCellType listing in the file does not pass through,
while others do.
* isPassCellPosList: Specify whether the passCellFile is in positive listing. Default is
1.
* mapFile: Specify the file name containing the module port mapping that jumps
through while tracing. The mapping should be 1-1 or 1-N or N-1 relationship. N-N is
not supported. Wildcard supported. If one line has first character `#', it is treated as
comment line.
* Style:
1-1: modName in1 out1
N-1: modName { in1 in2 } out1
1-N: modName in1 { out1 out2 }
linkFile

Specify the file name containing the full actual name / npiNlFullName of link points.
A link point is a npiNlPort or a npiNlInstPort that user particularly want to observe in the
network graph. The graph recognizes the link point as a node, thus also reported in the
network result.
Wildcard is supported. If one line has first character `#', it is treated as comment line.
* isToBit: Specify whether the start port should split to bits before tracing. Default is 0.
If the start ports is itself a npiNlPseudoPort name. For example, top.a[2:3]
from a npiNlPort top.a[0:3], it is always automatically split to bits.
* isEndAtModule: Specify whether the end file is stated in the "full actual name /
npiNlFullName" style (0), or the "module name" style (1) or mixed style(2). Default is 0.
* detailMode: Specify how detail the network is, and how it affects the result of report
path or network. By default, 0, the network graph contains:
The start ports and end ports
Both sides of ports of mapping module.

Link ports that you want to observe.
The stop ports or instports and literal net that meet the stop conditions.
0: The instports from the passCellFile is not a node in the network
graph for less complexity.
1: Adding all past ports of module into the graph.
2: Adding all instports of instance from symbol library.
3: Adding all past ports of module, and the past instports from the
passCellFile into the graph.

* networkStyle: Specify which style the network file should be dumped.
0: Text view (default).
1: json style.
Text view and json style shows the actual name of each node in graph, along with
its type, direction if it is a port or instport, connected net if it is an instport, and value
if it is a literal net.
It shows its instance information, including instance name, module name, cell type,
file name and begin line number. It also shows the driver or load relationship of
each node.
2: Tree view.
Each tree starts from a no-driver node.
3: Tree view readable.
Similar to 2. However for instport with non-intuitive netlist-gen name, it shows its
connected net's name instead for readability.

npi_nl_trace_network_sig_2_sig
Report tracing result and the network between start nets and end nets based on NPI
Netlist model.
A general trace connection app is provided. The function starts tracing from the nets listed
in the startFile. When tracing to a module listed in the modMap, it does not go into the
module. Instead, it goes to the corresponding port and keeps tracing.
There are some conditions for the program to stop tracing:
1. It meets the floating ports/instports or constant-tied signal.
2. It meets the nets listed in the endFile.
3. It meets the instports of flip-flop cell.
4. It meets the instports of an instance whose npiNlCellType is not npiNlModule nor
listed in the passCellFile.
5. It meets ports of the top boundary module of the whole design.
6. It meets the instports of an instance whose module name is listed in the stopModFile.
7. Finally, if the tracing level exceed the depth user specified, it stops tracing. Then, the
tracing result of each ports is dumped to the resultFile.
The whole graph network of the points mentioned above (start points, jump points, end
points and stop points) are dumped to the networkFile.

Tcl
proc ::npi_L1::npi_nl_trace_network_sig_2_sig { startFile endFile
resultFile
networkFile
{ passCellFile "" } { isPassCellPosList 1 }
{ mapFile "" } {linkFile "" }
{ isToBit 0 }
{ detailMode 0 } { networkStyle 0 } { depth 20 }
{ stopModFile "" }}

startFile

Specify the file name containing the full actual name / npiNlFullName of start nets, and the
trace direction of each net.

Format:
net_full_actual_name npiNlDriver/npiNlLoad Does not support wildcard.
endFile

Specify the file name containing the full actual name / npiNlFullName of end nets.
Wildcard supported. If one line has first character `#', it is treated as comment line.
resultFile

Specify the file name where the trace results of each start net is shown.
networkFile

Specify the file name where the network relationship is shown. To specify the complexity of
the network please refer to: detailMode.
passCellFile

Specify the file name containing the npiNlCellType that pass through and keep tracing. Nospecified type: tracing passes through module boundaries by default(npiNlCellType ==
npiNlModuleCell). If one line has first character `#', it is treated as comment line.
isPassCellPosList = 1, only the npiNlCellType listing in the file + npiNlModuleCell passes,
while others do not.
isPassCellPosList = 0, then npiNlCellType listing in the file does not pass through, while
others do.
isPassCellPosList

Specify whether the passCellFile is in positive listing. Default is 1.
mapFile

Specify the file name containing the module port mapping that jumps through while
tracing. The mapping should be 1-1 or 1-N or N-1 relationship. N-N is not supported.
Wildcard is supported. If one line has first character `#', it is treated as comment line.
Style:
1-1: modName in1 out1
N-1: modName { in1 in2 } out1
1-N: modName in1 { out1 out2 }
linkFile

Specify the file name containing the full actual name /npiNlFullNameof link points. A
link point is a npiNlPort or a npiNlInstPort that you want to observe in the network
graph. The graph recognizes the link point as a node, and therefore is also reported in
the network result. Wildcard is supported. If one line has first character `#', it is treated as
comment line.
isToBit

Specify whether the start net should split to bits before tracing. Default is 0.
detailMode

Specify how detail the network is, and how it affects the result of report path or network. By
default, 0, the network graph contains:
* the start ports and end ports,
* both sides of ports of mapping module,
* link ports that user wants to observe,
* the stop ports/instports and literal net that meet the stop conditions.
Note: The instports from the passCellFile are not a node in the network
graph for less complexity.
1. 1: adding all past ports of module into the graph.
2. 2: adding all instports of instance from symbol library.
3. 3: adding all past ports of module, and the past instports from the passCellFile into the
graph.

networkStyle

Specify which style the network file should be dumped. Default is 0, Text view.
1: json style

Text view and json style shows the actual name of each node in graph, along with its type,
direction if it is a port or instport, connected net if it is an instport, and value if it is a literal
net. It shows its instance information, including instance name, module name, cell type, file
name and begin line number. Also, it shows the driver/ load relationship of each node.
2: Tree view
Each tree starts from a no-driver node.
3: Tree view readable
Similar to 2. However for instport with non-intuitive netlist-gen name, it shows its
connected net's name instead for readability.

npi_nl_trace_network_sig_2_inst
Report tracing result and the network between start nets and end instances based
on NPI Netlist model.
A general trace connection app is provided. The function starts tracing from the nets listed
in the startFile. When tracing to a module listed in the modMap, it does not go into the
module. Instead, it goes to the corresponding port and keeps tracing.
There are some conditions for the program to stop tracing:
1. It meets the floating ports or instports or constant-tied signal.
2. It meets the ports of end instance listed in the endFile.
3. It meets the instports of flip-flop cell.
4. It meets the instports of an instance whose npiNlCellType is not npiNlModule nor
listed in the passCellFile.
5. It meets ports of the top boundary module of the whole design.
6. It meets the instports of an instance whose module name is listed in the stopModFile.
7. Finally, if the tracing level exceed the depth user specified, it stops tracing. Then, the
tracing result of each ports is dumped to the resultFile.
The whole graph network of the points mentioned above (start points, jump points, end
points and stop points) are dumped to the networkFile.

Tcl
proc ::npi_L1::npi_nl_trace_network_sig_2_inst { startFile endFile
resultFile
networkFile
{ passCellFile "" } { isPassCellPosList 1 }
{ mapFile "" } {linkFile "" }
{ isToBit 0 } { isEndAtModule 0 }
{ detailMode 0 } { networkStyle 0 } { depth 20 } }
{ stopModFile "" } }

* startFile: Specify the file name containing the full actual name or npiNlFullName of
start nets, and the trace direction of each net.
Format:
net_full_actual_name npiNlDriver/npiNlLoad

Does not support wildcard.
* endFile: Specify the file name containing the end instances. It can be module name,
or the full actual name or npiNlFullName of end instances, according to the flag
isEndAtModule.
isEndAtModule = 0: full actual name / npiNlFullName of instances
isEndAtModule = 1: module name

Wildcard supported.
* resultFile: Specify the file name where the trace results of each start port is shown.
* networkFile: Specify the file name where the network relationship is shown. To
specify the complexity of the network, refer to detailMode.
* passCellFile: Specify the file name containing the npiNlCellType that passes through
and keep tracing.

No-specified type: tracing passes through module boundaries by default.
(npiNlCellType == npiNlModuleCell). If one line has first character `#', it is treated
as comment line.
isPassCellPosList = 1, only the npiNlCellType listing in the file + npiNlModuleCell
passes, while others do not.
isPassCellPosList = 0, then npiNlCellType listing in the file does not pass through,
while others do.
* isPassCellPosList: Specify whether the passCellFile is in positive listing. Default is
1.
* mapFile: Specify the file name containing the module port mapping that jumps through
while tracing.
The mapping should be 1-1 or 1-N or N-1 relationship. N-N is not supported. Wildcard
is supported. If one line has first character `#', it is treated as comment line.
* Style:
1-1: modName in1 out1
N-1: modName { in1 in2 } out1
1-N: modName in1 { out1 out2 }

* linkFile: Specify the file name containing the full actual name /npiNlFullName of
link points.
A link point is a npiNlPort or a npiNlInstPort that you want to observe in the
network graph.
The graph recognizes the link point as a node, and therefore is also reported in the
network result. Wildcard is supported. If one line has first character `#', it is treated as
comment line.
* isToBit: Specify whether the start net should split to bits before tracing. Default is 0.

* depth: Specify the maximum tracing level. Default is 20.
* stopModFile: Specify the file name containing the module names that stops tracing.
If the tracing program ended gracefully, the total number of start ports is returned.
Otherwise, returns 0.

module top (w1, w2, w3 ,w5, w6, clk);
input [3:0] w2;
input [1:0] w1, w3;
clk;

[1:0] w0;

assign w7[1] = w0[1];
Mix inst(w1, w2, w3, w4, w0, w5, clk);
w6 = 2'b00;
end
always @ (posedge clk) begin

Default

and base (example: {2'b10,2'b01}). Note that the full name exists in the netlist model, and
some signal in FSDB might be flattened in the netlist model that cannot set value.

Dump the FSDB scope tree to a file.
The hierarchical tree view of a scope, specified by its name root_scope, is dumped into a
text file. If root_scope is NULL, the hierarchy tree from the top modules in the FSDB file is
dumped.

vc_array }

vc_array

(Output) the array of value changes (Key: time, Data: value) (Note: time value is unique

npi_l1_fsdb_sig_by_property
Query the signals by given property with specified FSDB file.

Predefine Data Type
There are several new data types related to this API.
1. typedef enum npiFsdbL1Bool
typedef enum npiFsdbL1Bool {
npiFsdbL1Unset = 0,
npiFsdbL1True,
npiFsdbL1False
npiFsdbL1Bool;
2. typedef struct npiFsdbL1PropertyStruct
This is the struct type for users to set querying constraints.
typedef struct npiFsdbL1Property_s{
const char* sigName = "";
npiFsdbL1Bool real = npiFsdbL1Unset;
npiFsdbL1Bool MDA = npiFsdbL1Unset;
const char* leftRange = "";
const char* rightRange = "";
const char* rangeSize = "";
const char* direction = "";
const char* assertionType = "";
const char* compositeType = "";
} npiFsdbL1PropertyStruct;

For all the constraints except sigIsReal, they are defined as constant character pointer
type and the simple expression is supported.
For example, if the querying constraints are as below.
1. Signal name is "i_BJsource" or "MAselect".
2. Range size is between 10 and 20.
3. Direction type is input or inout.

To set these constraints, the following is a partial extract of sample code.
npiFsdbL1Property_spropStruct;
propStruct.sigName = " sig == \"i_BJsource\" || sig == \" MAselect \" ";
propStruct.rangeSize = "sig>10 && sig< 20";
propStruct.direction = "sig == \"input\" || sig == \"inout\"";

There are several rules that need to be noticed.
1. Except sigName, all constraints are not case sensitive which means both lowercase
and capital are acceptable. For example, propStruct.direction = "input" and
propStruct.direction = "INPUT" are with same meaning, which is to set the
direction as input.
2. For the non-numeral identifier , it should be marked by "\" ". As the example above, the
signal name expression is
propStruct.sigName = " sig == \"i_BJsource\" || sig == \" MAselect \"
";

The two identifier, i_BJsource and MAselect are marked as \"i_BJsource\" and \"
MAselect \".
3. For each equivalence, the operand name should be "sig". Any other operand name is
invalid and makes this API calling invalid.
For example, propStruct.rangeSize = "a>10 && a< 20" ; is an invalid expression
since the operand name is a instead of sig.
Signal Name Constraint
For querying array signal, the expression should be declaration name without the
dimension. For example, if there is a signal array named "Card[3:0]", to querying this
signal, the given constraint should be as below.
propStruct.sigName = " sig == \"Card\" ";

The following expressions are not legal for this case.
propStruct.sigName = " sig == \"Card[3:0]\" "; // invalid. Should not
include dimension
propStruct.sigName = " sig == \"Card[1]\" "; // invalid. Should not
include dimension

MDA Constraint
For the querying constraint MDA, it means if the signal has the array with more than two
dimension or not. If this constraint is true, all the signals which have the array with more
than two dimension is queried. Note that the any two dimension or multi-dimension arrays
inside composite signals (struct, union, ) are not considered in this constraint.

Direction Constraint
For the constraint direction, the allowable const char* is as below.
* Input
* Output
* Inout
These are not case sensitive but it is failed if any other const char* is given.
There is an example for this constraint.
npiFsdbL1Property_spropStruct;
propStruct.direction = "sig == \"INOUT\""; // legal, since it is not case
sensitive

Assertion Type Constraint
For the constraint assertion type, the allowable const char* is as below.
* Assert
* Assume

* Restrict
These are not case sensitive but it is failed if any other const char* is given.
Composite Type Constraint
* Array
* Struct
* Union
* TaggedUnion
* Record
These are not case-sensitive but it is failed if any other const char* is given.

Supported Logic Symbols
For this API, there are several symbols supported in expression, such as the following:
1. && (AND)
2. || (OR)
3. == (equal)
4. <= (Less than or equal to)
5. < (Less than)
6. >= (Greater than or equal to)
7. > (Greater than)
8. * (wildcard, signal name constraint only)

up until the point at which the object is ended; however, only the last specified value is
associated with the attribute. It supports more than 64 bits.

npiFsdbwRadix radix = npiFsdbwHex);

Specifies the UID of the object to be modified. For illegal case, see Illegal Cases for Object
ID.

Specifies the attribute value. For each bit, its value can be 0,1,x(X),z(Z).

Note that the attribute length more than 64 bits is supported.
num_bits (SystemVerilog only)

For SystemVerilog, this is the size of the bit-vector. For example, if the definition of the bitvector to be stored is bit [15:0] data, the value of this parameter must be set to 16. If the
value of this parameter exceeds NPI_TR_WRITER_BV_MAX_WIDTH, the stored value is
pruned (and thus data could be lost).

Specifies the expected attribute value. If this value differs from "attribute_value", the
object is marked as having an error condition. If the attribute value length is not equal to
expected value length, this API is failed and returns 0.

set_object_attribute_value_int
This method specifies the value of an integer attribute for an object. This method can be
called up until the point at which the object is ended; however, only the last specified value
is associated with the attribute.

NPI_INT32 set_object_attribute_value_int(
cosnt char* attribute_name,
NPI_INT64
NPI_INT64
expected_value,
npiTrIntBits num_bits,
npiFsdbwRadix radix = npiFsdbwDec);

Specifies the UID of the object to be modified. For illegal case, see Illegal Cases for Object
ID.

Specifies the attribute value. The data types are as following.
NPI_INT64: it represents long integer type.
NPI_UINT64: it represents unsigned long integer type.

Specifies the expected attribute value. If this value differs from "attribute_value", the object
num_bits (NPI_INT64 only)

Number of bits of integer attribute.
The enumerate type is as below.
typedef enum npiTrIntBits {
npiTrInt8B, // 8 bits integer
npiTrInt16B, // 16 bits integer
npiTrInt32B, // 32 bits integer
npiTrInt64B // 64 bits integer
}npiTrIntBits;
Note that for unsigned integer (NPI_UINT64), the bit size is 64 bits only.

Specifies the name of the FSDB file. If it is NULL, an error is issued and this API fails.

unit (C-based)
Specifies the scale unit of this file. For example, if the scale unit should be set as 10 ns,
you can provide a string "10 ns" as a unit for this API. The legal scale unit should be as [1,
10, 100] [s, ms, us, ns, ps, fs] (these are case sensitive and only lower cases are allowed).
An error is issued and it is set as 1 ns if any other value is provided.
time (C-based)
Specifies the begin time of simulation for this FSDB file. If the provided time is a negative
value, a warning is issued and it is set as 0.

npi_hier_tree_trv_register_cb
Register callback function for npi_hier_tree_trv.
The npi_hier_tree_trv_register_cb API associates a user-defined callback function and
data with npi_hier_tree_trv.
You can register callbacks for object types that can be iterated from a scope.
npi_hier_tree_trv calls the registered callback when it traverses the corresponding object
type.
Also refer to npi_hier_tree_trv, npi_hier_tree_trv_chk_skip_cb and
npi_hier_tree_trv_reset_cb.
The object (npiHandle) is passed as an argument to the callback function and
be released when the execution of callback function is done. If users want to
preserve the object, npi_set_permanent_handle can be used to set the object
as "permanent".

npi_hier_tree_trv_chk_skip_cb
Register callback function to skip traverse for npi_hier_tree_trv

The API npi_hier_tree_trv_chk_skip_cb provides a solution to determine whether
the traverse can be stopped during execution of npi_hier_tree_trv. The API
npi_hier_tree_trv_chk_skip_cb creates the association between npi_hier_tree_trv
and user-defined callback function/data for specified object types. When a handle
is retrieved by npi_hier_tree_trv, the registered callback function is called. The
callback function must return a boolean value. Once the returned value returns 'true',
npi_hier_tree_trv stops exploring any relationship of the handle; likewise, if the
callback function returns false, the traverse continues and the callback function of
npi_hier_tree_trv_register_cb is executed. The registered callback function/data is
reset by the API npi_hier_tree_trv_reset_cb.
Also refer to npi_hier_tree_trv, npi_hier_tree_trv_register_cb, and
npi_hier_tree_trv_reset_cb.
The object (npiHandle) is passed as an argument to the callback function and
be released when the execution of callback function is done. If users want to
preserve the object, npi_set_permanent_handle can be used to set the object
as "permanent".
Object types recognized by npi_hier_tree_trv_chk_skip_cb are identical with
npi_hier_tree_trv_register_cb.

{

npi_nl_set_black_box
Set a module as black box.
This API affects the trace results of APIs: npi_nl_trace_driver/load series,
npi_nl_sig_2_reg_conn series including fanIn/fanOut, and npi_nl_trace_network series.

npi_nl_set_black_box ( const char* modName );

modname

Specify the module name.
If success, return true.

Tcl
proc ::npi_L1:: npi_nl_set_black_box { modName }

modname

Specify the module name.
If success, return 1.
If a module is set to be black box, then its instances (cell should be npiNlModuleCell) are
treated as black boxes.
When tracing from outside of those black box instances, it does not trace into the instance.
Instead, it passes through the instance according to the direction of its instports.
Basically the behavior is the same as npiNlMacroCell:
1. When tracing load of an input instport (pi), it gets all the output (po) and inout (pio)
instports of the instance.
2. When tracing driver of an output instport (po), it gets all the input (pi) and inout (pio)
instports of the instance.
3. When tracing load of an inout (pio) instport, it gets all the output (po) and inout instports
of the instance despite itself, and the load of the other side (p).
4. When tracing driver of an inout (pio) instport, it gets all the input (pi) and inout instports
of the instance despite itself, and the driver of the other side.

npi_tr_writer_create_bit_vector_value
This method is to create a multiple bits vector. You can use it to create a bit vector as
argument of method set_object_attribute_value_bit_vector().
string bitVector = npi_tr_writer_create_bit_vector_value
// bitVector: "00000000101"
tr_writer-> set_object_attribute_value_bit_vector(obj_id,
"attr_bit_vec", bitVector);
(5, 11);

const char* bitVector =
npi_tr_writer_create_bit_vector_value (bitVector, "x1z1", 11);
//
bitVector: "0000000x1z1"
tr_writer-> set_object_attribute_value_bit_vector(obj_id,
"attr_bit_vec", bitVector);

string npi_tr_writer_create_bit_vector_value(
NPI_INT64 value, unsigned int num_bits);
const char* value, unsigned int num_bits);

value (NPI_INT64 or const char*)

The target value. It can be either 64-bits integer or string.
For example, if this argument is set to integer "7" and the num_bits is set to 4, the
vector_value is "0111". If it is set to string "01xz" and the num_bits is set to 6, the
vector_value is "0001xz".
num_bits

The number of bits in vector_value.
If num_bits is less than value length, the value is truncated to fit the exact size.
On success, the bit vector string is returned.

$value
$num_bits
$value_type

// vecValue: "0001X"

"attr_bit_vec " vecValue

value (NPI_INT64 or const char*)

The target value. It can be either 64-bits integer or string.
For example, if this argument is set to "7" and the num_bits is set to 4, the vector_value is
"0111". If it is set to string "01xz" and the num_bits is set to 6, the vector_value is "0001xz".
num_bits

The number of bits in vector_value.
value_type

The given value type. It can be set to the following.
1. STRING
2. NPI_INT64
set vecValue [::npi_L1::npi_tr_writer_set_attr_value_bit 5 5
NPI_INT64] // vecValue: "00101"
::npi_L1::npi_tr_writer_set_attr_value_bit_vector $writer $object
"attr_bit_vec " vecValue

// vecValue: "0001X"
::npi_L1::npi_tr_writer_set_attr_value_bit_vector $writer $object
"attr_bit_vec " vecValue.

On success, returns bit vector.
On failure, returns empty string.

npi_tr_writer_FSDB_open
This method constructs a new instance of the "npi_tr_writer" class.

NPI_INT32 npi_tr_writer_FSDB_open(
const char* name,
const char* unit,
npiFsdbTime time = 0);

Specifies the name of the FSDB file. If it is NULL, an error is issued and this API fails.
Each FSDB file must have a unique name. If the name is same as any of the existing
FSDB files, this API fails and returns a NULL pointer.
unit (C-based)
Specifies the scale unit of this file. For example, if the scale unit should be set as 10 ns,
you can provide a string "10 ns" as a unit for this API. The legal scale unit should be as [1,
10, 100] [s, ms, us, ns, ps, fs] (these are case sensitive and only lower cases are allowed).
An error is issued and it is set as 1 ns if any other value is provided.
time (C-based)
Specifies the begin time of simulation for this FSDB file. If the provided time is a negative
value, a warning is issued and it is set as 0.

{

}

Tcl
npi_tr_writer_FSDB_open {
unit
{ time "0" }
}

file_name

Specifies the name of the FSDB file.
scale_unit

Specifies the scale unit of this file. For example, if the scale unit needs to be set as 10 ns,
you can provide a string "10 ns" as a unit for this API. The legal scale unit must be as [1,

10, 100] [s, ms, us, ns, ps, fs] (these are case sensitive and only lower cases are allowed).
An error is issued and scale unit is set as 1 ns if any other value is provided.

Specifies the begin time of simulation for this FSDB file. If time is omitted, the begin time
of this file is set as 0. It must be a positive number and the maximum number of digits
allowed is 64; an error is issued if this is violated.

npi_hier_tree_trv_register_cb
Register callback function for npi_hier_tree_trv.
The npi_hier_tree_trv_register_cb API associates a user-defined callback function and
data with npi_hier_tree_trv.
You can register callbacks for object types that can be iterated from a scope.
npi_hier_tree_trv calls the registered callback when it traverses the corresponding object
type.
Also refer to npi_hier_tree_trv, npi_hier_tree_trv_chk_skip_cb and
npi_hier_tree_trv_reset_cb.
The object (npiHandle) is passed as an argument to the callback function and
be released when the execution of callback function is done. If users want to
preserve the object, npi_set_permanent_handle can be used to set the object
as "permanent".

npi_mod_define_dump_design
Dump the complete source code of a module definition.
Locates the definition of a module specified by its name mod_name, and then dumps its
complete source code into a file.

int npi_mod_define_dump_design ( char * mod_name , FILE * pFile );

Specify the definition name of the target module.

Returns 0 if the corresponding module definition cannot be found. Otherwise, returns a
positive integer indicating the number of source code segments dumped.
Output Format
The dumped output begins with a comment line in the format "//File: /full/path/
to/source_file".
This comment indicates the original source file location.
The output then includes the complete module definition from the module declaration
through endmodule.
All macros are expanded in the output.

DATA_WIDTH 8
MAX_COUNT 255
RESET_VALUE 8'h00
MIN(a, b) ((a) < (b) ? (a) : (b))

output logic [DATA_WIDTH-1:0] count
);
count <= RESET_VALUE;
count <= MIN(count + 1'b1, MAX_COUNT);
end
module top_design (
output logic [DATA_WIDTH-1:0] count_out
);
counter u_counter (
.clk (clk),
.rst_n (rst_n),
.enable (enable),
.count (count_out)

);

{
npi_mod_define_dump_design("counter", stdout);

}

//File: example.v

);
count <= 8'h00;
count <= ((count + 1'b1) < (255) ? (count + 1'b1) : (255));
end

npi_nl_set_black_box
Set a module as black box.
This API affects the trace results of APIs: npi_nl_trace_driver/load series,
npi_nl_sig_2_reg_conn series including fanIn/fanOut, and npi_nl_trace_network series.

npi_nl_set_black_box ( const char* modName );

modname

Specify the module name.
If success, return true.

Tcl
proc ::npi_L1:: npi_nl_set_black_box { modName }

modname

Specify the module name.
If success, return 1.
If a module is set to be black box, then its instances (cell should be npiNlModuleCell) are
treated as black boxes.
When tracing from outside of those black box instances, it does not trace into the instance.
Instead, it passes through the instance according to the direction of its instports.
Basically the behavior is the same as npiNlMacroCell:
1. When tracing load of an input instport (pi), it gets all the output (po) and inout (pio)
instports of the instance.
2. When tracing driver of an output instport (po), it gets all the input (pi) and inout (pio)
instports of the instance.
3. When tracing load of an inout (pio) instport, it gets all the output (po) and inout instports
of the instance despite itself, and the load of the other side (p).
4. When tracing driver of an inout (pio) instport, it gets all the input (pi) and inout instports
of the instance despite itself, and the driver of the other side.

npi_nl_bit_trace_driver_by_hdl
Find the bit-level drivers of a net/port/instport handle based on the NPI Netlist
The handles of the driver ports or instance ports, specified by input handle, are collected
into the specified vector (C++) or list (Tcl).
The API does not traverse across a module boundary.
It does not pass through assign statements. An assign cell is treated as a primitive cell.

npi_get_sig_elem_range
Get the element range of specified signal handle (see the definition of
npi_ut_is_signal) based on the NPI Language Model. However, any range selected
signal like npiPartSelect is not an invalid input signal.
The output left and right value means the range value of input signal's element.

int npi_get_sig_elem_range(npiHandle sig, int &left, int &right, int
vhRngIdx=0);

sig

Specify the target signal.

The left range value that is assigned after executing this API.

The right range value that is assigned after executing this API.
vhRngIdx

Specify the index number for VHDL signal with multiple range index. (start from 0; default
value is 0).
If input signal is valid, return 1 for existing element range and return 0 for no element
range. Otherwise return -1 due to invalid input signal.
logic [1:0][2:0] a [3:0];
logic [1:1] b;
logic [1:0] a;
logic [1:0][2:0] c [3:0];
} st_t;
st_t svar;

Here are some examples for different kinds of signal and their results.
1. Input signal "top.a":
return value = 1, left = 3, right = 0.
2. Input signal "top.a[1][0][1]":
return value = 0, left = -1, right = -1

3. Input signal "top.b":
return value = 1, left = 1, right = 1.
4. Input signal "top.svar.a":
return value = 1, left = 1, right = 0.
5. Input signal "top.svar.b":
return value = 0, left = -1, right = -1.
6. Input signal "top.svar.c[1:0]":
return value = -1, left = -1, right = -1.

type MY_BOOL_2D_ARR is array (NATURAL range <>, NATURAL range <>) of
BOOLEAN;
type MY_SUB_2D_ARR

is array (NATURAL range <>) of MY_BOOL_2D_ARR;

std_logic_vector(0 to 0);

signal c:

MY_SUB_2D_ARR(2 downto 0)(0 to 1, 4 to 5);

Here are some examples for different kinds of signal and their results.

1. Input signal "top.a":
return value = 1, left = 31, right = 0.
2. Input signal "top.a(0)":
return value = 0, left = -1, right = -1.
3. Input signal "top.b":
return value = 1, left = 0, right = 0.
4. Input signal "top.c":
return value = 1, left = 2, right = 0.
5. Input signal "top.c(0)", vhRngIdx = 1
return value = 1, left = 4, right = 5.
6. Input signal "top.c(0)(0, 4)":
return value = 0, left = -1, right = -1.

npi_ut_is_signal) based on the NPI Language Model. However, any range selected
signal like npiPartSelect is not an invalid input signal.
The bit-blasted signal handles obtained by this API are collected into a specified vector (C
++) or list (Tcl).

sig

not a valid signal, return -1.
logic [1:0][2:0] a [3:0];

npi_nl_trace_load_by_inst_hdl_dump
Dump the information of loads of a primitive instance based on the NPI Netlist Model.
npi_nl_trace_load_by_inst_hdl_dump finds the connected nets of load instance ports of
the given primitive cell, and then find the driver ports or instance ports of those net objects
based on the NPI Netlist model.
Finally, the load information obtained is dumped into the specified file pointer "pFile".

npi_expr_decompile
Decompile the target expression. The expression includes SV expression and VHDL
expression.
The API npi_expr_decompile decompiles the npiHandle object and return a string
functionally equivalent to the original source code.

const char* npi_expr_decompile ( npiHandle exprHdl, bool constSize=false,
resConstOpr=false );

constSize

If this variable is true, the value of size appends before constant. The default value is
false.
resConstOpr

Option to resolve value of operations that are composed by constants or generate
variables. The default value is false. This option is only available in SystemVerilog.
A string representing the decompiled result of the given expression handle. If the input
handle is not an expression, an empty string ("") is returned.

include"npi.h"
include"npi_L1.h"
int main(int argc,char** argv)
{

// Usage of constSize
npiHandle paramHdl = npi_handle_by_name("top.P2",NULL);
npiHandle paramRhsHdl = npi_handle(npiExpr, paramHdl);
printf("RHS of P2: %s\n", npi_expr_decompile(paramRhsHdl));
printf("RHS of P2 with constant size: %s\n",
npi_expr_decompile(paramRhsHdl, true/*constSize*/));
// Usage of resConstOpr
npiHandle varHdl = npi_handle_by_name("top.a", NULL);
npiHandle varRhsHdl = npi_handle(npiExpr, varHdl);
printf("RHS of a: %s\n", npi_expr_decompile(varRhsHdl));
printf("RHS of a and resolve operation: %s\n",
npi_expr_decompile(varRhsHdl, false/*constSize*/, true/*resConstOpr*/));

}

npi_nl_ut_filter_port_instport
Filter npiNlHandles of a specific npiNlPortType from a vector.
The NPI Netlist API npi_nl_ut_filter_port_instport filters the npiNlPortType of all handles in
a specified vector (C++) or array (Tcl).
Filtering uses either a positive or negative list.
The filtered result is collected into another specified vector (C++) or array (Tcl).

npi_get_bit_blasted_expr
Resolve an expression handle to a bit vector.
The API npi_get_bit_blasted_expr resolves an expression to a bit vector. The bit
vector contains full name of a signal handle or 1-bit constant value.

typedef std::vector<string> stringVec_t;
int npi_get_bit_blasted_expr ( npiHandle exprHdl, stringVec_t&
bitVec/*O*/ );

bitVec

title: 0 } { isComposeFullName 0 } }
text:
A vector of bit information. The bit information is one of the following types:
(1) A constant: 1'b1, 1'b0, 1'bx, or 1'bz
(2) Full name of a signal, for example, top.mod.sig
The vector stores information from MSB to LSB. bitVec[0] is MSB and
bitVec[bitVec.size()-1] is LSB.
Bit length of the expression. If the expression is not supported, the API returns -1.

The API npi_scope_explore_register_cb creates the association between userdefined callback function/data and npi_scope_explore. Object types that can be iterated
from scope are allowed to register callback functions. The registered callback function is
called by npi_scope_explore when the corresponding object type is traversed.
Also refer to npi_scope_explore and npi_scope_explore_reset_cb.
The object (npiHandle) is passed as an argument to the callback function and
be released when the execution of callback function is done. If users want to

* Text Model Limitations

Text Model Limitations
1. The same file name cannot exist in design files. Always try to use the full file name to
specify a file.
In the current NPI Text Model, the simple file name is unique.
If two files in different directories share the same file name and you pass the simple
name to npi_text_file_by_name, only one file handle is returned.
The returned handle belongs to the first loaded file with that simple name.
In this case, use npi_text_file_by_name.
Pass a full name as the input argument to get the correct file handle object.
2. The change of macro text of a macro does not take effect until the changed macro text
file is written out and the files that use this macro in Verdi system are imported again.
This also means that if you change macro text and call npi_text_expand_macro, text

Introduction
As designs incorporate more (and more complex) standard protocols, the engineers
tasked with verifying the behavior of those designs find themselves faced with a variety
of new challenges. Not only must they understand the domain-specific aspects of the
design they are verifying, they must also understand the operation of the incorporated
protocols and how those protocol interfaces interact with the design. Learning about a
new protocol, or coming up to speed on updates to a well-established protocol might
represent significant effort for design verification teams. Large SOCs that incorporate
multiple protocol blocks further exacerbate these issues.
The complexity of modern protocols also creates a significant challenge for many
traditional debug methodologies.
Some methodologies use a bottom-up approach. This approach extracts information from
simulation log or waveform dump files. It then attempts to transform this low-level data into
more easily analyzed higher-level representations. But this approach assumes not only
that all of the required high-level information can be inferred from the low-level data. It also
assumes that this approach is reasonably efficient.
Alternatively, the debug process might use a top-down approach. That is, this approach
might be forced, particularly when a test environment focuses primarily on higher-level
transactions. But top-down methodologies rarely offer adequate insight into the underlying
simulation details. These details are often required to uncover the ultimate cause of
unexpected behavior.

The scope of complex protocol definitions is broad. It extends from the lowest physical
details (such as the analog behavior exhibited by a PHY) up to the edge of (and
sometimes into) the software domain. This highlights the challenges faced by verification
teams who want to add home-grown support for a particular protocol to a verification
environment.
This also illustrates two important requirements for a protocol-oriented analysis tool.
First, a protocol-oriented analysis tool must be able to represent and view protocol data
at multiple levels of abstraction. Second, the tool must be extensible, such that these
protocol-oriented analysis capabilities can be made available for in-house, internallydeveloped or proprietary protocol VIPs.
The Verdi Protocol Analyzer is designed to address these challenges. The Verdi Protocol
Analyzer accelerates the investigation of protocol behavior by providing protocol-oriented

analysis and debugging capabilities in verification environments that use Synopsys
Verification IP.
These capabilities not only reduce the time required to identify the source of bugs that
can be directly attributed to protocol behavior, but also provide insight into aspects of the
operation of a design that might otherwise be overlooked. With the addition of VC Apps
Protocol Analyzer, these same benefits can be extended to in-house, internally-developed
or proprietary protocol VIPs.
Starting with the Verdi L-2016.06 release, the VC Apps Protocol Analyzer APIs were
enhanced to support the recording of memory data of in-house, internally-developed
or proprietary protocol VIPs. The use of these APIs allow you to visualize memory data
using the Verdi Memory Browser. This is fully integrated with other transaction-based and
general Verdi capabilities.
This document describes the overall VC Apps Protocol Analyzer integration process
as well as the specific steps that are required to integrate a protocol VIP into the Verdi
Protocol Analyzer environment.

Tool Flow
In the hardware world, bus analyzers and packet analyzers are widely used to debug
hardware issues. These analyzers display information at a higher level of abstraction than
more traditional logic analyzers that work at the signal level.
The Verdi Protocol Analyzer provides similar capabilities for verification engineers who
are working with RTL and face many of the same debug challenges. The Verdi Protocol
Analyzer brings all of the design and test environment debug information into one place
and provides a protocol aware environment to simplify root-cause analysis.
During simulation, the VIP captures protocol-specific data using code that is either
designed into the Synopsys VIP or added to an in-house or custom VIP as part of the VC
Apps Protocol Analyzer integration process. As the VIP interacts with the design, it creates
a high-level record of transactions and other interesting protocol-specific activity such as
the values of internal state machines. This protocol-specific (and simulation-specific) data

Integration Process Overview

is stored in a common FSDB database along with the other design information, such as
waveforms, source code, stack traces, and so on.
The Verdi Protocol Analyzer uses this data in conjunction with protocol knowledge
provided by the Synopsys VIP (or created as part of the VC Apps Protocol Analyzer
integration process) to create a higher-level, interactive display of the protocol-related
activity and provide comprehensive protocol-oriented analysis and debug capabilities.
The protocol-related activity can also be synchronized with other design-related debug
information (such as signal activity and simulation log messages) to enable easy
correlation of errors (or other unexpected behavior) with protocol activity.

Integration Process Overview
VC Apps Protocol Analyzer provides an open interface that enables integration of nonSynopsys VIPs (in-house or custom VIPs or other protocol-like components) into the Verdi
environment so as to facilitate access to the comprehensive protocol-specific debugging
capabilities provided by the Verdi platform.
In this flow, protocol-related data from these VIPs can be recorded into a common
FSDB file. This data is then processed in conjunction with a protocol extension definition
to enable the protocol-oriented debug and analysis capabilities of the Verdi Protocol
Analyzer.

Integration Process Overview

The VC Apps Protocol Analyzer integration process involves the following two steps:
1. In the first step, existing custom or in-house SystemVerilog VIP code is annotated
with calls to the VC Apps Protocol Analyzer SystemVerilog API. This is defined in the
verdi_pa_writer class that is delivered as part of the Verdi installation. This API
enables the recording of protocol-related activity to an FSDB file during simulation.
2. In the second step, you can create a protocol extension definition, which describes the
specific characteristics of the protocol information that was captured during simulation.

Protocol Objects and Object Types
Verdi Protocol Analyzer is a protocol-oriented debug and analysis environment. The goal
of the tool is to provide visualization and analysis of protocol objects. The term protocol
object refers to any description of data that is found in a protocol specification.
For example, consider a protocol specification that defines a packet object as a particular
sequence of bytes.
It defines a transfer object as a particular collection of packets.
In the Verdi Protocol Analyzer environment, packet and transfer are referred to as object
types.
The packets and transfers that are generated as a result of a particular simulation are
referred to as objects.
In other words, a protocol object definition is simply a way to associate a name with a
collection of data that is related in some way.
The motivation for defining object types in a protocol specification is to facilitate discussion
of the protocol features at various levels of abstraction.

Stacked Protocols or Abstraction Layers

The behavior of a protocol is expressed in terms of its own specific object types. Thus, the
first step to learn a new protocol is to become familiar with the structure and the behavior
of those protocol-specific object types and their relationships to one another.
Once an engineer becomes well-versed in the operation of a protocol, analysis or
debugging of protocol-specific behavior becomes most productive.
That productivity is highest when behavior is represented in terms of these protocolspecific objects.
In order to capitalize on such productivity, the Verdi Protocol Analyzer enables protocol
behavior to be explored in terms of protocol-specific objects and the relationships between
those objects.

Stacked Protocols or Abstraction Layers
The complexity of protocols varies greatly; for example, consider the vast difference in
complexity between a basic UART and a USB 3.0 host (or device). To fully explore the
capabilities of the Verdi Protocol Analyzer, this section examines a complex protocol.
Specifically, the SuperSpeed aspects of the USB 3.0 protocol.
The USB 3.0 protocol is a stacked protocol. This means that the behavior of the protocol
is defined across multiple layers. These layers are, from less abstract to more abstract the
physical layer, the link layer, and the protocol layer. Complex protocols are almost always
stacked. In contrast, a simple protocol is likely to be defined by only a single layer.
A protocol specification defines the activity that occurs in each layer. It also defines the
data that are associated with the activity of that layer. Additionally, the manner in which the
data is communicated between the layers.

Stacked Protocols or Abstraction Layers

For protocols with multiple layers, perhaps the most fundamental relationship between
protocol objects is the parent or child relationship. The relationship between the parent
object and the child objects is one of composition. The data model of the Verdi Protocol
Analyzer supports the specification of composite relationships. Thus, it understands the
complete relationship tree for any particular protocol object.
A protocol specification defines the object types associated with each level of abstraction.
The least abstract object types, that is, the objects types associated with the lowest level
of abstraction are likely to correspond closely to the signal patterns observed directly
on the protocol bus interface. Conversely, the most abstract object types are likely to
represent complex, high-level data objects that are far removed from the detailed bus
activity.
The following figure shows the fundamental object types defined by the USB 3.0 protocol.
It also shows the relationships between those object types in terms of their level of
abstraction. This type of figure is extremely useful for any protocol. It not only highlights
the protocol object types that are likely to be most useful when debugging protocol-related
issues, but it also suggests how the protocol data can be organized and presented.
Figure 6

USB 3.0 (SuperSpeed) Objects Organized by Level of Abstraction

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
For example, USB 3.0 (SuperSpeed) Objects Organized by Level of Abstraction shows
USB 3.0 objects that are captured by the Synopsys USB 3.0 VIP. The objects are
organized into three columns: labeled Transfers, Transactions, and Packets. These are
ordered from left to right by decreasing level of abstraction.
This approach of organizing protocol activity according to the level of abstraction makes
it easy to analyze protocol-related issues in the most efficient manner. Some issues can
be most easily observed and understood at a very high level of abstraction. Other issues
might require analysis at lower levels of abstraction.
For most protocols, the data objects that are manipulated in each layer can be considered
as (and thus represented by) transactions. Ideally, a VIP captures the activity related to
any of these objects. As previously discussed, the data should be organized according to
the abstraction layer with which the data is associated.
There might be additional activity of interest that aids the protocol debug process. For
example, the USB 3.0 protocol defines a state machine (called the LTSSM) that resides
in the link layer. The ability to capture and display the LTSSM state can greatly accelerate

the debug process. For example, to identify a scenario where the LTSSM is stuck in a
particular state.
Another example of additional activity of interest that aids the debug of USB 3.0 scenarios
is the behavior of the Low-Frequency Periodic Signaling (LFPS) transmitter and receiver.
These are primarily used to establish the initial communication between a host and a
device and for low-power activities.
Note that both of these items are shown in the previous figure, and are located in the
figure according to their relative level of abstraction. Ideally, a VIP captures this additional
protocol-related data.

Parent or Child Relationships
For any stacked protocol and even for many simple protocols, there is a hierarchical
relationship between objects. For example, for USB 3.0, a transfer is composed of one
or more transactions. A transaction is composed of multiple packets; and a packet is
represented by a specific sequence of symbols. As USB 3.0 supports multiple concurrent
transfers and transactions, it is extremely important to understand the relationship
between these objects when debugging.

Hierarchical Object Types
An additional complexity is that the object types (such as transfers, transactions, packets,
and symbols in the case of USB 3.0) are rarely monolithic. It is common for objects of a
particular type to have multiple possible representations. For example, there are different
kinds of USB 3.0 transfers, transactions, packets, and so on. When debugging a protocol,
it is not only important to know the type of each object. It is also important to be able to
distinguish between the various sub-types of objects of a particular type.
USB 3.0 (SuperSpeed) Objects Organized by Level of Abstraction provided a comparative
view of the base object types (such as transfers, transactions, and packets). These base
object types are used to define the general behavior of the protocol.
Each object type is used to discuss a common set of functionality. For the majority of these
object types, the protocol also defines more strictly-defined variations of the object type
that are applicable to a specific task. In a protocol extension, each variation is referred to
as an object sub-type. This is equivalent to a specialization in the software realm.
Note that in Hierarchical Relationships Between Objects Shown in the Verdi Protocol
Analyzer, the four child objects are shown in the lower-right portion. Even though the child
objects are all USB 3.0 transactions, each is a different kind of transaction. Also note that
these transactions have different labels: SETUP, OUT, and STATUS. These three object
types are examples of USB 3.0 transaction object sub-types.
In the USB 3.0 protocol, there is not only an object type hierarchy for transactions, there
is also an object type hierarchy for packets. A packet is a base object type, with certain
characteristics. However, the protocol later describes four different packet sub-types: Link
Management Packet (LMP), Transaction Packet (TP), Data Packet (DP), and Isochronous
Timestamp Packet (ITP). Two of these packet sub-types (LMPs and TPs) also have a
number of sub-types.
The following figure shows all of the different USB 3.0 packet object types and how they
relate to one another:

Object Fields or Attributes

For any particular protocol, the object type hierarchy can be multiple levels deep,
depending on the complexity of the protocol.

Object Fields or Attributes
Any data associated with the operation of the protocol defines the attributes that provide
detailed information about the specific protocol objects that are captured.
At the most basic level, each object that is captured by the VIP must have attributes to
specify the start time, the end time, and the type of object for use during debug.
In addition, protocol specifications typically define other attributes that are associated with
the different object types that are manipulated by the protocol.
For example, USB 3.0 transaction packets have a number of associated attributes, such
as an endpoint number and a sequence number.
Even though these attributes are ultimately represented by a number of bits in the
transaction object, it is much easier to debug transaction-related issues when the values of
these attributes are easily observable.
Figure 10

title: Verification ContinuumTM
text:
The ability to view the values of object attributes is an essential aid to debug protocolrelated issues.
Not only are these attributes made available for analysis, each attribute is typed to provide
robust search and filtering capabilities within the Verdi Protocol Analyzer debugging
environment.
That is, by typing an attribute as an integer, a [simulation] time, a floating-point number, or
a string (for example), sophisticated searching and filtering capabilities can be provided.
For example, applying comparison operators (such as '<' and '>') to an attribute whose
values are represented as strings can produce completely different results.
The same operators applied to an attribute (with the same values) whose values are
represented as integers can produce different results.

Predecessor or Successor Relationships

Predecessor or Successor Relationships
Hierarchical relationships are previously discussed. These are composite relationships,
as they describe how one object is composed of other objects. This document uses the
familiar term for a composite relationship: a parent/child relationship.
But some protocols can have a different kind of relationship between objects that is causal
in nature. In other words, one object is the reason for (or cause of) the creation of one or
more other objects. The more familiar term for a composite relationship is a predecessor/
successor relationship.
To explain the value of being able to visualize such relationships, a different protocol
is considered. Namely ACE (AXI Coherence Extensions) of the AMBA 4 protocol from
ARM. This protocol enables system-level cache coherency across clusters of multicore processors. That is, the system can use multiple components that each has a local
memory cache. The use of a local cache can greatly increase the performance of an
individual component.
However, to maintain high performance of the overall system, it is necessary to ensure the
caches of the various local components are synchronized. It is also necessary to maximize
the use of cached data across the system, so as to minimize access to the main memory,
which is comparatively expensive in terms of performance.
In the AMBA 4 protocol, these coherency checks and optimizations are performed
by a system interconnect. The various components are connected along with special
transactions called snoop transactions. These snoop transactions enables the system
interconnect to query other components about their local cached data.
For example, a simple AMBA 4 might contain two components, each of which has a
cache. These two components are connected to the system interconnect, along with the
main memory. If the first component needs to read the value of a particular variable, it
issues a read transaction and transmits that transaction to the system interconnect.
The system interconnect, in turn, generates a snoop transaction and transmits that
transaction to the second component. This is essentially to "ask" that component if it
already has a valid value for the variable of interest. The second component generates a
snoop response transaction. This response either includes the requested data or indicates
that it does not have that data in its cache. In the latter scenario, the system interconnect
reads the requested data from the main memory and sends that data back to the first
component.
While many details of the ACE protocol are omitted from the explanation above,
the purpose of the example is to highlight the relationship between the two types of
transactions that were introducedin that explanation: read transactions and snoop
transactions.

Channels

In the scenario described, the snoop transaction is generated as a result of the read
transaction. That is, the read transaction caused the creation of the snoop transaction. The
AMBA 4 protocol supports multiple, concurrent read transactions, and write transactions.
Due to this complexity, it is useful to understand the relationship between coherent nonsnoop transactions and the corresponding snoop transactions that are generated by the
system interconnect.

Channels
Verdi Protocol Analyzer must be aware of the object type hierarchy to be able to display
the protocol objects in the most meaningful manner for the debugging process. For
example, all packets should be grouped together, independent of their sub-type.
However, in the following figure, note that not all packet objects are displayed in a single
row; there are two rows, labeled Rx and Tx. In Verdi Protocol Analyzer, these sub-rows are
referred to as channels, and provide a mechanism for separating objects of the same base
object type into separate groups (which are then displayed in separate rows). In this case,
the Rx channel displays packets that are received by the USB VIP and the Tx channel
displays packets that the USB VIP has transmitted.

Low-Level Memory Data
There are two types of low-level memory activity that can be written to the FSDB and
visualized in the Memory Protocol Analyzer:
* Front door memory actions that refer to memory activity initiated by changes to the bus
(that is, as a result of pin wiggles)
* Back door memory actions that refer to memory activity initiated by the test
environment.
The difference between front door and back door memory access is illustrated in the
following figure:
Figure 12

Front Door and Back Door Memory Access

Memories are passive components. In other words, memories do not generate activity on
their own. Memories respond to requests that are made using the memory bus.
There are two kinds of front door memory operations: memory read operations and
memory write operations.

title: Verification ContinuumTM

sive components. In other words, memories do not generate activity on
their own. Memories respond to requests that are made using the memory bus.
There are two kinds of front door memory operations: memory read operations and
memory write operations. Memory write operations can be further sub-divided into
normal writes and masked writes. A masked write is the equivalent of a read-modify-write
operation.
Since this is now a relatively common feature of contemporary memories, the VC Apps
Protocol Analyzer APIs support these two types of write operations and can distinguish
between them. Thus, there are different memory actions for these two types of write
operations. There are three front door memory actions: read, write, and write_masked.
However, a robust memory VIP should provide a verification engineer with other ways
to access the memory without having to access the memory bus. For example, a

scoreboard. It should also allow injecting an incorrect data value into a specific memory
location. It should also be possible for the test environment to quickly initialize a memory
with a pattern or with data from a file.

Correlating Memory Transactions With Memory Actions
For Synopsys Memory VIPs, it is possible to synchronize high-level memory protocol
transactions with the subsequent front door memory actions. When selection
synchronization is enabled in both Protocol Analyzer and Memory Protocol Analyzer, the
selection of a protocol transaction causes a memory action to be selected, and vice-versa.

This selection synchronization is shown in the following figure:
Figure 16
Selection Synchronization Between High-Level Memory Transactions and
Low-Level Memory Actions

This selection synchronization is also available for custom memory VIPs, but it requires
that certain conventions be followed. As illustrated in the previous figure, the following two
rules must be followed:
* For read memory protocol transactions, the corresponding read memory action must
be recorded at the time the protocol transaction is started.
* For write memory protocol transactions, the corresponding write (or write_masked)
memory action must be recorded at the time the protocol transaction is ended.
These two rules ensure that time is synchronized correctly between the two windows. In
order to synchronize the memory address between the two windows, the memory protocol
transaction must have an attribute called logical_address. The value of logical_address
should be the address of the memory location with which the high-level transaction is
associated.
Selection synchronization only works if all of these rules are followed.

Integration Process
VC Apps Protocol Analyzer provides an open interface that enables integration of nonSynopsys VIPs (in-house or custom VIPs or other protocol-like components) into the Verdi
environment so as to facilitate access to the comprehensive protocol-specific debugging
capabilities provided by the Verdi platform.
In this flow, protocol-related data from these VIPs can be recorded into a common
FSDB file. This data is then processed in conjunction with a protocol extension definition
to enable the protocol-oriented debug and analysis capabilities of the Verdi Protocol
Analyzer.
The VC Apps Protocol Analyzer integration process involves the following two steps:
1. In the first step, existing custom or in-house SystemVerilog VIP code is annotated
with calls to the VC Apps Protocol Analyzer SystemVerilog API, which is defined in
the verdi_pa_writer class that is delivered as part of the Verdi installation. This API
enables the recording of protocol-related activity to an FSDB file during simulation.
2. In the second step, you can create a protocol extension definition, which describes the
specific characteristics of the protocol information that was captured during simulation.
This section describes about the following topics:
* Data Recorded During Simulation
* Protocol Characteristics
* Protocol Analysis and Object Type Identification

of the VIPs that are configured to capture such data:

Optional composite (that is, parent or child) relationships with other objects.
Optional causal (that is, predecessor or successor) relationships with other objects.

The following general protocol information is captured as part of the protocol extension

The visual attributes of the protocol, such as, display text, a brief description, and

the Verdi Protocol Analyzer?" The answer to this question is: Almost anything.
The reason that this answer is both very simple and yet very general is that the base
Protocol Analyzer technology can be viewed as being essentially protocol-agnostic. This
idea can be most easily understood by considering the basic characteristics of the object

The display and the analysis capabilities of the Verdi Protocol Analyzer can be applied
to any of the objects that are recorded by the VIP during a simulation. While this object
model shows how objects can easily represent protocol-related transactions, a VIP often
has knowledge of other activity that can expedite the debugging and analysis of protocol

In other words, any activity of interest with respect to the operation of the VIP should be
taken into consideration as a potential object to be recorded by the VIP during simulation.
Some examples of such activity are as follows:
* Transitions of internal state machines.
* State changes for other internal structures (such as, reaching the high/low watermarks
of a FIFO).
* Reconfigurations that modify the behavior of the VIP.
* Other internal VIP activity that can be represented by the object model (such as, can
be viewed as having a start and end time, even if that activity is not represented by the
VIP as a transaction)

Thus, the first step of the integration process is to evaluate the protocol and the VIP to
identify the types of objects associated with the protocol and the VIP. The goal of this step
is to identify the protocol-related data that most enhances protocol-oriented debug and
analysis productivity.
During this process, note the following points:
* Consider both big picture protocol-centric debugging and the detailed protocol analysis.
* List any activity of interest that aids protocol debug.
* Start by listing transactions (on the VIP or layer boundaries).
* Consider other internal activity and processing performed by the VIP.
* Consider the relationships between objects (both parent/child and predecessor/
successor).
Once the top-level object types are identified, the next step in the process is to sub-divide
each of the top-level object types into object type hierarchies.

The following figure shows the complete object type hierarchy for the packet object type
(that is, for both SuperSpeed and USB 2.0), as defined in the protocol extension definition
of the Synopsys USB 3.0 VIP:
Figure 19

Complete packet Object Type Hierarchy for Synopsys USB 3.0 VIP

An object type hierarchy is analogous to a class hierarchy. Child object types (or subtypes) are variants of their parent type. For example, a Port Cfg Resp packet is also an
LMP packet, an SS Packet, and a Packet.
An object type hierarchy can greatly simplify protocol debug. Different packet sub-types
have different display text. This text is drawn within the rectangle that represents each
packet in the timeline display within the Protocol Analyzer. Different object types can
also have different colors. Different colors can be used to indicate different behavior. For
example, for both SuperSpeed and USB 2.0 packets, bad responses (NRDY and NAK,
respectively) are drawn in a light red color, whereas good responses (ACK and ERDY)
are drawn in a light green color. Using this differentiation, the general flow of traffic can be
quickly ascertained with a quick look at the timeline display.
A robust object type hierarchy also enhances searching, filtering, and general analysis
capabilities that are available in the Protocol Analyzer. For example, the timeline display
can be easily configured to only display certain types of packets. The object type hierarchy
and the number of objects of each type are also shown in the Summary tab.

Figure 20

Summary Tab Showing Object Type Hierarchy and Number of Each Object Type

Even if all of the different kinds of packets are represented in the VIP by a single
SystemVerilog class, the different kinds of packets can still be recorded as different object
types when they are written to the FSDB.
For example, if a single class is used to represent every kind of packet, but that class
includes a field to distinguish the various kinds of packets (perhaps defined using an
enumerated type) The code that is added to the VIP to record packets can check the
value of that field and assign the appropriate corresponding object type when creating the
packet object.
VIP can be instrumented to record other non-transaction protocol activity that is of use
during the debug process. For example, it is very useful to be able to observe the state
changes that occur for the state machine that is described in the link layer of the USB 3.0
protocol (called the LTSSM), particularly during certain operations, such as SuperSpeed
role swapping. Here a USB SuperSpeed host and device switch roles).

Directory Structure and Files
For each protocol that is integrated with the Verdi Protocol Analyzer, there is information
about the protocol that only needs to be captured once. This information is stored in a
collection of files, referred to as the protocol extension definition. The overall directory
structure and files that comprise a protocol extension definition are described this chapter.
The purpose of a protocol extension definition is to provide the Verdi Protocol Analyzer
with protocol-specific information . This enables the tool to organize and display the
protocol-related data that was generated during a simulation. The organization and display
are tailored to support protocol-oriented debugging.
The extension definition for each protocol is contained in a directory structure. The name
of the top-most directory is the internal name of the protocol. This name cannot contain
any spaces or non-alphanumeric characters, with the exception of underscore (`_')
characters. For simplicity, it is recommended to use all lower-case letters. To avoid naming
collisions, consider adding a prefix or suffix that clearly differentiates the protocol name
(such as, snps_xyzbus or xyzbus_snps).
When a VIP (or other SystemVerilog code) is annotated using the verdi_pa_writer
class, the protocol name that is specified in the class constructor must match the name
that is specified for the top-level of the protocol extension definition directory.
Figure 23

Directory Structure for a Protocol Extension Definition

The next level in the directory structure of the protocol extension definition is a subdirectory that represents the version of the protocol extension definition.

Chapter 4: Directory Structure and Files

Every protocol extension definition is versioned. This enables changes or enhancements
to be made to a protocol extension definition without the risk of breaking the existing
flows of current users. For example, a VIP might be enhanced to capture additional
protocol-related data during simulation. This new data might come from new features that
are added to the protocol over time. Alternatively, the new data might come from enduser requests that additional information be captured during simulation. Either of these
scenarios would certainly require modifications to the protocol extension definition.
The version string cannot contain any spaces or non-alphanumeric characters, with the
exception of underscore (`_') and dot (`.') characters. For simplicity, it is recommended
to use all lower-case letters. While any version string is permitted, a simple versioning
scheme is recommended (such as, 1.0, 1.1, 2.0_beta, 2.0, and so on).
For each version of the VIP that has been annotated using the verdi_pa_writer class,
there should be a corresponding version of a protocol extension definition for that VIP. This
means that there should be a sub-directory whose name is the same as the version string
passed to the verdi_pa_writer constructor in the VIP SystemVerilog code.
Note that when a VIP (or other SystemVerilog code) is annotated using the
verdi_pa_writer class, both the protocol name and the protocol version are specified in
the class constructor.

As shown in Directory Structure for a Protocol Extension Definition, there is a symbolic
link called "latest" at the same level in the directory structure as the extension definition
versions. The version of the protocol extension definition that this link points to indicates
the default version of the extension definition.
This link is only used if there is no directory that corresponds to the information captured
during simulation. There is no directory that corresponds the version reported by the
VIP. If the versions of both the annotated VIPs and the protocol extension definitions
are managed appropriately, this situation should not occur. Also, note that under these
conditions, errors or warnings might be generated when the data is read into the Verdi
Protocol Analyzer.
Within the version sub-directory is another sub-directory that must be called pa. This
additional layer is included in the directory hierarchy to separate information related to

Chapter 4: Directory Structure and Files

the Verdi Protocol Analyzer from any other protocol-related data. While this is completely
optional, this allows the protocol extension definition directory structure to be used as a
common location to store other protocol-related files, such as, documentation, code, or
any other data, if needed.
The pa directory contains the following two items:
* A file - extension.xml. The extension.xml file is an XML file (as implied by its extension)
and defines all of the protocol-related information required by the Verdi Protocol
Analyzer.
* A subdirectory - icons. The icons directory contains icons that provide visual
representations for protocol-specific object types that are defined for the protocol.
These icons are used by the Verdi Protocol Analyzer throughout the GUI to provide
visual cues to aid protocol debug.
